questions.a: Arrows show what goes where next, as in a water cycle, and can also show which way a part is being pressed. A thick arrow may mean a lot and a thin one a little.

questions.q:
diagram: a drawing that shows how something works.
cycle: something that goes around and starts again.
Describe the connection between following the arrows and understanding the diagram.
questions.a: Follow the arrows in order before reading the words, because the order they make is the thing the diagram is about.

articles.note: Give the class a diagram with the words covered. The arrows alone will carry most of the meaning.

articles.title: Then and Now Pictures
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Explain how specific images, such as a diagram showing how a machine works, contribute to and clarify a text.
 Spiral: RI.2.2 main topic · RI.2.3 connections · RI.2.5 text features · RI.2.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 330 – 430

paras.label: A
paras.text: Some history books put two pictures side by side. One of them is old. The other was taken from the same spot today.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The pair does something one picture cannot. It shows change without saying a word about it.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Look for what stayed. A church, a hill, or a bend in the river is often in both pictures.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Then look for what went. A streetcar line, a row of trees, or a whole block of houses may be gone.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The things that stayed are how you know it is the same place. The things that went are the story.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Some history books put two pictures side by side. One is old. One is from today.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The pair does what one picture cannot. It shows change without words.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Look for what stayed. A church, a hill, or a bend in the river is often in both.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Then look for what went. A row of trees or a block of houses may be gone.

paras.label: E
paras.text: What stayed tells you it is the same place. What went is the story.

questions.q: What do two pictures side by side show?
questions.a: They show change, because one is old and the other was taken from the same spot today.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. what stayed) and paragraph D (i.e. what went).
Summarize how to read a then and now pair.
questions.a: Look for what stayed, such as a church, a hill or a bend in the river, and then look for what went, such as a row of trees or a block of houses.

questions.q:
spot: the exact place where someone stood.
streetcar: a train that ran along a city street.
Describe the connection between the things that stayed and the things that went.
questions.a: The things that stayed are how you know it is the same place, and the things that went are the story.

articles.note: A local pair works best. Photograph the view outside the school and set it beside an old picture of the same corner.

articles.title: A Picture That Shows Size
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Explain how specific images, such as a diagram showing how a machine works, contribute to and clarify a text.
 Spiral: RI.2.2 main topic · RI.2.3 connections · RI.2.5 text features · RI.2.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 330 – 430

paras.label: A
paras.text: A picture of an animal does not tell you how big it is. A beetle and a bear can fill the same page.

paras.label: B
paras.text: So books add something for scale. A small drawing of a hand, a coin, or a person stands next to the animal.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Now the page means something. If the beetle is half as long as a hand, you know.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Some books use a ruler line instead. A short bar under the picture is marked with inches or centimeters.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Always look for the scale before you decide a thing is huge. Without it, every picture is the size of the page.

paras.text: Some books use a ruler line. A short bar is marked with inches.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Look for the scale first. Without it, every picture is the size of the page.

questions.q: Why do books put a hand or a coin next to an animal?
questions.a: A picture of an animal does not tell you how big it is, so the hand or coin gives you a scale.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. the hand or coin) and paragraph D (i.e. the ruler line).
Summarize how a picture shows size.
questions.a: A small drawing of a hand, a coin or a person stands next to the animal, or a short bar marked in inches sits under the picture, so a reader can tell how big the thing really is.

questions.q:
scale: something that shows how big a thing really is.
bar: a short straight line used as a measure.
Describe the connection between having no scale and thinking something is huge.
questions.a: Without a scale, every picture is the size of the page, so a beetle and a bear can look the same.

articles.note: Show two animal pictures with no scale and ask which is bigger. Then show the scale bars.

articles.title: Why the Bus Has Rules
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Describe how reasons support specific points the author makes in a text.
 Spiral: RI.2.1 key details · RI.2.6 author's purpose · RI.2.9 comparing texts · RI.2.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 330 – 430

paras.label: A
paras.text: A school bus has a short list of rules. Each one has a reason. The reasons are not written on the sign, but they exist.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Stay seated. A bus can stop fast. A person standing has nothing to hold them in place.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Keep the aisle clear. If the bus must be left in a hurry, a bag in the aisle slows everyone behind it.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Keep your voice low. The driver has to hear a train, a siren, or a horn through an open window.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The rules are not about being good. Each one answers a danger the driver already knows about.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A school bus has a short list of rules. Each rule has a reason behind it.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Stay seated. A bus can stop fast. A standing person has nothing to hold them.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Keep the aisle clear. If the bus must be left fast, a bag slows everyone.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Keep your voice low. The driver must hear a train or a siren.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The rules are not about being good. Each one answers a real danger.

questions.q: Why does the rule say stay seated?
questions.a: A bus can stop fast, and a person standing has nothing to hold them in place.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the clear aisle) and paragraph D (i.e. a low voice).
Summarize the rules and their reasons.
questions.a: Stay seated because a bus can stop fast. Keep the aisle clear because a bag slows everyone leaving in a hurry. Keep your voice low because the driver has to hear a train, a siren or a horn.

questions.q:
aisle: the open path to walk between two rows of seats.
siren: a loud warning sound from a fire truck or police car.
Describe the connection between the driver's hearing and the voice rule.
questions.a: The driver has to hear a train, a siren or a horn through an open window, so the rule says keep your voice low.

articles.note: Pair each rule with its reason on the board. RI.2.8 is about that pairing, not about the rules themselves.

articles.title: Why Trees Are Planted on Streets
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Describe how reasons support specific points the author makes in a text.
 Spiral: RI.2.1 key details · RI.2.6 author's purpose · RI.2.9 comparing texts · RI.2.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 330 – 430

paras.label: A
paras.text: Cities spend money putting trees along streets. A tree costs more than a lamp post. There are reasons they do it anyway.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first reason is heat. A street with trees can be ten degrees cooler than the same street with none.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second reason is water. Roots and soil soak up rain that would otherwise run straight into a drain and flood it.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The third reason is air. Leaves catch dust and soot, and the dirt stays on the leaf instead of in a lung.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A fourth reason is harder to measure. People walk more on a street with trees, and shops on those streets do better.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Cities spend money putting trees on streets. A tree costs more than a lamp post. There are reasons.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first reason is heat. A street with trees can be ten degrees cooler.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second reason is water. Roots and soil soak up rain. Less rain runs into the drain.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The third reason is air. Leaves catch dust. The dirt stays on the leaf.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A fourth reason is harder to measure. People walk more on a street with trees.

questions.q: What is the first reason given for planting street trees?
questions.a: Heat: a street with trees can be ten degrees cooler than the same street with none.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. water) and paragraph E (i.e. the reason that is hard to measure).
Summarize the reasons for street trees.
questions.a: Trees make a street about ten degrees cooler, their roots and soil soak up rain that would flood a drain, their leaves catch dust and soot, and people walk more on streets with trees.

questions.q:
soot: black dust left behind by smoke.
drain: a hole that carries water away from a street.
Describe the connection between roots and a flooded drain.
questions.a: Roots and soil soak up rain that would otherwise run straight into a drain and flood it.

articles.note: Four reasons, four paragraphs. Ask which one a student finds strongest and make them say why.

articles.title: Why the Library Is Quiet
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Describe how reasons support specific points the author makes in a text.
 Spiral: RI.2.1 key details · RI.2.6 author's purpose · RI.2.9 comparing texts · RI.2.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 330 – 430

paras.label: A
paras.text: A library asks people to be quiet. Some children think it is just an old rule. There are reasons behind it.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first reason is reading. Reading uses the same part of the brain that listens. A loud voice pulls that part away.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second reason is sharing. One room holds many people doing different work. A quiet room belongs to all of them.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The third reason is help. A librarian answering a question needs to hear it the first time.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Notice that every reason is about other people. The rule is not there to make the room dull.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A library asks people to be quiet. Some think it is just an old rule. There are reasons.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first reason is reading. Reading uses the part of the brain that listens.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second reason is sharing. One room holds many people doing different work.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The third reason is help. A librarian needs to hear a question the first time.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Every reason is about other people. The rule is not there to make the room dull.

questions.q: Why does reading need quiet?
questions.a: Reading uses the same part of the brain that listens, so a loud voice pulls that part away.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. sharing the room) and paragraph E (i.e. what the reasons have in common).
Summarize the reasons a library is quiet.
questions.a: Reading uses the part of the brain that listens, one room holds many people doing different work, and a librarian needs to hear a question the first time.

questions.q:
librarian: the person who helps people find books.
share: to use one thing together with others.
Describe the connection between all three reasons.
questions.a: Every reason is about other people, because the rule is not there to make the room dull.

articles.note: Paragraph E does something the others do not: it finds what the three reasons have in common. That is a step past RI.2.8 and worth praising.

articles.title: Why Bikes Need Helmets
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Describe how reasons support specific points the author makes in a text.
 Spiral: RI.2.1 key details · RI.2.6 author's purpose · RI.2.9 comparing texts · RI.2.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 330 – 430

paras.label: A
paras.text: A helmet looks like a hard shell. Most of the work is done by the soft foam inside it.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A head stops faster than a brain does. The brain keeps moving for a moment and hits the inside of the skull.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Foam crushes slowly. That gives the head a few more milliseconds to stop, and those milliseconds are what protect the brain.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A crushed helmet has done its job. It cannot do it twice, so a helmet in a crash is replaced, not reused.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Fit is a reason too. A loose helmet slides off the forehead, and the part that matters is no longer over the part that matters.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A helmet looks like a hard shell. The soft foam inside does most of the work.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A head stops faster than a brain. The brain keeps moving for a moment.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Foam crushes slowly. That gives the head more time to stop. That time protects the brain.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A crushed helmet has done its job. It cannot do it twice. It must be replaced.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Fit is a reason too. A loose helmet slides off the forehead.

questions.q: What part of a helmet does most of the work?
questions.a: The soft foam inside does most of the work, not the hard shell.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the foam) and paragraph D (i.e. replacing a helmet).
Summarize why a helmet protects a brain.
questions.a: A head stops faster than a brain does, so the brain keeps moving and hits the skull. Foam crushes slowly and gives the head a few more milliseconds to stop, which is what protects the brain.

questions.q:
foam: a soft light material full of tiny holes.
skull: the bone around the brain.
Describe the connection between a crushed helmet and buying a new one.
questions.a: A crushed helmet has done its job and cannot do it twice, so a helmet in a crash is replaced, not reused.

articles.note: Paragraph A is the surprise. Most students will say the hard shell, and the text says the opposite.

articles.title: Why Dogs Must Be on a Leash
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Describe how reasons support specific points the author makes in a text.
 Spiral: RI.2.1 key details · RI.2.6 author's purpose · RI.2.9 comparing texts · RI.2.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 330 – 430

paras.label: A
paras.text: Most parks ask that dogs be kept on a leash. Dog owners sometimes argue about it. The rule has several reasons.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first is other people. A friendly dog running toward a stranger does not look friendly to that stranger.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second is other dogs. Two dogs meeting at full speed start more fights than two dogs meeting slowly.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The third is wildlife. A dog off a leash chases birds off their nests, and the eggs cool while the parent is away.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The fourth is the dog. A leash is what stops a dog from reaching a road before its owner can call it back.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Most parks ask that dogs be kept on a leash. The rule has several reasons.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first is other people. A friendly dog running at a stranger does not look friendly.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second is other dogs. Two dogs meeting fast start more fights.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The third is wildlife. A dog off a leash chases birds off their nests.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The fourth is the dog. A leash stops a dog from reaching a road.

questions.q: What is the fourth reason for a leash?
questions.a: The dog itself: a leash is what stops a dog from reaching a road before its owner can call it back.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. wildlife) and paragraph E (i.e. the dog).
Summarize the reasons for a leash rule.
questions.a: A friendly dog running at a stranger does not look friendly, two dogs meeting at full speed start more fights, a loose dog chases birds off their nests, and a leash stops a dog reaching a road.

questions.q:
leash: a strap used to hold a dog while walking.
wildlife: wild animals living in a place.
Describe the connection between a dog off a leash and eggs in a nest.
questions.a: A dog off a leash chases birds off their nests, and the eggs cool while the parent is away.

articles.note: Paragraph A names the disagreement openly. Students with dogs will have opinions, and the reasons are there to argue with.

articles.title: Two Books About Bats
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Compare and contrast the most important points presented by two texts on the same topic.
 Spiral: RI.2.2 main topic · RI.2.6 author's purpose · RI.2.8 reasons · RI.2.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 330 – 430

paras.label: A
paras.text: Two books on the shelf are both about bats. They do not say the same things. Reading both is better than reading one twice.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first book is about how bats find food. It spends most of its pages on sound. A bat calls out and listens for the echo.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second book is about where bats live. It shows caves, bridges, and hollow trees. It barely mentions sound at all.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Both books agree on two points. Bats are mammals, and most bats eat insects. Those facts are in each one.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The books differ on one thing. The first says a bat can eat a thousand insects an hour. The second says hundreds. Neither is lying; they counted in different places.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Two books are both about bats. They do not say the same things. Reading both is better.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first book is about how bats find food. A bat calls out and listens for the echo.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second book is about where bats live. It shows caves and hollow trees.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Both books agree on two points. Bats are mammals. Most bats eat insects.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The books differ on one thing. One says a thousand insects an hour. One says hundreds.

questions.q: What do both books agree on?
questions.a: Both books agree that bats are mammals and that most bats eat insects.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. the first book) and paragraph C (i.e. the second book).
Summarize how the two books are the same and different.
questions.a: One book is about how bats find food using sound and echoes, and the other is about where bats live in caves, bridges and hollow trees. Both say bats are mammals and most eat insects, but they give different numbers of insects.

questions.q:
echo: a sound that bounces back from something.
mammal: an animal that has fur and feeds its young milk.
Describe the connection between the two different numbers.
questions.a: The first says a bat can eat a thousand insects an hour and the second says hundreds, and neither is lying because they counted in different places.

articles.note: Paragraph E is the hard idea and the valuable one. Two true books can give two numbers.

articles.title: Two Books About Trains
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Compare and contrast the most important points presented by two texts on the same topic.
 Spiral: RI.2.2 main topic · RI.2.6 author's purpose · RI.2.8 reasons · RI.2.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 330 – 430

paras.label: A
paras.text: One shelf holds two books about trains. One of them is about how a train works. The other is about the people who ride them.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The how book has diagrams. It shows the engine, the wheels, and the track. Almost nobody appears in the pictures.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The people book has photographs. It shows a conductor, a family with bags, and a man asleep in a seat.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Both say trains carry more weight than trucks. That point shows up in each book, in different words.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The two books feel very different, but neither one is wrong. They simply picked different parts of the same subject.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Two books on a shelf are about trains. One is about how a train works. One is about people.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The how book has diagrams. It shows the engine, the wheels, and the track.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The people book has photographs. It shows a conductor and a family with bags.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Both say trains carry more weight than trucks. That point is in each book.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The two books feel different. Neither one is wrong.

questions.q: What do both books say about trains?
questions.a: Both say trains carry more weight than trucks.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. the how book) and paragraph C (i.e. the people book).
Summarize how the two train books differ.
questions.a: One has diagrams of the engine, wheels and track with almost nobody in the pictures, and the other has photographs of a conductor and a family with bags. Both say trains carry more weight than trucks.

questions.q:
conductor: the person who works on a train and checks tickets.
diagram: a drawing that shows how something works.
Describe the connection between the two books and the same subject.
questions.a: The two books feel very different but neither is wrong, because they simply picked different parts of the same subject.

articles.note: Diagrams against photographs is the clue. What a book chooses to picture tells you what it is about.

articles.title: Two Books About Rain
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Compare and contrast the most important points presented by two texts on the same topic.
 Spiral: RI.2.2 main topic · RI.2.6 author's purpose · RI.2.8 reasons · RI.2.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 330 – 430

paras.label: A
paras.text: Two books on rain sit side by side. One explains where rain comes from. One tells what people do when it falls.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The science book starts with the sea. Water rises, cools, makes clouds, and falls again. The whole book is that circle.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The other book starts with a boot. It shows umbrellas, puddles, drains, and a city that must move water off its streets.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Both books use the word evaporation. The science book explains it. The city book just uses it.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Reading both gives you something neither gives alone. You learn where rain comes from and what a town has to do about it.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Two books on rain sit side by side. One tells where rain comes from. One tells what people do.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The science book starts with the sea. Water rises, cools, makes clouds, and falls.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The other book starts with a boot. It shows umbrellas, puddles, and drains.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Both books use the word evaporation. One explains it. One just uses it.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Reading both gives you more. You learn where rain comes from and what a town does.

questions.q: What does the science book explain?
questions.a: It explains where rain comes from: water rises from the sea, cools, makes clouds, and falls again.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the city book) and paragraph D (i.e. the shared word).
Summarize how the two rain books differ.
questions.a: One starts with the sea and follows water as it rises, cools, makes clouds and falls. The other starts with a boot and shows umbrellas, puddles, drains and a city moving water off its streets.

questions.q:
evaporation: when water turns into tiny bits that float in the air.
umbrella: a thing you hold over your head to keep rain off.
Describe the connection between the two books and the word evaporation.
questions.a: Both books use the word evaporation, but the science book explains it and the city book just uses it.

articles.note: Paragraph D is a small, sharp observation. A word can appear in two books and be doing different work.

articles.title: Two Books About Firefighters
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Compare and contrast the most important points presented by two texts on the same topic.
 Spiral: RI.2.2 main topic · RI.2.6 author's purpose · RI.2.8 reasons · RI.2.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 330 – 430

paras.label: A
paras.text: Two books about firefighters were written forty years apart. Put together they show what the job is and how it changed.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The older book is mostly about fire. Every picture has flames in it. The trucks carry ladders and hoses and nothing else.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The newer book says something surprising. Most calls today are not fires. Firefighters go to car crashes and medical calls far more often.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Both books make the same main point. Firefighters train constantly, because the work has to be done the same way every time.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A reader with both books knows two things. What firefighters do, and that the answer has not stayed the same.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Two books about firefighters were written forty years apart. Together they show how the job changed.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The older book is mostly about fire. Every picture has flames. The trucks carry ladders and hoses.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The newer book says something surprising. Most calls today are not fires. Many are medical calls.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Both books make the same point. Firefighters train all the time.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A reader with both books knows more. The answer has not stayed the same.

questions.q: What does the newer book say that is surprising?
questions.a: Most calls today are not fires; firefighters go to car crashes and medical calls far more often.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. the older book) and paragraph C (i.e. the newer book).
Summarize how the two firefighter books compare.
questions.a: The older book is mostly about fire, with flames in every picture and trucks carrying ladders and hoses. The newer book says most calls are not fires. Both say firefighters train constantly.

questions.q:
medical: having to do with helping someone who is sick or hurt.
constantly: all the time, again and again.
Describe the connection between the age of a book and what it says.
questions.a: The two books were written forty years apart, so together they show what firefighters do and that the answer has not stayed the same.

articles.note: Check the copyright date on two books about the same job. Second graders can do that, and it changes how they read both.

articles.title: Two Books About the Sun
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Compare and contrast the most important points presented by two texts on the same topic.
 Spiral: RI.2.2 main topic · RI.2.6 author's purpose · RI.2.8 reasons · RI.2.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 330 – 430

paras.label: A
paras.text: Two books about the sun are open on a table. One is about the sun itself. One is about what the sun does for us.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first book gives numbers. The sun is a star. It is about 93 million miles away and far bigger than the Earth.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second book gives examples. Plants use sunlight to make food. Skin makes vitamin D. Solar panels turn light into power.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Both books say the same thing about light. Light from the sun takes about eight minutes to reach us.

paras.label: E
paras.text: One book is mostly about a thing. One is mostly about effects. The topic is the same and the point of view is not.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Two books about the sun are open on a table. One is about the sun. One is about what it does for us.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first book gives numbers. The sun is a star. It is far bigger than the Earth.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second book gives examples. Plants use sunlight to make food. Solar panels make power.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Both books say the same thing about light. It takes about eight minutes to reach us.

paras.label: E
paras.text: One book is about a thing. One is about effects. The topic is the same.

questions.q: What do both books say about light?
questions.a: Both say light from the sun takes about eight minutes to reach us.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. the numbers) and paragraph C (i.e. the examples).
Summarize how the two sun books differ.
questions.a: One gives numbers about the sun itself, that it is a star about 93 million miles away and far bigger than the Earth. The other gives examples of what the sun does, like plants making food and solar panels making power.

questions.q:
solar: having to do with the sun.
vitamin: something the body needs a small amount of to stay well.
Describe the connection between the two books having the same topic.
questions.a: One book is mostly about a thing and one is mostly about effects, so the topic is the same and the point of view is not.

articles.note: A thing and its effects is a split that shows up everywhere. Name it here and students will spot it again.

articles.title: The Statue That Came in Pieces
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of the year, read and comprehend informational texts, including history/social studies, science, and technical texts, in the grades 2-3 text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.
 Spiral: RI.2.1 key details · RI.2.2 main topic · RI.2.4 word meaning · RI.2.8 reasons
 Lower range: LL 330 – 430

paras.label: A
paras.text: The Statue of Liberty did not arrive standing up. It came across the ocean in 214 wooden crates.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The statue was built in France first. Workers put the whole thing together in a Paris yard, then took it apart again.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Each piece was numbered. Without the numbers, nobody in New York would have known which sheet of copper went where.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The copper skin is thinner than two pennies stacked. It is held on an iron frame, the way skin is held on bones.

paras.label: E
paras.text: It took four months to put back together. The crates sat on an island for almost a year first, because the base was not ready.

paras.label: A
paras.text: The Statue of Liberty did not arrive standing up. It came in 214 wooden crates.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The statue was built in France first. Workers put it together, then took it apart.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Each piece was numbered. Without the numbers, nobody would know which piece went where.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The copper skin is very thin. It is held on an iron frame, like skin on bones.

paras.label: E
paras.text: It took four months to put back together. The crates waited almost a year first.

questions.q: How did the statue cross the ocean?
questions.a: It came across the ocean in 214 wooden crates.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the numbers) and paragraph E (i.e. the wait).
Summarize how the Statue of Liberty got to New York.
questions.a: It was built in France, put together in a Paris yard, then taken apart with each piece numbered and shipped in 214 crates. The crates waited almost a year because the base was not ready, and it took four months to rebuild.

questions.q:
crate: a strong wooden box for shipping things.
copper: an orange-brown metal that turns green over time.
Describe the connection between the numbers on the pieces and rebuilding the statue.
questions.a: Each piece was numbered, because without the numbers nobody in New York would have known which sheet of copper went where.

articles.note: Two pennies stacked is the detail students repeat at dinner. Let them hold two pennies while you read paragraph D.

articles.title: The Tree That Grows in Salt Water
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of the year, read and comprehend informational texts, including history/social studies, science, and technical texts, in the grades 2-3 text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.
 Spiral: RI.2.1 key details · RI.2.2 main topic · RI.2.4 word meaning · RI.2.8 reasons
 Lower range: LL 330 – 430

paras.label: A
paras.text: Most trees die in salt water. A mangrove lives in it. It grows where a river meets the sea.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Salt is the problem. A plant pulls water up through its roots, and salt comes along with it.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Mangroves solve it in two ways. Some roots block most of the salt. Some leaves push salt out, and it dries in white crystals on top.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The mud is a second problem. It holds almost no air. So mangroves grow roots that stick up out of the water to breathe.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Those tangled roots do a job for everyone else. They slow a storm wave before it reaches land, and young fish hide between them.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Most trees die in salt water. A mangrove lives in it. It grows where a river meets the sea.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Salt is the problem. A plant pulls water up through its roots. Salt comes too.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Mangroves solve it in two ways. Some roots block the salt. Some leaves push salt out.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The mud is another problem. It holds almost no air. So some roots stick up to breathe.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Those roots help everyone. They slow a storm wave. Young fish hide between them.

questions.q: Why is salt a problem for a plant?
questions.a: A plant pulls water up through its roots, and salt comes along with it.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. two ways to handle salt) and paragraph D (i.e. roots that breathe).
Summarize how a mangrove survives in salt water.
questions.a: Some of its roots block most of the salt and some of its leaves push salt out, which dries in white crystals. Because the mud holds almost no air, it also grows roots that stick up out of the water to breathe.

questions.q:
mangrove: a tree that grows in salt water near a coast.
crystal: a small hard piece that forms as something dries.
Describe the connection between the tangled roots and a storm wave.
questions.a: The tangled roots slow a storm wave before it reaches land, and young fish hide between them.

articles.note: Two problems, two solutions, and then a paragraph about everyone else. That shape is worth naming out loud.

articles.title: The Town with No Cars
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of the year, read and comprehend informational texts, including history/social studies, science, and technical texts, in the grades 2-3 text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.
 Spiral: RI.2.1 key details · RI.2.2 main topic · RI.2.4 word meaning · RI.2.8 reasons
 Lower range: LL 330 – 430

paras.label: A
paras.text: There is an island in Michigan where cars have been against the law since 1898. About five hundred people live there all year.

paras.label: B
paras.text: People get around on bicycles, on foot, and in carriages pulled by horses. There are more than five hundred horses on the island in summer.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Everything arrives by boat. Furniture, food, and building supplies are unloaded at a dock and moved by wagon.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Even an emergency runs on horses. The ambulance is a sled in winter and a horse-drawn wagon the rest of the year.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The rule started because the first cars frightened the horses. It stayed because people decided they liked the island the way it was.

paras.label: A
paras.text: There is an island in Michigan where cars are against the law. The rule began in 1898.

paras.label: B
paras.text: People get around on bikes, on foot, and in carriages pulled by horses.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Everything arrives by boat. Food and supplies come to a dock. Wagons move them.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Even an emergency runs on horses. The ambulance is a sled in winter.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The rule started because cars frightened the horses. It stayed because people liked it.

questions.q: How do people get around on the island?
questions.a: They get around on bicycles, on foot, and in carriages pulled by horses.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. arriving by boat) and paragraph E (i.e. why the rule stayed).
Summarize life on the island without cars.
questions.a: Cars have been against the law since 1898, so people use bicycles, their feet and horse-drawn carriages. Everything arrives by boat and moves by wagon, and even the ambulance is a sled or a wagon.

questions.q:
carriage: a cart with seats that a horse pulls.
dock: a place at the edge of water where boats are loaded.
Describe the connection between the first cars and the rule.
questions.a: The rule started because the first cars frightened the horses, and it stayed because people decided they liked the island the way it was.

articles.note: Paragraph E separates why a rule began from why it lasted. Those are rarely the same thing.

articles.title: The Ants That Grow Their Own Food
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of the year, read and comprehend informational texts, including history/social studies, science, and technical texts, in the grades 2-3 text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.
 Spiral: RI.2.1 key details · RI.2.2 main topic · RI.2.4 word meaning · RI.2.8 reasons
 Lower range: LL 330 – 430

paras.label: A
paras.text: Some ants do not hunt for food. They grow it. Leafcutter ants have been farming for millions of years.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A line of ants carries pieces of leaf back to the nest. The leaves are not what they eat. They cannot digest a leaf at all.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Underground, the ants chew the leaves into a soft mush. They plant a fungus in it. The fungus grows, and that is the food.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The nest is kept clean on purpose. Workers pull out any mold that is not the right kind and carry it far away.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A big nest can hold millions of ants and reach deeper than a person is tall. All of it is built around one crop.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Some ants do not hunt for food. They grow it. Leafcutter ants are farmers.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A line of ants carries leaf pieces to the nest. The leaves are not what they eat.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Underground, they chew the leaves into mush. They plant a fungus in it. The fungus is the food.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The nest is kept clean. Workers pull out the wrong kind of mold.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A big nest can hold millions of ants. All of it is built around one crop.

questions.q: What do leafcutter ants actually eat?
questions.a: They eat a fungus they grow, not the leaves, because they cannot digest a leaf at all.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. growing the fungus) and paragraph D (i.e. keeping the nest clean).
Summarize how leafcutter ants farm.
questions.a: Ants carry pieces of leaf underground and chew them into a soft mush, then plant a fungus in it. The fungus grows and that is their food, and workers pull out any mold that is the wrong kind.

questions.q:
fungus: a living thing like a mushroom or a mold.
crop: a plant that people or animals grow for food.
Describe the connection between the leaves and the ants' food.
questions.a: The ants cannot digest a leaf, so they chew the leaves into mush and plant a fungus in it, and the fungus is what they eat.

articles.note: Paragraph B is the twist. Every student will assume the ants eat the leaves, and the second sentence says no.

articles.title: The Room Made for Children
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of the year, read and comprehend informational texts, including history/social studies, science, and technical texts, in the grades 2-3 text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.
 Spiral: RI.2.1 key details · RI.2.2 main topic · RI.2.4 word meaning · RI.2.8 reasons
 Lower range: LL 330 – 430

paras.label: A
paras.text: For a long time, libraries had no room for children. Many would not let anyone under fourteen through the door at all.

paras.label: B
paras.text: In 1890, a librarian in Brookline, Massachusetts set aside one room with low shelves and small chairs. It was one of the first.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The idea spread quickly. Within thirty years most city libraries had a children's room, and some had a librarian who worked only there.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Those librarians changed what got published. They asked for books with bigger print and better pictures, and companies made them.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A children's room looks ordinary now. It was an argument once, and somebody had to win it.

paras.label: A
paras.text: For a long time, libraries had no room for children. Many would not let them in at all.

paras.label: B
paras.text: In 1890, a librarian in Massachusetts set aside one room. It had low shelves and small chairs.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The idea spread. Within thirty years most city libraries had a children's room.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Those librarians changed what got published. They asked for bigger print and better pictures.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A children's room looks ordinary now. It was an argument once.

questions.q: What did libraries used to do about children?
questions.a: Many libraries would not let anyone under fourteen through the door at all.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. the first room) and paragraph D (i.e. changing the books).
Summarize how children's rooms began.
questions.a: In 1890 a librarian in Brookline, Massachusetts set aside a room with low shelves and small chairs. Within thirty years most city libraries had one, and those librarians asked publishers for bigger print and better pictures.

questions.q:
librarian: the person who helps people find books.
published: printed and sold as a book.
Describe the connection between the children's librarians and the books that were made.
questions.a: They asked for books with bigger print and better pictures, and companies made them.

articles.note: Read this one in the children's room. The last sentence is the whole point and the room is the evidence.

articles.title: The Race to Nome
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Ask and answer questions to demonstrate understanding of a text, referring explicitly to the text as the basis for the answers.
 Spiral: RI.3.2 main idea · RI.3.3 connections · RI.3.4 word meaning · RI.3.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: In January of 1925, a doctor in Nome, Alaska sent an urgent telegram. Children in his town were sick with diphtheria. Without medicine, the disease could kill most of them. The nearest supply was a thousand miles away.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Nome was frozen in. The port was iced over until spring. The two airplanes in the territory had open cockpits and engines that would not start in the cold. That left one way in: dog sled.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The plan was a relay. The medicine traveled by train as far as the rails went, to a town called Nenana. From there, twenty mushers and about 150 sled dogs would carry it in stages across 674 miles of frozen Alaska.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The weather was brutal. Temperatures dropped near sixty degrees below zero. One musher, Leonhard Seppala, took a shortcut straight across the frozen sea ice of Norton Sound during a blizzard. If the ice had broken, his whole team would have gone into the water.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The final stretch belonged to a musher named Gunnar Kaasen and his lead dog, Balto. Wind flipped the sled and buried the package of medicine in the snow. Kaasen dug it out with his bare hands. He reached Nome on the morning of February 2nd.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The relay took five and a half days. The medicine arrived frozen but unbroken. A statue of Balto still stands in Central Park in New York, and every year the Iditarod sled dog race follows part of the same trail.

paras.label: A
paras.text: In January of 1925, a doctor in Nome, Alaska sent an urgent message. Children in his town were sick. Without medicine, many of them could die. The nearest medicine was a thousand miles away.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Nome was frozen in. The port was iced over until spring. The airplanes would not start in the cold. That left one way in. Dog sled.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The plan was a relay. A train carried the medicine as far as the tracks went. From there, twenty mushers and about 150 sled dogs would carry it in stages. The trip was 674 miles.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The weather was terrible. It was almost sixty degrees below zero. One musher, Leonhard Seppala, went straight across frozen sea ice in a blizzard. If the ice had broken, his whole team would have fallen in.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The last stretch belonged to Gunnar Kaasen and his lead dog, Balto. Wind flipped the sled and buried the medicine in the snow. Kaasen dug it out with his bare hands. He reached Nome on February 2nd.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The relay took five and a half days. The medicine arrived frozen but safe. A statue of Balto still stands in New York.

questions.q: Why could the medicine not be flown or shipped to Nome?
questions.a: It could not be shipped because the port was frozen over until spring, and it could not be flown because the only two airplanes had open cockpits and engines that would not start in the cold.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. trapped) and paragraph E (i.e. Balto).
Summarize how the medicine reached Nome.
questions.a: Twenty mushers and about 150 sled dogs carried the medicine 674 miles in a relay. They traveled through blizzards near sixty degrees below zero. Gunnar Kaasen and his lead dog Balto ran the final stretch and reached Nome in five and a half days.

questions.q:
urgent: Urgent means it cannot wait. The doctor needed the medicine right away or children would die.
relay: A relay is when a team takes turns, each member carrying something part of the way.
Describe the connection between the weather and the danger the mushers faced.
questions.a: Because temperatures were near sixty below and a blizzard was blowing, the mushers risked frostbite, and Seppala risked breaking through the sea ice with his entire team.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "the port was iced over until spring" or "Kaasen dug the medicine out with his bare hands." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: Why Your Stomach Growls
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Ask and answer questions to demonstrate understanding of a text, referring explicitly to the text as the basis for the answers.
 Spiral: RI.3.2 main idea · RI.3.3 connections · RI.3.4 word meaning · RI.3.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: You are sitting in a quiet classroom and your stomach makes a long, loud noise. Everyone hears it. The sound has less to do with hunger than you might think.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Your stomach and intestines are muscular tubes. About every ninety minutes, whether you have eaten or not, those muscles squeeze in a wave that pushes everything forward. The wave is called peristalsis. It works the way you squeeze toothpaste out of a tube.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Inside those tubes there is always some liquid and some gas. When the muscles squeeze, the gas and liquid get pushed through narrow spaces. That is what makes the sound. Your body is not empty and rumbling. It is full and moving.

paras.label: D
paras.text: So why does it seem louder when you are hungry? There are two reasons. Food muffles the noise, the way a full water bottle sloshes less than an empty one. And when you have not eaten for a couple of hours, your body runs an extra strong wave to sweep out leftovers.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A growling stomach is not a problem to fix. It is a sign that the machinery is running.

paras.label: A
paras.text: You are in a quiet classroom and your stomach makes a loud noise. Everyone hears it. Why does that happen?

paras.label: B
paras.text: Your stomach and intestines are tubes made of muscle. About every ninety minutes those muscles squeeze in a wave. The wave pushes everything forward, like squeezing a tube of toothpaste.

paras.label: C
paras.text: There is always some liquid and some gas inside the tubes. When the muscles squeeze, the gas and liquid get pushed through tight spaces. That is the sound you hear.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Why is it louder when you are hungry? Food muffles the sound, the way a full water bottle sloshes less than an empty one. Also, when you have not eaten in a while, your body runs an extra strong wave to sweep out leftovers.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A growling stomach is not a problem. It means your body is working.

questions.q: Why does a stomach with food in it make less noise?
questions.a: A stomach with food in it makes less noise because the food muffles the sound, the way a full water bottle sloshes less than an empty one.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. squeezing) and paragraph D (i.e. hunger).
Summarize what causes the sound of a growling stomach.
questions.a: The stomach and intestines squeeze in waves about every ninety minutes. Those squeezes push gas and liquid through narrow spaces, and that makes the growling sound. It is louder when you are hungry because there is no food to muffle it.

questions.q:
peristalsis: Peristalsis is the wave of squeezing that pushes food through your stomach and intestines.
muffles: Muffles means makes a sound quieter. Food in the stomach makes the noise quieter.
Describe the connection between an empty stomach and a louder growl.
questions.a: Because there is no food to muffle the sound and the body runs an extra strong cleaning wave, an empty stomach growls louder than a full one.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "the muscles squeeze every ninety minutes" or "there is always gas and liquid inside." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: The Hats That Almost Ended the Birds
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Ask and answer questions to demonstrate understanding of a text, referring explicitly to the text as the basis for the answers.
 Spiral: RI.3.2 main idea · RI.3.3 connections · RI.3.4 word meaning · RI.3.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: In the 1890s, the most fashionable hats in America were covered in feathers. Not small feathers. Whole wings. Sometimes an entire stuffed bird sat on the brim.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The demand was enormous. Hunters shot herons, egrets, and terns by the millions. Egrets were hunted hardest, because their finest feathers grow only during nesting season. Killing the adults left the chicks to starve. Some species came close to disappearing.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Two women in Boston, Harriet Hemenway and Minna Hall, decided to act. Neither could vote. So they used what they did have: an invitation list. They asked the wealthiest women in the city to tea and asked them to stop wearing feathers.

paras.label: D
paras.text: It worked. Hundreds agreed. The group they formed became the Massachusetts Audubon Society. Similar groups appeared in other states, and together they pushed for laws.

paras.label: E
paras.text: In 1918, Congress passed a law making it illegal to hunt most wild birds for their feathers. Egret populations recovered. The next time you see a snowy egret standing in shallow water, remember that it is there partly because of a tea party.

paras.label: A
paras.text: In the 1890s, the most stylish hats in America were covered in feathers. Some hats had whole wings on them. Some had a whole stuffed bird.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Hunters shot millions of birds to sell the feathers. Egrets were hunted the most. Their best feathers only grow during nesting season, so killing the adults left the chicks to starve. Some birds almost disappeared.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Two women in Boston decided to act. Their names were Harriet Hemenway and Minna Hall. Neither one could vote. So they invited rich women to tea and asked them to stop wearing feathers.

paras.label: D
paras.text: It worked. Hundreds agreed. The group became the Massachusetts Audubon Society. Groups in other states pushed for laws.

paras.label: E
paras.text: In 1918, Congress made it illegal to hunt most wild birds for their feathers. The egrets came back.

questions.q: Why were egrets hunted harder than other birds?
questions.a: Egrets were hunted hardest because their finest feathers grow only during nesting season, so hunters killed the adult birds while they had chicks.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. tea) and paragraph E (i.e. law).
Summarize how the feather trade was stopped.
questions.a: Two women in Boston invited wealthy women to tea and asked them to stop wearing feathers. Hundreds agreed, and their group became the Massachusetts Audubon Society. Groups like it pushed for laws, and in 1918 Congress made hunting wild birds for feathers illegal.

questions.q:
demand: Demand means how much people want to buy something. So many people wanted feathered hats that hunters killed millions of birds.
recovered: Recovered means got better and grew back. The egret population grew again after the law passed.
Describe the connection between nesting season and the danger to egret chicks.
questions.a: Because the finest feathers grew only during nesting season, hunters killed the adult egrets while they had chicks, and the chicks starved without their parents.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "neither woman could vote" or "similar groups formed in other states." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: Cities Under Our Feet
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Ask and answer questions to demonstrate understanding of a text, referring explicitly to the text as the basis for the answers.
 Spiral: RI.3.2 main idea · RI.3.3 connections · RI.3.4 word meaning · RI.3.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: Step on a sidewalk crack in summer and there is a good chance you are standing over a city. Ant colonies can run for yards underground, with rooms, roads, and jobs.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A colony begins with a single queen. After her mating flight she lands, breaks off her own wings, digs a small chamber, and lays her first eggs. She feeds those first larvae using her wing muscles, which she will never need again.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Once workers hatch, they take over. Some dig. Some forage for food. Some care for the young. Some do almost nothing for days at a time, which scientists think is a reserve crew for emergencies.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The rooms have purposes. There are nurseries held at a steady temperature, food storage rooms, and a waste room kept far from everything else. Leafcutter ants add a farm room where they grow a fungus on chewed leaves. The fungus, not the leaves, is their food.

paras.label: E
paras.text: No ant is in charge. The queen lays eggs; she does not give orders. Each ant follows simple rules and responds to chemical signals from its neighbors. Out of thousands of small decisions, a city runs.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Step on a sidewalk crack and you may be standing over a city. Ant colonies run for yards underground. They have rooms, roads, and jobs.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A colony starts with one queen. She lands, breaks off her own wings, digs a small room, and lays her first eggs.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Once workers hatch, they take over. Some dig. Some look for food. Some care for the young. Some rest, and scientists think they are a backup crew.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The rooms have jobs. There are nurseries, food rooms, and a trash room kept far away. Leafcutter ants even grow a fungus on chewed leaves and eat that.

paras.label: E
paras.text: No ant is the boss. The queen lays eggs but gives no orders. Each ant follows simple rules and signals from its neighbors. That is how the city runs.

questions.q: What does the queen use to feed her very first larvae?
questions.a: The queen feeds her first larvae using her own wing muscles, which she no longer needs after she breaks off her wings.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. rooms) and paragraph E (i.e. rules).
Summarize how an ant colony is organized.
questions.a: One queen starts the colony and lays all the eggs. Workers then dig, forage, and care for the young. The colony has separate rooms for nurseries, food, and waste. No ant is in charge; each one follows simple rules and chemical signals.

questions.q:
forage: Forage means to go out and search for food.
colony: A colony is a large group of ants that live and work together in one nest.
Describe the connection between simple rules and a working colony.
questions.a: Because each ant follows simple rules and reacts to signals from its neighbors, thousands of small decisions add up, and the whole colony works without anyone in charge.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "the waste room is kept far from everything else" or "leafcutter ants grow a fungus." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: The Glue That Failed
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Ask and answer questions to demonstrate understanding of a text, referring explicitly to the text as the basis for the answers.
 Spiral: RI.3.2 main idea · RI.3.3 connections · RI.3.4 word meaning · RI.3.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1968, a scientist named Spencer Silver was trying to invent a very strong glue. He failed. What he made instead was a glue that stuck lightly and peeled off without leaving a mark.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Silver thought it was useful. Nobody else did. For five years he gave talks inside his own company trying to find someone who wanted a weak glue. No one took it.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Then a coworker named Art Fry got annoyed at church. He sang in the choir, and the paper scraps he used to mark the hymns kept sliding out of his book. He remembered Silver’s glue.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Fry coated small pieces of paper with it. The markers stayed in the book, then peeled out clean. He made batches for people around the office, and those people would not stop asking for more.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The first stores barely sold any. So in 1980 the company mailed free samples to offices in one city. Nine out of ten people who tried them ordered more. The notes went on sale everywhere that year.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A glue that was too weak became one of the most common objects in the world. Silver had not failed. He had solved a problem nobody had asked about yet.

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1968, a scientist named Spencer Silver tried to invent a very strong glue. He failed. He made a glue that stuck lightly and peeled off with no mark.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Silver thought it was useful. No one else did. For five years he looked for someone who wanted a weak glue. No one took it.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Then a coworker named Art Fry got annoyed at church. The paper he used to mark songs kept sliding out of his book. He remembered Silver’s glue.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Fry put the weak glue on small pieces of paper. The markers stayed in the book and peeled out clean. He made some for people in his office. They kept asking for more.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The first stores barely sold any. So the company mailed free samples to offices in one city. Nine out of ten people who tried them ordered more.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A glue that was too weak became one of the most common things in the world.

questions.q: Why did Art Fry think of Spencer Silver’s glue?
questions.a: Art Fry thought of the glue because the paper scraps he used to mark hymns in his choir book kept sliding out, and he needed a marker that would stay put and still peel off clean.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. rejected) and paragraph E (i.e. samples).
Summarize how a failed glue became a useful product.
questions.a: Spencer Silver accidentally made a weak glue and could not find a use for it. Art Fry used it to make paper markers that stayed in his choir book and peeled off clean. After free samples convinced people to try them, the notes sold everywhere.

questions.q:
samples: Samples are free pieces of a product that a company gives away so people will try it.
batches: Batches are groups of something made at one time. Fry made groups of sticky notes for his coworkers.
Describe the connection between the weak glue and the usefulness of the paper markers.
questions.a: Because the glue was weak, the markers stuck in the book but peeled out without tearing the page, which is exactly what Fry needed.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "Silver spent five years looking for a use" or "nine out of ten people who got samples ordered more." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: The Town That Moved
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine the main idea of a text; recount the key details and explain how they support the main idea.
 Spiral: RI.3.1 key details · RI.3.3 connections · RI.3.4 word meaning · RI.3.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: Kiruna is a town in the far north of Sweden. It sits on top of the largest iron mine in the world. For a hundred years the mine has paid for the town. Now the mine is taking the town back.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Digging under Kiruna has made the ground unsteady. Cracks are spreading toward the buildings. Engineers say that if nothing is done, parts of the town will sink.

paras.label: C
paras.text: So Sweden decided to move the town. Not rebuild it somewhere else. Move it. Workers lift whole buildings onto trailers and drive them two miles east.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The church went first. It is more than a hundred years old and built of wood. Crews cut it into pieces, drove each piece down the road, and put it back together.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Not everything can travel. Most homes are being torn down and rebuilt instead. Families have been given apartments in the new center. Some people are glad. Others say the new town does not feel like home.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The move started in 2014 and will not finish until the 2030s. About six thousand people will end up with new addresses without ever leaving Kiruna.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Kiruna is a town in the far north of Sweden. It sits on top of the largest iron mine in the world. The mine paid for the town. Now the mine is taking the town back.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Digging under Kiruna has made the ground weak. Cracks are spreading toward the buildings. If nothing is done, parts of the town will sink.

paras.label: C
paras.text: So Sweden decided to move the town. Workers lift whole buildings onto trailers and drive them two miles east.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The church went first. It is over a hundred years old and made of wood. Crews cut it into pieces, drove each piece down the road, and put it back together.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Not everything can move. Most homes are torn down and rebuilt. Families get new apartments. Some people are glad. Others say the new town does not feel like home.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The move started in 2014 and will not finish until the 2030s.

questions.q: Why does Kiruna have to move?
questions.a: Kiruna has to move because digging in the iron mine underneath has made the ground unsteady, and cracks are spreading toward the buildings.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. moving) and paragraph E (i.e. feelings).
Summarize what is happening in Kiruna and why.
questions.a: Mining under Kiruna made the ground unsafe, so Sweden is moving the whole town two miles east. Some buildings, like the wooden church, are cut apart and driven to the new site. Most homes are torn down and rebuilt. The move began in 2014 and will take until the 2030s.

questions.q:
unsteady: Unsteady means not firm or safe. The ground under Kiruna can shift and sink.
crews: Crews are teams of workers who do a job together.
Describe the connection between the mine and the cracks in the ground.
questions.a: Because the mine removes rock from underneath the town, the ground above has less holding it up, so it shifts and cracks.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "the church was cut into pieces" or "the move will take until the 2030s." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: The Dogs That Find Whales
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine the main idea of a text; recount the key details and explain how they support the main idea.
 Spiral: RI.3.1 key details · RI.3.3 connections · RI.3.4 word meaning · RI.3.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: Scientists who study killer whales have a problem. The whales live underwater. You cannot weigh one, check its health, or find out what it ate. Most of what a researcher wants to know is out of reach.

paras.label: B
paras.text: There is one exception. Whale scat, which is whale waste, floats for about half an hour before it sinks. A sample tells researchers what the whale ate, whether it is pregnant, and how stressed it is.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Finding it is the hard part. A boat crew scanning the water might spot one sample in a long day. So researchers turned to dogs.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A dog named Tucker was trained to smell whale scat from up to a mile away. He stood at the bow of the boat and leaned toward the scent. The crew steered wherever he leaned. When the boat got close, his body language changed, and the crew scooped the sample out of the water.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Dogs like Tucker found four times more samples than people scanning alone. What the samples showed mattered: these whales were not starving from a shortage of salmon, the way scientists had assumed. They were eating, but they were stressed by boat traffic.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The dogs never see a whale. They only smell what one left behind.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Scientists who study killer whales have a problem. The whales live underwater. You cannot weigh one or check its health.

paras.label: B
paras.text: There is one way. Whale waste floats for about half an hour before it sinks. A sample shows what the whale ate and how healthy it is.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Finding it is hard. A crew watching the water might find one sample all day. So researchers used dogs.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A dog named Tucker was trained to smell whale waste from a mile away. He stood at the front of the boat and leaned toward the smell. The crew steered where he leaned.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Dogs like Tucker found four times more samples than people alone. The samples showed the whales were eating, but they were stressed by boat traffic.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The dogs never see a whale. They only smell what one left behind.

questions.q: Why do researchers want samples of whale scat?
questions.a: A sample tells researchers what the whale ate, whether it is pregnant, and how stressed it is, which they cannot learn any other way.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. Tucker) and paragraph E (i.e. results).
Summarize how dogs help scientists study killer whales.
questions.a: Killer whales are hard to study because they live underwater, but their floating scat holds useful information. Dogs trained to smell it from up to a mile away point the boat toward samples, and crews find four times more that way. The samples showed the whales were stressed by boat traffic rather than starving.

questions.q:
samples: Samples are small amounts collected so scientists can test and study them.
stressed: Stressed means under strain or pressure. Boat traffic put pressure on the whales.
Describe the connection between the dogs and what scientists learned about the whales.
questions.a: Because the dogs found four times more samples, scientists had enough evidence to see that the whales were eating but stressed by boat traffic, which changed what they had assumed.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "scat floats for about half an hour" or "the dogs found four times more samples." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: How a Seed Crosses an Ocean
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine the main idea of a text; recount the key details and explain how they support the main idea.
 Spiral: RI.3.1 key details · RI.3.3 connections · RI.3.4 word meaning · RI.3.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: A new island rises out of the sea with no life on it at all. Within a few years, plants are growing there. They had to get there somehow, and plants cannot move.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Wind carries the smallest seeds. Orchid seeds are as fine as dust. A single pod releases millions of them, and a few ride the wind for hundreds of miles.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Birds carry others. A seed with a hook catches in feathers. A seed inside a berry gets eaten, rides in the bird’s gut for hours, and lands in a new place already surrounded by fertilizer.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The ocean carries the biggest travelers. A coconut has a thick husk full of air pockets, so it floats, sometimes for months. Salt water cannot get through the shell to the seed inside. Coconuts have crossed thousands of miles of open water and sprouted on beaches where no coconut palm had ever grown.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Not every traveler survives. Most seeds land in salt water or on bare rock and die. But a plant does not need most of its seeds to make it. It only needs one.

paras.label: A
paras.text: An island rises out of the sea with no life on it. Plants show up anyway. They cannot move, so how do they get there?

paras.label: B
paras.text: Wind carries the smallest seeds. Orchid seeds are as fine as dust. One pod lets out millions, and a few ride the wind for hundreds of miles.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Birds carry others. A seed with a hook sticks in feathers. A seed inside a berry gets eaten and lands far away in the bird’s waste.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The ocean carries the biggest seeds. A coconut has a thick husk full of air. It floats for months, and salt water cannot reach the seed inside. Coconuts have crossed thousands of miles and grown on new beaches.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Most seeds land in salt water or on bare rock and die. But a plant does not need most of its seeds to make it. It only needs one.

questions.q: How does a coconut survive a long trip across the ocean?
questions.a: A coconut has a thick husk full of air pockets so it floats, and the hard shell keeps salt water from reaching the seed inside.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. birds) and paragraph D (i.e. floating).
Summarize the three ways seeds travel to new places.
questions.a: Wind carries dust-sized seeds like orchid seeds for hundreds of miles. Birds carry seeds that hook onto feathers or pass through their guts. The ocean floats big seeds like coconuts for months. Most seeds die on the way, but a plant only needs one to survive.

questions.q:
husk: A husk is the thick outer covering of a seed or fruit. The coconut husk is full of air pockets.
fertilizer: Fertilizer is material that helps plants grow. Bird droppings act as fertilizer around a seed.
Describe the connection between the coconut husk and where coconut palms grow.
questions.a: Because the air-filled husk lets a coconut float for months and the shell keeps salt water out, coconuts can drift thousands of miles and sprout on beaches where no palm grew before.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "orchid seeds are as fine as dust" or "a seed in a berry lands surrounded by fertilizer." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: The Woman Who Got Tired of Broken Dishes
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine the main idea of a text; recount the key details and explain how they support the main idea.
 Spiral: RI.3.1 key details · RI.3.3 connections · RI.3.4 word meaning · RI.3.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: Josephine Cochrane owned fine china that had been in her family for generations. In the 1880s she threw large dinner parties, and her servants kept chipping the plates while washing them.

paras.label: B
paras.text: She decided to wash them herself. She did not like that either. So she measured every dish she owned and built wire compartments shaped to hold each one.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Then she mounted the compartments in a wheel inside a copper boiler. A motor turned the wheel while a pump sprayed hot soapy water up from the bottom. In 1886 she received a patent for it.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Selling it turned out to be harder than building it. Families did not want one. Washing dishes by hand was cheap, and most homes could not make water hot enough. So Cochrane went to hotels and restaurants, where washing hundreds of plates by hand was slow and expensive. They bought.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Her machine won an award at the 1893 World’s Fair in Chicago. She ran her company until she died in 1913. Home dishwashers did not become common until the 1950s, about seventy years after she built the first one.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Josephine Cochrane owned fine china that had been in her family for years. In the 1880s she had big dinner parties. Her servants kept chipping the plates while washing them.

paras.label: B
paras.text: She tried washing them herself. She did not like that either. So she measured every dish she owned and built wire holders shaped to fit each one.

paras.label: C
paras.text: She put the holders in a wheel inside a copper tub. A motor turned the wheel while a pump sprayed hot soapy water up from the bottom. In 1886 she got a patent.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Selling it was harder than building it. Families did not want one, because washing by hand was cheap. So she sold to hotels and restaurants, where washing hundreds of plates took a long time.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Her machine won an award at the 1893 World’s Fair. Home dishwashers did not become common until the 1950s.

questions.q: Why did Cochrane sell her machine to hotels instead of to families?
questions.a: She sold to hotels and restaurants because families found hand washing cheap and most homes could not make water hot enough, while hotels had hundreds of plates to wash and it was slow and expensive.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. machine) and paragraph D (i.e. selling).
Summarize how and why Josephine Cochrane invented the dishwasher.
questions.a: Cochrane was tired of her servants chipping her family china. She measured her dishes, built a wire compartment for each one, and mounted them in a wheel inside a boiler with a pump that sprayed hot water. She patented it in 1886 and sold it to hotels and restaurants, which needed it more than families did.

questions.q:
compartments: Compartments are separate spaces that each hold one thing. Each dish had its own wire compartment.
patent: A patent is a legal document saying that an inventor owns the rights to an invention.
Describe the connection between the chipped plates and the design of the machine.
questions.a: Because plates were being chipped during hand washing, Cochrane measured every dish and built a compartment shaped to hold each one, so nothing could knock against anything else.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "she measured every dish she owned" or "her machine won an award in 1893." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: Why Bridges Have Gaps
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine the main idea of a text; recount the key details and explain how they support the main idea.
 Spiral: RI.3.1 key details · RI.3.3 connections · RI.3.4 word meaning · RI.3.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: Walk across a long bridge and at some point you will step over a metal comb set into the road. The teeth fit together but do not touch. That gap is not damage. It is one of the most important parts of the bridge.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Steel and concrete expand when they get hot and shrink when they get cold. The change is tiny for a short piece, but a bridge is not short. A steel span a mile long can grow more than a foot between a January night and a July afternoon.

paras.label: C
paras.text: If both ends were bolted down, that extra length would have nowhere to go. The bridge would push against its own supports with enormous force. Concrete would crack. Steel would buckle.

paras.label: D
paras.text: So engineers build in expansion joints. One end of the span rests on rollers or a sliding plate. The comb-shaped gap opens in winter and closes in summer, and the road stays smooth enough to drive over either way.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The same idea shows up in sidewalks, railroad tracks, and pipelines. Anything long and rigid that sits outside needs somewhere to put the extra length. Engineers do not fight the expansion. They plan a place for it to go.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Walk across a long bridge and you will step over a metal comb in the road. The teeth fit together but do not touch. That gap is not damage. It is important.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Steel and concrete grow when they get hot and shrink when they get cold. A bridge a mile long can grow more than a foot from a winter night to a summer day.

paras.label: C
paras.text: If both ends were bolted down, that growth would have nowhere to go. The bridge would push hard on its own supports. Concrete would crack. Steel would bend.

paras.label: D
paras.text: So engineers leave gaps called expansion joints. One end of the bridge rests on rollers. The gap opens in winter and closes in summer.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The same idea shows up in sidewalks, train tracks, and pipes. Anything long that sits outside needs a place to put the extra length.

questions.q: What would happen if both ends of a long bridge were bolted down?
questions.a: If both ends were bolted down, the extra length from expansion would have nowhere to go, so the bridge would push against its supports until the concrete cracked or the steel buckled.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. expansion) and paragraph D (i.e. joints).
Summarize why bridges are built with gaps in them.
questions.a: Steel and concrete expand in heat and shrink in cold, and a mile-long span can grow more than a foot. Bolted at both ends it would crack or buckle, so engineers leave expansion joints where the extra length can go. The same idea is used in sidewalks, tracks, and pipelines.

questions.q:
expand: Expand means to get bigger or longer. Steel expands when it heats up.
rigid: Rigid means stiff and not able to bend easily. Bridges and rails are long and rigid.
