Describe the connection between heat and damage to a bridge with no gaps.
questions.a: Because heat makes the steel and concrete grow longer, a bridge bolted at both ends would press against its supports with great force, and the concrete would crack or the steel would buckle.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "one end rests on rollers" or "the gap opens in winter." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: How a Cave Is Carved
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Describe the relationship between a series of historical events, scientific ideas or concepts, or steps in technical procedures in a text, using language that pertains to time, sequence, and cause/effect.
 Spiral: RI.3.1 key details · RI.3.2 main idea · RI.3.4 word meaning · RI.3.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: A cave does not get dug out. It gets dissolved.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It starts with rain. As a raindrop falls it picks up a little carbon dioxide from the air, and it picks up more as it soaks through soil. That turns the water slightly acidic, like very weak lemon juice.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Next the water sinks into the ground and reaches limestone. Limestone is a soft rock made from ancient sea shells, and weak acid dissolves it the way water dissolves sugar. Over thousands of years, water trickling along one crack widens it into a passage.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Then the water table drops. The passage drains, and for the first time there is air inside. Now the cave is a room instead of a pipe.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Water still drips in from above, and each drop carries dissolved limestone. When a drop hangs from the ceiling, a little of that limestone stays behind. Drop after drop builds a stone icicle called a stalactite. What splashes on the floor builds a stalagmite pointing up.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A stalactite may grow about the thickness of a sheet of paper in a year. The formations in a large cave took longer to build than humans have existed.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A cave is not dug out. It is dissolved.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It starts with rain. A falling raindrop picks up carbon dioxide from the air and from the soil. That makes the water a weak acid.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The water sinks down and reaches limestone. Limestone is a soft rock made from old sea shells. Weak acid dissolves limestone. Over thousands of years, water trickling along a crack makes it wider.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Then the water drains away. Air fills the passage. Now the cave is a room.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Water still drips from above. Each drop carries a little dissolved limestone. When a drop hangs from the ceiling, some limestone stays behind. Drop after drop makes a stone icicle called a stalactite. What splashes down makes a stalagmite.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A stalactite may grow as thick as a sheet of paper in one year.

questions.q: What makes rainwater able to dissolve solid rock?
questions.a: Rainwater picks up carbon dioxide from the air and from the soil, which makes it slightly acidic, and weak acid dissolves limestone.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. dissolving) and paragraph E (i.e. building).
Summarize the steps that form a cave.
questions.a: Rain picks up carbon dioxide and becomes a weak acid. It sinks into limestone and slowly dissolves a crack into a passage. When the water table drops, the passage drains and fills with air. Dripping water then leaves limestone behind, building stalactites from the ceiling and stalagmites from the floor.

questions.q:
dissolves: Dissolves means breaks apart into a liquid until it disappears, the way sugar dissolves in water.
formations: Formations are the shapes built up inside a cave, such as stalactites and stalagmites.
Describe the connection between the draining water and the cave filling with air.
questions.a: Because the water table drops, the water drains out of the passage, and air moves into the empty space, turning a flooded pipe into an open cave room.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "limestone is made from ancient sea shells" or "a stalactite grows a paper’s thickness in a year." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: The Long Road of a Banana
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Describe the relationship between a series of historical events, scientific ideas or concepts, or steps in technical procedures in a text, using language that pertains to time, sequence, and cause/effect.
 Spiral: RI.3.1 key details · RI.3.2 main idea · RI.3.4 word meaning · RI.3.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: A banana in a Michigan grocery store in February grew on a plant that has never felt frost. Getting it there takes about three weeks, and it is never allowed to ripen on its own.

paras.label: B
paras.text: First, workers cut the bunch while the bananas are still hard and green. A ripe banana would turn to mush on the trip.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Next the bunches are washed in tanks to remove the sticky sap, cut into the smaller clusters you see in stores, and boxed. The boxes go into a refrigerated ship held at about 56 degrees, cold enough to slow ripening but not cold enough to damage the fruit.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The ship takes one to two weeks. For the entire trip the bananas stay green and hard.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Then comes the part most people never hear about. At a warehouse near the store, the boxes go into a sealed room and the room is filled with a gas called ethylene. Bananas make this gas themselves as they ripen, so adding it starts the process on schedule. In three to eight days the fruit turns yellow.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Only then does the banana go to the store. The ripening did not happen on a farm. It happened in a room, on a timer, a few miles from you.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A banana in a Michigan store in February grew somewhere it never freezes. Getting it there takes about three weeks.

paras.label: B
paras.text: First, workers cut the bunch while the bananas are hard and green. A ripe banana would turn to mush on the trip.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Next the bunches are washed, cut into small clusters, and boxed. The boxes go into a cold ship at about 56 degrees. That slows ripening without hurting the fruit.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The ship takes one to two weeks. The bananas stay green the whole time.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Then the boxes go into a sealed room near the store. The room is filled with a gas called ethylene. Bananas make this gas themselves when they ripen. In three to eight days the fruit turns yellow.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Only then does the banana go to the store.

questions.q: Why are bananas picked while they are still green and hard?
questions.a: They are picked green because a ripe banana would turn to mush during the three-week trip to the store.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. shipping) and paragraph E (i.e. ripening).
Summarize the trip a banana takes to reach the store.
questions.a: Workers cut the bunches green so they survive the trip. The fruit is washed, cut into clusters, boxed, and shipped cold for one to two weeks. Near the store the boxes go into a sealed room filled with ethylene gas, which ripens them in three to eight days. Then they go on the shelf.

questions.q:
refrigerated: Refrigerated means kept cold on purpose. The ship holds the bananas at about 56 degrees.
sealed: Sealed means closed up tight so that nothing can get in or out.
Describe the connection between the ethylene gas and the color of the banana.
questions.a: Because ethylene is the gas bananas give off when they ripen, filling the room with it starts ripening on schedule, so the green fruit turns yellow in three to eight days.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "the ship is held at 56 degrees" or "bananas make ethylene themselves." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: How a Broken Bone Heals
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Describe the relationship between a series of historical events, scientific ideas or concepts, or steps in technical procedures in a text, using language that pertains to time, sequence, and cause/effect.
 Spiral: RI.3.1 key details · RI.3.2 main idea · RI.3.4 word meaning · RI.3.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: A bone is not a dry stick. It is living tissue with blood running through it. That is why it can repair itself and a chair leg cannot.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The moment a bone breaks, blood vessels inside it tear. Blood pools around the break and clots. Within hours that clot forms a soft collar around both ends, which is why a fresh break swells.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Over the next week, cells arrive and turn the clot into a soft callus made of collagen, the same stretchy material in your ears. The bone is joined now, but it would bend under weight. This is the stage the cast protects.

paras.label: D
paras.text: During the following weeks the body replaces the soft callus with a hard one. Cells lay down minerals, mostly calcium, until the bridge is real bone. By six to eight weeks most breaks can carry weight again.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Then comes the part that takes longest. The hard callus is a lumpy patch, thicker than the original bone. For months, sometimes years, the body shaves the outside down and rebuilds the inside along the lines of force the bone actually feels.

paras.label: F
paras.text: When that work is finished, an X-ray may show no sign that anything ever happened.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A bone is not a dry stick. It is alive and has blood running through it. That is why it can fix itself.

paras.label: B
paras.text: When a bone breaks, blood vessels inside it tear. Blood pools around the break and clots. In a few hours the clot forms a soft collar. That is why a new break swells.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Over the next week, cells turn the clot into a soft callus. The bone is joined, but it would bend under weight. That is why you wear a cast.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Over the next weeks the body makes the callus hard. Cells add minerals like calcium until it is real bone. By six to eight weeks most breaks can hold weight.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Then comes the slowest part. The hard patch is lumpy and too thick. For months the body shaves it down and rebuilds the inside.

paras.label: F
paras.text: When it is done, an X-ray may show no sign of the break.

questions.q: Why does a fresh break swell?
questions.a: A fresh break swells because torn blood vessels let blood pool around the break, and within hours that blood clots into a soft collar around both ends.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. soft) and paragraph D (i.e. hardening).
Summarize the stages of a bone healing.
questions.a: Blood pools at the break and clots into a collar. Cells turn the clot into a soft callus that joins the bone but bends under weight. The body then adds minerals until the bridge is hard bone, usually within six to eight weeks. Finally it spends months reshaping the lumpy patch back to normal.

questions.q:
callus: A callus here is the patch of new material the body builds across a break to join the two pieces.
minerals: Minerals are substances such as calcium that the body uses to make bone hard.
Describe the connection between the soft callus and the need for a cast.
questions.a: Because the soft callus joins the bone but would bend under weight, the cast holds the pieces in place until the body replaces it with hard bone.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "collagen is the same material as in your ears" or "most breaks carry weight by eight weeks." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: How a Wildfire Starts and Stops
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Describe the relationship between a series of historical events, scientific ideas or concepts, or steps in technical procedures in a text, using language that pertains to time, sequence, and cause/effect.
 Spiral: RI.3.1 key details · RI.3.2 main idea · RI.3.4 word meaning · RI.3.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: A fire needs three things: fuel, oxygen, and heat. Take away any one and it goes out. Everything firefighters do in a forest comes back to that.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The fuel builds up first, often for decades. Dead needles, fallen branches, and dry brush pile on the forest floor. A wet year grows more grass, which dies and adds to the pile.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Then comes the spark. Lightning starts some fires. People start most of them, usually by accident.

paras.label: D
paras.text: What happens next depends on the wind. Wind pushes flame into fresh fuel and heats that fuel before the flame arrives, so the fire moves faster and faster in one direction. A fire running uphill behaves the same way, because heat rises into the slope above it.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Firefighters cannot remove the oxygen and usually cannot remove the heat, so they remove the fuel. Crews cut and scrape a strip of bare dirt, called a fire line, ahead of the flames. When the fire reaches that line, there is nothing left to burn.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Sometimes crews light a fire on purpose, burning the fuel between the line and the wildfire before the wildfire gets there. It looks reckless. It is the same idea: get the fuel out of the way first.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A fire needs three things: fuel, oxygen, and heat. Take one away and the fire goes out.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The fuel builds up first, often for years. Dead needles, branches, and dry brush pile up on the forest floor.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Then comes the spark. Lightning starts some fires. People start most of them by accident.

paras.label: D
paras.text: What happens next depends on the wind. Wind pushes flame into new fuel and heats it early, so the fire moves faster. A fire going uphill does the same thing, because heat rises.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Firefighters cannot take away the oxygen or the heat. So they take away the fuel. Crews scrape a strip of bare dirt called a fire line. When the fire reaches it, there is nothing left to burn.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Sometimes crews light a fire on purpose to burn the fuel first. It is the same idea.

questions.q: Why do firefighters build a fire line instead of trying to cool the fire?
questions.a: A fire needs fuel, oxygen, and heat. Crews cannot remove the oxygen and usually cannot remove the heat, so they scrape away the fuel and the fire has nothing left to burn.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. wind) and paragraph E (i.e. fire line).
Summarize how a wildfire builds and how crews stop it.
questions.a: Dead needles, branches, and brush pile up for decades as fuel. A spark from lightning or a person starts the fire, and wind or a slope pushes it into fresh fuel and speeds it up. Since crews cannot remove oxygen or heat, they scrape a bare fire line to take the fuel away, sometimes burning fuel on purpose first.

questions.q:
fuel: Fuel is anything a fire can burn, such as dead needles, branches, and dry brush.
reckless: Reckless means careless about danger. Lighting a fire on purpose looks reckless but is carefully planned.
Describe the connection between wind and the speed of a fire.
questions.a: Because wind pushes the flame into fresh fuel and heats that fuel before the flame arrives, the fuel catches sooner, so the fire moves faster and faster in one direction.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "a wet year grows more grass" or "people start most fires by accident." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: From Sand to Window Glass
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Describe the relationship between a series of historical events, scientific ideas or concepts, or steps in technical procedures in a text, using language that pertains to time, sequence, and cause/effect.
 Spiral: RI.3.1 key details · RI.3.2 main idea · RI.3.4 word meaning · RI.3.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: The window you are looking through started as sand. Not beach sand exactly, but sand made mostly of quartz.

paras.label: B
paras.text: First the sand is mixed with two other powders. Soda ash lowers the melting point so the mix melts at a temperature a furnace can actually reach. Limestone keeps the finished glass from slowly dissolving in water.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Next the mixture goes into a furnace at about 2,900 degrees. The grains lose their shape and become a thick glowing liquid, closer to honey than to water.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Then comes the clever part. The liquid glass is poured onto a shallow bath of melted tin. Glass floats on tin and does not mix with it, and because the tin is perfectly flat, the glass spreads out perfectly flat too, on both sides at once. Before this method, window glass had to be ground and polished for hours.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The sheet cools as it travels down the bath and comes off solid but still hot. It then moves slowly through a long oven that cools it by degrees. Cooling too fast would leave stress locked inside, and the glass would shatter later for no clear reason.

paras.label: F
paras.text: At the end, a machine cuts the ribbon into panes. The whole trip, from sand to cut glass, runs without ever stopping.

paras.label: A
paras.text: The window you are looking through started as sand.

paras.label: B
paras.text: First the sand is mixed with two powders. Soda ash makes the mix melt at a lower heat. Limestone keeps the glass from slowly dissolving in water.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Next the mix goes into a furnace at about 2,900 degrees. The grains melt into a thick glowing liquid.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Then the liquid glass is poured onto a bath of melted tin. Glass floats on tin and does not mix with it. The tin is perfectly flat, so the glass spreads out flat on both sides.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The sheet cools as it moves down the bath. Then it goes slowly through a long oven. Cooling too fast would leave stress in the glass, and it could shatter later.

paras.label: F
paras.text: At the end, a machine cuts the ribbon into panes.

questions.q: Why is the liquid glass poured onto melted tin?
questions.a: Glass floats on tin without mixing with it, and because the tin is perfectly flat, the glass spreads out perfectly flat on both sides at once instead of needing hours of grinding.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. melting) and paragraph E (i.e. cooling).
Summarize how sand becomes a window.
questions.a: Sand is mixed with soda ash to lower the melting point and limestone to keep the glass from dissolving. The mix melts in a furnace near 2,900 degrees. The liquid is floated on melted tin so it spreads perfectly flat, cooled slowly in a long oven so it will not shatter later, and finally cut into panes.

questions.q:
furnace: A furnace is a chamber built to hold very high heat, hot enough here to melt sand.
stress: Stress here means hidden strain left inside the glass. Cooling too fast leaves stress that can crack it later.
Describe the connection between cooling speed and glass breaking later.
questions.a: Because cooling too fast locks stress inside the sheet, the glass can shatter later for no clear reason, so it is cooled slowly in a long oven instead.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "soda ash lowers the melting point" or "the glass is cut into panes at the end." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: Life in a Tide Pool
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of general academic and domain-specific words and phrases in a text relevant to a grade 3 topic or subject area.
 Spiral: RI.3.1 key details · RI.3.2 main idea · RI.3.3 connections · RI.3.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: Twice a day the ocean pulls back and leaves puddles behind in the rocks. These puddles are tide pools, and each one is a small world that gets rebuilt every twelve hours.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Living there is hard. When the tide is out, the water heats up in the sun and gets saltier as it evaporates. A rainstorm can make it almost fresh. Then the tide returns and slams the pool with cold waves. An animal in a tide pool has to survive all of it.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Different animals solve the problem differently. A barnacle glues itself to the rock and seals its shell shut, trapping enough water inside to last until the tide comes back. A limpet clings so tightly with its muscular foot that waves cannot pry it loose.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A sea star has a weapon most animals do not. Hundreds of tiny tube feet on its underside grip the rock and also grip prey. A sea star can hold a mussel closed shut and pull, hour after hour, until the mussel tires and opens.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Tide pools are organized in zones. The highest pools dry out longest and hold the toughest animals. Lower pools stay wet nearly all the time and hold species that could not survive higher up. Walk down a rocky shore and the residents change every few feet.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Twice a day the ocean pulls back and leaves puddles in the rocks. These are tide pools. Each one is a small world rebuilt every twelve hours.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Living there is hard. When the tide is out, the water heats up and gets saltier. Rain can make it almost fresh. Then cold waves come crashing back.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Animals solve the problem in different ways. A barnacle glues itself to the rock and shuts its shell, trapping water inside. A limpet clings so tightly with its foot that waves cannot pull it off.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A sea star has hundreds of tiny tube feet. They grip the rock and grip prey too. A sea star can pull on a mussel for hours until it tires and opens.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Tide pools are set in zones. The highest pools dry out the longest and hold the toughest animals. Lower pools stay wet and hold animals that could not live higher up.

questions.q: Why is a tide pool a hard place for an animal to live?
questions.a: When the tide is out the water heats up and gets saltier as it evaporates, rain can make it almost fresh, and then the returning tide slams it with cold waves. One animal has to survive all of those changes.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. holding on) and paragraph E (i.e. zones).
Summarize how tide pool animals survive.
questions.a: Tide pool animals have to handle heat, changing saltiness, and crashing waves. A barnacle glues itself down and seals water inside its shell. A limpet clings with a strong foot. A sea star uses tube feet to grip rock and pull mussels open. Animals are sorted into zones by how much drying they can take.

questions.q:
evaporates: Evaporates means turns into a gas and goes into the air. As pool water evaporates, the salt left behind makes it saltier.
zones: Zones are bands or levels along the shore. Each zone stays wet for a different amount of time and holds different animals.
Describe the connection between how long a pool stays dry and which animals live in it.
questions.a: Because higher pools are out of the water longest, only animals that can survive heat, salt, and drying live there, while lower pools stay wet and hold species that could not last higher up.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "a barnacle seals water inside its shell" or "the highest pools hold the toughest animals." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: The Parts of a Volcano
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of general academic and domain-specific words and phrases in a text relevant to a grade 3 topic or subject area.
 Spiral: RI.3.1 key details · RI.3.2 main idea · RI.3.3 connections · RI.3.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: A volcano is not just a mountain with fire in it. It is a delivery system, and every part has a job.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It starts deep underground with a magma chamber, a pocket of melted rock. Magma is lighter than the solid rock around it, so it pushes upward whenever it finds a way.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The way up is the conduit, a pipe running through the mountain. At the top of the conduit is the vent, the opening where material escapes. Some volcanoes have one main vent. Others have side vents opening partway down the slope.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The bowl around the vent is the crater. When an eruption empties the magma chamber, the ground above can collapse into the hole it left, forming a much larger pit called a caldera. Crater Lake in Oregon fills a caldera six miles wide.

paras.label: E
paras.text: What comes out depends on the magma. Runny magma flows out as lava and builds wide, gently sloped shields, like the volcanoes of Hawaii. Thick, sticky magma traps gas until the pressure blows it apart, sending up ash and rock and building the steep cone shape most people picture.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Geologists read those shapes backward. The shape of a volcano tells them what kind of eruption built it.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A volcano is not just a mountain with fire in it. Every part has a job.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It starts deep underground with a magma chamber, a pocket of melted rock. Magma is lighter than the rock around it, so it pushes up.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The way up is the conduit, a pipe through the mountain. At the top is the vent, the opening where material comes out. Some volcanoes also have side vents on the slope.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The bowl around the vent is the crater. When an eruption empties the chamber, the ground can fall into the hole and make a much bigger pit called a caldera.

paras.label: E
paras.text: What comes out depends on the magma. Runny magma flows as lava and builds wide, gentle slopes. Thick, sticky magma traps gas until the pressure blows it apart, sending up ash and building a steep cone.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Geologists read the shape of a volcano to learn what kind of eruption built it.

questions.q: Why do some volcanoes have gentle slopes and others have steep cones?
questions.a: Runny magma flows out as lava and spreads into wide, gently sloped shields. Thick, sticky magma traps gas until pressure blows it apart, throwing out ash and rock that pile into a steep cone.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. pathway) and paragraph E (i.e. shape).
Summarize the parts of a volcano and what each one does.
questions.a: A magma chamber underground holds melted rock that pushes upward. The conduit is the pipe it travels through, and the vent is the opening where it escapes. The crater is the bowl around the vent, and a caldera is the much larger pit left when the ground collapses into an emptied chamber.

questions.q:
conduit: A conduit is a pipe or channel that carries something through. In a volcano it carries magma up to the vent.
caldera: A caldera is the large pit left when the ground collapses into an emptied magma chamber.
Describe the connection between an emptied magma chamber and a caldera.
questions.a: Because the eruption drains the magma chamber, the rock above it has nothing holding it up, so the ground collapses into the empty space and leaves a pit far wider than the original crater.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "some volcanoes have side vents" or "Crater Lake fills a six-mile caldera." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: How Birds Migrate
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of general academic and domain-specific words and phrases in a text relevant to a grade 3 topic or subject area.
 Spiral: RI.3.1 key details · RI.3.2 main idea · RI.3.3 connections · RI.3.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: Every fall, billions of birds leave the places where they hatched and travel toward warmer ground. The Arctic tern makes the longest trip of any animal, flying from the Arctic to Antarctica and back, roughly 44,000 miles a year.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Birds migrate because food moves, not because they dislike cold. A warbler that eats insects has nothing to eat in a frozen northern forest. Chickadees, which can find seeds and dormant insects under bark, stay all winter.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Finding the way is the harder problem. Birds navigate using several tools at once. Many read the position of the sun, correcting for the time of day. Night migrants use the stars, and young birds appear to learn the pattern of rotation around the North Star before they ever fly.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Birds also sense the Earth’s magnetic field. The strength and angle of that field change as you move north or south, which gives a bird something like a built-in latitude reading. Landmarks help too: rivers, coastlines, and mountain ranges act as highways.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Migration is expensive. Small birds nearly double their weight in fat before leaving, then burn it in flights that can last more than sixty hours without landing. Many do not survive the trip. Enough do that the whole pattern repeats the next year.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Every fall, billions of birds leave the places where they hatched and travel toward warmer ground. The Arctic tern flies from the Arctic to Antarctica and back, about 44,000 miles a year.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Birds migrate because their food moves, not because they hate cold. A warbler that eats insects has nothing to eat in a frozen forest. Chickadees can find seeds under bark, so they stay.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Finding the way is harder. Many birds read the position of the sun. Night fliers use the stars, and young birds seem to learn the pattern around the North Star before they ever fly.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Birds can also sense the Earth’s magnetic field, which changes as you move north or south. Rivers, coastlines, and mountains work like highways too.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Migration is hard work. Small birds nearly double their weight in fat before leaving, then burn it on flights lasting more than sixty hours without landing.

questions.q: Why do some birds migrate while others stay all winter?
questions.a: Birds migrate because their food disappears. A warbler eats insects, which are gone from a frozen forest, while a chickadee can find seeds and dormant insects under bark and so can stay.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. navigation) and paragraph E (i.e. cost).
Summarize why birds migrate and how they find their way.
questions.a: Birds migrate because the food they eat disappears in winter. They navigate with several tools at once: the position of the sun, the pattern of stars around the North Star, the Earth’s magnetic field, and landmarks like rivers and coastlines. They fuel the trip by nearly doubling their weight in fat.

questions.q:
migrate: Migrate means to travel from one region to another at the same time each year, and then back again.
navigate: Navigate means to find and follow the right route to a place.
Describe the connection between what a bird eats and whether it migrates.
questions.a: Because a warbler eats insects that vanish from a frozen forest, it has to leave, while a chickadee can find seeds and dormant insects under bark, so it has no reason to go.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "the Arctic tern flies 44,000 miles a year" or "small birds nearly double their weight in fat." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: Deserts Are Not Always Hot
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of general academic and domain-specific words and phrases in a text relevant to a grade 3 topic or subject area.
 Spiral: RI.3.1 key details · RI.3.2 main idea · RI.3.3 connections · RI.3.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: Most people picture a desert as hot sand. Heat is not what makes a desert. Dryness is.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A place counts as a desert if it is arid, meaning it receives less than about ten inches of precipitation in a year. Precipitation is any water that falls from the sky: rain, snow, sleet, or hail. By that measure the largest desert on Earth is Antarctica, which gets about two inches a year, almost all of it as snow.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Deserts form for different reasons. Some sit in the rain shadow of a mountain range: air rising over the mountains drops its moisture on the near side and arrives dry on the far side. Others sit under bands of sinking air that hold no rain. Antarctica is dry because cold air cannot hold much moisture in the first place.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Only about a fifth of the world’s deserts are covered in sand. The rest are gravel, bare rock, or salt flats. Where there is sand, wind piles it into dunes that move a few yards a year as grains blow up the gentle side and tumble down the steep one.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Desert plants survive by storing water, growing shallow roots that catch rain quickly, or waiting. Some seeds can sit in dry soil for years and sprout within days of a single storm.

paras.label: A

paras.label: B
paras.text: A place is a desert if it is arid, meaning it gets less than about ten inches of precipitation a year. Precipitation is any water that falls from the sky. By that rule the largest desert on Earth is Antarctica, which gets about two inches a year, almost all snow.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Deserts form for different reasons. Some sit behind a mountain range that takes the rain out of the air. Others sit under sinking air that holds no rain. Antarctica is dry because cold air cannot hold much moisture.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Only about a fifth of deserts are sand. The rest are gravel, bare rock, or salt flats. Where there is sand, wind piles it into dunes that move a few yards a year.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Desert plants survive by storing water or by waiting. Some seeds sit in dry soil for years and sprout days after one storm.

questions.q: Why is Antarctica considered a desert?
questions.a: A desert is any place that gets less than about ten inches of precipitation a year. Antarctica gets about two inches, almost all of it snow, so it qualifies even though it is freezing.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. causes) and paragraph D (i.e. surfaces).
Summarize what makes a place a desert.
questions.a: A desert is defined by dryness, not heat: less than about ten inches of precipitation a year. Deserts form behind mountain ranges, under bands of sinking air, or in cold places where the air cannot hold moisture. Only about a fifth are sandy, and the plants there store water or wait years for rain.

questions.q:
arid: Arid means very dry, with little rain or snow.
precipitation: Precipitation is any water that falls from the sky: rain, snow, sleet, or hail.
Describe the connection between a mountain range and the dry land behind it.
questions.a: Because air rising over the mountains drops its moisture on the near side, it arrives on the far side already dry, so little rain falls there and a desert forms.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "Antarctica gets about two inches a year" or "dunes move a few yards a year." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: What Makes an Earthquake
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of general academic and domain-specific words and phrases in a text relevant to a grade 3 topic or subject area.
 Spiral: RI.3.1 key details · RI.3.2 main idea · RI.3.3 connections · RI.3.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: The outer shell of the Earth is broken into large pieces called tectonic plates. They float on hotter, softer rock below and move about as fast as your fingernails grow.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Where two plates meet, there is a crack called a fault. The plates try to slide past each other along the fault, but rock is rough, and friction locks the two sides together. The plates keep pushing anyway, and the rock near the fault bends and stores the strain, like a stick you are slowly bending.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Eventually the friction gives. The two sides snap past each other in seconds, the bent rock springs back, and all the stored energy is released at once. That release is the earthquake.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The energy travels outward as seismic waves. Some waves push and pull the ground the way sound moves through air. Others shake it side to side. A seismograph records the waves as a jagged line, and the height of that line tells scientists how much energy was released.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The spot underground where the rock slips is the focus. The point on the surface directly above it is the epicenter, and that is usually where shaking is strongest.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Faults do not stop moving after a quake. They lock again and begin storing strain for the next one.

paras.label: A
paras.text: The outer shell of the Earth is broken into large pieces called tectonic plates. They move about as fast as your fingernails grow.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Where two plates meet there is a crack called a fault. The plates try to slide past each other, but the rock is rough and friction locks them together. The plates keep pushing, and the rock bends and stores the strain.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Finally the friction gives. The two sides snap past each other in seconds and all the stored energy is released at once. That is the earthquake.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The energy travels out as seismic waves. Some push and pull the ground. Others shake it side to side. A seismograph draws the waves as a jagged line.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The spot underground where the rock slips is the focus. The point on the surface right above it is the epicenter, where shaking is usually strongest.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Faults do not stop after a quake. They lock again and start storing strain for the next one.

questions.q: Why does the ground shake instead of the plates sliding smoothly?
questions.a: Rock is rough, so friction locks the two sides of a fault together while the plates keep pushing. The rock bends and stores strain until the friction gives, and then everything snaps past at once, releasing the energy as shaking.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. strain) and paragraph E (i.e. location).
Summarize what causes an earthquake.
questions.a: Tectonic plates try to slide past each other along a fault, but friction locks them and the rock bends, storing strain. When the friction finally gives, the sides snap past each other and release all that energy at once as seismic waves. The fault then locks again and starts over.

questions.q:
fault: A fault is a crack in the Earth’s crust where two blocks of rock can move past each other.
epicenter: The epicenter is the point on the surface directly above where the rock slipped underground.
Describe the connection between stored strain and the strength of an earthquake.
questions.a: Because the bending rock stores energy the whole time the fault stays locked, all of it is released in the instant the rock finally slips, so the longer the strain builds the more energy the quake can release.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "plates move as fast as fingernails grow" or "a seismograph draws a jagged line." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: Inside a Beehive
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Use text features and search tools (e.g., key words, sidebars, hyperlinks) to locate information relevant to a given topic efficiently.
 Spiral: RI.3.1 key details · RI.3.2 main idea · RI.3.4 word meaning · RI.3.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: A beehive looks like chaos. It is one of the most organized places in nature.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Every hive has one queen. She does one job: she lays eggs, up to two thousand a day in summer. She does not give orders. The hive runs without a boss.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Almost every other bee is a female worker, and her job changes as she ages. For her first days she cleans cells. Then she feeds larvae. Then she builds wax comb. Only in the last part of her life does she leave the hive to gather nectar.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Foragers share what they find by dancing. A bee that has located flowers runs in a figure eight on the comb. The angle of the run tells the other bees the direction relative to the sun, and the length of the waggle tells them how far.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The male bees, called drones, do no work at all. They cannot sting and cannot feed themselves. In fall the workers push them out of the hive.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Through winter the workers cluster around the queen and shiver their flight muscles, holding the center near 95 degrees while snow sits on the roof.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A beehive looks like chaos. It is one of the most organized places in nature.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Every hive has one queen. She lays eggs, up to two thousand a day. She does not give orders.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Almost every other bee is a female worker. Her job changes as she gets older. First she cleans cells. Then she feeds babies. Then she builds wax. Last, she leaves to gather nectar.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Bees that find flowers share the news by dancing. The angle of the dance tells the direction. The length tells how far.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The male bees, called drones, do no work. They cannot sting or feed themselves. In fall the workers push them out.

paras.label: F
paras.text: In winter the workers cluster around the queen and shiver to keep the center warm.

questions.q: Use the index. You want to know how bees stay warm in cold weather. Which pages should you turn to, and why?
questions.a: Pages 31–33, listed under "Winter cluster." That entry matches the topic of bees keeping warm in winter.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. jobs) and paragraph D (i.e. dancing).
Summarize how work is divided in a beehive.
questions.a: The queen only lays eggs and gives no orders. Female workers move through a series of jobs as they age, from cleaning cells to feeding larvae to building comb to foraging. Drones do no work and are pushed out in fall. In winter the workers shiver to keep the cluster warm.

questions.q:
foragers: Foragers are the bees that leave the hive to search for nectar and bring it back.
cluster: A cluster is a tight group. In winter bees pack into a cluster to share heat.
Describe the connection between the waggle dance and finding flowers.
questions.a: Because the angle of the dance shows the direction relative to the sun and the length of the waggle shows the distance, other bees can fly straight to the flowers without searching.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "a queen lays two thousand eggs a day" or "drones cannot feed themselves." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: The Layers of the Rainforest
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Use text features and search tools (e.g., key words, sidebars, hyperlinks) to locate information relevant to a given topic efficiently.
 Spiral: RI.3.1 key details · RI.3.2 main idea · RI.3.4 word meaning · RI.3.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: A rainforest is not one habitat. It is four stacked on top of each other, and most animals spend their whole lives in just one.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The top layer is the emergent layer, where a few giant trees push above everything else. Up there the wind is strong and the sun is harsh. Eagles nest in it.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Below that is the canopy, a roof of branches so thick it blocks most of the light. This is the crowded layer. Roughly half of all rainforest species live here, including monkeys that can travel for miles without touching the ground.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The understory sits in shade. Plants there grow enormous leaves to catch what little light gets through, and the air stays still and humid.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The forest floor is the darkest. Only about two percent of sunlight reaches it. Little grows, but the floor is where everything breaks down. A fallen leaf rots in about six weeks, compared with a year in a forest farther north.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That fast breakdown is why rainforest soil is surprisingly thin. Nutrients do not build up in the ground; they go straight back into the trees.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A rainforest is not one habitat. It is four stacked on top of each other.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The top layer is the emergent layer. A few giant trees push above the rest. The wind is strong and the sun is harsh.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Below that is the canopy, a roof of branches that blocks most of the light. About half of all rainforest animals live here.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The understory sits in shade. Plants grow huge leaves to catch the little light that gets through.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The forest floor is darkest. Only about two percent of sunlight reaches it. A fallen leaf rots in about six weeks.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That is why rainforest soil is thin. The nutrients go straight back into the trees.

questions.q: Use the headings. Which one would you read to learn about monkeys, and how do you know?
questions.a: Heading 2, "The Canopy: Where Half the Species Live." The canopy is the crowded layer where monkeys travel through the branches.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. crowded) and paragraph E (i.e. dark).
Summarize the four layers of a rainforest.
questions.a: The emergent layer holds a few giant trees in strong wind and harsh sun. The canopy is a thick roof of branches where about half of all species live. The understory is shady, so plants grow huge leaves. The forest floor is nearly dark, and fallen material rots there in about six weeks.

questions.q:
canopy: The canopy is the thick roof of branches and leaves near the top of the forest.
nutrients: Nutrients are the substances plants need to grow, taken in through their roots.
Describe the connection between how fast leaves rot and how thin the soil is.
questions.a: Because fallen material breaks down in about six weeks and the trees take the nutrients up immediately, nothing piles up in the ground, so the soil stays thin.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "only two percent of sunlight reaches the floor" or "eagles nest in the emergent layer." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: Reading a Weather Map
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Use text features and search tools (e.g., key words, sidebars, hyperlinks) to locate information relevant to a given topic efficiently.
 Spiral: RI.3.1 key details · RI.3.2 main idea · RI.3.4 word meaning · RI.3.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: A weather map is packed with symbols, and once you know four of them you can predict tomorrow reasonably well.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The big letters come first. An H marks high pressure, where air is sinking. Sinking air does not form clouds, so an H usually means clear skies. An L marks low pressure, where air rises, cools, and forms clouds. An L usually means rain.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The lines with triangles and half circles are fronts, the boundaries where two air masses meet. Blue triangles mark a cold front: cold air shoving under warm air, which lifts it fast and can build thunderstorms in an hour. Red half circles mark a warm front: warm air sliding up over cold, which brings steady rain for longer.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Thin curving lines without symbols are isobars. Each one connects places with the same air pressure. When isobars are packed close together, the pressure changes sharply over a short distance, and that means wind.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Colors usually show precipitation on radar, from green for light rain to red for heavy.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Put those together and a map stops being decoration. It becomes a forecast you can read yourself.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A weather map is full of symbols. Once you know four of them, you can guess at tomorrow.

paras.label: B
paras.text: An H marks high pressure, where air sinks. That usually means clear skies. An L marks low pressure, where air rises and forms clouds. That usually means rain.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Lines with triangles or half circles are fronts, where two air masses meet. Blue triangles mean a cold front, which can build storms fast. Red half circles mean a warm front, which brings steady rain.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Thin curving lines are isobars. Each one connects places with the same air pressure. When they are packed close, expect wind.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Colors show rain on radar, from green for light to red for heavy.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Put those together and a map becomes a forecast you can read yourself.

questions.q: Use the key. A map shows an L over your town with isobars packed tightly around it. What kind of day should you expect?
questions.a: A rainy, windy day. The L means rising air and clouds, and tightly packed isobars mean the pressure changes sharply, which brings wind.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. fronts) and paragraph D (i.e. wind).
Summarize what the four main weather map symbols tell you.
questions.a: H marks high pressure and sinking air, so clear skies. L marks low pressure and rising air, so clouds and rain. Fronts show where air masses meet, with cold fronts building storms fast and warm fronts bringing steady rain. Isobars connect equal pressure, and packed isobars mean wind.

questions.q:
fronts: A front is the boundary where two different air masses meet.
isobars: Isobars are lines on a map connecting places that have the same air pressure.
Describe the connection between a cold front and a sudden storm.
questions.a: Because cold air shoves underneath warm air and lifts it fast, clouds build quickly, so a cold front can produce a thunderstorm within an hour.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "a cold front can build storms in an hour" or "green means light rain on radar." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: The Road to the Vote
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Use text features and search tools (e.g., key words, sidebars, hyperlinks) to locate information relevant to a given topic efficiently.
 Spiral: RI.3.1 key details · RI.3.2 main idea · RI.3.4 word meaning · RI.3.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: When the United States began, most states allowed only white men who owned property to vote. Widening that circle took nearly two hundred years and a great deal of argument.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Property rules fell first. By the 1850s most states had dropped them, so a white man could vote whether or not he owned land.

paras.label: C
paras.text: After the Civil War, the Fifteenth Amendment said a state could not deny the vote because of race. In practice, poll taxes, literacy tests, and outright threats kept most Black citizens in the South from voting for another ninety years.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Women organized for seventy years before winning the vote. The Nineteenth Amendment passed in 1920, and it came down to a single vote in the Tennessee legislature, cast by a young man whose mother had written to him asking him to support it.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The Voting Rights Act of 1965 finally banned the tests and sent federal officials to register voters in places that had blocked them. Registration in Mississippi went from about 7 percent of Black adults to nearly 60 percent in four years.

paras.label: F
paras.text: In 1971 the voting age dropped from 21 to 18, driven by men being drafted at an age when they could not vote.

paras.label: A
paras.text: When the United States began, most states let only white men who owned property vote. Widening that circle took almost two hundred years.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Property rules fell first. By the 1850s most states had dropped them.

paras.label: C
paras.text: After the Civil War, the Fifteenth Amendment said a state could not deny the vote because of race. But poll taxes, reading tests, and threats kept most Black citizens in the South from voting for ninety more years.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Women organized for seventy years before winning the vote in 1920. It came down to a single vote in Tennessee.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The Voting Rights Act of 1965 banned the tests. In Mississippi, Black voter registration went from about 7 percent to nearly 60 percent in four years.

paras.label: F
paras.text: In 1971 the voting age dropped from 21 to 18.

questions.q: Use the timeline. How many years passed between the Fifteenth Amendment and the Voting Rights Act?
questions.a: Ninety-five years, from 1870 to 1965. The amendment banned denial by race, but the tests and taxes were not outlawed until 1965.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. blocked) and paragraph E (i.e. enforcement).
Summarize how voting rights expanded in the United States.
questions.a: At first only white men with property could vote. Property rules fell by the 1850s. The Fifteenth Amendment banned denial by race in 1870, though tests and taxes blocked Black voters for ninety more years. Women won the vote in 1920, the Voting Rights Act enforced the earlier promise in 1965, and the age dropped to 18 in 1971.

questions.q:
amendment: An amendment is a change added to the Constitution.
register: To register is to sign up officially so that you are allowed to vote.
Describe the connection between the Voting Rights Act and the change in Mississippi.
questions.a: Because the act banned literacy tests and sent federal officials to sign people up, the barriers that had kept Black citizens off the rolls were removed, and registration rose from about 7 percent to nearly 60 percent in four years.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "the Nineteenth Amendment came down to one vote" or "the voting age dropped in 1971." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: What Lives in the Deep Ocean
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Use text features and search tools (e.g., key words, sidebars, hyperlinks) to locate information relevant to a given topic efficiently.
 Spiral: RI.3.1 key details · RI.3.2 main idea · RI.3.4 word meaning · RI.3.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: Sunlight runs out about 650 feet down. Below that is the largest habitat on Earth, and almost none of it has ever been seen.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The pressure is the first problem. It increases by about one atmosphere every 33 feet, so two miles down a body is squeezed by the weight of roughly 300 atmospheres. Deep sea animals survive it because they have no air pockets to crush. Their bodies are mostly water, which barely compresses.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Food is the second problem. Nothing grows without light, so most of the deep depends on "marine snow," a slow drift of dead material falling from above. It can take weeks to reach the bottom.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Many deep sea animals make their own light, a trick called bioluminescence. A chemical reaction in their bodies produces a cold glow. They use it to lure prey, to startle predators, and to find mates in the dark.

paras.label: E
paras.text: In the 1970s scientists found something that broke the rules: hot vents on the sea floor where whole communities live without sunlight at all. Bacteria there make food from the chemicals in the vent water, and tube worms, crabs, and clams live off them.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Sunlight runs out about 650 feet down. Below that is the largest habitat on Earth, and almost none of it has been seen.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Pressure is the first problem. It grows the deeper you go. Deep sea animals survive because they have no air pockets to crush. Their bodies are mostly water.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Food is the second problem. Nothing grows without light, so most of the deep lives on "marine snow," dead material drifting down from above.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Many deep sea animals make their own light. A chemical reaction makes a cold glow. They use it to catch food and to find mates.

paras.label: E
paras.text: In the 1970s scientists found hot vents on the sea floor. Whole communities live there without sunlight. Bacteria make food from chemicals in the vent water.

questions.q: Use the diagram. At 5,000 feet, which zone are you in, and what is the light like?
questions.a: The midnight zone, which runs from 3,300 to 13,000 feet. It is fully dark, so animals there rely on marine snow drifting down.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. food) and paragraph E (i.e. vents).
Summarize how animals survive in the deep ocean.
questions.a: They handle crushing pressure because their bodies are mostly water and have no air pockets. Most feed on marine snow drifting down, since nothing grows without light. Many make their own light to lure prey and find mates. At hot vents, bacteria make food from chemicals and support whole communities.

questions.q:
pressure: Pressure is the weight of the water pressing in from every side. It grows the deeper you go.
bioluminescence: Bioluminescence is light made by a living thing through a chemical reaction in its body.
Describe the connection between having no air pockets and surviving deep pressure.
questions.a: Because pressure crushes air but barely compresses water, an animal whose body is mostly water and holds no air pockets has nothing for the pressure to squeeze, so it survives depths that would collapse an air-filled body.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "marine snow takes weeks to reach the bottom" or "vents were found in the 1970s." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: Homework in Elementary School
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Distinguish their own point of view from that of the author of a text.
 Spiral: RI.3.1 key details · RI.3.2 main idea · RI.3.4 word meaning · RI.3.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: I taught third grade for eleven years, and I stopped assigning homework in my fourth year. I want to explain why, because I know not everyone agrees.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The research on elementary homework is thin. Studies find little connection between homework in the early grades and how much students learn. The connection gets stronger in high school, but that is not who I teach.

paras.label: C
paras.text: What I did see was the cost. Homework arrived finished for the students whose parents had time to sit down with them, and unfinished for the students whose parents worked nights. The assignment measured the household, not the child.

paras.label: D
paras.text: I replaced it with one request: read for twenty minutes, anything you like. No log, no signature. Reading volume is one thing that does predict how well children read later.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Some families were unhappy. They said homework builds discipline and prepares children for middle school. I understand that argument. I think eight-year-olds build discipline in other ways, and I would rather they spend the evening at dinner or outside.

paras.label: F
paras.text: You may weigh these things differently than I do. That is a fair thing to do. What matters is knowing which parts of what you just read were evidence and which were my opinion.

paras.label: A
paras.text: I taught third grade for eleven years. I stopped giving homework in my fourth year. I want to explain why.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Studies find little connection between homework in the early grades and how much students learn. The connection is stronger in high school, but that is not who I teach.

paras.label: C
paras.text: I also saw the cost. Homework came back finished for students whose parents had time to help, and unfinished for students whose parents worked nights.

paras.label: D
paras.text: I asked for one thing instead: read for twenty minutes, anything you like. How much a child reads does predict how well they read later.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Some families were unhappy. They said homework builds discipline. I understand that. I think eight-year-olds build discipline in other ways.

paras.label: F
paras.text: You may weigh these things differently than I do. That is fair.

questions.q: What is the author’s point of view about homework, and what is her job?
questions.a: The author is a third grade teacher of eleven years who believes elementary homework is not worth assigning. She replaced it with twenty minutes of free reading.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. unfairness) and paragraph E (i.e. disagreement).
Summarize the author’s reasons for dropping homework.
questions.a: Research shows little connection between elementary homework and learning. The author also saw that finished homework tracked which families had free evenings rather than which children tried. She replaced it with free reading because reading volume does predict later reading ability.

questions.q:
discipline: Discipline here means the habit of doing work steadily even when you do not feel like it.
volume: Volume here means how much of something. Reading volume is how much a child reads.
Describe the connection between a family’s schedule and whether homework came back finished.
questions.a: Because homework was done at home, students whose parents were free in the evening got help finishing it, while students whose parents worked nights did not, so the grade reflected the household instead of the child.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "no log, no signature" or "the connection gets stronger in high school." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: Should Zoos Exist?
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Distinguish their own point of view from that of the author of a text.
 Spiral: RI.3.1 key details · RI.3.2 main idea · RI.3.4 word meaning · RI.3.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: I work at a zoo, so you should know my point of view before you read further. I believe good zoos are worth keeping. I also think most people, including me, should be harder on the bad ones.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Here is the case against zoos. A tiger in the wild ranges over dozens of square miles. No enclosure comes close. Animals in small spaces often pace or rock, behaviors they do not show in the wild. Those are real problems and I am not going to argue them away.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Here is my case for zoos. Several species are alive today only because zoos bred them. The California condor was down to twenty-two birds in 1982. Every condor flying now descends from those twenty-two, raised in captivity and released.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Zoos also fund fieldwork. A share of every ticket at my zoo goes to protecting habitat in places most visitors will never see.

paras.label: E
paras.text: And zoos change people. It is hard to care about an animal you have only seen on a screen.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A reader could accept every fact in this article and still conclude that zoos should close. The facts are not the whole argument. What you think an animal is owed is the rest of it, and that part is yours.

paras.label: A
paras.text: I work at a zoo, so you should know my point of view before you read on. I believe good zoos are worth keeping.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Here is the case against zoos. A tiger in the wild ranges over dozens of square miles. No cage comes close. Animals in small spaces often pace, which they do not do in the wild.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Here is my case for zoos. Some species are alive only because zoos bred them. The California condor was down to twenty-two birds in 1982. Every condor now comes from those birds.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Zoos also pay for fieldwork. Part of every ticket goes to protecting habitat far away.

paras.label: E
paras.text: And zoos change people. It is hard to care about an animal you have only seen on a screen.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A reader could accept every fact here and still say zoos should close. That part is yours to decide.

questions.q: Why does the author tell you where he works in the first sentence?
questions.a: He works at a zoo, so he has a stake in the argument. He tells the reader up front so they can weigh his point of view while reading.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. against) and paragraph C (i.e. for).
Summarize the author’s position and the argument he admits is strong.
questions.a: The author believes good zoos are worth keeping because zoo breeding saved species like the California condor, ticket money funds habitat protection, and seeing animals in person makes people care. He admits that no enclosure matches a wild animal’s range and that confined animals pace.

questions.q:
enclosure: An enclosure is the fenced or walled space an animal is kept in.
captivity: Captivity means living under human care rather than in the wild.
Describe the connection between agreeing with the facts and disagreeing with the author.
questions.a: Because the facts do not settle what an animal is owed, a reader can accept every fact the author gives and still weigh those facts differently, reaching the opposite conclusion.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "twenty-two condors were left in 1982" or "a tiger ranges over dozens of square miles." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: A Letter About the New Skate Park
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Distinguish their own point of view from that of the author of a text.
 Spiral: RI.3.1 key details · RI.3.2 main idea · RI.3.4 word meaning · RI.3.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: To the editor: I have lived on Water Street for thirty-one years, and I am writing against the skate park proposed for the lot behind the fire station.

paras.label: B
paras.text: My reasons are practical. That lot has no parking. Skaters will park on Water Street, which is narrow enough that two cars already cannot pass when someone parks on both sides.

paras.label: C
paras.text: I also expect noise. Skateboards on concrete carry a long way, and the lot is forty feet from the nearest bedroom window, which is mine.

paras.label: D
paras.text: I want to be clear about what I am not saying. I am not saying teenagers are trouble. I hear that argument at every meeting and I think it is nonsense. The kids in this neighborhood shovel my walk.

paras.label: E
paras.text: I would support this park on the school property, where there is a parking lot already and no houses within two hundred feet. I have said so at three meetings.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A reader who does not live on a narrow street may weigh the parking problem differently than I do. A reader who skates certainly will. I am telling you where I stand and why, so you can decide what my reasons are worth.

paras.label: A
paras.text: To the editor: I have lived on Water Street for thirty-one years. I am writing against the skate park planned for the lot behind the fire station.

paras.label: B
paras.text: My reasons are practical. That lot has no parking. Skaters will park on Water Street, which is already too narrow for two cars to pass.

paras.label: C
paras.text: I also expect noise. Skateboards on concrete carry a long way. The lot is forty feet from the nearest bedroom window, which is mine.

paras.label: D
paras.text: I am not saying teenagers are trouble. I hear that at every meeting and I think it is nonsense. The kids here shovel my walk.

paras.label: E
paras.text: I would support this park at the school, where there is already a parking lot and no houses nearby.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A reader who skates will weigh this differently than I do.

questions.q: What is the writer against, and what is he for?
questions.a: He is against building the skate park on the lot behind the fire station because of parking and noise. He is for building the same park on school property, which already has parking and no nearby houses.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. parking) and paragraph D (i.e. clarification).
Summarize the writer’s objections and his alternative.
questions.a: He objects to the fire station lot because it has no parking and Water Street is too narrow, and because skateboard noise would carry to his bedroom forty feet away. He explicitly rejects the argument that teenagers are trouble, and he supports building the park at the school instead.

questions.q:
proposed: Proposed means suggested and not yet decided.
practical: Practical reasons are about how something works day to day, not about feelings or beliefs.
Describe the connection between the writer mentioning shoveling and the argument he rejects.
questions.a: Because he wants readers to know his objection is about parking and noise rather than about teenagers, he offers the shoveling as proof that he thinks well of the neighborhood kids.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "the kids shovel my walk" or "he has said so at three meetings." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: Why I Changed My Mind About Wolves
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Distinguish their own point of view from that of the author of a text.
 Spiral: RI.3.1 key details · RI.3.2 main idea · RI.3.4 word meaning · RI.3.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: I ranched cattle in Montana for twenty years, and for most of them I believed wolves should be shot on sight. I want to tell you what changed and what did not.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Wolves were removed from Yellowstone by 1926 and brought back in 1995. I opposed the return. I had lost calves to predators and I did not want more.

paras.label: C
paras.text: What changed my thinking was watching the park. Without wolves, elk had grazed the riverbanks bare. When wolves returned, elk stopped standing in the open bottoms, and willow and aspen grew back. Beavers followed the willows. Songbirds followed the trees.

paras.label: D
paras.text: I am not going to tell you wolves never take livestock. They do. I lost a heifer in 2011 and I was not philosophical about it.

paras.label: E
paras.text: What I changed my mind about is narrower than people assume. I now think wolves belong in wild country. I still think a rancher should be paid promptly for a confirmed kill, and I still think the people who argue loudest for wolves mostly do not live near any.

paras.label: F
paras.text: If you have never lost an animal, you may find my remaining objections too strong. If you ranch, you may find I gave up too much. Both of those are points of view, including mine.

paras.label: C

paras.label: D
paras.text: I am not saying wolves never take livestock. They do. I lost a heifer in 2011.

questions.q: What changed the author’s mind, and what did not change?
questions.a: Watching the park recover changed his mind: elk stopped grazing the riverbanks bare, and willow, aspen, beavers, and songbirds returned. He still believes ranchers should be paid promptly for confirmed kills.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. recovery) and paragraph E (i.e. limits).
Summarize how the return of wolves changed Yellowstone.
questions.a: Without wolves, elk grazed the riverbanks bare. After wolves returned in 1995, elk stopped standing in the open bottoms, so willow and aspen grew back, beavers followed the willows, and songbirds followed the trees.

questions.q:
predators: Predators are animals that hunt and eat other animals.
confirmed: Confirmed means checked and proven true. A confirmed kill has been verified as a wolf’s.
Describe the connection between wolves returning and songbirds returning.
questions.a: Because wolves kept elk from standing in the open riverbanks, willow and aspen grew back, and those trees gave songbirds the cover and nesting places they had lost.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "wolves were gone by 1926" or "he lost a heifer in 2011." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: Two Views of the Cell Phone Rule
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Distinguish their own point of view from that of the author of a text.
 Spiral: RI.3.1 key details · RI.3.2 main idea · RI.3.4 word meaning · RI.3.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: Our district banned phones during the school day this year. Two people who live with that rule wrote about it.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A principal wrote: "I expected complaints and I got them, for about three weeks. Then the lunchroom got loud again, in a good way. Teachers report fewer arguments that started as group texts. I am aware that a rule which is convenient for adults is not automatically good for children, so we tracked it. Discipline referrals are down a fifth. I support the ban."

paras.label: C
paras.text: A seventh grader wrote: "I take the city bus home and my mom works until six. Before the ban I texted her when I got on. Now I cannot, and the office phone has a line. Adults keep saying we are addicted. Some kids are. I am trying to tell my mother I am safe."

paras.label: D
paras.text: Both of these people are describing the same rule honestly. Neither is making anything up.

paras.label: E
paras.text: They differ because they are standing in different places. The principal is responsible for three hundred students and measures the rule by what happens to all of them. The student is responsible for getting herself home.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A reader has to decide what weight to give each view. That decision is the reader’s, not the writers’.

questions.q: Why do the principal and the student disagree, according to the text?
questions.a: They disagree because they are standing in different places. The principal is responsible for three hundred students and judges the rule by what happens to all of them, while the student is responsible for getting herself home safely.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. principal) and paragraph C (i.e. student).
Summarize each writer’s view of the phone ban.
questions.a: The principal supports the ban: complaints stopped after three weeks, the lunchroom got livelier, teachers report fewer arguments, and referrals are down a fifth. The student objects because she rides the bus home and can no longer text her mother, who works until six, and the office phone has a line.

questions.q:
referrals: Referrals are reports sent to the office when a student breaks a rule.
responsible: To be responsible for something is to be the person who has to take care of it.
Describe the connection between what a person is responsible for and how they judge a rule.
questions.a: Because the principal answers for three hundred students, she measures the rule by totals like referral counts, while the student answers only for her own trip home, so she measures it by whether she can reach her mother.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "referrals are down a fifth" or "the office phone has a line." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: The Oregon Trail
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Use information gained from illustrations (e.g., maps, photographs) and the words in a text to demonstrate understanding of the text (e.g., where, when, why, and how key events occur).
 Spiral: RI.3.1 key details · RI.3.2 main idea · RI.3.4 word meaning · RI.3.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: Between 1840 and 1869, roughly 400,000 people walked from Missouri to Oregon and California. The trail ran about 2,000 miles and took four to six months.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Timing mattered more than anything. Leave too early and there is no grass yet for the oxen. Leave too late and snow closes the mountains before you reach them. Most families left in April or May.

paras.label: C
paras.text: They walked. Wagons were packed with food and tools, not people, and were pulled by oxen rather than horses because oxen live on prairie grass and horses need grain.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The hardest stretches came last. By the time families reached the mountains, the oxen were thin and the food was low. Furniture was pushed off the trail to lighten the load.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Accidents and disease killed far more travelers than anything else. Cholera spread through camps sharing river water. Roughly one in ten people who started the trail died on it.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The railroad finished in 1869 made the same trip in a week. Within a few years, the wagon trail was nearly empty.

questions.q: Use the map. How far is it from Fort Kearny to South Pass?
questions.a: Fort Kearny is at mile 320 and South Pass is at mile 1,100, so the distance between them is 780 miles.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. timing) and paragraph E (i.e. disease).
Summarize why the Oregon Trail was so dangerous.

By the mountains the oxen were thin and food was low. Disease, especially cholera from shared river water, killed about one traveler in ten.

questions.q:
oxen: Oxen are strong cattle trained to pull wagons and plows.
cholera: Cholera is a disease that spreads through dirty water and killed many travelers in camp.
Describe the connection between the food oxen eat and why they were chosen.
questions.a: Because oxen can live on the prairie grass growing along the trail while horses need grain that had to be carried, oxen let families use the wagon space for food and tools instead.
