articles.title: Inside a Volcano Eruption
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Use information gained from illustrations (e.g., maps, photographs) and the words in a text to demonstrate understanding of the text (e.g., where, when, why, and how key events occur).
 Spiral: RI.3.1 key details · RI.3.2 main idea · RI.3.4 word meaning · RI.3.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: On May 18, 1980, the north face of Mount St. Helens slid off the mountain. It was the largest landslide ever recorded.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Pressure had been building for two months. Magma pushing up inside the mountain made the north slope swell outward about five feet per day. Scientists watched the bulge grow and knew something would give.

paras.label: C
paras.text: An earthquake at 8:32 that morning shook the bulge loose. The entire north face collapsed, and that removed the lid holding the pressure in.

paras.label: D
paras.text: What followed went sideways instead of up. A blast of superheated gas and rock shot north at hundreds of miles an hour, flattening forest for nineteen miles. Trees were laid down in rows all pointing away from the mountain.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Then the vertical column rose. Ash reached the stratosphere within fifteen minutes and fell on eleven states. In Yakima, Washington, streetlights came on at noon.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Fifty-seven people died. Life returned faster than expected: within five years, plants sprouted from roots that survived under the ash, and elk were grazing on the blast plain.

questions.a: The earthquake hit at 8:32:11 and the blast began at 8:32:30, so about nineteen seconds later.

Summarize what happened on the morning of May 18, 1980.

questions.q:
bulge: A bulge is a swelling that pushes outward. Magma made the mountain’s north slope bulge.
blast: A blast is a sudden violent rush of gas and rock away from an explosion.
Describe the connection between the landslide and the sideways blast.
questions.a: Because the collapsing north face removed the rock that had been holding the pressure in, the trapped gas escaped through the open side of the mountain, sending the blast north instead of straight up.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "trees lay in rows pointing away" or "streetlights came on at noon." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: A Day in the Life of a Coral Reef
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Use information gained from illustrations (e.g., maps, photographs) and the words in a text to demonstrate understanding of the text (e.g., where, when, why, and how key events occur).
 Spiral: RI.3.1 key details · RI.3.2 main idea · RI.3.4 word meaning · RI.3.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: A coral reef is not a rock and it is not a plant. It is thousands of tiny animals called polyps, each one living inside a cup of limestone it built itself.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Each polyp holds algae inside its body. The algae make food from sunlight and share it with the polyp; the polyp gives the algae a safe place to live. That trade is why reefs grow only in shallow, clear water where light reaches.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The reef runs on a schedule. By day, parrotfish and surgeonfish graze algae off the coral, and the polyps stay closed. At dusk the day fish retreat into crevices and the polyps open, spreading tentacles to catch drifting plankton.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Night belongs to different hunters. Octopuses come out, and moray eels leave their holes to hunt sleeping fish.

paras.label: E
paras.text: When water gets too warm, the polyps expel their algae. The coral turns white, which is called bleaching. A bleached coral is not dead yet, but it is starving, and if the heat lasts it will die.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor and shelter about a quarter of all ocean species.

questions.q: Use the chart. What is happening on the reef at 10 p.m.?
questions.a: At 10 p.m. the polyps are open and catching plankton, octopuses are hunting, and moray eels are out of their holes while the day fish sleep.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. trade) and paragraph E (i.e. bleaching).
Summarize how a coral polyp and its algae help each other.
questions.a: The algae live inside the polyp, make food from sunlight, and share it. The polyp gives the algae a safe place to live. Because the algae need light, reefs grow only in shallow clear water, and when heat drives the algae out the coral turns white and starves.

questions.q:
polyps: Polyps are the tiny animals that build a coral reef, each living in a limestone cup.
bleaching: Bleaching is when a coral pushes out its algae and turns white, leaving it starving.
Describe the connection between sunlight and where reefs can grow.
questions.a: Because the algae inside each polyp need sunlight to make the food they share, reefs can only survive in shallow, clear water where enough light reaches the coral.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "each polyp builds a limestone cup" or "reefs shelter a quarter of ocean species." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: How a City Gets Its Water
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Use information gained from illustrations (e.g., maps, photographs) and the words in a text to demonstrate understanding of the text (e.g., where, when, why, and how key events occur).
 Spiral: RI.3.1 key details · RI.3.2 main idea · RI.3.4 word meaning · RI.3.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: New York City drinks water that falls as rain a hundred miles away, and almost none of it is pumped. Gravity does the work.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It starts in the Catskill Mountains, where streams feed reservoirs built by flooding valleys. Several towns were bought and emptied to make room.

paras.label: C
paras.text: From the reservoirs, water enters tunnels bored through solid rock, some of them six hundred feet underground. The tunnels slope gently downhill the whole way, so the water keeps moving on its own.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Before it reaches taps, the water is treated. It is screened for debris, disinfected with ultraviolet light and chlorine, and fluoride is added. Most cities also filter their water; New York is one of the few large cities allowed to skip that step, because the land around its reservoirs is protected from development.

paras.label: E
paras.text: City Tunnel No. 3 has been under construction since 1970 and is still not finished. It is meant to let the older tunnels be shut off and inspected. Neither has been closed since it opened.

paras.label: F
paras.text: About a billion gallons a day arrive this way, without a single pump for most of the journey.

questions.q: Use the diagram. What happens to the water between the reservoir and the city mains?
questions.a: It travels downhill through an aqueduct tunnel cut six hundred feet through rock, then it is screened, disinfected with ultraviolet light and chlorine, and given fluoride.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. tunnels) and paragraph D (i.e. treatment).
Summarize how water gets from the mountains to a city tap.
questions.a: Rain falls in the Catskills and fills reservoirs made by flooding valleys. The water then runs downhill through tunnels bored hundreds of feet through rock, needing no pumps. It is screened, disinfected, and treated with fluoride before entering the pipes under the streets.

questions.q:
reservoirs: Reservoirs are large artificial lakes built to store water for people to use.
aqueduct: An aqueduct is a channel or tunnel built to carry water a long distance.
Describe the connection between the slope of the tunnels and the need for pumps.
questions.a: Because every part of the tunnel is slightly lower than the part before it, gravity keeps the water moving on its own, so the city does not need pumps for most of the journey.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "several towns were emptied" or "a billion gallons a day." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: The Underground Railroad
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Use information gained from illustrations (e.g., maps, photographs) and the words in a text to demonstrate understanding of the text (e.g., where, when, why, and how key events occur).
 Spiral: RI.3.1 key details · RI.3.2 main idea · RI.3.4 word meaning · RI.3.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: The Underground Railroad was not underground and not a railroad. It was a network of people who helped enslaved men, women, and children escape north, and it used railroad words as code.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A conductor was a guide. A station was a house where someone could hide. A stationmaster was the person who lived there and risked everything by opening the door.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Most travel happened at night, often on foot, following creeks so dogs could not track a scent. The North Star pointed the way, and travelers who could not see it felt for moss on the north side of trees.

paras.label: D
paras.text: After 1850, escaping to a free northern state was no longer enough. A new federal law required officials in free states to return escapees, so many continued all the way to Canada.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Harriet Tubman escaped in 1849 and then went back into slave territory at least thirteen times to lead others out. She later said she never lost a passenger.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Nobody knows the true number. Historians estimate that tens of thousands reached freedom this way, though records were deliberately never kept.

questions.a: A stationmaster was the person who lived at a station, a house or barn, and sheltered people escaping slavery, risking everything by opening the door.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. navigation) and paragraph D (i.e. Canada).
Summarize how the Underground Railroad worked.
questions.a: A network of guides called conductors led people escaping slavery from one hiding place to the next, using railroad words as code. Travel happened at night, often along creeks so dogs could not track them, guided by the North Star. After 1850 many continued all the way to Canada.

questions.q:
network: A network is a group of people connected to each other and working toward the same purpose.
conductor: A conductor here was a guide who led people along the escape route, not someone on a train.
Describe the connection between the 1850 law and travelers going to Canada.
questions.a: Because the new law required officials in free northern states to send escapees back, reaching the North was no longer safe, so many people kept going until they crossed into Canada.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "the Big Dipper was called the drinking gourd" or "Tubman went back thirteen times." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: Why Leaves Change Color
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Describe the logical connection between particular sentences and paragraphs in a text (e.g., comparison, cause/effect, first/second/third in a sequence).
 Spiral: RI.3.1 key details · RI.3.2 main idea · RI.3.4 word meaning · RI.3.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: The red and orange in a fall leaf were there all summer. You just could not see them.

paras.label: B
paras.text: All summer, a leaf is full of chlorophyll, the green chemical that turns sunlight into food. There is so much of it that it hides every other color in the leaf.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Then the days get shorter. The tree senses the change in daylight, not the cold, and begins shutting the leaves down. It stops making new chlorophyll, and the green already there breaks apart.

paras.label: D
paras.text: As the green fades, the yellows and oranges underneath finally show. Those pigments were in the leaf the whole time, doing quiet work alongside the chlorophyll.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Red is different. Red is made fresh in the fall, and only in some trees. A bright red maple needs warm sunny days and cool nights to produce it, which is why the same tree looks brilliant one year and dull the next.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Finally the tree seals off each leaf at the stem. The leaf falls, and the tree spends the winter on food it stored while those leaves were still green.

paras.text: The red and orange in a fall leaf were there all summer. You just could not see them.

paras.label: B

paras.label: C

paras.label: F

questions.q: What signals the tree to start shutting the leaves down?
questions.a: The tree senses that the days are getting shorter. It responds to the change in daylight, not to cold weather.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. shutdown) and paragraph E (i.e. red).
Summarize the steps that turn a green leaf into a fallen one.
questions.a: Chlorophyll fills the leaf all summer and hides the other colors. Shorter days make the tree stop producing it, and the green breaks apart. Yellow and orange, already present, become visible. Some trees make red fresh. Finally the tree seals the stem and the leaf falls.

questions.q:
chlorophyll: Chlorophyll is the green chemical in a leaf that turns sunlight into food for the tree.
pigments: Pigments are the substances that give something its color.
Describe the connection between the green fading and the yellow appearing.
questions.a: Because the chlorophyll was so strong that it covered every other color, the yellows and oranges only become visible once the green breaks apart, even though they were in the leaf all along.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "the tree senses daylight, not cold" or "red needs warm days and cool nights." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: The First Public Library
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Describe the logical connection between particular sentences and paragraphs in a text (e.g., comparison, cause/effect, first/second/third in a sequence).
 Spiral: RI.3.1 key details · RI.3.2 main idea · RI.3.4 word meaning · RI.3.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: Two hundred years ago, owning books meant being wealthy. A single book could cost a week of a worker’s pay.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first answer was the subscription library. Readers paid a yearly fee and shared a collection. This helped, but it only helped people who could afford the fee, which was the same people who could mostly afford books.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The idea that changed things was simple and strange at the time: a library paid for by taxes and free to everyone, whether they paid taxes or not.

paras.label: D
paras.text: People argued against it. Some said free books would make readers lazy. Others said taxpayers should not fund something they might never use. Supporters answered that a town full of readers is worth more than the tax, and that argument slowly won.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Boston opened the first large free public library in 1854. Anyone could walk in.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Between 1883 and 1929, Andrew Carnegie paid to build more than 1,600 library buildings in the United States, on one condition: the town had to promise to pay for the books and staff forever. He built the shell. The town had to mean it.

paras.label: B

questions.q: Why did the subscription library not solve the problem?

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. free) and paragraph F (i.e. Carnegie).
Summarize how free public libraries came to exist.
questions.a: Books were too expensive for most people. Subscription libraries helped only those who could pay the fee. The new idea was a library funded by taxes and free to all. Objections about laziness and cost lost out, Boston opened one in 1854, and Carnegie later funded 1,600 buildings.

questions.q:
subscription: A subscription is a fee paid regularly for the right to use something.
taxpayers: Taxpayers are the people who pay taxes that fund public services.
Describe the connection between Carnegie’s condition and the towns that got libraries.
questions.a: Because Carnegie paid only for the building and required the town to fund books and staff forever, a town had to commit its own money before it could receive one, which proved the library would last.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "a book cost a week of pay" or "Carnegie required a permanent promise." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: How Salmon Find Their River
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Describe the logical connection between particular sentences and paragraphs in a text (e.g., comparison, cause/effect, first/second/third in a sequence).
 Spiral: RI.3.1 key details · RI.3.2 main idea · RI.3.4 word meaning · RI.3.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: A salmon hatches in a small freshwater stream, swims to the ocean, lives there for years, and then returns to the exact stream where it was born. Some travel two thousand miles to do it.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The journey out happens in stages. First the young salmon drifts downstream. Then, in the estuary where fresh water meets salt, its body rebuilds itself to survive in the ocean, a change that takes weeks.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Once at sea, it grows. A salmon spends one to five years in the ocean before the return trip begins.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Finding the way back uses two different tools. Far out at sea, the salmon reads the Earth’s magnetic field, which tells it roughly where the coast is. That gets it close, but not to the right stream.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Close to shore, it switches to smell. Every stream carries its own chemical signature from the rocks and plants around it, and the salmon memorized that smell as a young fish. It follows the scent upstream, choosing at every fork.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Then it spawns and dies. Its body decays in the stream, feeding the insects that its own young will eat the following spring.

paras.text: A salmon hatches in a small stream, swims to the ocean, lives there for years, and then returns to the exact stream where it was born.

paras.label: B

paras.label: C

paras.label: D
paras.text: Finding the way back uses two tools. Far out at sea, the salmon reads the Earth’s magnetic field. That gets it close to the right coast.

paras.label: E

paras.label: F

questions.q: Why does a salmon need two different ways of navigating?
questions.a: The magnetic field gets it near the right coast but cannot identify one small stream. Smell identifies the exact stream but only works close to shore, so each tool covers what the other cannot.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. changing) and paragraph E (i.e. smell).
Summarize the journey a salmon makes.
questions.a: A salmon hatches in a stream, drifts downstream, and rebuilds its body in the estuary to survive salt water. It grows at sea for one to five years, then navigates back by magnetic field until it nears the coast, switches to smell to find its exact stream, spawns, and dies.

questions.q:
estuary: An estuary is the place where a river’s fresh water meets the ocean’s salt water.
signature: A signature here is a unique mark. Each stream has its own chemical smell.
Describe the connection between a salmon dying and its young having food.
questions.a: Because the adult’s body decays in the same stream where it spawned, it feeds the insects living there, and those insects become food for its young the following spring.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "some travel two thousand miles" or "its body feeds the insects." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: Two Ways to Build a House
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Describe the logical connection between particular sentences and paragraphs in a text (e.g., comparison, cause/effect, first/second/third in a sequence).
 Spiral: RI.3.1 key details · RI.3.2 main idea · RI.3.4 word meaning · RI.3.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: A house can be built on a site or built in a factory. Both end up looking like houses. Almost everything else is different.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A site-built house is assembled in place, in order. The foundation goes in, then the frame, then the roof, then everything inside. Each stage waits for the one before it, and all of it waits on weather.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A factory-built house is made in sections indoors. Walls are built flat on a table and stood up. Because the building is never rained on during construction, the wood never swells and dries.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Speed is the biggest difference. A factory house can be finished in weeks, because the foundation is poured at the site while the house itself is being built somewhere else. Two things happen at once instead of in line.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Site building wins on changes. If you decide halfway through that a room should be larger, a site crew can adjust. A factory section is already built.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Cost usually favors the factory, but not always. The sections have to be trucked to the site and lifted by crane, and a house going up a narrow mountain road can cost more to deliver than it saved.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A site-built house is put together in place, in order. Foundation, then frame, then roof, then the inside. Each stage waits for the one before it, and all of it waits on weather.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A factory-built house is made in sections indoors. Walls are built flat and stood up. The wood is never rained on.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Speed is the biggest difference. A factory house can be done in weeks, because the foundation is poured while the house is built somewhere else.

paras.label: E

paras.label: F
paras.text: Cost usually favors the factory, but not always. The sections must be trucked and lifted by crane.

questions.q: Why can a factory-built house be finished so much faster?
questions.a: The foundation is poured at the site while the house itself is being built in the factory, so two stages happen at the same time instead of one waiting for the other.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. indoors) and paragraph E (i.e. changes).
Summarize how the two building methods compare.
questions.a: A site-built house is assembled in order and waits on weather, but the crew can change the plan partway through. A factory house is built indoors in sections while the foundation is poured, so it finishes in weeks and the wood never gets wet, but the design is fixed and delivery can be costly.

questions.q:
foundation: A foundation is the solid base a house is built on.
sections: Sections are the finished pieces of a house, built separately and joined together.
Describe the connection between building in order and delays.
questions.a: Because each stage on a site cannot start until the one before it is done, a rainy week that stops the framing also pushes back the roof and everything inside.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "walls are built flat on a table" or "sections are lifted by crane." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: What Happened to the Passenger Pigeon
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Describe the logical connection between particular sentences and paragraphs in a text (e.g., comparison, cause/effect, first/second/third in a sequence).
 Spiral: RI.3.1 key details · RI.3.2 main idea · RI.3.4 word meaning · RI.3.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1860 the passenger pigeon was probably the most numerous bird on Earth. A single flock could take three days to pass overhead and darken the sky while it did.

paras.label: B
paras.text: By 1914 there were none. The last one died in a zoo in Cincinnati.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Two things happened at the same time, and either alone might not have been enough. First, the forests were cut. Passenger pigeons ate beech and oak nuts, and those forests were cleared for farms across the eastern United States.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Second, they were hunted on a scale that is hard to picture. New railroads could carry barrels of pigeons to city markets, and the telegraph let hunters send word of where the flocks had landed. Nesting colonies were emptied in a few days.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Their own biology worked against them. Passenger pigeons nested in enormous colonies, which protected them by sheer numbers: a hawk could only eat so many. Below a certain size, that protection stopped working, and a small flock was worse off than a small flock of any ordinary bird.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That is why the collapse was so fast at the end. The species did not fade gradually. It fell off a cliff.

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1860 the passenger pigeon was probably the most common bird on Earth. One flock could take three days to pass overhead.

paras.label: B
paras.text: By 1914 there were none. The last one died in a zoo in Cincinnati.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Two things happened at the same time. First, the forests were cut. Passenger pigeons ate beech and oak nuts, and those forests were cleared for farms.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Second, they were hunted on a huge scale. Railroads carried barrels of pigeons to city markets, and the telegraph told hunters where flocks had landed.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Their own biology worked against them. They nested in huge colonies, which protected them by numbers. Below a certain size, that protection stopped working.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That is why the end came so fast. The species did not fade slowly. It fell off a cliff.

questions.q: How did the railroad and telegraph contribute to the extinction?
questions.a: The telegraph let hunters send word of where flocks had landed, and railroads carried barrels of pigeons to city markets, so nesting colonies could be emptied in a few days.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. hunting) and paragraph E (i.e. colonies).
Summarize why the passenger pigeon disappeared.
questions.a: The beech and oak forests they fed on were cleared for farms. At the same time, railroads and the telegraph made hunting possible on an enormous scale. Their defense was nesting in huge colonies, so once the numbers fell below a certain point that protection failed and the collapse was sudden.

questions.q:
colonies: Colonies are large groups of the same animal living and nesting together.
collapse: A collapse is a sudden fall or failure, rather than a slow decline.
Describe the connection between nesting in huge colonies and the sudden collapse.
questions.a: Because their only defense was numbers so large that predators could not eat them all, shrinking below that size removed the protection entirely, so the last flocks died far faster than the decline had begun.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "a flock took three days to pass" or "the last bird died in Cincinnati." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: Two Texts: Honeybees and Wild Bees
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Compare and contrast the most important points and key details presented in two texts on the same topic.
 Spiral: RI.3.1 key details · RI.3.2 main idea · RI.3.4 word meaning · RI.3.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: TEXT 1 · Honeybees live in hives with one queen and thousands of workers. Beekeepers move the hives from farm to farm in trucks.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A single hive can hold 50,000 bees. The workers share food, share heat in winter, and follow one another to flowers they have already found.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Farmers rent honeybee hives because a whole colony arrives at once and gets to work on one crop.

paras.label: D
paras.text: TEXT 2 · Most bees are not honeybees. North America has about 4,000 wild bee species, and almost all of them live alone.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A female mason bee digs her own tunnel, lays her eggs, and dies before they hatch. She has no hive, no queen, and no helpers.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Wild bees are often better pollinators. A mason bee carries loose, dry pollen that falls off easily, so more of it lands on the next flower.

paras.label: A
paras.text: TEXT 1 · Honeybees live in hives with one queen and thousands of workers. Beekeepers move the hives from farm to farm.

paras.label: B
paras.text: One hive can hold 50,000 bees. The workers share food and share heat in winter.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Farmers rent honeybee hives because a whole colony comes at once and works on one crop.

paras.label: D
paras.text: TEXT 2 · Most bees are not honeybees. North America has about 4,000 wild bee kinds, and almost all live alone.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A female mason bee digs her own tunnel and lays her eggs. She has no hive and no helpers.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Wild bees are often better pollinators. A mason bee carries loose, dry pollen that falls off easily onto the next flower.

questions.q: Use both texts to explain how a mason bee is different from a honeybee.
questions.a: A honeybee lives in a hive of up to 50,000 with a queen and workers who share food and heat. A mason bee digs her own tunnel, lays eggs, and has no hive, no queen, and no helpers.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. sharing) and paragraph E (i.e. alone).
What is the most important point in each text?
questions.a: Text 1 says honeybees work together in huge colonies, which is why farmers can rent a whole hive. Text 2 says most bees are wild and live alone, and that those solitary bees often move pollen better.

questions.q:
colony: A colony is a large group of animals that live and work together.
pollinators: Pollinators are animals that carry pollen between flowers so plants can make seeds.
Describe the connection between dry pollen and better pollinating.
questions.a: Because loose, dry pollen falls off a mason bee easily, more of it lands on the next flower she visits instead of staying packed on her body.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "workers share heat in winter" or "mason bee pollen is loose and dry." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: Two Texts: The First Flight
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Compare and contrast the most important points and key details presented in two texts on the same topic.
 Spiral: RI.3.1 key details · RI.3.2 main idea · RI.3.4 word meaning · RI.3.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: TEXT 1 · From a museum sign. On December 17, 1903, Orville Wright flew 120 feet in twelve seconds at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina. It was the first powered flight by a machine carrying a person.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Five people watched. One of them took the photograph that is now in every textbook.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The brothers flew three more times that morning. The last flight covered 852 feet and lasted 59 seconds.

paras.label: D
paras.text: TEXT 2 · From a book about inventing. The Wrights were bicycle makers, not scientists. That turned out to matter.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Other inventors tried to build planes that would stay steady on their own. The Wrights knew a bicycle is not steady on its own. The rider balances it.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So they built a plane the pilot had to balance, using wires that twisted the wingtips. That choice is why their machine turned and the others did not.

paras.label: A
paras.text: TEXT 1 · From a museum sign. On December 17, 1903, Orville Wright flew 120 feet in twelve seconds at Kitty Hawk. It was the first powered flight with a person aboard.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Five people watched. One of them took the photo that is now in every textbook.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The brothers flew three more times that morning. The last flight went 852 feet and lasted 59 seconds.

paras.label: D
paras.text: TEXT 2 · From a book about inventing. The Wrights were bicycle makers, not scientists. That mattered.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Other inventors tried to build planes that stayed steady by themselves. The Wrights knew a bicycle is not steady by itself. The rider balances it.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So they built a plane the pilot had to balance, using wires that twisted the wingtips. That is why their machine could turn.

questions.q: Use both texts to explain why the Wright plane could turn.
questions.a: The brothers built the plane to be balanced by the pilot, the way a rider balances a bicycle. Wires twisted the wingtips, which let the pilot steer, while other inventors were trying to make planes that stayed steady on their own.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. improving) and paragraph E (i.e. balancing).
What is the most important point in each text?
questions.a: Text 1 records the first flight: 120 feet in twelve seconds, watched by five people, with a last flight of 852 feet. Text 2 explains that the brothers succeeded because being bicycle makers led them to build a plane the pilot balances.

questions.q:
powered: A powered flight uses an engine instead of only gliding on the wind.
steady: Steady means staying level without tipping.
Describe the connection between riding a bicycle and designing a plane.
questions.a: Because the brothers knew a bicycle only stays up when the rider keeps balancing it, they designed a plane meant to be balanced by its pilot rather than one that had to hold itself level.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "five people watched" or "other inventors wanted steady planes." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: Two Texts: What Happened to the Dinosaurs
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Compare and contrast the most important points and key details presented in two texts on the same topic.
 Spiral: RI.3.1 key details · RI.3.2 main idea · RI.3.4 word meaning · RI.3.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: TEXT 1 · About 66 million years ago, an asteroid about six miles wide struck the sea near what is now Mexico. The crater is still there, buried under rock.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The impact threw dust and rock into the sky. The dust blocked sunlight for months. Plants died, then the animals that ate plants, then the animals that ate those animals.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Around three quarters of all species on Earth disappeared, including every dinosaur except the group that became birds.

paras.label: D
paras.text: TEXT 2 · The asteroid is not the whole story. For about 300,000 years before the impact, enormous volcanoes in India were erupting almost without stopping.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Those eruptions poured gas into the air and changed the climate. Some scientists find that dinosaur numbers were already dropping before the asteroid arrived.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Most scientists now say both mattered. The volcanoes weakened life on Earth, and the asteroid finished it in a single afternoon.

paras.label: A
paras.text: TEXT 1 · About 66 million years ago, an asteroid about six miles wide hit the sea near what is now Mexico. The crater is still there under the rock.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The crash threw dust into the sky. The dust blocked sunlight for months. Plants died, then the animals that ate plants.

paras.label: C
paras.text: About three quarters of all species disappeared, including every dinosaur except the group that became birds.

paras.label: D

paras.label: E
paras.text: Those eruptions poured gas into the air and changed the climate. Some scientists find dinosaur numbers were already falling.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Most scientists now say both mattered. The volcanoes weakened life, and the asteroid finished it in one afternoon.

questions.q: Use both texts to explain what killed the dinosaurs.
questions.a: Volcanoes in India erupted for about 300,000 years and changed the climate, so dinosaur numbers were already dropping. Then an asteroid six miles wide struck near Mexico and threw up dust that blocked the sun for months, ending it.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. darkness) and paragraph F (i.e. agreement).
What is the most important point in each text?
questions.a: Text 1 says an asteroid strike near Mexico blocked the sun and wiped out about three quarters of all species. Text 2 says volcanoes erupting for 300,000 years had already weakened life, so both causes together explain the extinction.

questions.q:
crater: A crater is the bowl-shaped hole left where something struck the ground hard.
erupting: Erupting is when a volcano bursts open and sends out lava, ash, and gas.
Describe the connection between blocked sunlight and animals starving.
questions.a: Because plants need sunlight to grow, months of dust in the sky killed them, and once the plants were gone the animals that ate them starved, followed by the animals that ate those animals.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "the crater is still there" or "birds are the dinosaurs that survived." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: Two Texts: Living on a Submarine
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Compare and contrast the most important points and key details presented in two texts on the same topic.
 Spiral: RI.3.1 key details · RI.3.2 main idea · RI.3.4 word meaning · RI.3.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: TEXT 1 · From a navy fact sheet. A submarine crew of 130 lives inside a steel tube for up to three months without surfacing.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Machines make oxygen from seawater and scrub carbon dioxide from the air. Fresh water is made from seawater too. Food is the only thing that runs out, and it sets the length of the trip.

paras.label: C
paras.text: There are fewer beds than sailors. Three sailors share two beds, taking turns by shift.

paras.label: D
paras.text: TEXT 2 · From a sailor’s interview. "The thing nobody tells you is that you stop knowing what time it is. There are no windows. The lights change color to tell you it is night."

paras.label: E
paras.text: "You run on an eighteen-hour day, six on and twelve off. Your body never quite agrees to it. After a month you stop arguing."

paras.label: F
paras.text: "The food matters more than you would think. When the fresh fruit runs out, around week three, everybody notices. That is the calendar."

paras.label: A
paras.text: TEXT 1 · From a navy fact sheet. A submarine crew of 130 lives inside a steel tube for up to three months without coming up.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Machines make oxygen from seawater and clean carbon dioxide out of the air. Food is the only thing that runs out, and it sets how long the trip can be.

paras.label: C
paras.text: There are fewer beds than sailors. Three sailors share two beds, taking turns by shift.

paras.label: D
paras.text: TEXT 2 · From a sailor’s interview. "Nobody tells you that you stop knowing what time it is. There are no windows. The lights change color to tell you it is night."

paras.label: E
paras.text: "You run on an eighteen-hour day, six hours on and twelve off. Your body never quite agrees."

paras.label: F
paras.text: "The food matters more than you would think. When the fresh fruit runs out, around week three, everybody notices."

questions.q: Use both texts to explain why a patrol cannot last forever.
questions.a: Machines make the oxygen and fresh water from seawater, so those do not run out. Food is the one thing that cannot be made aboard, and the sailor notices it first when the fresh fruit is gone around week three.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. supplying) and paragraph E (i.e. adjusting).
What is the most important point in each text?
questions.a: Text 1 explains that machines supply the crew’s air and water, so only food limits the patrol. Text 2 explains what that life feels like: no windows, colored lights for night, an eighteen-hour day, and fruit gone by week three.

questions.q:
scrub: To scrub the air means to clean a gas out of it.
patrol: A patrol is one trip a submarine takes before returning to port.
Describe the connection between having no windows and losing track of time.
questions.a: Because there is no daylight to mark morning or evening, the crew has nothing to tell the hour by, so the ship changes the color of its lights to stand in for night.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "three sailors share two beds" or "the lights change color at night." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: Two Texts: The Great Wall
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Compare and contrast the most important points and key details presented in two texts on the same topic.
 Spiral: RI.3.1 key details · RI.3.2 main idea · RI.3.4 word meaning · RI.3.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: TEXT 1 · The Great Wall of China is not one wall. It is many walls, built by different rulers over 2,000 years, and later joined together.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The parts most visitors see were built in the 1400s and 1500s of brick and cut stone. Older sections, far to the west, were made of packed earth and have mostly worn away.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Together the walls run more than 13,000 miles, though no one ever walked the whole thing at once.

paras.label: D
paras.text: TEXT 2 · The Wall was built to stop riders from the north. It rarely did. Armies went around it, or paid a guard to open a gate.

paras.label: E
paras.text: What it did well was slow people down. A raider on horseback could cross the border in an hour. Getting a herd of stolen animals back over a wall took much longer, and that was long enough for soldiers to arrive.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The Wall also carried signal fires along its towers. A warning could travel hundreds of miles in a day, faster than any rider.

paras.label: A
paras.text: TEXT 1 · The Great Wall of China is not one wall. It is many walls, built by different rulers over 2,000 years and later joined.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The parts most visitors see were built in the 1400s and 1500s from brick and stone. Older parts in the west were packed earth and have worn away.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Together the walls run more than 13,000 miles.

paras.label: D
paras.text: TEXT 2 · The Wall was built to stop riders from the north. It rarely did. Armies went around it or paid a guard to open a gate.

paras.label: E
paras.text: What it did well was slow people down. A raider could cross the border in an hour, but getting stolen animals back over a wall took much longer. That was long enough for soldiers to come.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The Wall also carried signal fires on its towers. A warning could travel hundreds of miles in a day.

questions.q: Use both texts to explain how the Wall helped even when raiders got past it.
questions.a: A raider could cross the border in an hour, but driving stolen animals back over a wall took much longer, which gave soldiers time to arrive. Signal fires on the towers also spread a warning hundreds of miles in a day.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. materials) and paragraph E (i.e. delaying).
What is the most important point in each text?
questions.a: Text 1 says the Great Wall is many walls built over 2,000 years from different materials, running more than 13,000 miles in total. Text 2 says it rarely stopped anyone outright but worked by slowing raiders down and carrying warnings by signal fire.

questions.q:
raider: A raider is someone who makes a quick attack to steal and then leave.
signal: A signal is a sign sent to pass a message, like a fire lit on a tower.
Describe the connection between slowing raiders down and soldiers catching them.
questions.a: Because stolen animals could not be hurried over a wall, the raiders lost hours getting back, and those hours were enough for soldiers who had seen the signal fires to reach them.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "older sections were packed earth" or "guards were sometimes paid to open a gate." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: The Library That Rides a Donkey
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of the year, read and comprehend informational texts, including history/social studies, science, and technical texts, at the high end of the grades 2–3 text complexity band independently and proficiently.
 Spiral: RI.3.1 key details · RI.3.2 main idea · RI.3.3 connections · RI.3.4 word meaning · RI.3.7 images
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: In the mountains of Colombia, some villages have no road wide enough for a truck. Children there had no library until a teacher named Luis Soriano loaded books onto two donkeys.

paras.label: B
paras.text: He named the donkeys Alfa and Beto, which together make the Spanish word for alphabet. Each weekend he walked them into the hills with about 120 books strapped to their backs.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A child could keep a book for a week. Soriano wrote the loans in a notebook. Almost every book came back.

paras.label: D
paras.text: He kept going for more than twenty years, through heat, rain, and one robbery. A broken leg from a fall did not stop him either.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Other places copied the idea. There are book boats in Bangladesh, camel libraries in Kenya, and a book bicycle in the Philippines.

paras.label: F
paras.text: All of them solve the same problem in the same way. If people cannot reach the library, the library travels.

loans: A loan is something lent for a while and then returned.
alphabet: An alphabet is the set of letters used to write a language.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "almost every book came back" or "he kept going for twenty years." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: How Ice Cream Freezes
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of the year, read and comprehend informational texts, including history/social studies, science, and technical texts, at the high end of the grades 2–3 text complexity band independently and proficiently.
 Spiral: RI.3.1 key details · RI.3.2 main idea · RI.3.3 connections · RI.3.4 word meaning · RI.3.7 images
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: Ice cream is mostly cream, sugar, and air. Getting all three to hold together is harder than it sounds.

paras.label: B
paras.text: If you froze cream in a cup, you would get a solid block. The water in it would form large ice crystals, and large crystals feel gritty on the tongue.

paras.label: C
paras.text: So ice cream is stirred the whole time it freezes. Stirring breaks the crystals before they can grow. Smaller crystals mean a smoother scoop.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Stirring also folds in air. A good ice cream is about a quarter air by volume. Without it, the frozen mix would be too hard to scoop.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Sugar does something else. Sugar water freezes at a lower temperature than plain water, so some of the mix stays soft even in a freezer.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That is why ice cream can be scooped at a temperature where a block of ice would be solid stone.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Ice cream is mostly cream, sugar, and air. Getting all three to hold together is harder than it sounds.

paras.label: B
paras.text: If you froze cream in a cup, you would get a solid block. The water in it would form big ice crystals, and big crystals feel gritty.

paras.label: C
paras.text: So ice cream is stirred the whole time it freezes. Stirring breaks the crystals before they grow. Smaller crystals mean a smoother scoop.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Stirring also folds in air. A good ice cream is about a quarter air. Without it, the mix would be too hard to scoop.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Sugar water freezes at a lower temperature than plain water, so some of the mix stays soft in the freezer.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That is why ice cream can be scooped when a block of ice would be solid.

questions.q: Use the diagram to explain why ice cream is stirred while it freezes.
questions.a: Stirring does two jobs. It breaks ice crystals before they grow large, which keeps the texture smooth instead of gritty, and it folds in the air that makes about a quarter of the volume and keeps the ice cream soft enough to scoop.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. stirring) and paragraph E (i.e. sweetening).
What is the main idea of this text?
questions.a: Ice cream is smooth and scoopable because of three things working together: constant stirring to keep ice crystals small, air folded into the mix, and sugar that lowers the freezing temperature.

questions.q:
crystals: Crystals are solid pieces that form in a regular shape as a liquid freezes.
volume: Volume is how much space something takes up.
Describe the connection between sugar and ice cream staying soft.
questions.a: Because sugar lowers the temperature at which the mix freezes, part of the ice cream stays unfrozen at freezer temperature, which keeps it soft enough to scoop.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "large crystals feel gritty" or "sugar water freezes at a lower temperature." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: The Town That Moved
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of the year, read and comprehend informational texts, including history/social studies, science, and technical texts, at the high end of the grades 2–3 text complexity band independently and proficiently.
 Spiral: RI.3.1 key details · RI.3.2 main idea · RI.3.3 connections · RI.3.4 word meaning · RI.3.7 images
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: Kiruna is a mining town in northern Sweden. Below it is the largest underground iron mine in the world.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The mining has gone on for more than a hundred years. Over that time, the tunnels reached under the town itself, and the ground above began to crack and sink.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Sweden had two choices: stop the mine, which employs most of the town, or move the town. It chose to move the town.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The move began in 2014 and will take decades. The new center sits two miles east. Some buildings were pulled down and rebuilt. Others were lifted whole onto trailers and driven.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The wooden church, built in 1912 and voted the most beautiful building in Sweden, was cut into pieces and carried in a slow parade to its new place.

paras.label: F
paras.text: About 6,000 people will have moved house by the time the work is done.

questions.q: Why did Sweden move the town instead of closing the mine?

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. sinking) and paragraph D (i.e. moving).
What is the main idea of this text?
questions.a: Mining under Kiruna made the ground unsafe, so rather than close the mine that provides the town’s jobs, Sweden is moving the whole town two miles east, a project that will take decades and relocate about 6,000 people.

questions.q:
tunnels: Tunnels are passages dug underground.
relocate: To relocate is to move something to a new place.
Describe the connection between digging tunnels and the ground cracking.
questions.a: Because the miners removed rock from beneath the town, the ground above lost its support and began to sink and crack, which made the buildings unsafe to leave where they were.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "the church was built in 1912" or "the new center sits two miles east." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: The Bird That Sews
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of the year, read and comprehend informational texts, including history/social studies, science, and technical texts, at the high end of the grades 2–3 text complexity band independently and proficiently.
 Spiral: RI.3.1 key details · RI.3.2 main idea · RI.3.3 connections · RI.3.4 word meaning · RI.3.7 images
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: Most birds build nests by piling things up. The tailorbird does something else. It sews.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The bird finds a large green leaf still growing on a branch. Using its beak, it punches a row of small holes along both edges.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Then it pulls plant fiber or spider silk through the holes, one hole at a time, and knots the ends so the thread will not slip back out.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The leaf folds into a pocket. The bird lines the inside with soft grass and lays its eggs there.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Because the leaf is still alive and still attached, it stays green. From a few feet away the nest looks like an ordinary leaf, which is exactly the point.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A tailorbird weighs less than a slice of bread. It cannot fight off a snake. Hiding is the whole defense.

paras.text: Most birds build nests by piling things up. The tailorbird does something else. It sews.

paras.text: The bird finds a large green leaf still growing on a branch. With its beak it punches small holes along both edges.

paras.label: F

questions.q: Use the diagram to explain why the bird leaves the leaf attached to the branch.
questions.a: A leaf still attached keeps growing and stays green, so the nest blends in with the rest of the plant. A picked leaf would brown and give the nest away.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. sewing) and paragraph F (i.e. hiding).
What is the main idea of this text?
questions.a: The tailorbird protects its eggs by sewing a living leaf into a hidden pocket, because it is far too small to defend a nest any other way.

questions.q:
fiber: A fiber is a thin thread from a plant or animal.
defense: A defense is anything that protects you from harm.
Describe the connection between the leaf staying alive and the eggs staying safe.
questions.a: Because the leaf is still attached and still green, the nest looks like every other leaf on the plant, so a snake or larger bird passes it without noticing the eggs inside.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "it knots the ends of the thread" or "it lines the pocket with grass." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: The Clock That Runs on Water
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of the year, read and comprehend informational texts, including history/social studies, science, and technical texts, at the high end of the grades 2–3 text complexity band independently and proficiently.
 Spiral: RI.3.1 key details · RI.3.2 main idea · RI.3.3 connections · RI.3.4 word meaning · RI.3.7 images
 Lower range: LL 500 – 580

paras.label: A
paras.text: Long before gears and springs, people told time with water. A water clock is a jar that leaks on purpose.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The simplest kind is a bowl with a small hole in the bottom, floating in a larger basin. Water seeps in, the bowl sinks, and the time it takes to sink is always the same.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Egyptian water clocks worked the other way. A jar with markings inside slowly drained, and the falling water level showed the hour.

paras.label: D
paras.text: There is a problem. Water drains faster when the jar is full, because the weight above pushes harder. So the early hours ran short and the late hours ran long.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Clockmakers solved it by shaping the jar. If the jar is wider at the top, the level falls slowly at first, and the hours come out even.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That shape was worked out more than three thousand years ago by people who had no way to measure pressure. They found it by trying.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The simplest kind is a bowl with a small hole, floating in a larger basin. Water seeps in, the bowl sinks, and the sinking always takes the same time.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Egyptian water clocks worked the other way. A jar with marks inside slowly drained, and the water level showed the hour.

paras.label: D

paras.label: E

paras.label: F
paras.text: People worked that shape out more than three thousand years ago by trying it.

questions.q: Use the diagram to explain why a straight-sided water clock keeps poor time.
questions.a: When the jar is full, the weight of water above pushes the flow out faster, so the level drops quickly and the first hours are short. As the jar empties the push weakens, the flow slows, and the last hours are too long.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. the problem) and paragraph E (i.e. the fix).
What is the main idea of this text?
questions.a: Water clocks told time by letting water drain, but the flow changed as the jar emptied, so early clockmakers shaped the jar wider at the top to make every hour the same length.

questions.q:
seeps: To seep is to pass slowly through a small opening.
drained: Drained means emptied out slowly through a hole.
Describe the connection between the shape of the jar and even hours.
questions.a: Because a wide top holds more water in each layer, it takes longer for the level to fall one mark while the flow is fast, which balances out the slower flow later and makes the hours match.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "the bowl sinks at the same rate every time" or "Egyptian jars had markings inside." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: The Ship in the Desert
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Refer to details and examples in a text when explaining what the text says explicitly and when drawing inferences from the text.
 Spiral: RI.4.2 main idea · RI.4.3 explaining events · RI.4.4 word meaning · RI.4.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: In the town of Moynaq, Uzbekistan, rusting fishing boats sit in sand. There is no water for sixty miles. Fifty years ago, Moynaq was a busy port on the Aral Sea, the fourth largest lake in the world.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The Aral Sea was fed by two rivers. In the 1960s, planners decided to redirect those rivers into canals to irrigate cotton fields in the desert. The cotton grew. The sea began to shrink.

paras.label: C
paras.text: At first the change was slow enough to ignore. Then it accelerated. By 2000 the sea had split in two. By 2014 the eastern half had dried completely for the first time in six hundred years. The lake had lost about ninety percent of its water.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The damage went far beyond the shoreline. The exposed seabed was full of salt and pesticide residue from the cotton fields. Wind lifted that dust and dropped it on towns hundreds of miles away. Rates of lung disease and certain cancers climbed. Twenty-four species of fish that lived nowhere else disappeared, and sixty thousand fishing jobs went with them.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The weather changed too. A large lake moderates temperature. Without it, summers in the region grew hotter and winters grew colder.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Not all of it is lost. In 2005 Kazakhstan finished a dam across the northern section. Water levels there rose, the salt level dropped, and fish returned. Boats are working the northern Aral again. The southern half is still desert.

questions.q: Why did the Aral Sea begin to shrink?
questions.a: The sea shrank because planners redirected the two rivers that fed it into canals to irrigate cotton fields, so the water that had always refilled the lake never arrived.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. fallout) and paragraph F (i.e. recovery).
Summarize what happened to the Aral Sea and why.
questions.a: Two rivers that fed the Aral Sea were diverted in the 1960s to water cotton. The lake lost about ninety percent of its water and split in two. Salt and pesticide dust from the dry seabed sickened people, fish species died out, and sixty thousand jobs vanished. A dam finished in 2005 brought part of the northern sea back.

questions.q:
irrigate: Irrigate means to bring water to crops through canals or pipes.
accelerated: Accelerated means sped up. The shrinking happened faster and faster over time.
Describe the connection between the exposed seabed and illness in nearby towns.
questions.a: Because the dry seabed was full of salt and pesticide residue, wind lifted that dust and carried it hundreds of miles, and breathing it raised rates of lung disease and some cancers.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "the eastern half dried completely in 2014" or "wind carried salt dust hundreds of miles." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: The Woman Who Mapped the Ocean Floor
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Refer to details and examples in a text when explaining what the text says explicitly and when drawing inferences from the text.
 Spiral: RI.4.2 main idea · RI.4.3 explaining events · RI.4.4 word meaning · RI.4.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1952, almost nobody knew what the bottom of the Atlantic Ocean looked like. Ships had taken depth readings along their routes for decades, but the readings sat in notebooks as columns of numbers.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Marie Tharp was a geologist at Columbia University. She was not allowed on the research ships; at the time, women were considered bad luck at sea. So she stayed on shore and turned the numbers into pictures. Line by line, she drew the profile of the sea floor.

paras.label: C
paras.text: What appeared was not a flat plain. It was a mountain range running down the middle of the Atlantic, longer than the Andes, Rockies, and Himalayas combined. And down the center of that range ran a deep valley.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The valley was the problem. A crack that long suggested the sea floor was splitting apart, which supported the idea that continents move. Most geologists rejected that idea outright. Tharp’s colleague Bruce Heezen called her finding "girl talk" and told her to do it over.

paras.label: E
paras.text: She did it over. The valley was still there. Then an assistant plotted the locations of Atlantic earthquakes on the same map, and the earthquakes fell in a line directly inside Tharp’s valley. Heezen changed his mind.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Their maps, published over the next twenty years, helped convince a generation of scientists that the plates of the Earth move. Tharp’s name did not appear on the first paper announcing the discovery.

questions.q: Why did Marie Tharp work from shore instead of aboard the research ships?
questions.a: Tharp worked from shore because women were not allowed on the research ships at the time; they were considered bad luck at sea.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. doubt) and paragraph E (i.e. proof).
Summarize how Marie Tharp changed what scientists believed.
questions.a: Tharp turned columns of depth readings into drawings of the Atlantic sea floor and found a mountain range with a deep valley down its center. The valley suggested the sea floor was splitting apart. When Atlantic earthquakes turned out to fall inside her valley, her doubting colleague accepted it, and their maps helped convince scientists that Earth’s plates move.

questions.q:
geologist: A geologist is a scientist who studies the Earth, its rocks, and how it changes over time.
profile: A profile here is a side-view drawing showing the shape of the sea floor as it rises and falls.
Describe the connection between the earthquake locations and Heezen changing his mind.
questions.a: Because the Atlantic earthquakes fell in a line directly inside the valley Tharp had drawn, the valley could no longer be dismissed as her error, so Heezen accepted the finding.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "the range is longer than three mountain ranges combined" or "her name was left off the first paper." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: Why Venice Is Sinking
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Refer to details and examples in a text when explaining what the text says explicitly and when drawing inferences from the text.
 Spiral: RI.4.2 main idea · RI.4.3 explaining events · RI.4.4 word meaning · RI.4.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: Venice, Italy is built on 118 small islands in a lagoon. Its buildings do not rest on rock. They rest on millions of wooden posts driven down into mud, a technique that has held for more than a thousand years.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The city is sinking and the water is rising, and those two problems have completely different causes.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The sinking has two sources. Some of it is natural: the soft ground compacts slowly under the weight of the city. The rest was self-inflicted. In the middle of the twentieth century, factories on the mainland pumped groundwater out from under the lagoon, and the ground above the emptied space settled. Venice dropped about twelve centimeters before the pumping was banned in the 1970s.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The rising is global. Warmer oceans expand, and melting ice adds volume. Sea level in the northern Adriatic has climbed roughly thirty centimeters over the last century.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Combined, the two effects flood St. Mark’s Square more than sixty times a year. A century ago it flooded fewer than ten.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Venice’s answer is a set of 78 steel gates that lie flat on the sea floor at the three entrances to the lagoon. When a high tide is forecast, compressed air pushes the water out of the gates and they swing up into a wall. The system first protected the city in 2020. It cost more than five billion euros and took eighteen years to finish.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Venice, Italy is built on 118 small islands. Its buildings do not sit on rock. They sit on millions of wooden posts driven into the mud.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The city is sinking and the water is rising. The two problems have different causes.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Some of the sinking is natural. The soft ground slowly squeezes down under the weight of the city. The rest was caused by people. Factories nearby pumped water out from under the lagoon, and the ground settled. Venice dropped about twelve centimeters before the pumping was banned.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The rising is global. Warm ocean water takes up more space, and melting ice adds more water. The sea near Venice has risen about thirty centimeters in a hundred years.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Together, the two problems flood St. Mark’s Square more than sixty times a year. A century ago it flooded fewer than ten.
