questions.q: What caused the part of Venice’s sinking that was not natural?
questions.a: Factories on the mainland pumped groundwater out from under the lagoon, and the ground settled into the emptied space, dropping the city about twelve centimeters.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. sinking) and paragraph F (i.e. gates).
Summarize the two problems Venice faces and how the city is responding.
questions.a: Venice is sinking, partly because soft ground compacts and partly because factories pumped out groundwater. At the same time the sea is rising because warm water expands and ice melts. Together they flood St. Mark’s Square more than sixty times a year. Venice built 78 steel gates that rise from the sea floor to block high tides.

questions.q:
lagoon: A lagoon is a shallow body of water separated from the open sea by islands or sandbars.
compacts: Compacts means presses together into less space. The soft ground squeezes down under the weight of the city.
Describe the connection between pumping groundwater and the height of the city.
questions.a: Because factories pumped water out from under the lagoon, the space that water had filled collapsed, the ground above settled, and the whole city dropped about twelve centimeters.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "the buildings rest on wooden posts" or "the gates took eighteen years to build." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: The Night the Radio Lied
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Refer to details and examples in a text when explaining what the text says explicitly and when drawing inferences from the text.
 Spiral: RI.4.2 main idea · RI.4.3 explaining events · RI.4.4 word meaning · RI.4.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: On October 30, 1938, the Mercury Theatre broadcast a radio play based on H.G. Wells’s novel The War of the Worlds. The script was written as a series of news bulletins interrupting a program of dance music.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The format mattered. Listeners heard what sounded like a real reporter describing a cylinder opening in a New Jersey field, then a heat ray, then the broadcast itself collapsing into static. An announcer stated at the opening that the program was fiction, but many people tuned in late.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Newspapers the next morning described mass panic: crowds in the streets, jammed switchboards, families fleeing cities. The story became famous, and it is still repeated in classrooms today.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Later researchers questioned it. Ratings data showed that relatively few people were listening, because a popular comedy program held most of the audience in that hour. Surveys taken afterward found that most listeners who did hear the show understood it was a play.

paras.label: E
paras.text: So why did the panic story spread? Newspapers at the time were losing advertising money to radio. A story about radio being reckless and dangerous served their interests. Historians now believe the papers inflated a small number of frightened phone calls into a national event.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The broadcast is still a useful lesson, though perhaps not the one usually taught. The audience was not as gullible as the story claims. The people who repeated the story were.

paras.label: A
paras.text: On October 30, 1938, a radio show told a story about aliens invading Earth. The script was written to sound like news bulletins breaking into a music program.

paras.label: B
paras.text: That choice mattered. Listeners heard what sounded like a real reporter describing a cylinder opening in a New Jersey field. An announcer said at the start that it was fiction, but many people tuned in late.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The next morning, newspapers said people had panicked. They wrote about crowds in the streets and jammed phone lines. That story is still repeated today.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Later researchers doubted it. Ratings showed few people were listening. Surveys found that most who did hear it knew it was a play.

paras.label: E
paras.text: So why did the panic story spread? Newspapers were losing money to radio. A story about radio being dangerous helped them. Historians think the papers turned a few scared phone calls into a national panic.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The broadcast still teaches a lesson, but maybe not the usual one. The listeners were not as easily fooled as the story says. The people repeating the story were.

questions.q: What evidence made later researchers doubt the panic story?
questions.a: Ratings data showed relatively few people were listening because a popular comedy held most of the audience, and surveys afterward found most listeners who did hear the show knew it was a play.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. format) and paragraph E (i.e. motive).
Summarize why the story of the 1938 panic may not be accurate.
questions.a: The broadcast was written as fake news bulletins, and newspapers reported the next day that listeners had panicked. But ratings showed few people were listening and surveys showed most knew it was fiction. Newspapers were losing money to radio and had a reason to exaggerate, so historians think the panic was largely invented.

questions.q:
bulletins: Bulletins are short news reports that interrupt regular programming to announce something urgent.
gullible: Gullible means easily fooled, or quick to believe something without checking it.
Describe the connection between newspaper advertising money and the panic story.
questions.a: Because newspapers were losing advertising money to radio, a story showing radio as reckless served their interests, so they had a reason to inflate a few frightened calls into a national panic.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "an announcer said at the start it was fiction" or "a popular comedy held most of the audience." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: Reading the Rings
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Refer to details and examples in a text when explaining what the text says explicitly and when drawing inferences from the text.
 Spiral: RI.4.2 main idea · RI.4.3 explaining events · RI.4.4 word meaning · RI.4.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: Cut across a tree trunk and you see rings. Each ring is one year of growth: a pale band of fast spring growth and a dark band of slow summer growth. Counting them gives the tree’s age. Measuring them gives much more.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A wide ring means a good year with plenty of water. A narrow ring means drought. Because every tree in a region lives through the same weather, trees of the same species in the same place share the same pattern of wide and narrow rings, a little like a barcode.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That shared pattern is what makes the method powerful. A scientist can overlap the rings of a living tree with the outer rings of an older dead log, then overlap that log with an even older beam, and keep stepping backward. In the American Southwest, this chain of overlaps reaches back more than two thousand years.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Archaeologists use it to date buildings. A wooden beam in a cliff dwelling can be matched to the master pattern, which gives the exact year that tree was cut. That is how we know the largest structures at Chaco Canyon went up in bursts of building rather than steadily.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Climate scientists use it differently. The rings preserve a record of rainfall from long before anyone was measuring rainfall. Tree rings show that a drought in the Southwest in the late 1200s lasted more than twenty years, which matches the period when many cliff dwellings were abandoned.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The tree does not know it is keeping records. It simply grows more in a wet year than a dry one. Everything else is us learning to read.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Cut across a tree trunk and you see rings. Each ring is one year of growth. Counting them gives the tree’s age. Measuring them tells you much more.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A wide ring means a good year with plenty of water. A narrow ring means drought. Trees in the same area live through the same weather, so they share the same pattern of wide and narrow rings.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That shared pattern is the key. A scientist can match the rings of a living tree to an older dead log, then match that log to an even older beam, and keep stepping back. In the Southwest, the chain reaches back more than two thousand years.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Archaeologists use it to date buildings. A wooden beam in a cliff dwelling can be matched to the pattern, which gives the exact year the tree was cut.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Climate scientists use it another way. The rings record rainfall from before anyone measured rainfall. They show a drought in the late 1200s that lasted more than twenty years. That is when many cliff dwellings were left empty.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The tree does not know it is keeping records. It just grows more in a wet year. The reading is up to us.

questions.q: Why can scientists date wood that is far older than any living tree?
questions.a: Because trees in one region share the same pattern of wide and narrow rings, a scientist can overlap a living tree with an older dead log, then that log with an even older beam, stepping backward thousands of years.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. pattern) and paragraph E (i.e. climate).
Summarize what tree rings can tell us and how scientists read them.
questions.a: Each ring is one year, and its width shows how wet that year was. Trees in one region share the same pattern, so scientists overlap living trees with older and older wood to build a chain going back thousands of years. Archaeologists use it to date buildings to the exact year, and climate scientists use it to find droughts that happened before rainfall was ever measured.

questions.q:
drought: A drought is a long stretch of time with much less rain than normal.
archaeologists: Archaeologists are scientists who study people of the past by examining what they built and left behind.
Describe the connection between the drought of the late 1200s and the cliff dwellings.
questions.a: Because tree rings show a drought lasting more than twenty years in the late 1200s, and that is the same period when many cliff dwellings were abandoned, the drought is a likely reason people left.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "a narrow ring means drought" or "the Southwest chain reaches back two thousand years." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: The Clock That Found the Longitude
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine the main idea of a text and explain how it is supported by key details; summarize the text.
 Spiral: RI.4.1 details and inferences · RI.4.3 explaining events · RI.4.4 word meaning · RI.4.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: For centuries, a ship at sea could tell how far north or south it was by measuring the sun. Nobody could reliably tell how far east or west. Ships missed islands by hundreds of miles. Crews starved. In 1707, four British warships ran into rocks off England and about fourteen hundred men died.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The math was not the hard part. The Earth turns fifteen degrees every hour. If a sailor knew the exact time at home and the exact time where the ship was, the difference would give the longitude. The problem was knowing the time back home.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Clocks of the day used a swinging pendulum. On a rolling ship a pendulum is useless. Heat, cold, and salt air threw the mechanism off further. Britain offered a prize worth millions in today’s money to anyone who could solve it.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Most experts worked on maps of the moon and stars. A carpenter named John Harrison built a clock instead. He replaced the pendulum with springs that balanced each other, so rocking did not matter. He used two metals that expanded at different rates, so the clock corrected itself as the temperature changed.

paras.label: E
paras.text: His fourth version was the size of a large pocket watch. On a voyage to Jamaica in 1761 it lost about five seconds in eighty-one days.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The board that judged the prize was full of astronomers, and they kept demanding new trials. Harrison spent forty years on the clocks and most of his life arguing for the money. He was finally paid at the age of eighty.

questions.q: Why could sailors find their latitude but not their longitude?
questions.a: Sailors could measure the sun to find how far north or south they were, but finding east or west required knowing the exact time back home, and no clock of the day could keep accurate time on a rolling ship.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. obstacle) and paragraph D (i.e. solution).
Summarize the longitude problem and how Harrison solved it.
questions.a: Ships could not tell how far east or west they were, and wrecks killed thousands. Longitude could be calculated from the time difference between home and the ship, but pendulum clocks failed at sea. John Harrison replaced the pendulum with balanced springs and used two metals to correct for temperature. His fourth clock lost only about five seconds in eighty-one days.

questions.q:
pendulum: A pendulum is a weight that swings back and forth to keep a clock running at a steady rate.
trials: Trials are tests done to prove whether something works.
Describe the connection between the two metals in the clock and its accuracy.
questions.a: Because the two metals expanded at different rates, they pulled against each other as the temperature changed, which corrected the mechanism and kept the clock running at the same speed in heat and cold.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "the Earth turns fifteen degrees an hour" or "the clock lost five seconds in eighty-one days." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: The River That Wants to Move
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine the main idea of a text and explain how it is supported by key details; summarize the text.
 Spiral: RI.4.1 details and inferences · RI.4.3 explaining events · RI.4.4 word meaning · RI.4.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: Rivers do not stay where we put them. Over thousands of years the Mississippi has swung back and forth across southern Louisiana, building land in one place and abandoning it for another. Roughly every thousand years it finds a shorter path to the sea and takes it.

paras.label: B
paras.text: By the 1950s it had found one. A smaller river called the Atchafalaya offered a route to the Gulf less than half as long as the Mississippi’s own. Water flows toward the steeper, shorter path. Each year a little more of the Mississippi went that way.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The consequences would have been enormous. Baton Rouge and New Orleans sit on the Mississippi. So do oil refineries, chemical plants, and the port that handles much of the country’s grain. If the river left, their water would turn salty and their shipping channel would become a shallow bay.

paras.label: D
paras.text: So the Army Corps of Engineers built the Old River Control Structure: a set of concrete gates that lets exactly thirty percent of the flow into the Atchafalaya and holds the rest in the Mississippi. It opened in 1963.

paras.label: E
paras.text: In 1973 a flood nearly ended it. Water scoured a hole under one of the structures deep enough to swallow a building. Engineers dropped boulders in for weeks. The structure held, but a wing of it collapsed, and afterward the Corps built a second structure beside the first as backup.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The river has not stopped trying. Every year the gates hold a continent’s worth of water on a path it no longer wants to take.

paras.text: Rivers do not stay where we put them. Over thousands of years the Mississippi has swung back and forth across southern Louisiana. About every thousand years it finds a shorter path to the sea and takes it.

questions.q: Why would it matter economically if the Mississippi changed course?
questions.a: Baton Rouge, New Orleans, oil refineries, chemical plants, and a major grain port all sit on the Mississippi. If the river left, their water would turn salty and the shipping channel would become a shallow bay.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. shortcut) and paragraph E (i.e. flood).
Summarize why the Old River Control Structure was built and what it does.
questions.a: The Mississippi was shifting toward the shorter Atchafalaya route, which would have cut off the cities, industries, and port built along it. Engineers built concrete gates that send exactly thirty percent of the flow down the Atchafalaya and hold the rest in the Mississippi. A 1973 flood nearly destroyed the structure, so a backup was added.

questions.q:
consequences: Consequences are the results that follow from something happening.
scoured: Scoured means scraped or dug away. The flood water dug out the ground beneath the structure.
Describe the connection between the length of the two routes and the river’s behavior.
questions.a: Because the Atchafalaya route to the Gulf is less than half as long, it drops more steeply, and water always flows toward the steeper path, so more of the Mississippi moved that way every year.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "the Atchafalaya route is less than half as long" or "the gates pass exactly thirty percent." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: The Vault Inside the Mountain
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine the main idea of a text and explain how it is supported by key details; summarize the text.
 Spiral: RI.4.1 details and inferences · RI.4.3 explaining events · RI.4.4 word meaning · RI.4.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: On a frozen island between Norway and the North Pole, a concrete wedge sticks out of a mountainside. A tunnel runs four hundred feet into the rock. At the end are three rooms holding seeds.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The Svalbard Global Seed Vault is a backup copy of the world’s crops. Countries send duplicate samples of their seeds, sealed in foil packets and boxed. It holds more than a million varieties: thousands of kinds of rice, wheat, beans, and potatoes that most people have never heard of.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Variety is the point. A crop grown from one single variety can be wiped out by one disease. When a blight destroyed Ireland’s potatoes in the 1840s, nearly all of them were the same kind. Old and rare varieties carry traits, like resistance to a fungus or tolerance for salty soil, that plant breeders may need later.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The location was chosen for physics, not scenery. The rock stays below freezing on its own, so even if the power failed the seeds would stay cold for weeks. The vault sits well above sea level.

paras.label: E
paras.text: It has been used once. The seed bank in Aleppo, Syria was damaged in the civil war, and researchers withdrew samples from Svalbard to restart their collection in Lebanon and Morocco. They later sent replacements back.

paras.label: F
paras.text: No country owns the seeds inside. Each depositor keeps ownership of its own boxes, and only that depositor can open them. The vault is a safe-deposit box, not a library.

paras.label: A
paras.text: On a frozen island between Norway and the North Pole, a concrete wedge sticks out of a mountain. A tunnel runs four hundred feet into the rock. At the end are three rooms full of seeds.

questions.q: Why does the vault store so many different varieties of the same crop?
questions.a: Because a crop grown from a single variety can be wiped out by one disease, as happened to Ireland’s potatoes, and rare varieties carry useful traits like disease resistance that breeders may need later.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. variety) and paragraph D (i.e. location).
Summarize what the Svalbard vault is and why it exists.
questions.a: The Svalbard Global Seed Vault is a backup copy of the world’s crop seeds, stored in rooms at the end of a tunnel inside an Arctic mountain. It holds over a million varieties because relying on one variety makes a crop easy to wipe out. The rock stays frozen without power, and depositors keep ownership of their own boxes.

questions.q:
varieties: Varieties are the different kinds within one type of plant, like thousands of different rices.
resistance: Resistance is the ability to survive something harmful, such as a plant that a fungus cannot kill.
Describe the connection between the Irish potato blight and the purpose of the vault.
questions.a: Because nearly all of Ireland’s potatoes were one variety, a single disease destroyed the whole crop. The vault stores many varieties so that no single disease can wipe out a crop everywhere.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "the tunnel runs four hundred feet into rock" or "Aleppo’s seed bank was restarted from it." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: The Girl Who Named a Planet
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine the main idea of a text and explain how it is supported by key details; summarize the text.
 Spiral: RI.4.1 details and inferences · RI.4.3 explaining events · RI.4.4 word meaning · RI.4.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: In March 1930, an eleven-year-old named Venetia Burney was eating breakfast in Oxford, England. Her grandfather read aloud from the newspaper: astronomers in Arizona had found a ninth planet, and it did not have a name yet.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Venetia had been studying Greek and Roman myths at school. The planet was the farthest from the sun, cold and dark and never visited. She suggested Pluto, the Roman god of the underworld.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Her grandfather had worked at the Bodleian Library and knew an astronomy professor. He passed the suggestion along. The professor cabled it to the observatory in Arizona.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The staff there were already voting on names. Pluto won unanimously, partly for the myth and partly because the first two letters were the initials of Percival Lowell, the astronomer whose observatory had begun the search. The name was announced on May 1, 1930.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Venetia received five pounds from her grandfather and went back to school. She became a teacher and rarely mentioned it.

paras.label: F
paras.text: In 2006, astronomers reclassified Pluto as a dwarf planet. Venetia, then eighty-seven, said she was a little disappointed but supposed that at her age these things did not matter much. The following year a dust counter aboard a spacecraft heading for Pluto was named the Venetia Burney Student Dust Counter. It reached Pluto in 2015, three years after she died.

paras.text: In March 1930, an eleven-year-old named Venetia Burney was eating breakfast in Oxford, England. Her grandfather read from the newspaper. Astronomers had found a ninth planet, and it had no name yet.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Venetia had been studying Greek and Roman myths at school. The new planet was the farthest from the sun, cold and dark. She suggested Pluto, the Roman god of the underworld.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Her grandfather knew an astronomy professor. He passed the idea along. The professor sent it to the observatory in Arizona.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The staff there were already voting on names. Pluto won every vote. The first two letters were also the initials of Percival Lowell, who had started the search. The name was announced on May 1, 1930.

paras.text: Venetia got five pounds from her grandfather and went back to school. She became a teacher and rarely talked about it.

paras.label: F
paras.text: In 2006, astronomers called Pluto a dwarf planet instead. Venetia, then eighty-seven, said she was a little disappointed. A tool on a spacecraft heading to Pluto was later named for her. It arrived in 2015, three years after she died.

questions.q: Give two reasons the observatory staff liked the name Pluto.
questions.a: They liked that Pluto was the Roman god of the underworld, which fit a cold, dark, distant planet, and that the first two letters were the initials of Percival Lowell, whose observatory began the search.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. idea) and paragraph F (i.e. afterward).
Summarize how Pluto got its name.
questions.a: Eleven-year-old Venetia Burney heard about the new planet at breakfast and suggested Pluto, the Roman god of the underworld, because the planet was cold and dark. Her grandfather passed the idea to an astronomy professor, who sent it to the observatory in Arizona. The staff voted for it unanimously and announced it in May 1930.

questions.q:
unanimously: Unanimously means everyone voted the same way, with nobody against it.
reclassified: Reclassified means put into a different group. Pluto was moved from planet to dwarf planet.
Describe the connection between Percival Lowell’s initials and the vote.
questions.a: Because the first two letters of Pluto are P and L, the name honored Percival Lowell as well as the myth, which gave the staff a second reason to choose it.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "she had been studying myths at school" or "a dust counter was named for her." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: What the Forest Is Saying
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine the main idea of a text and explain how it is supported by key details; summarize the text.
 Spiral: RI.4.1 details and inferences · RI.4.3 explaining events · RI.4.4 word meaning · RI.4.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: A forest looks like a collection of separate trees. Underground, it is closer to a single connected system.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Almost every tree root is wrapped in fungus. The fungus threads are far thinner than roots and reach into spaces roots cannot. They pull water and minerals out of the soil and hand them to the tree. In exchange the tree hands back sugar it made from sunlight. Neither one can thrive without the other.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The same fungal network usually connects to many trees at once. Researchers have injected a tree with a traceable form of carbon and found it days later inside a different tree twenty feet away. The carbon traveled through the fungus.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The transfers are not random. A large old tree in full sun often sends sugar to shaded seedlings that cannot make enough of their own. A dying tree has been observed dumping its stored carbon into the network rather than keeping it.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Warnings travel too. When a tree is attacked by insects, chemical signals move through the network, and neighboring trees begin producing defensive compounds before the insects arrive.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Scientists disagree about how to describe this. Some call it cooperation. Others point out that fungi benefit from keeping their hosts alive and may be managing the trees as much as serving them. What is not in dispute is the plumbing: cut the fungal network and the forest grows differently.

paras.label: C

questions.q: What does the tree give the fungus, and what does the fungus give the tree?
questions.a: The fungus pulls water and minerals from soil spaces that roots cannot reach and hands them to the tree. The tree hands back sugar it made from sunlight.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. evidence) and paragraph F (i.e. debate).
Summarize how trees in a forest are connected and what moves between them.
questions.a: Fungus wrapped around tree roots forms a network linking many trees. The fungus trades water and minerals for sugar from the trees. Carbon has been traced moving from one tree to another twenty feet away, older trees send sugar to shaded seedlings, and chemical warnings about insects travel through the network too.

questions.q:
traceable: Traceable means it can be followed and identified later, so researchers can tell where it ended up.
compounds: Compounds are substances made of combined chemicals. Trees make defensive compounds to fight insects.
Describe the connection between an insect attack on one tree and the defenses of its neighbors.
questions.a: Because the attacked tree sends chemical signals through the fungal network, neighboring trees receive the warning and start producing defensive compounds before the insects reach them.

articles.title: The Winter the Thames Froze
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Explain events, procedures, ideas, or concepts in a historical, scientific, or technical text, including what happened and why, based on specific information in the text.
 Spiral: RI.4.1 details and inferences · RI.4.2 main idea · RI.4.4 word meaning · RI.4.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: In January 1814 Londoners walked out onto the middle of the River Thames, set up tents, and held a fair. There were swings, printing presses selling souvenirs, and an elephant led across the ice below Blackfriars Bridge.

paras.label: B
paras.text: These frost fairs happened more than once. The river froze solid enough to hold crowds at least two dozen times between the 1300s and 1814. Two conditions had to line up.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The first was climate. Europe was passing through a stretch of unusually cold centuries now called the Little Ice Age. Winters ran longer and harder than they do today.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The second was the river itself. Old London Bridge sat on nineteen wide stone piers, and those piers left only narrow gaps for water to pass. The bridge acted like a dam. Upstream the current slowed almost to nothing, and slow shallow water freezes far more easily than fast deep water.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The 1814 fair was the last one. In 1831 the old bridge was replaced with a new one on fewer, wider arches, and the river ran faster. Embankments built later narrowed and deepened the channel, speeding it further.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So the fairs did not end only because the climate warmed. They ended because people rebuilt the river. Even in the coldest winters since, the Thames through London has not frozen across.

paras.label: A
paras.text: In January 1814 Londoners walked out onto the middle of the frozen River Thames and held a fair. There were tents, swings, and even an elephant led across the ice.

paras.label: B
paras.text: These frost fairs happened more than once. The river froze hard enough to hold crowds at least two dozen times before 1814. Two things had to line up.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The first was the weather. Europe was going through a stretch of very cold centuries. Winters were longer and harder than they are today.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The second was the river. Old London Bridge sat on nineteen wide stone piers with only narrow gaps between them. The bridge acted like a dam. Above it the water barely moved, and slow shallow water freezes much more easily.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The 1814 fair was the last one. In 1831 the old bridge was replaced with one on fewer, wider arches, and the river ran faster. Later walls made the channel narrower and deeper, speeding it up more.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So the fairs did not end only because the weather warmed. They ended because people rebuilt the river.

questions.q: Explain the two conditions that had to line up for the Thames to freeze.
questions.a: First, Europe was in the Little Ice Age, so winters were longer and colder. Second, Old London Bridge’s nineteen wide piers acted like a dam, slowing the water upstream, and slow shallow water freezes much more easily.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. bridge) and paragraph F (i.e. cause).
Summarize why the frost fairs happened and why they stopped.
questions.a: Unusually cold centuries combined with Old London Bridge, whose wide piers slowed the river almost to a stop, let the Thames freeze solid enough for fairs. After 1831 the bridge was replaced with wider arches and embankments deepened the channel, so the river ran too fast to freeze across.

questions.q:
piers: Piers are the heavy supports that hold a bridge up from the riverbed.
embankments: Embankments are walls built along a river to hold the water in a narrower channel.
Describe the connection between the shape of Old London Bridge and the ice on the river.
questions.a: Because the bridge’s nineteen wide piers left only narrow gaps, water backed up and slowed almost to a stop upstream, and slow shallow water freezes far more easily than fast deep water.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "an elephant was led across the ice" or "the old bridge had nineteen piers." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: How a Vaccine Teaches the Body
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Explain events, procedures, ideas, or concepts in a historical, scientific, or technical text, including what happened and why, based on specific information in the text.
 Spiral: RI.4.1 details and inferences · RI.4.2 main idea · RI.4.4 word meaning · RI.4.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: Your immune system is good at fighting an enemy it has already met. The first time a germ arrives, it takes about a week to build the right defense, and you are sick for that week. The second time, the defense is ready in hours and you may never notice.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A vaccine is a way of getting the practice without the illness.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Here is what happens. A vaccine delivers a harmless piece of a germ: a dead virus, a weakened one, a single protein from its surface, or instructions for your own cells to build that protein. None of these can make you sick, because none of them is the working germ.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Your immune cells find the piece and treat it as an intruder. They build antibodies shaped to lock onto it, the way a key fits one lock. Then, and this is the important part, some of those cells become memory cells and stay in your body for years.

paras.label: E
paras.text: If the real germ ever arrives, the memory cells recognize the shape immediately and the antibodies are produced fast enough to stop the infection before it spreads.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Soreness or a mild fever after a shot is not the vaccine making you ill. It is the immune system doing the work. The training is uncomfortable for a day. The illness it prevents can last much longer.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Your immune system is good at fighting an enemy it has met before. The first time a germ arrives, building the right defense takes about a week, and you are sick that week. The second time, the defense is ready in hours.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A vaccine is a way to get the practice without the illness.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A vaccine delivers a harmless piece of a germ. It may be a dead virus, a weakened one, or just one protein from its surface. None of these can make you sick, because none of them is the working germ.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Your immune cells find the piece and treat it as an intruder. They build antibodies shaped to lock onto it. Some of those cells become memory cells and stay in your body for years.

paras.label: E
paras.text: If the real germ ever arrives, the memory cells know the shape right away. Antibodies are made fast enough to stop the infection before it spreads.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A sore arm or mild fever after a shot is not the vaccine making you ill. It is your immune system doing the work.

questions.q: Explain why a vaccine cannot give you the disease it protects against.
questions.a: A vaccine delivers only a harmless piece of the germ, such as a dead or weakened virus or a single surface protein. None of those is the working germ, so none can cause the illness.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. memory) and paragraph F (i.e. soreness).
Summarize how a vaccine protects a person.
questions.a: A vaccine introduces a harmless piece of a germ. Immune cells treat it as an intruder and build antibodies shaped to lock onto it, and some become memory cells that last for years. When the real germ arrives, those memory cells recognize it at once and antibodies stop the infection before it spreads.

questions.q:
antibodies: Antibodies are proteins the body builds in a shape that locks onto one particular germ.
intruder: An intruder is something that gets in where it does not belong. Immune cells treat the vaccine piece as one.
Describe the connection between memory cells and how quickly you recover.
questions.a: Because memory cells already know the germ’s shape, antibodies are produced in hours instead of a week, so the infection is stopped before it can spread and make you sick.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "the first defense takes about a week" or "antibodies fit like a key in a lock." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: The Bridge That Danced
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Explain events, procedures, ideas, or concepts in a historical, scientific, or technical text, including what happened and why, based on specific information in the text.
 Spiral: RI.4.1 details and inferences · RI.4.2 main idea · RI.4.4 word meaning · RI.4.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: The Tacoma Narrows Bridge opened in Washington State in July 1940 and collapsed four months later. Film of the collapse is still shown in engineering classes, because the bridge did not fall the way anyone expected.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It was built long, narrow, and unusually light. Instead of an open truss under the roadway, the designers used solid steel plate girders eight feet deep along the sides. Those plates were the problem: wind could not pass through them, so it had to go around.

paras.label: C
paras.text: From the first days, the deck rippled up and down in ordinary wind. Drivers came for the ride. Locals called the bridge Galloping Gertie. Engineers attached cables and hydraulic devices to damp the motion, and the rippling continued.

paras.label: D
paras.text: On November 7, 1940, a steady wind near forty miles an hour did something different. The deck stopped rippling and began to twist, one edge rising as the other fell. Wind curling off the solid girders shed swirls of air in a rhythm, and that rhythm matched the bridge’s own natural twisting motion. Each gust arrived at the moment that pushed the twist further, the way timing your legs makes a swing go higher.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The twisting grew for about an hour until the deck tore loose and fell into the water. Nobody died. A dog left in an abandoned car did not survive.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Bridges built since are tested as models in wind tunnels, and most use open trusses or shaped decks that let wind slip past instead of catching it.

paras.label: A
paras.text: The Tacoma Narrows Bridge opened in Washington State in July 1940 and fell down four months later. Film of the collapse is still shown in classes, because it did not fall the way anyone expected.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It was built long, narrow, and very light. Instead of an open frame under the road, the sides were solid steel plates eight feet deep. Wind could not pass through them, so it had to go around.

paras.label: C
paras.text: From the first days, the road rippled up and down in normal wind. People drove across for the ride. Locals called it Galloping Gertie.

paras.label: D
paras.text: On November 7, 1940, a steady wind near forty miles an hour did something new. The deck stopped rippling and started to twist, one edge rising as the other fell. Wind curling off the solid plates came in a rhythm that matched the bridge’s own twisting. Each gust pushed the twist further, the way timing your legs makes a swing go higher.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The twisting grew for about an hour until the deck tore loose and fell into the water. Nobody died.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Bridges built since are tested as models in wind tunnels, and most let wind slip past instead of catching it.

questions.q: Explain why the solid side girders caused a problem.
questions.a: Wind could not pass through the eight-foot solid plates, so it curled around them and shed swirls of air in a rhythm. That rhythm matched the bridge’s natural twisting motion and pushed the twist further with each gust.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. warning) and paragraph D (i.e. twisting).
Summarize what happened to the Tacoma Narrows Bridge and why.
questions.a: The bridge was long, narrow, and light, with solid plate girders that blocked the wind instead of letting it through. It rippled in ordinary wind from the day it opened. In a steady forty-mile wind the deck began twisting, and because the wind’s rhythm matched the bridge’s own, the twist grew until the deck tore loose and fell.

questions.q:
girders: Girders are the large beams that run along a bridge and carry the weight of the roadway.
damp: To damp a motion is to slow it down or absorb it so it does not build up.
Describe the connection between the rhythm of the wind and the size of the twisting.
questions.a: Because each swirl of wind arrived at exactly the moment that pushed the twist further, the motion added up instead of cancelling out, so the twisting grew larger and larger until the deck failed.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "locals called it Galloping Gertie" or "the twisting grew for about an hour." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: When the Sahara Was Green
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Explain events, procedures, ideas, or concepts in a historical, scientific, or technical text, including what happened and why, based on specific information in the text.
 Spiral: RI.4.1 details and inferences · RI.4.2 main idea · RI.4.4 word meaning · RI.4.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: In the middle of the Sahara, on rock walls in southern Algeria and Libya, there are paintings of people swimming. There are herds of cattle, hippos, crocodiles, and giraffes. The nearest permanent water today is hundreds of miles away.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The paintings are not imaginary. Between roughly 11,000 and 5,000 years ago the Sahara was grassland dotted with lakes. Lake Chad covered an area larger than the Caspian Sea. Rivers ran where there is now nothing but sand.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The cause was the tilt and wobble of the Earth. Our planet’s axis shifts slowly over tens of thousands of years, changing how much summer sunlight reaches each latitude. During that period, North Africa received more summer sun. Hotter land pulled moist air inland from the ocean, and the monsoon rains that now stop far to the south reached deep into the desert.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Vegetation made it stronger. Plants hold moisture and release it back into the air, and dark leaves absorb more heat than pale sand does. Green ground pulls in more rain, which grows more green ground.

paras.label: E
paras.text: That same loop ran in reverse when the sunlight faded. Less rain killed plants, bare sand reflected sunlight back into space, the land cooled, and the rain retreated further. The change was not gradual everywhere; in some places the record suggests it took only a few centuries.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The wobble continues. On the current cycle, the monsoon is expected to reach into the Sahara again in roughly 15,000 years.

paras.label: A
paras.text: In the middle of the Sahara there are rock paintings of people swimming. There are cattle, hippos, and giraffes. The nearest water today is hundreds of miles away.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The paintings are not made up. Between about 11,000 and 5,000 years ago the Sahara was grassland with lakes. Rivers ran where there is now only sand.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The cause was the tilt of the Earth. Our planet wobbles slowly over tens of thousands of years, changing how much summer sun each part gets. Back then North Africa got more summer sun. Hotter land pulled wet air in from the ocean, and rains reached deep into the desert.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Plants made it stronger. Plants hold water and give it back to the air, and dark leaves soak up more heat than pale sand. Green ground pulls in more rain, which grows more green ground.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The same loop ran backward when the sunlight faded. Less rain killed plants, bare sand bounced sunlight away, the land cooled, and the rain pulled back further.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The wobble continues. The rains are expected to reach the Sahara again in about 15,000 years.

questions.q: Explain what caused the Sahara to become green.
questions.a: The slow shift in Earth’s tilt gave North Africa more summer sunlight. The hotter land pulled moist ocean air inland, so monsoon rains that now stop far to the south reached deep into the desert.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. feedback) and paragraph E (i.e. reversal).
Summarize how the Sahara became green and then became desert again.
questions.a: A shift in Earth’s tilt sent more summer sunlight to North Africa, which pulled monsoon rains far inland and turned the Sahara to grassland with lakes. Plants strengthened the pattern by returning moisture to the air. When the sunlight faded, plants died, bare sand reflected heat away, and the rains retreated, in some places within a few centuries.

questions.q:
monsoon: A monsoon is a seasonal wind that carries heavy rain inland from the ocean.
vegetation: Vegetation is all the plant life growing in an area.
Describe the connection between bare sand and the loss of rain.
questions.a: Because bare sand reflects sunlight back into space instead of absorbing it, the land cooled, which weakened the pull of moist air inland, so even less rain fell and still more plants died.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "Lake Chad was larger than the Caspian Sea" or "dark leaves absorb more heat than pale sand." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: How a Lock Lifts a Ship
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Explain events, procedures, ideas, or concepts in a historical, scientific, or technical text, including what happened and why, based on specific information in the text.
 Spiral: RI.4.1 details and inferences · RI.4.2 main idea · RI.4.4 word meaning · RI.4.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: The Panama Canal connects two oceans, but it does not run at sea level. Ships crossing it are raised eighty-five feet, carried across a lake, and lowered again. There are no pumps involved in the lifting.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A lock is a concrete chamber with a watertight gate at each end. A ship enters through the lower gate, which then closes behind it.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Next, valves open in tunnels connecting the chamber to the water above it. That water is higher, so gravity pushes it in. The chamber fills, and the ship floats up with the rising water. When the level inside matches the level above, the upper gate opens and the ship moves on.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Going the other direction, valves at the bottom open instead, and the water drains out to the lower level. The ship settles with it.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Each fill takes about eight minutes and moves roughly 26 million gallons. That water is not recovered. It runs to the ocean, which is why the canal depends on rainfall into Gatun Lake and why droughts force the canal to limit traffic.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Ships do not drive through the locks under their own power. Small electric locomotives called mules run on tracks along the walls, holding the ship centered with cables. The clearance in the older locks is about two feet on each side.

paras.label: A
paras.text: The Panama Canal connects two oceans, but it does not run at sea level. Ships are raised eighty-five feet, carried across a lake, and lowered again. No pumps do the lifting.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A lock is a concrete chamber with a watertight gate at each end. A ship enters through the lower gate, and the gate closes behind it.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Next, valves open in tunnels that connect the chamber to the water above it. That water is higher, so gravity pushes it in. The chamber fills and the ship floats up. When the levels match, the upper gate opens and the ship moves on.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Going the other way, valves at the bottom open and the water drains out. The ship settles down with it.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Each fill takes about eight minutes and uses about 26 million gallons. That water runs to the ocean and is not reused, so droughts force the canal to limit traffic.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Ships do not drive through the locks. Small electric engines called mules run on tracks along the walls and hold the ship centered with cables.

questions.q: Explain how a ship is raised without any pumps.
questions.a: Valves open tunnels between the chamber and the higher water above it. Because that water is higher, gravity pushes it into the chamber, the chamber fills, and the ship floats up with the rising water.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. filling) and paragraph E (i.e. water).
Summarize how a ship gets from one ocean to the other through the canal.
questions.a: A ship enters a lock chamber and the gate closes. Valves let higher water flow in by gravity until the ship has floated up to the next level, and the upper gate opens. The ship crosses the lake eighty-five feet up, then descends the same way as valves drain each chamber. Electric mules keep it centered.

questions.q:
valves: Valves are controls that open and close to let water flow through a pipe or tunnel.
clearance: Clearance is the space left between two things, here between the ship and the lock wall.
Describe the connection between rainfall and how many ships can use the canal.
questions.a: Because every lift dumps about 26 million gallons into the ocean and none of it is recovered, the canal depends on rain refilling Gatun Lake, so a drought forces it to run fewer ships.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "each fill uses 26 million gallons" or "there is about two feet of clearance." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: The Currency of Salt
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of general academic and domain-specific words or phrases in a text relevant to a grade 4 topic or subject area.
 Spiral: RI.4.1 details and inferences · RI.4.2 main idea · RI.4.3 explaining events · RI.4.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: Before refrigeration, salt was not a seasoning. It was the only reliable way to keep food from rotting, and that made it valuable enough to fight wars over.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Salt preserves meat by pulling water out of it. Bacteria need moisture to multiply, so a salted ham is a place where bacteria cannot get started. A cut of pork that would spoil in two days lasts two years.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Because it was essential and hard to get, salt became a commodity, a good traded in bulk at a set price. Roman soldiers received an allowance to buy it, and the Latin word for that payment, salarium, is where the English word salary comes from.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Governments noticed. A tax on salt is difficult to avoid, because everyone needs it and there is no substitute. France collected the gabelle, a salt tax so resented it helped fuel a revolution. In India, British law made it illegal to collect salt from the sea, and in 1930 Gandhi walked 240 miles to the coast to break that law in public.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Refrigeration ended salt’s monopoly in about fifty years. Today it is one of the cheapest minerals on Earth, spread on roads by the ton.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Its value never came from the substance. It came from scarcity, and from the fact that nothing else would do.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Before refrigerators, salt was not just a seasoning. It was the only sure way to keep food from rotting. That made it worth fighting over.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Salt keeps meat by pulling water out of it. Bacteria need water to grow, so they cannot get started in salted meat. Pork that would spoil in two days lasts two years.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Because everyone needed it, salt became a commodity, a good traded in bulk at a set price. Roman soldiers were given money to buy it. The Latin word for that payment is where we get the word salary.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Governments noticed. A salt tax is hard to avoid, because everyone needs salt. In India, British law made it illegal to collect salt from the sea. In 1930 Gandhi walked 240 miles to the coast to break that law.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Refrigeration ended all of it in about fifty years. Today salt is one of the cheapest minerals on Earth.

questions.q: Explain how salt preserves meat.
questions.a: Salt pulls the water out of meat. Bacteria need moisture to multiply, so without it they cannot get started, and pork that would spoil in two days lasts two years.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. trade) and paragraph D (i.e. taxes).
Summarize why salt was once so valuable and why it is not now.
questions.a: Salt was the only reliable way to keep food from spoiling, and because it was essential and hard to get, it was traded as a commodity, paid to soldiers, and taxed by governments. Refrigeration gave people another way to preserve food, so salt lost its scarcity and became cheap.

questions.q:
commodity: A commodity is a basic good traded in large amounts at a set price, like salt, grain, or oil.
scarcity: Scarcity is a short supply of something people need. Salt was valuable because of scarcity, not because of what it was.
Describe the connection between a good having no substitute and a government taxing it.
questions.a: Because everyone needs salt and nothing else will do the job, people cannot avoid buying it, so a tax on salt collects money from nearly every household.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "salary comes from the Latin word for salt money" or "Gandhi walked 240 miles." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: How Antibiotics Stop Working
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of general academic and domain-specific words or phrases in a text relevant to a grade 4 topic or subject area.
 Spiral: RI.4.1 details and inferences · RI.4.2 main idea · RI.4.3 explaining events · RI.4.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1928 Alexander Fleming noticed that mold growing on a forgotten dish had killed the bacteria around it. That accident became penicillin, and infections that routinely killed people became treatable within twenty years.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Fleming warned about the problem himself. Bacteria reproduce every twenty minutes, and each generation carries small random mutations. In any large population, a few bacteria happen to carry a mutation that lets them survive a given drug.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That is where selection takes over. When the antibiotic kills the vulnerable bacteria, the resistant few are left with no competition and multiply freely. The drug did not create the resistance. It cleared the field for it.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Two habits speed this up. Taking antibiotics for a viral illness like a cold does nothing to the virus but exposes the bacteria in your body to the drug for no reason. Stopping a prescription early because you feel better leaves the hardiest bacteria alive to rebuild.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Some infections are now resistant to nearly every drug available. Developing a new antibiotic takes about a decade, and resistance to it can appear within a few years.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The strategy now is to slow the process down: use the drugs only when they will work, finish the course, and hold the strongest ones in reserve.

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1928 Alexander Fleming noticed that mold on a forgotten dish had killed the bacteria around it. That accident became penicillin.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Fleming warned about the problem himself. Bacteria reproduce every twenty minutes, and each new generation has small random changes. A few happen to survive a given drug.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Then selection takes over. The drug kills the weak bacteria, and the resistant few are left with no competition. The drug did not create the resistance. It cleared the field for it.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Two habits speed this up. Taking antibiotics for a cold does nothing to the virus but exposes your bacteria to the drug for no reason. Stopping early leaves the toughest bacteria alive.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Some infections now resist nearly every drug. A new antibiotic takes about ten years to develop, and resistance can appear within a few years.

questions.q: Explain why the author says the drug did not create the resistance.
questions.a: The resistant bacteria were already there, carrying random mutations. The antibiotic killed the vulnerable ones, which left the resistant few with no competition and room to multiply.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. selection) and paragraph D (i.e. habits).
Summarize how bacteria become resistant to antibiotics.
questions.a: Bacteria reproduce every twenty minutes with small random mutations, so a few in any population survive a given drug. When the antibiotic kills the rest, those survivors multiply without competition. Using antibiotics on viruses or stopping a course early speeds the process up.

questions.q:
mutation: A mutation is a small random change in a living thing’s instructions. Some mutations let a bacterium survive a drug.
resistant: Resistant means able to survive something that would normally kill it.
Describe the connection between stopping a prescription early and stronger bacteria.
questions.a: Because the weakest bacteria die first, quitting once you feel better leaves the hardiest ones alive, and those are the bacteria that rebuild the infection and pass on their resistance.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "Fleming warned about this himself" or "a new antibiotic takes a decade." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: Reading the Rings of a Tree
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of general academic and domain-specific words or phrases in a text relevant to a grade 4 topic or subject area.
 Spiral: RI.4.1 details and inferences · RI.4.2 main idea · RI.4.3 explaining events · RI.4.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: Cut across a tree trunk and you find a record of every year it lived. Each ring is one growing season, and the rings are not all alike.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A tree grows by adding a layer just under the bark. In spring, when water is plentiful, it produces large thin-walled cells that look pale. Later in the season growth slows and the cells are small and dense, forming a dark band. One pale layer plus one dark band equals one year.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The width of a ring records the conditions of that year. A wet year with a long season leaves a wide ring. A drought leaves a narrow one. A scar in the ring records a fire that the tree survived.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The science of reading these records is called dendrochronology. Because every region shares the same weather, trees in one area produce the same distinctive sequence of wide and narrow rings, like a barcode. Researchers can match the outer rings of a living tree to the inner rings of an older dead one, then to a beam in an ancient building, extending the record backward thousands of years.

paras.label: E
paras.text: This is how archaeologists date a wooden roof beam to an exact year rather than a rough century.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Trees in the tropics are less useful. Where there is no winter, growth never pauses, and no clear rings form.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Cut across a tree trunk and you find a record of every year it lived. Each ring is one growing season.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A tree grows by adding a layer just under the bark. In spring the cells are large and pale. Later in the year they are small and dark. One pale layer plus one dark band equals one year.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The width of a ring records that year. A wet year leaves a wide ring. A drought leaves a narrow one. A scar records a fire the tree lived through.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Trees in one area share the same weather, so they show the same pattern of wide and narrow rings, like a barcode. Researchers match a living tree to an older dead one, then to a beam in an old building, going back thousands of years.

paras.label: E
paras.text: This is how a wooden beam can be dated to an exact year.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Tropical trees are less useful. With no winter, growth never pauses and no clear rings form.

questions.q: Explain how one year shows up in a tree trunk.
questions.a: In spring the tree makes large, pale, thin-walled cells, and later in the season it makes small, dense, dark cells. One pale layer plus one dark band is one year of growth.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. weather) and paragraph D (i.e. matching).
Summarize how tree rings let researchers date old wood.
questions.a: Each ring is one year, and its width records that year’s weather, so trees in one region share a distinctive pattern of wide and narrow rings. Researchers match the rings of a living tree to an older dead tree, then to a beam in an ancient building, extending the record back thousands of years.

questions.q:
dendrochronology: Dendrochronology is the science of dating events by studying the rings in trees.
sequence: A sequence is a set of things in a particular order. The order of wide and narrow rings works like a barcode.
Describe the connection between a region having no winter and its trees having no rings.
questions.a: Because rings form when growth slows in a cold or dry season, a tropical tree that grows steadily all year never makes the dark dense band that marks the end of a year.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "a scar records a fire" or "tropical trees form no clear rings." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: The Grid That Powers Your House
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of general academic and domain-specific words or phrases in a text relevant to a grade 4 topic or subject area.
 Spiral: RI.4.1 details and inferences · RI.4.2 main idea · RI.4.3 explaining events · RI.4.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: Electricity is the only major product that is consumed the instant it is made. There is almost no warehouse for it. Supply has to match demand second by second, all day, forever.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Power leaves a plant as alternating current and immediately enters a transformer that raises the voltage, sometimes above 300,000 volts. High voltage is not about power; it is about loss. Pushing the same energy at higher voltage means less current in the wire, and less current means less energy wasted as heat over long distances.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Near your town, substations step the voltage back down in stages, and a final transformer on a pole or pad drops it to the 120 volts in your outlet.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The whole network has to hold a steady frequency of 60 cycles per second. When demand rises, generators are pulled slightly slower and the frequency dips. Operators watch that number constantly and add generation to hold it.

paras.label: E
paras.text: This is why a blackout can cascade. If one line fails, its load shifts to neighboring lines, which may overload and shut down in turn, shifting still more load. In 2003 a single overloaded line in Ohio touched off a chain that darkened parts of eight states in about eight minutes.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The grid is not one machine. It is thousands of machines forced to stay in step with each other.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Electricity is used the instant it is made. There is almost no way to store it. Supply has to match demand second by second.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Power leaves a plant and goes straight into a transformer that raises the voltage very high. High voltage means less current in the wire, and less current means less energy wasted as heat over long distances.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Near your town, substations step the voltage back down. A final transformer on a pole drops it to the 120 volts in your outlet.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The whole network has to hold a steady frequency of 60 cycles a second. When demand rises, the frequency dips, and operators add power to hold it steady.

paras.label: E
paras.text: This is why a blackout can spread. If one line fails, its load shifts to other lines, which may overload and shut down too. In 2003 one overloaded line in Ohio darkened parts of eight states in about eight minutes.

questions.q: Explain why power is sent at very high voltage.
questions.a: Pushing the same energy at higher voltage means less current in the wire, and less current wastes less energy as heat over long distances.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. frequency) and paragraph E (i.e. cascade).
Summarize how electricity gets from a power plant to an outlet.
questions.a: Power leaves the plant and a transformer raises the voltage so less energy is lost as heat on the way. Substations near town step it back down in stages, and a final transformer drops it to 120 volts. Throughout, operators hold the frequency at 60 cycles per second by matching supply to demand.

questions.q:
transformer: A transformer is a device that raises or lowers the voltage of electricity.
cascade: A cascade is a failure that spreads from one part to the next, each one triggering the following.
Describe the connection between one failed line and a blackout across eight states.
questions.a: Because the failed line’s load shifts onto neighboring lines, those lines overload and shut down too, passing still more load along, so one failure spreads through the network in minutes.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "the grid holds 60 cycles per second" or "eight states went dark in eight minutes." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: What a Census Counts
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of general academic and domain-specific words or phrases in a text relevant to a grade 4 topic or subject area.
 Spiral: RI.4.1 details and inferences · RI.4.2 main idea · RI.4.3 explaining events · RI.4.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: Every ten years the United States tries to count every person living in the country. Not citizens. Not voters. Everyone.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The count is written into the Constitution, and it decides how the 435 seats in the House of Representatives are divided among the states. A state that grows faster than its neighbors gains seats. A state that grows slower loses them, even if its population went up.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Money follows the count too. Federal programs distribute hundreds of billions of dollars each year using census figures, so an undercount in one county means fewer dollars for its roads, clinics, and school lunches for a full decade.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Getting an accurate count is harder than it sounds. Some households never return the form, so census takers visit in person. Some people are difficult to reach at a fixed address, and some are counted twice, such as college students recorded both at school and at home.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The Census Bureau estimates its own error afterward by comparing results against a separate survey. Historically, young children, renters, and rural residents have been undercounted.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Individual answers are confidential by law for seventy-two years. That is why genealogists can read the 1950 census in full, but not the most recent one.

paras.text: Every ten years the United States tries to count every person living in the country. Not citizens. Not voters. Everyone.

paras.label: B

paras.label: F

questions.q: Explain why a state can lose House seats even when its population grows.
questions.a: The 435 seats are divided among the states by comparison, so what matters is how fast a state grows relative to the others. A state that grows more slowly than its neighbors loses seats even though it gained people.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. funding) and paragraph D (i.e. difficulty).
Summarize why the census matters and why it is hard to get right.
questions.a: The census decides how House seats are divided and how hundreds of billions of federal dollars are distributed for a decade. It is hard to get right because some households never return the form, some people are hard to reach, and others are counted twice, so children, renters, and rural residents are often undercounted.

questions.q:
undercount: An undercount is a count lower than the real number. An undercounted county loses funding for ten years.
confidential: Confidential means kept private. Individual census answers stay confidential for seventy-two years.
Describe the connection between an undercount and a county’s schools.
questions.a: Because federal money is handed out using census figures, a county counted short receives fewer dollars for every year until the next census, which reaches programs like school lunches.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "answers stay private for seventy-two years" or "census takers visit in person." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: The Lead in the Pipes
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Describe the overall structure (e.g., chronology, comparison, cause/effect, problem/solution) of events, ideas, concepts, or information in a text or part of a text.
 Spiral: RI.4.1 details and inferences · RI.4.2 main idea · RI.4.4 word meaning · RI.4.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: The problem was invisible. Lead does not change the color, smell, or taste of water, and in small amounts it does not make anyone immediately sick. It accumulates in the body over years, and in children it damages the developing brain.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The source was the pipes themselves. Lead service lines, the pipe running from the street main into a house, were standard in American cities until 1986. Millions are still in the ground.

paras.label: C
paras.text: For decades the solution was chemical rather than physical. Utilities added orthophosphate to the water, which coats the inside of the pipe with a mineral film. Water then touches the film instead of the lead.

paras.label: D
paras.text: That solution has a weakness: it only works if nothing disturbs the film. In 2014 Flint, Michigan switched water sources without adding corrosion control. The new water stripped the coating, and lead began entering homes within weeks.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Residents reported discolored water and rashes. Officials said the water met standards. Independent testing by a Virginia Tech team and a local pediatrician’s review of children’s blood tests eventually forced the city to reverse course.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The lasting solution is the expensive one: dig up the lines and replace them. Cities are now doing it, at a cost measured in billions and a timeline measured in decades.

paras.text: The problem was invisible. Lead does not change the color, smell, or taste of water. It builds up in the body over years, and in children it damages the growing brain.

paras.label: B
