questions.q: Explain why the chemical coating was only a partial solution.
questions.a: The coating works only as long as nothing disturbs it. When Flint switched water sources without corrosion control, the new water stripped the film away and lead entered homes within weeks.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. coating) and paragraph F (i.e. replacement).
Summarize the problem and the solutions described.
questions.a: Lead service lines, standard until 1986, leach lead into drinking water where it cannot be seen or tasted. Utilities coated the pipes chemically, which works only while the film stays intact. Flint stripped that film in 2014. The lasting solution is digging up and replacing the lines.

questions.q:
accumulates: Accumulates means builds up little by little over time.
corrosion: Corrosion is the slow eating away of metal. Corrosion control keeps water from stripping the pipe.
Describe the connection between lead being invisible and the problem going unnoticed.
questions.a: Because lead does not change how water looks, smells, or tastes, and causes no immediate illness, families kept drinking it for years while the damage accumulated unnoticed.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "lead lines were standard until 1986" or "a pediatrician reviewed blood tests." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: Two Ways to Power a Car
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Describe the overall structure (e.g., chronology, comparison, cause/effect, problem/solution) of events, ideas, concepts, or information in a text or part of a text.
 Spiral: RI.4.1 details and inferences · RI.4.2 main idea · RI.4.4 word meaning · RI.4.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: A gasoline car and an electric car do the same job by opposite methods. Comparing them part by part shows where each one wins.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Start with the engine. A gasoline engine has hundreds of moving parts and converts roughly a quarter of the fuel’s energy into motion; the rest becomes heat. An electric motor has about a dozen moving parts and converts most of its energy into motion.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Refueling flips the advantage. A gasoline tank fills in five minutes anywhere in the country. Charging a battery takes twenty minutes on the fastest chargers and many hours on a household outlet.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Maintenance favors electric again. No oil changes, no spark plugs, no exhaust system. Brakes last longer because the motor does much of the slowing.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Manufacturing favors gasoline. Building a battery takes mining lithium, nickel, and cobalt, and an electric car leaves the factory with a larger carbon footprint than a gasoline car does.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Over a lifetime, the picture reverses again. Most studies find an electric car makes up its manufacturing deficit within one to two years of driving and emits less overall after that, though how much less depends on how the local electricity is generated.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A gasoline car and an electric car do the same job in opposite ways. Comparing them part by part shows where each one wins.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Start with the engine. A gasoline engine has hundreds of moving parts and turns about a quarter of the fuel into motion. An electric motor has about a dozen and turns most of its energy into motion.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Refueling flips it. A gas tank fills in five minutes anywhere. Charging takes twenty minutes on a fast charger and many hours at home.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Upkeep favors electric again. No oil changes, no spark plugs. Brakes last longer because the motor does much of the slowing.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Building favors gasoline. Making a battery takes mining lithium and nickel, so an electric car starts out with a bigger carbon footprint.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Over a lifetime it reverses again. Most studies find an electric car makes up that difference within one to two years.

questions.q: Explain why an electric car starts out with a larger carbon footprint.
questions.a: Building its battery requires mining lithium, nickel, and cobalt, so the car has already caused more emissions by the time it leaves the factory than a gasoline car has.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. refueling) and paragraph E (i.e. manufacturing).
Summarize how the two kinds of car compare.
questions.a: The electric motor is simpler and wastes far less energy, and an electric car needs less maintenance. Gasoline wins on refueling speed and on manufacturing, since battery materials must be mined. Over one to two years of driving, the electric car makes up that deficit and emits less overall.

questions.q:
efficiency: Efficiency is how much of the energy put in actually does useful work.
footprint: A carbon footprint is the total amount of greenhouse gas something causes to be released.
Describe the connection between where electricity comes from and how clean an electric car is.
questions.a: Because an electric car runs on power from the grid, its emissions depend on how that power was generated, so the same car is cleaner in a region using wind or hydro than one burning coal.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "a gasoline engine wastes three quarters of its energy" or "brakes last longer on an electric car." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: The Year Without a Summer
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Describe the overall structure (e.g., chronology, comparison, cause/effect, problem/solution) of events, ideas, concepts, or information in a text or part of a text.
 Spiral: RI.4.1 details and inferences · RI.4.2 main idea · RI.4.4 word meaning · RI.4.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: In April 1815, Mount Tambora in Indonesia erupted with more force than any volcano in recorded history. The explosion was heard sixteen hundred miles away.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The eruption threw an enormous quantity of sulfur gas into the stratosphere, far above the weather. There it formed a haze of tiny droplets that reflected sunlight back into space. Because the stratosphere has no rain to wash particles out, the haze spread worldwide and stayed for years.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Global temperatures fell roughly one degree Fahrenheit. That sounds trivial. It was enough to shorten growing seasons across the Northern Hemisphere.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The following year, 1816, became known as the year without a summer. Snow fell in New England in June. Frost killed crops in August. Grain prices in Europe doubled, and famine followed in Ireland, Switzerland, and parts of China.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The effects reached beyond hunger. Thousands of New England families gave up and moved west, accelerating the settlement of Indiana and Illinois. In Switzerland, a group of writers kept indoors by relentless rain held a contest to write ghost stories. One of them, eighteen years old, wrote Frankenstein.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A single mountain, on the far side of the world, changed what people ate, where they lived, and what they wrote, for years afterward.

paras.label: A
paras.text: In April 1815, Mount Tambora in Indonesia erupted with more force than any volcano in recorded history. The explosion was heard sixteen hundred miles away.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The eruption threw sulfur gas high above the weather. There it formed a haze that reflected sunlight back into space. With no rain that high to wash it out, the haze spread worldwide and stayed for years.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Temperatures fell about one degree. That sounds small. It was enough to shorten growing seasons across the north.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The next year, 1816, became known as the year without a summer. Snow fell in New England in June. Frost killed crops in August. Grain prices doubled and famine followed.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The effects went further. Thousands of families moved west. In Switzerland, writers kept indoors by rain held a ghost story contest. One of them wrote Frankenstein.

paras.label: F
paras.text: One mountain changed what people ate, where they lived, and what they wrote.

questions.q: Explain why the haze from one eruption lasted for years.
questions.a: The sulfur reached the stratosphere, above the weather. Because there is no rain that high to wash particles out, the haze spread around the globe and stayed aloft for years.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. cooling) and paragraph E (i.e. consequences).
Summarize the chain of effects from the eruption.
questions.a: Tambora erupted in 1815 and threw sulfur into the stratosphere, where it formed a haze that reflected sunlight. Global temperatures fell about one degree, shortening growing seasons. Crops failed in 1816, grain prices doubled, famine spread, families migrated west, and a rainy Swiss summer produced Frankenstein.

questions.q:
stratosphere: The stratosphere is a layer of the atmosphere above where weather happens.
famine: A famine is a severe shortage of food across a whole region.
Describe the connection between a one-degree drop and crops failing.
questions.a: Because a small drop in average temperature shortens the frost-free season at both ends, crops that need the full season did not ripen before frost killed them.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "snow fell in New England in June" or "the explosion was heard sixteen hundred miles away." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: How the Interstate Was Built
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Describe the overall structure (e.g., chronology, comparison, cause/effect, problem/solution) of events, ideas, concepts, or information in a text or part of a text.
 Spiral: RI.4.1 details and inferences · RI.4.2 main idea · RI.4.4 word meaning · RI.4.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1919 the United States Army sent a convoy of trucks from Washington to San Francisco to test whether the country could move an army by road. The trip took sixty-two days. Vehicles broke through wooden bridges and sank in mud.

paras.label: B
paras.text: One of the officers on that convoy was a young Dwight Eisenhower. Twenty-five years later, as a general in Germany, he drove on the autobahn and saw what a national highway system could do.

paras.label: C
paras.text: In 1956, as president, Eisenhower signed the Federal-Aid Highway Act. It authorized 41,000 miles of interstate, paid ninety percent by the federal government, funded by a tax on gasoline.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Construction ran for thirty-five years. Engineers set uniform standards: twelve-foot lanes, no traffic lights, grades gentle enough for loaded trucks, and curves banked for seventy miles an hour.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The routes were not neutral. Urban interstates were often driven straight through Black and immigrant neighborhoods, where land was cheapest and residents had the least political power. Tens of thousands of homes were demolished, and some cities are now studying how to remove those highways.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The last original segment opened in 1992, seventy-three years after the convoy that started the argument.

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1919 the Army sent a convoy of trucks from Washington to San Francisco to test whether an army could move by road. The trip took sixty-two days. Trucks broke through wooden bridges and sank in mud.

paras.label: B
paras.text: One officer on that trip was a young Dwight Eisenhower. Twenty-five years later he drove on Germany’s highways and saw what a national system could do.

paras.label: C
paras.text: In 1956, as president, Eisenhower signed a law authorizing 41,000 miles of interstate, paid mostly by the federal government and funded by a gas tax.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Building took thirty-five years. Engineers set the same standards everywhere: twelve-foot lanes, no traffic lights, gentle grades for trucks.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The routes were not neutral. City interstates were often run straight through Black and immigrant neighborhoods, where land was cheap. Tens of thousands of homes were torn down.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The last original stretch opened in 1992.

questions.q: Explain what the 1919 convoy had to do with the interstate system.
questions.a: The convoy took sixty-two days and kept breaking through bridges and sinking in mud, which showed how poor the roads were. A young officer on that trip, Dwight Eisenhower, later signed the law creating the interstates.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. standards) and paragraph E (i.e. cost).
Summarize how the interstate system came to be built.
questions.a: A 1919 Army convoy exposed how bad American roads were. Eisenhower, who rode on it, later saw Germany’s autobahn and as president signed the 1956 Highway Act funding 41,000 miles. Construction ran to 1992 under uniform standards, and urban routes displaced tens of thousands of families.

questions.q:
convoy: A convoy is a group of vehicles traveling together.
uniform: Uniform means the same everywhere, with no variation.
Describe the connection between cheap land and which neighborhoods were demolished.
questions.a: Because planners chose routes where land cost least and residents had the least political power, urban interstates were run through Black and immigrant neighborhoods, destroying tens of thousands of homes.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "twelve-foot lanes and no traffic lights" or "funded by a tax on gasoline." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: The Fish That Ate the River
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Describe the overall structure (e.g., chronology, comparison, cause/effect, problem/solution) of events, ideas, concepts, or information in a text or part of a text.
 Spiral: RI.4.1 details and inferences · RI.4.2 main idea · RI.4.4 word meaning · RI.4.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: In the 1970s, catfish farmers in Arkansas had a problem. Algae clouded their ponds and clogged their equipment.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Their solution was biological. They imported silver carp and bighead carp from Asia, fish that filter algae out of water in enormous quantities. In the ponds, the carp worked exactly as intended.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Then the rivers flooded. Ponds overflowed into the Mississippi watershed, and the carp went with them. In open water they encountered no predator large enough to control them and no competitor that fed the same way.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The consequences compounded. An adult silver carp eats up to twenty percent of its body weight in plankton daily, starving the native fish that depend on the same food. Populations exploded; in some stretches of the Illinois River, carp now make up most of the fish by weight.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A second problem was unforeseen. Silver carp leap when startled by boat motors, sometimes ten feet into the air, and have broken the noses and jaws of boaters.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The current response is containment rather than removal. An electric barrier in a Chicago canal is meant to keep the carp out of Lake Michigan, where they could reach the entire Great Lakes system. Nobody has proposed a plan to get them out of the Mississippi.

paras.label: A
paras.text: In the 1970s, catfish farmers in Arkansas had a problem. Algae clouded their ponds and clogged their equipment.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Their solution used living things. They brought in silver carp and bighead carp from Asia, fish that filter algae out of water. In the ponds, the carp worked as planned.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Then the rivers flooded. Ponds spilled into the Mississippi, and the carp went with them. In open water nothing was big enough to eat them.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The problems piled up. A silver carp eats up to a fifth of its weight in plankton every day, starving native fish. In parts of the Illinois River, carp are now most of the fish by weight.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A second problem was a surprise. Silver carp leap when boat motors startle them, sometimes ten feet up, and have injured boaters.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The plan now is to contain them, not remove them. An electric barrier near Chicago is meant to keep them out of Lake Michigan.

questions.q: Explain why the carp spread so quickly once they reached the rivers.
questions.a: In open water they met no predator large enough to control them and no competitor feeding the same way, so nothing limited their numbers while they ate the plankton native fish needed.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. explosion) and paragraph F (i.e. containment).
Summarize how a solution became a bigger problem.
questions.a: Catfish farmers imported Asian carp to clear algae from their ponds, and it worked. Floods then washed the carp into the Mississippi, where nothing controlled them. They now starve native fish, injure boaters by leaping, and the only plan is an electric barrier keeping them out of the Great Lakes.

questions.q:
compounded: Compounded means added up and got worse, each problem making the next one bigger.
containment: Containment means keeping something from spreading further, rather than getting rid of it.
Describe the connection between the Chicago barrier and the Great Lakes.
questions.a: Because the canal connects the Mississippi watershed to Lake Michigan, carp reaching it could spread through the entire Great Lakes system, so the electric barrier is meant to block that one route.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "carp leap ten feet when startled" or "they eat a fifth of their weight daily." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: The Night the Lights Went Out
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Compare and contrast a firsthand and secondhand account of the same event or topic; describe the differences in focus and the information provided.
 Spiral: RI.4.1 details and inferences · RI.4.2 main idea · RI.4.4 word meaning · RI.4.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: FIRSTHAND · Nurse, county hospital: "The lights went at 4:10. The generator caught after about eight seconds, which felt much longer than eight seconds. I was holding a chart and I remember thinking about the third floor, where two patients were on ventilators."

paras.label: B
paras.text: "The generator runs the critical floors, not the elevators. So we carried meals up four flights. A man in the waiting room held his phone as a flashlight for six hours and would not take a break."

paras.label: C
paras.text: "I went home at midnight and my own street was dark. That was the strange part. At the hospital the emergency had a shape. At home it was just quiet."

paras.label: D
paras.text: SECONDHAND · From a report by the state utility commission: The outage began at 4:08 p.m. when a transmission line contacted an untrimmed tree near Carlton.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The fault shifted load to two parallel lines, which exceeded their thermal limits and disconnected within ninety seconds. Approximately 210,000 customers lost service across four counties.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Power was restored to 90 percent of customers within seven hours. The commission recommended a revised vegetation-management schedule and found no evidence of equipment failure.

paras.text: FIRSTHAND · Nurse, county hospital: "The lights went at 4:10. The generator caught after about eight seconds, which felt much longer. I remember thinking about the third floor, where two patients were on ventilators."

paras.label: B

paras.label: C
paras.text: "I went home at midnight and my own street was dark. At the hospital the emergency had a shape. At home it was just quiet."

paras.label: D
paras.text: SECONDHAND · From a state utility report: The outage began at 4:08 p.m. when a power line touched an untrimmed tree near Carlton.

paras.label: E

paras.label: F
paras.text: Power came back for 90 percent of customers within seven hours.

questions.q: Explain what caused the outage, and which account tells you.
questions.a: A transmission line touched an untrimmed tree near Carlton, which shifted load to two other lines that overheated and disconnected. Only the secondhand report gives the cause; the nurse never knew it.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. coping) and paragraph E (i.e. cascade).
Summarize what each account tells you that the other does not.
questions.a: The nurse describes the eight seconds before the generator caught, carrying meals up four flights, and a stranger holding a phone as a flashlight. The commission report gives the cause, the ninety-second cascade, the 210,000 customers affected, and the seven-hour restoration.

questions.q:
generator: A generator is a backup machine that makes electricity when the normal supply fails.
vegetation: Vegetation is plant growth. Vegetation management means trimming trees away from power lines.
Describe the connection between one line failing and 210,000 people losing power.
questions.a: Because the first line’s load shifted onto two parallel lines, those lines exceeded their heat limits and shut down too, so a single tree contact spread into an outage across four counties.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "two patients were on ventilators" or "no evidence of equipment failure." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: Climbing Denali
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Compare and contrast a firsthand and secondhand account of the same event or topic; describe the differences in focus and the information provided.
 Spiral: RI.4.1 details and inferences · RI.4.2 main idea · RI.4.4 word meaning · RI.4.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: FIRSTHAND · From a climber’s journal, day eleven: "Woke at 2 a.m. because the wind changed pitch. You learn the sound of a tent about to go."

paras.label: B
paras.text: "We are at 14,200 feet. I have a headache that has not left in three days. Eating is work. I made myself finish the oatmeal and it took twenty minutes. Nobody talks much up here, and I used to think that was about the cold. It is not. Thinking is slow."

paras.label: C
paras.text: "Tomorrow we carry loads to 16,200 and come back down to sleep. Going up to come down sounds foolish and it is the only thing that works."

paras.label: D
paras.text: SECONDHAND · From a park service guide: Denali rises to 20,310 feet, the highest peak in North America. Its high latitude means the air at the summit is thinner than at the same elevation in the Himalaya.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Roughly half of those who attempt the summit reach it. The most common reason for turning back is weather, and the second is altitude illness.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Climbers reduce that risk by acclimatizing: carrying supplies to a higher camp, then descending to sleep lower. The body responds by making more red blood cells. Standard expeditions take 17 to 21 days.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Climbers lower the risk by acclimatizing: carrying loads high, then sleeping low. The body makes more red blood cells. Most trips take 17 to 21 days.

questions.q: Explain why climbers carry loads up and then come back down to sleep.
questions.a: It is called acclimatizing. Going high and sleeping low lets the body respond by making more red blood cells, which lowers the risk of altitude illness.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. exhaustion) and paragraph F (i.e. acclimatizing).
Summarize what each account adds to your understanding of Denali.
questions.a: The journal shows what altitude feels like: a headache that will not leave, twenty minutes to eat oatmeal, and thinking that slows down. The park guide explains why, giving the height, the thin air caused by high latitude, the roughly even odds of summiting, and the purpose of acclimatizing.

questions.q:
acclimatizing: Acclimatizing is letting the body adjust to thin air by going high and sleeping lower.
latitude: Latitude is how far north or south a place is. Denali’s high latitude makes its air thinner.
Describe the connection between thin air and how the climber describes thinking.
questions.a: Because there is less oxygen reaching the brain at 14,200 feet, the climber’s thinking slows and conversation stops, which she first mistook for an effect of the cold.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "the wind changed pitch" or "weather is the top reason for turning back." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: The Day the Levees Broke
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Compare and contrast a firsthand and secondhand account of the same event or topic; describe the differences in focus and the information provided.
 Spiral: RI.4.1 details and inferences · RI.4.2 main idea · RI.4.4 word meaning · RI.4.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: FIRSTHAND · Resident, Lower Ninth Ward, recorded 2006: "The storm passed. That is the part people get wrong. The wind stopped and we thought we had come through it."

paras.label: B
paras.text: "The water came later, in the morning, and it came fast. Not like rain filling up a street. Like something poured. We went to the attic. My neighbor kept an axe up there, which everyone said was paranoid, and that axe got four of us onto the roof."

paras.label: C
paras.text: "I had lived on that block forty-one years. I did not recognize it from above."

paras.label: D
paras.text: SECONDHAND · From an engineering investigation, 2007: Hurricane Katrina made landfall on August 29, 2005. Failures occurred at more than fifty points in the New Orleans flood-protection system.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The investigation found that most breaches occurred below the design storm surge. Floodwalls along the Industrial Canal failed when water pressure caused the soil beneath them to shift, a mechanism the original design had not accounted for.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The report concluded that the flooding was primarily the result of engineering and organizational failure rather than an unforeseeable natural event. Roughly 80 percent of the city flooded.

paras.text: Most breaks happened below the level the walls were built to handle. Water pressure moved the soil under the floodwalls, something the original design had not planned for.

paras.label: F

questions.q: Explain why the floodwalls failed, according to the investigation.
questions.a: Water pressure caused the soil beneath the floodwalls to shift, a mechanism the original design had not accounted for, so most breaches happened below the storm surge the walls were built to handle.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. escape) and paragraph E (i.e. failure).
Summarize what each account tells you about the flooding.
questions.a: The resident describes believing the danger had passed, then water arriving fast the next morning, and escaping through the attic with a neighbor’s axe. The engineering report explains that the system failed at more than fifty points because soil shifted beneath the floodwalls, flooding 80 percent of the city.

questions.q:
breaches: Breaches are places where a wall or barrier broke open and let water through.
unforeseeable: Unforeseeable means impossible to predict. The report said the flooding was not unforeseeable.
Describe the connection between the storm passing and people being caught by surprise.
questions.a: Because the wind stopped and residents believed the danger was over, they were still in their homes when the levees failed the next morning and the water arrived fast.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "the wind stopped first" or "most breaches were below the design surge." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: Working the Night Shift at the Zoo
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Compare and contrast a firsthand and secondhand account of the same event or topic; describe the differences in focus and the information provided.
 Spiral: RI.4.1 details and inferences · RI.4.2 main idea · RI.4.4 word meaning · RI.4.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: FIRSTHAND · Night keeper, large city zoo: "People assume the zoo is asleep at night. Half of it is just waking up."

paras.label: B
paras.text: "My rounds start at ten. The big cats are awake and following me along the fence, which took a long time to stop finding unnerving. The elephants sleep standing, mostly, and lie down for maybe an hour. I have seen the older female lie down exactly twice in six years."

paras.label: C
paras.text: "The part nobody warns you about is listening. You learn each animal’s normal noise. When something is wrong, you usually hear it before you see it. I called a vet at 3 a.m. once because a giraffe was breathing differently. I was right."

paras.label: D
paras.text: SECONDHAND · From a veterinary text on captive animal care: Nocturnal and crepuscular species constitute a substantial share of zoo collections, and their activity peaks outside public hours.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Overnight monitoring serves several functions. Keepers observe feeding, social interaction, and locomotion that daytime visitors never see. Early detection of abnormal behavior is the most reliable indicator of illness in species that instinctively conceal symptoms.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Many prey species mask signs of weakness, an adaptation that helps in the wild and delays diagnosis in captivity. Continuous observation partially offsets that difficulty.

paras.label: A
paras.text: FIRSTHAND · Night keeper, city zoo: "People assume the zoo is asleep at night. Half of it is just waking up."

paras.label: B
paras.text: "My rounds start at ten. The big cats are awake and follow me along the fence. The elephants sleep standing and lie down for maybe an hour. I have seen the older female lie down exactly twice in six years."

paras.label: C
paras.text: "The part nobody warns you about is listening. You learn each animal’s normal noise. I called a vet at 3 a.m. once because a giraffe was breathing differently. I was right."

paras.label: D
paras.text: SECONDHAND · From a book on caring for zoo animals: Many zoo species are most active at night or at dusk, outside public hours.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Overnight watching lets keepers see feeding and movement that visitors never see. Noticing unusual behavior early is the best sign of illness in animals that hide symptoms.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Many prey animals hide weakness. That helps them in the wild and makes illness harder to spot in a zoo.

questions.q: Explain why noticing a change early matters so much at a zoo.
questions.a: Many prey species instinctively hide signs of weakness, which helps them survive in the wild but delays diagnosis in captivity. Early detection of unusual behavior is the most reliable indicator that an animal is ill.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. listening) and paragraph F (i.e. masking).
Summarize how the two accounts explain the same work differently.
questions.a: The keeper describes rounds at ten, cats following the fence, an elephant that has lain down twice in six years, and calling a vet because a giraffe breathed differently. The veterinary text explains why: many species are active at night, and prey animals hide symptoms, so continuous observation catches illness early.

questions.q:
nocturnal: Nocturnal animals are active at night and rest during the day.
conceal: To conceal something is to hide it. Prey animals conceal signs of illness.
Describe the connection between hiding weakness in the wild and illness being missed in a zoo.
questions.a: Because an animal that shows weakness in the wild attracts predators, prey species evolved to hide symptoms, and that same instinct keeps keepers from noticing sickness until it is advanced.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "elephants sleep standing" or "activity peaks outside public hours." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: Apollo 13
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Compare and contrast a firsthand and secondhand account of the same event or topic; describe the differences in focus and the information provided.
 Spiral: RI.4.1 details and inferences · RI.4.2 main idea · RI.4.4 word meaning · RI.4.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: FIRSTHAND · Flight controller, Mission Control, recalling April 13, 1970: "The first thing was not the bang. It was the pattern of the lights. Too many alarms at once means either everything broke or one sensor lied, and you have about four seconds to decide which you believe."

paras.label: B
paras.text: "We had a room full of people who had each memorized one system. Somebody said the oxygen quantity was dropping and somebody else said his readout disagreed. That argument is what saved them. If we had all agreed early, we would have been wrong together."

paras.label: C
paras.text: "Nobody shouted. That surprises people. The room got quieter."

paras.label: D
paras.text: SECONDHAND · From a NASA mission summary: Fifty-five hours into the flight, an oxygen tank in the service module ruptured following an electrical short in its internal heater wiring.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The explosion damaged a second tank and disabled two of three fuel cells, eliminating the command module’s power, water, and oxygen supplies. The lunar landing was abandoned within an hour.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The crew moved into the lunar module, using it as a lifeboat, and returned on a free-return trajectory around the Moon. They splashed down on April 17. All three astronauts survived.

paras.label: A
paras.text: FIRSTHAND · Flight controller, Mission Control, on April 13, 1970: "The first thing was not the bang. It was the pattern of the lights. Too many alarms at once means either everything broke or one sensor lied, and you have about four seconds to decide which."

paras.label: B
paras.text: "We had a room full of people who had each memorized one system. Somebody said the oxygen was dropping and somebody else said his readout disagreed. That argument is what saved them."

paras.label: C
paras.text: "Nobody shouted. That surprises people. The room got quieter."

paras.label: D
paras.text: SECONDHAND · From a NASA summary: Fifty-five hours into the flight, an oxygen tank ruptured after an electrical short in its heater wiring.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The explosion damaged a second tank and knocked out two of three fuel cells, cutting the command module’s power, water, and oxygen. The Moon landing was called off within an hour.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The crew moved into the lunar module and used it as a lifeboat. They splashed down on April 17. All three survived.

questions.q: Explain what actually failed aboard Apollo 13.
questions.a: An electrical short in an oxygen tank’s internal heater wiring caused the tank to rupture. The explosion damaged a second tank and disabled two of three fuel cells, cutting the command module’s power, water, and oxygen.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. disagreement) and paragraph F (i.e. lifeboat).
Summarize what each account contributes.
questions.a: The controller describes the first seconds: too many alarms to trust, four seconds to judge them, and an argument between two readouts that kept the room from being wrong together. The NASA summary gives the cause, the systems lost, the decision to abandon the landing, and the April 17 splashdown.

questions.q:
ruptured: Ruptured means burst open suddenly under pressure.
trajectory: A trajectory is the path a moving object follows through space.
Describe the connection between the disagreement in the room and the crew surviving.
questions.a: Because two controllers reported different readings instead of accepting the first one, the room had to work out which instrument was lying, and that argument kept them from committing early to a wrong conclusion.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "each person had memorized one system" or "they used a free-return trajectory." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: How a Lock Lifts a Ship
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Interpret information presented visually, orally, or quantitatively (e.g., in charts, graphs, diagrams, time lines, animations, or interactive elements on Web pages) and explain how the information contributes to an understanding of the text in which it appears.
 Spiral: RI.4.1 details and inferences · RI.4.2 main idea · RI.4.4 word meaning · RI.4.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: A river does not run level. It drops. A boat traveling upstream on a canal has to climb, and it cannot climb a waterfall. A lock is the machine that solves this, and it works without a single pump.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A lock is a concrete chamber with a gate at each end. A boat headed upstream enters through the lower gate, which then closes behind it. The chamber is now sealed, holding the boat at the lower water level.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Valves in the upper gate open. Water from the higher stretch of canal flows in by gravity alone. The water level in the chamber rises, and the boat rises with it, floating the whole time.

paras.label: D
paras.text: When the chamber water matches the upper canal, the pressure on both sides of the upper gate is equal. Only then will the gate swing open. The boat motors out at the higher level, and the lock is ready for the next one.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A boat going downstream runs the same steps in reverse, draining instead of filling. Each cycle uses a chamber of water, which is why locks on a busy canal are often built in pairs so one can fill while the other empties.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The Panama Canal lifts ships 85 feet using three sets of locks. The physics is the same as a canal lock in Ohio. Only the scale is different.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A river does not run level. It drops. A boat going upstream has to climb, and it cannot climb a waterfall. A lock is the machine that solves this, and it uses no pumps.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A lock is a concrete box with a gate at each end. A boat headed upstream comes in through the lower gate. The gate closes behind it.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Valves in the upper gate open. Water from the higher part of the canal flows in on its own. The water rises, and the boat floats up with it.

paras.label: D
paras.text: When the water inside matches the water above, the pressure on both sides of the upper gate is equal. Only then can the gate swing open. The boat motors out at the higher level.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A boat going downstream runs the same steps backward, draining instead of filling. Each trip uses a chamber of water.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The Panama Canal lifts ships 85 feet using three sets of locks. The science is the same as a small canal lock. Only the size is different.

questions.q: Use the diagram to explain why the upper gate cannot open at Stage 2.
questions.a: At Stage 2 the chamber is still at low water, so the higher canal is pressing against the upper gate with much more force than the water inside. The gate can only swing open at Stage 4, when the levels match and the pressure on both sides is equal.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. filling) and paragraph E (i.e. reversing).
Explain how the diagram helps you understand paragraphs B through D.
questions.a: The paragraphs describe the stages in sentences, but the diagram lines them up in order so you can see that the boat starts low, the chamber seals, water enters by gravity, and only then does the upper gate open. Seeing the five stages together makes the sequence and the reason for the order clear.

questions.q:
chamber: A chamber is an enclosed space. In a lock it is the concrete box between the two gates.
gravity: Gravity is the force pulling things down. It moves the water into the lock without a pump.
Describe the connection between equal pressure and the gate opening.
questions.a: Because water pushes hard against a gate when the levels are different, the gate cannot be forced open. Once the chamber has filled to match the upper canal, the push is the same on both sides and the gate swings freely.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "water flows in by gravity alone" or "the Panama Canal lifts ships 85 feet." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: Reading a Hurricane Track Map
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Interpret information presented visually, orally, or quantitatively (e.g., in charts, graphs, diagrams, time lines, animations, or interactive elements on Web pages) and explain how the information contributes to an understanding of the text in which it appears.
 Spiral: RI.4.1 details and inferences · RI.4.2 main idea · RI.4.4 word meaning · RI.4.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: Three days before a hurricane reaches land, forecasters publish a map with a cone on it. The cone is the single most misread graphic in American weather reporting.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The cone does not show the size of the storm. It shows where the center of the storm might travel. Historically, the true center stays inside the cone about two thirds of the time.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The cone widens with time because forecasts get less certain the farther out they reach. At 12 hours the cone is narrow. At 120 hours it can be hundreds of miles across.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Damaging wind and rain routinely occur far outside the cone. A town 150 miles from the drawn line can flood while a town on the line stays dry. The line is a probability, not a promise.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Forecasters also publish a separate surge map and a wind-arrival map. Emergency managers use those, not the cone, when they decide whether to order evacuations.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The cone remains in public forecasts because people understand a line better than they understand a probability. Whether that trade is worth making is still argued.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Three days before a hurricane reaches land, forecasters publish a map with a cone on it. The cone is the most misread graphic in weather reporting.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The cone does not show how big the storm is. It shows where the center of the storm might go. The real center stays inside the cone about two thirds of the time.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The cone gets wider the farther out it goes, because forecasts get less certain with time. At 12 hours it is narrow. At 120 hours it can be hundreds of miles wide.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Heavy wind and rain often happen far outside the cone. A town 150 miles from the line can flood while a town on the line stays dry.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Forecasters also publish a surge map and a wind-arrival map. Emergency managers use those, not the cone, to decide about evacuations.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The cone stays in public forecasts because people understand a line better than a probability.

questions.q: Use the chart to explain why the cone gets wider farther into the future.
questions.a: The chart shows the cone growing from about 30 miles at 12 hours to more than 300 miles at 120 hours. It widens because a forecast is less certain the farther ahead it reaches, so the range of places the center could be gets larger.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. misreading) and paragraph E (i.e. deciding).
Explain how the chart changes what you understand about paragraph D.
questions.a: Paragraph D says damage happens far outside the cone. The chart explains why: the cone only tracks the center, and its last row states plainly that it shows nothing about storm size, wind reach, rainfall, or surge. Together they show that being outside the line is not the same as being safe.

questions.q:
probability: A probability is how likely something is, not a guarantee that it will happen.
surge: Storm surge is ocean water pushed inland by a storm, which floods the coast.
Describe the connection between the cone showing only the center and people misreading it.
questions.a: Because the drawn cone looks like the outline of the storm, readers assume everything inside is dangerous and everything outside is safe, when the cone only marks where the center might pass.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "the center stays inside about two thirds of the time" or "managers use the surge map instead." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: The Fastest Land Animals
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Interpret information presented visually, orally, or quantitatively (e.g., in charts, graphs, diagrams, time lines, animations, or interactive elements on Web pages) and explain how the information contributes to an understanding of the text in which it appears.
 Spiral: RI.4.1 details and inferences · RI.4.2 main idea · RI.4.4 word meaning · RI.4.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: A cheetah can reach 70 miles per hour. That number appears on posters and in trivia books, and by itself it explains almost nothing about how a cheetah hunts.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The cheetah holds that speed for roughly twenty seconds. After that its body temperature rises past what it can safely carry, and it must stop. Most chases end in under a minute whether or not the cheetah has caught anything.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A pronghorn antelope tops out slower, near 55 miles per hour, but can hold 30 miles per hour for many miles. It evolved alongside a predator that no longer exists, and it is now faster than anything that chases it.

paras.label: D
paras.text: An ostrich runs about 43 miles per hour and can sustain it far longer than a cheetah. A greyhound reaches 45 but tires quickly, much like the cheetah.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Comparing only top speed puts the cheetah first every time. Comparing distance held at speed puts the pronghorn first and moves the cheetah to last.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Neither ranking is wrong. They measure different things, which is why a single number about an animal is rarely enough.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A cheetah can reach 70 miles per hour. That number is on posters everywhere, and by itself it explains almost nothing about how a cheetah hunts.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The cheetah holds that speed for about twenty seconds. After that its body gets too hot and it has to stop. Most chases end in under a minute.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A pronghorn antelope is slower, near 55 miles per hour, but can hold 30 miles per hour for many miles. Nothing alive today can chase it that far.

paras.label: D
paras.text: An ostrich runs about 43 miles per hour and holds it much longer than a cheetah. A greyhound reaches 45 but tires fast.

paras.label: E
paras.text: If you compare only top speed, the cheetah wins. If you compare how far an animal can hold speed, the pronghorn wins and the cheetah comes last.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Neither ranking is wrong. They measure different things.

questions.q: Use the graph to explain why the cheetah is both first and last.
questions.a: The graph ranks the animals two ways. By top speed the cheetah leads at 70 mph. By how long that speed is held, the cheetah manages about twenty seconds while the pronghorn keeps 30 mph for miles, so the cheetah drops to last.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. overheating) and paragraph E (i.e. comparing).
Explain how the graph supports the point made in paragraph F.
questions.a: Paragraph F says the two rankings measure different things and neither is wrong. The graph shows this directly by placing top speed and distance held side by side, so the same four animals come out in nearly opposite orders depending on which column you read.

questions.q:
sustain: To sustain a speed is to keep it going over time instead of only reaching it briefly.
evolved: Evolved means changed slowly over many generations to survive in a particular place.
Describe the connection between the cheetah’s body temperature and the length of its chases.
questions.a: Because sprinting heats the cheetah’s body faster than it can cool, it must stop after roughly twenty seconds, so its hunts are decided in under a minute whether or not it catches anything.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "the pronghorn evolved alongside a predator that no longer exists" or "greyhounds tire quickly." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: Where the Water Goes
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Interpret information presented visually, orally, or quantitatively (e.g., in charts, graphs, diagrams, time lines, animations, or interactive elements on Web pages) and explain how the information contributes to an understanding of the text in which it appears.
 Spiral: RI.4.1 details and inferences · RI.4.2 main idea · RI.4.4 word meaning · RI.4.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: A city receives rain the same way a field does. What happens next is not the same at all.

paras.label: B
paras.text: In a meadow, most rain soaks into the ground. Roots slow it, soil holds it, and it reaches the stream over hours or days. Only a small share runs off the surface.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Under a parking lot, none of that happens. Asphalt absorbs nothing. Rain hits it and moves immediately toward the nearest drain, arriving in the creek within minutes rather than hours.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The total amount of water is unchanged. The timing is what changes. A creek that would have risen slowly over a day instead rises sharply in twenty minutes, which is what causes flash flooding downstream.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Cities now build rain gardens, permeable pavement, and detention basins to delay runoff on purpose. None of these reduce the rainfall. They spread its arrival out again.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A city block with 20 percent of its surface paved behaves like a meadow. At 60 percent paved, it behaves like a roof.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A city gets rain the same way a field does. What happens next is not the same.

paras.label: B
paras.text: In a meadow, most rain soaks into the ground. Roots slow it and soil holds it. It reaches the stream over hours or days.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Under a parking lot, none of that happens. Asphalt soaks up nothing. Rain hits it and runs to the nearest drain, reaching the creek in minutes.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The amount of water is the same. The timing changes. A creek that would rise slowly over a day instead rises fast in twenty minutes, which causes flash flooding.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Cities now build rain gardens and special pavement to slow runoff on purpose. These do not reduce the rain. They spread out when it arrives.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A block with 20 percent paved acts like a meadow. At 60 percent paved, it acts like a roof.

questions.q: Use the graph to explain why the same storm floods a city but not a meadow.
questions.a: The graph shows a meadow absorbing about 90 of every 100 drops and releasing the rest over hours or days, while a parking lot absorbs almost none and sends nearly all of it to the creek within minutes. The rainfall is identical; the speed of arrival is what floods the city.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. runoff) and paragraph E (i.e. delaying).
Explain how the graph adds to what paragraph D tells you.
questions.a: Paragraph D states that the total water is unchanged and only the timing differs. The graph shows both halves of that at once: the soaks-in and runs-off rows account for the same inch of rain either way, and the last row shows the difference is hours versus minutes.

questions.q:
permeable: Permeable means able to let water pass through. Permeable pavement lets rain soak in.
detention: A detention basin is a dip in the ground that holds runoff for a while before releasing it.
Describe the connection between paved ground and flash flooding downstream.
questions.a: Because pavement sends rain to the drains at once instead of letting soil release it slowly, the creek receives a whole storm in twenty minutes and rises faster than its channel can carry, which floods the land below.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "asphalt absorbs nothing" or "at 60 percent paved a block behaves like a roof." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: The Longest Bridges Ever Built
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Interpret information presented visually, orally, or quantitatively (e.g., in charts, graphs, diagrams, time lines, animations, or interactive elements on Web pages) and explain how the information contributes to an understanding of the text in which it appears.
 Spiral: RI.4.1 details and inferences · RI.4.2 main idea · RI.4.4 word meaning · RI.4.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: Ask which bridge is the longest and you will get four different answers, all of them correct.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The Danyang–Kunshan Grand Bridge in China runs 102 miles. Almost all of it crosses farmland and rice paddies on short concrete spans. It is the longest bridge of any kind.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The Akashi Kaikyo Bridge in Japan has a main span of 6,532 feet. That is the distance between its two towers with nothing underneath. No bridge holds a longer single gap.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The Lake Pontchartrain Causeway in Louisiana stretches almost 24 miles over open water, the longest continuous bridge across water anywhere.

paras.label: E
paras.text: These are three different measurements: total length, longest single span, and length over water. A bridge can lead one list and not appear on another.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The main span matters most to engineers, because the gap a bridge can cross without a support is the hard problem. Total length is mostly a question of how many identical spans you are willing to pay for.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Ask which bridge is the longest and you will get four different answers, all correct.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The Danyang–Kunshan Grand Bridge in China runs 102 miles. Almost all of it crosses farmland on short concrete spans. It is the longest bridge of any kind.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The Akashi Kaikyo Bridge in Japan has a main span of 6,532 feet. That is the gap between its two towers with nothing underneath. No bridge has a longer single gap.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The Lake Pontchartrain Causeway in Louisiana runs almost 24 miles over open water. That is the longest bridge across water anywhere.

paras.label: E
paras.text: These are three different measurements: total length, longest single span, and length over water. A bridge can lead one list and miss another.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Engineers care most about the main span, because crossing a gap without a support is the hard problem.

questions.q: Use the chart to explain why the longest bridge is not the hardest to build.
questions.a: The chart shows Danyang–Kunshan leading total length at 102 miles, but its length comes from joining many short spans. The hardest measurement is the main span, where Akashi Kaikyo leads with 6,532 feet of gap that nothing supports in the middle.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. repeating) and paragraph F (i.e. engineering).
Explain how the chart makes paragraph E easier to understand.
questions.a: Paragraph E says there are three different measurements and a bridge can lead one list without appearing on another. The chart shows that directly: three different bridges in three different countries hold the three records, and no name repeats.

questions.q:
span: A span is the distance a bridge crosses between two supports.
causeway: A causeway is a raised road or bridge built across water or wet ground.
Describe the connection between building supports and how long a bridge can be.
questions.a: Because a bridge resting on many supports can simply repeat the same short span as far as the budget allows, total length is a matter of cost, while the span between two towers is limited by what the structure itself can hold up.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "most of Danyang–Kunshan crosses farmland" or "engineers care most about the main span." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: Start School Later
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Explain how an author uses reasons and evidence to support particular points in a text.
 Spiral: RI.4.1 details and inferences · RI.4.2 main idea · RI.4.4 word meaning · RI.4.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: Most American middle schools begin before 8:00 a.m. They should begin after 8:30, and the reasons have little to do with whether students are willing to go to bed.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first reason is biological. At puberty the body clock shifts later by about two hours. A thirteen-year-old told to sleep at 9:00 p.m. is being asked to fall asleep at what her body reads as 7:00. This shift is measurable in hormone levels and is not a matter of discipline.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second reason is safety. Crash rates for teenage drivers fall when start times move later. One district that shifted from 7:20 to 8:40 recorded 70 percent fewer teen crashes in the following two years.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The third reason is academic. Schools that delayed start times report higher attendance and fewer first-period failures. The gains are largest for students who ride the earliest buses.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The usual objection is athletics and bus scheduling. Both are real costs. Districts that made the change solved them by running buses in a different order and moving practice to mornings for some teams.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Costs that can be scheduled around are not the same as reasons to keep a start time that fights student biology every morning.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first reason is biology. At puberty the body clock shifts about two hours later. A thirteen-year-old told to sleep at 9:00 p.m. is being asked to sleep at what her body reads as 7:00.

paras.label: C

paras.label: D
paras.text: The third reason is school work. Schools that started later report better attendance and fewer first-period failures. The biggest gains go to students on the earliest buses.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The usual objection is sports and buses. Both are real costs. Districts fixed them by running buses in a different order and moving some practices to mornings.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Costs you can schedule around are not the same as reasons to keep a start time that fights student biology.

questions.q: Which reason has the strongest evidence behind it, and why?
questions.a: The safety reason. It offers a specific number from a specific district: a shift from 7:20 to 8:40 followed by 70 percent fewer teen crashes over two years. The academic reason reports a direction but gives no figures.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. biology) and paragraph E (i.e. objection).
Explain how the author uses reasons and evidence to support the claim.
questions.a: The author states the claim in paragraph A, then gives three reasons in order: a biological shift measurable in hormones, a crash-rate drop of 70 percent in one district, and better attendance with fewer first-period failures. Paragraph E then names the strongest objection and shows how districts solved it, so the claim is left standing.

questions.q:
biological: Biological means having to do with how a living body works, not with choices a person makes.
objection: An objection is a reason someone gives against an idea.
Describe the connection between the body clock shifting and an early start time being hard.
questions.a: Because puberty moves the body clock about two hours later, a teenager cannot fall asleep at the hour an early start requires, so the early bell costs sleep no matter what time she goes to bed.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "the shift is measurable in hormone levels" or "gains are largest for students on the earliest buses." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: Keep the Library Open on Sundays
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Explain how an author uses reasons and evidence to support particular points in a text.
 Spiral: RI.4.1 details and inferences · RI.4.2 main idea · RI.4.4 word meaning · RI.4.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: The city council has proposed closing the public library on Sundays to save money. The proposal would save less than it appears to and cost more than it admits.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Start with the savings. Sunday hours cost the library about $41,000 a year, which is under one percent of its budget. Closing would not solve the shortfall the council is trying to close.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Now the use. Sunday is the branch’s second-busiest day. The circulation desk counts an average of 610 visitors, compared with 380 on a typical Tuesday. Those visitors are not distributed evenly: most arrive between noon and 4:00.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Sunday is also the only day many patrons can come. Of the adults surveyed at the door, 44 percent said they work weekdays and cannot reach the library before it closes at 6:00.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The council argues that the bookmobile can absorb the demand. The bookmobile holds roughly 800 items and has no computers, no study rooms, and no staff librarian. The branch holds 94,000 items.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A one percent saving that removes the busiest access day for working adults is not a saving. It is a shift of the cost onto the people who have the fewest alternatives.

questions.q: Use the chart to explain why the author calls the bookmobile an inadequate replacement.
questions.a: The chart contrasts 800 items in the bookmobile with 94,000 in the branch, and notes the bookmobile has no computers, study rooms, or staff librarian. It cannot absorb what the branch provides, so the objection does not hold.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. demand) and paragraph E (i.e. substitute).
Explain how the author uses reasons and evidence to argue against the closure.
questions.a: The author gives three reasons, each with a number. The saving is $41,000, under one percent of the budget. Sunday draws 610 visitors against 380 on a Tuesday. Forty-four percent of adults surveyed cannot come on weekdays at all. Paragraph E then answers the council’s bookmobile proposal by comparing 800 items to 94,000.

questions.q:
circulation: Circulation is the counting and lending of library items, and the desk where that happens.
patrons: Patrons are the people who use a library or other public service.
Describe the connection between weekday work hours and Sunday library use.
questions.a: Because 44 percent of adults surveyed work while the library is open on weekdays, Sunday is the only day they can get there, which is why the second-busiest day would vanish rather than move.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "most Sunday visitors arrive between noon and 4:00" or "the branch closes at 6:00." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: Ban Plastic Bags? Read the Numbers First
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Explain how an author uses reasons and evidence to support particular points in a text.
 Spiral: RI.4.1 details and inferences · RI.4.2 main idea · RI.4.4 word meaning · RI.4.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: Cities that ban thin plastic grocery bags usually expect two results: less plastic in landfills and fewer bags in waterways. The first result is not what happens.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The reason is substitution. When the thin bags disappear, shoppers buy thicker reusable plastic bags and, separately, more small trash-can liners. A thin grocery bag weighs about 5 grams. A thick reusable plastic bag weighs about 80 grams.

paras.label: C
paras.text: One study of a large California ban found that plastic bag weight dropped by 40 million pounds a year, and that purchases of trash bags rose by 12 million pounds in the same area. The net reduction was real but far smaller than the headline number.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The second result, however, holds up. Litter surveys after bans consistently find fewer plastic bags in storm drains, on beaches, and in the stomachs of seabirds and turtles. A thicker bag that gets reused does not blow into a creek.

paras.label: E
paras.text: So the honest case for a bag ban is not mainly about landfill volume. It is about what escapes the waste stream, where a 5-gram bag does damage out of all proportion to its weight.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Arguing for the wrong reason is risky. When the landfill claim fails, opponents use the failure to dismiss the litter evidence, which is the stronger part of the case.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Cities that ban thin plastic grocery bags expect two results: less plastic in landfills and fewer bags in waterways. The first one does not happen.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The reason is substitution. When thin bags disappear, shoppers buy thicker reusable bags and more small trash-can liners. A thin bag weighs about 5 grams. A thick reusable bag weighs about 80 grams.

paras.label: C
paras.text: One study of a large California ban found plastic bag weight dropped by 40 million pounds a year, while trash bag purchases rose by 12 million pounds. The real drop was much smaller than the headline.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The second result holds up. Litter surveys after bans find fewer bags in storm drains, on beaches, and in the stomachs of seabirds and turtles.

paras.label: E
paras.text: So the honest case for a bag ban is not about landfill volume. It is about what escapes into the environment, where a 5-gram bag does great damage.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Arguing for the wrong reason is risky. When the landfill claim fails, opponents use it to dismiss the litter evidence, which is stronger.

questions.q: Use the chart to explain why the author calls Claim A weakened.
questions.a: The ban removed 40 million pounds of bag plastic but shoppers bought 12 million pounds more trash bags, and the replacement bags weigh about 80 grams against 5 grams. The reduction is real but much smaller than the headline figure suggests.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. substitution) and paragraph D (i.e. litter).
Explain how the author treats the two reasons differently.
questions.a: The author tests each reason against evidence. The landfill reason is weakened by the study showing trash-bag purchases rising and by the weight comparison between a 5-gram bag and an 80-gram one. The litter reason is supported by consistent survey findings in drains, on beaches, and in wildlife, so the author keeps it and drops the other.

questions.q:
substitution: Substitution is replacing one thing with another. Here, shoppers replace thin bags with thicker ones.
net: A net amount is what is left after gains and losses are counted together.
Describe the connection between arguing a weak reason and losing a strong one.
questions.a: Because opponents can disprove the landfill claim with the trash-bag numbers, they can then treat the whole argument as unreliable, and the litter evidence that the data does support gets dismissed along with it.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "a reused bag does not blow into a creek" or "opponents use the failed claim to dismiss the rest." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: Recess Is Not a Reward
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Explain how an author uses reasons and evidence to support particular points in a text.
 Spiral: RI.4.1 details and inferences · RI.4.2 main idea · RI.4.4 word meaning · RI.4.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: In many schools recess is withheld as a punishment for unfinished work or misbehavior. The practice takes the thing a struggling student most needs and removes it exactly when it is needed.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Consider what recess does. Physical activity raises blood flow to the brain and improves attention on the task that follows. Studies of elementary classrooms find measurable gains in on-task behavior in the twenty minutes after a break.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Now consider who loses recess. It is rarely the student who finished early. The students who lose it most often are the ones with attention difficulties, which is the group whose attention improves the most from movement.

paras.label: D
paras.text: There is also a fairness problem. Recess is the only part of the school day that is not academic, so taking it removes a student’s only chance to practice negotiating, taking turns, and settling a dispute without an adult.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Teachers who stop using recess as leverage need a replacement, and the honest answer is that consequences take longer that way. A conversation costs more minutes than a withheld recess.

paras.label: F
paras.text: But the minutes are spent on the problem instead of on making the next hour of the day harder for everyone in the room.

paras.text: In many schools recess is taken away as a punishment for unfinished work. The practice removes the thing a struggling student most needs, right when it is needed.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Consider what recess does. Moving raises blood flow to the brain and improves attention on the next task. Studies find real gains in on-task behavior in the twenty minutes after a break.

paras.label: C

paras.label: D
paras.text: There is also a fairness problem. Recess is the only part of the day that is not academic. Taking it removes a student’s only chance to practice taking turns and settling a dispute without an adult.

paras.label: E

paras.label: F
paras.text: But those minutes are spent on the problem instead of making the next hour harder for everyone.

questions.q: Use the chart to explain why the author calls the practice backwards.
questions.a: Reason 1 says attention improves in the twenty minutes after a break, and Reason 2 says the students who lose recess most often are those with attention difficulties. So recess is taken from exactly the students whose attention it would help most.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. mismatch) and paragraph E (i.e. cost).
Explain how the author supports the claim and handles the cost of it.
questions.a: The author gives three reasons: movement improves on-task behavior afterward, the students who lose recess are the ones who benefit most, and recess is the only non-academic time in the day. Paragraph E then admits the real cost, that a conversation takes longer than a withheld recess, and argues the minutes are better spent.

questions.q:
leverage: Leverage is something you hold over a person to make them do what you want.
negotiating: Negotiating is working out an agreement with someone by talking it through.
Describe the connection between physical activity and the work that follows a break.
questions.a: Because moving raises blood flow to the brain, students return to their seats better able to hold attention, so the twenty minutes after recess are measurably more productive than the same minutes without it.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "physical activity raises blood flow to the brain" or "a conversation costs more minutes." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: Why This Town Says No to a New Stadium
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Explain how an author uses reasons and evidence to support particular points in a text.
 Spiral: RI.4.1 details and inferences · RI.4.2 main idea · RI.4.4 word meaning · RI.4.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: A team owner has asked the city for $180 million toward a new stadium, promising jobs and downtown business. Nearly every study of past stadium deals says the promise does not arrive.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The jobs argument comes first. Stadium construction does create work, but it ends. Permanent stadium jobs are mostly part-time and seasonal: ushers, concessions, cleaning. Economists who have reviewed dozens of these deals find no measurable increase in regional employment.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The spending argument is the weaker one. Money spent at a game is not new money. A family that buys tickets is a family that did not spend that evening at a restaurant or a bowling alley in the same city. The dollars move; they do not multiply.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The cost, meanwhile, is fixed and public. $180 million is roughly what this city spends on street maintenance in nine years.

paras.label: E
paras.text: There is a genuine argument on the other side, and it is not economic. A team can be part of how a city sees itself, and that is worth something real that no study measures well.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A city may reasonably decide to pay for that. It should decide knowing it is buying identity, not jobs.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A team owner has asked the city for $180 million toward a new stadium, promising jobs and downtown business. Nearly every study of past deals says the promise does not arrive.

paras.label: B

paras.label: D
paras.text: The cost is fixed and public. $180 million is about what this city spends on street repair in nine years.

questions.q: Use the chart to explain why the author calls the spending promise the weaker one.
questions.a: Money spent at a game is not new money. A family buying tickets is not spending that evening at a local restaurant or bowling alley, so the dollars shift between businesses in the same city rather than adding up to more.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. shifting) and paragraph E (i.e. identity).
Explain how the author uses evidence to separate the strong argument from the weak ones.
questions.a: The author tests each promise. Jobs fail because construction work ends and permanent positions are part-time, with economists finding no regional gain. New spending fails because ticket dollars move from other local businesses. The $180 million cost is compared to nine years of street maintenance. Only the civic-identity argument survives, and the author concedes it is not economic.

questions.q:
permanent: Permanent means lasting. A permanent job continues after construction is finished.
civic: Civic means having to do with a city and the people who live in it.
Describe the connection between a family buying tickets and a nearby restaurant losing business.
questions.a: Because a family has one evening and one entertainment budget, the money it spends at the stadium is money it does not spend at a restaurant or bowling alley nearby, so the city’s total spending stays about the same.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "construction jobs end" or "$180 million equals nine years of street maintenance." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: Two Texts: Wolves Return to Yellowstone
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Integrate information from two texts on the same topic in order to write or speak about the subject knowledgeably.
 Spiral: RI.4.1 details and inferences · RI.4.2 main idea · RI.4.4 word meaning · RI.4.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: TEXT 1 · From a park history. Wolves were hunted out of Yellowstone by 1926. For nearly seventy years the park had none. In 1995 and 1996, fourteen wolves from Canada were released into the Lamar Valley.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The elk population had grown to roughly 19,000 and was browsing young willow and aspen faster than the trees could grow. Streambanks, held together by those roots, were collapsing.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Within fifteen years the elk herd fell by more than half. Willow returned along several creeks. Beaver colonies, which had dropped to one, rose to nine.

paras.label: D
paras.text: TEXT 2 · From an ecologist’s essay. The Yellowstone wolf story is usually told as a chain: wolves ate elk, willows grew back, rivers healed. The chain is real in places and overstated everywhere else.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Elk numbers fell partly from wolves and partly from drought, bear predation on calves, and a deliberate increase in hunting outside the park. Assigning the whole drop to wolves ignores three other pressures acting at once.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Willow recovery also varied. Where groundwater stayed high, willow returned strongly. Where it did not, willow stayed short even with no elk browsing. Wolves changed the system. They did not run it alone.

paras.label: A

paras.label: B
