paras.label: C
paras.text: Within fifteen years the elk herd fell by more than half. Willow came back along several creeks. Beaver colonies rose from one to nine.

paras.label: D
paras.text: TEXT 2 · From an ecologist’s essay. The wolf story is usually told as a chain: wolves ate elk, willows grew back, rivers healed. The chain is real in some places and overstated in others.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Elk numbers fell partly from wolves and partly from drought, bears eating calves, and more hunting outside the park. Giving wolves all the credit ignores three other causes.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Willow recovery varied too. Where groundwater stayed high, willow grew back strongly. Where it did not, willow stayed short even with no elk. Wolves changed the system, but not alone.

questions.q: Using both texts, explain why the elk population fell.
questions.a: Text 1 shows the herd dropping by more than half after wolves returned. Text 2 adds that drought, bears preying on calves, and increased hunting outside the park were acting at the same time, so wolves were one cause among several rather than the only one.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. recovery) and paragraph E (i.e. causes).
Combine both texts into an accurate summary of what wolves did to Yellowstone.
questions.a: Fourteen wolves were returned in 1995 and 1996 to a park that had none since 1926, where 19,000 elk were browsing willow faster than it grew. The herd then fell by more than half, willow returned along several creeks, and beaver colonies rose from one to nine. The second text shows the drop also owed to drought, bear predation, and hunting, and that willow only recovered fully where groundwater stayed high.

questions.q:
predation: Predation is one animal hunting and eating another.
groundwater: Groundwater is water held in the soil below the surface, which plant roots reach.
Describe the connection between elk browsing and collapsing streambanks.
questions.a: Because elk ate young willow faster than it could grow, the roots that held the soil along the creeks never developed, and the banks lost the structure that kept them from falling in.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "beaver colonies rose from one to nine" or "willow stayed short where groundwater was low." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: Two Texts: The Lost Colony of Roanoke
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Integrate information from two texts on the same topic in order to write or speak about the subject knowledgeably.
 Spiral: RI.4.1 details and inferences · RI.4.2 main idea · RI.4.4 word meaning · RI.4.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: TEXT 1 · From a school history. In 1587, about 115 English colonists settled on Roanoke Island. Their governor, John White, sailed back to England for supplies that same year.

paras.label: B
paras.text: War with Spain delayed his return for three years. When White finally landed in 1590, the settlement was empty. The houses had been taken down carefully rather than burned.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The word CROATOAN was carved into a post. White had arranged in advance that a carved cross would mean the colonists left in distress. There was no cross.

paras.label: D
paras.text: TEXT 2 · From a recent archaeology report. Croatoan was a real place and a real people, on what is now Hatteras Island, fifty miles south. Excavations there have recovered English items in layers dated to the right period.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The finds include a sword hilt, a slate writing tablet with a lead pencil, and fragments of English pottery, mixed with Native tools in the same layer rather than in a separate English area.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Mixed layers suggest people living together rather than trading at a distance. The evidence is suggestive, not conclusive: English goods also moved along trade routes without their owners.

paras.label: A
paras.text: TEXT 1 · From a school history. In 1587, about 115 English colonists settled on Roanoke Island. Their governor, John White, sailed back to England for supplies that year.

paras.label: B
paras.text: War with Spain delayed his return for three years. When White landed in 1590, the settlement was empty. The houses had been taken down carefully, not burned.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The word CROATOAN was carved into a post. White had arranged that a carved cross would mean the colonists left in danger. There was no cross.

paras.label: D
paras.text: TEXT 2 · From a recent archaeology report. Croatoan was a real place and a real people, on what is now Hatteras Island, fifty miles south. Digs there found English items from the right period.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The finds include a sword hilt, a slate writing tablet with a pencil, and English pottery, mixed with Native tools in the same layer.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Mixed layers suggest people living together, not trading from far away. The evidence is suggestive, not proof: English goods also traveled without their owners.

questions.q: Using both texts, explain why the carved word matters more than it first appears.
questions.a: Text 1 shows CROATOAN carved without the agreed distress cross, suggesting a planned departure to a named place. Text 2 shows Croatoan was a real people on Hatteras Island, where English objects turn up in dated layers, so the carving points somewhere the evidence can be checked.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. signal) and paragraph F (i.e. caution).
Integrate both texts into what can reasonably be said about the colony.
questions.a: About 115 colonists settled Roanoke in 1587 and were gone when their governor returned in 1590, leaving dismantled houses and the word CROATOAN carved without the agreed distress cross. Excavations on Hatteras, once Croatoan, have found a sword hilt, a slate tablet, and English pottery mixed with Native tools in period layers. That fits colonists living among the Croatoan, though trade could also carry such goods.

questions.q:
excavations: Excavations are careful digs made to uncover and study buried objects.
conclusive: Conclusive evidence settles a question. Suggestive evidence only points toward an answer.
Describe the connection between the war with Spain and the colony being lost.
questions.a: Because the war held White in England for three years instead of months, the colonists had to act on their own, and by the time he returned no one remained to explain where they had gone or why.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "the houses were taken down rather than burned" or "English goods moved along trade routes." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: Two Texts: Should Zoos Exist?
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Integrate information from two texts on the same topic in order to write or speak about the subject knowledgeably.
 Spiral: RI.4.1 details and inferences · RI.4.2 main idea · RI.4.4 word meaning · RI.4.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: TEXT 1 · From a conservation organization. Forty-one species now alive exist only because of zoos. The Arabian oryx was extinct in the wild in 1972 and was returned to the desert from zoo-bred herds.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Accredited zoos contribute about $230 million a year to field conservation. They also hold breeding populations for species whose wild habitat is not currently safe, which buys time that habitat work requires.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Public contact matters as well. Surveys find that visitors leave with greater knowledge of local species and higher stated willingness to support conservation funding.

paras.label: D
paras.text: TEXT 2 · From an animal-welfare researcher. The conservation figures are accurate and describe a small share of what zoos do. Of species held in accredited zoos, fewer than one in ten are part of any reintroduction program.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The welfare question is separate from the conservation question. Elephants in zoos show shortened lifespans and repetitive pacing behaviors. Large carnivores with wide natural ranges fare worst; small, territorial species often fare well.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A defensible zoo is not one that holds every animal a crowd expects. It is one that holds the animals it can house properly and sends the rest of its money into the field.

paras.label: A
paras.text: TEXT 1 · From a conservation group. Forty-one species alive today exist only because of zoos. The Arabian oryx was gone from the wild in 1972 and was returned to the desert from zoo-bred herds.

paras.label: B

paras.label: C
paras.text: Public contact matters too. Surveys find visitors leave knowing more about local species and more willing to support conservation.

paras.label: D

paras.label: E
paras.text: Welfare is a separate question. Elephants in zoos live shorter lives and pace repeatedly. Large carnivores with wide ranges do worst; small territorial species often do well.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A good zoo is not one that holds every animal a crowd expects. It is one that holds the animals it can house well.

questions.q: Using both texts, explain why the two authors do not actually contradict each other.
questions.a: Text 2 states that Text 1’s conservation figures are accurate. It argues they cover a small share of zoo activity, since fewer than one in ten species are in release programs, and it raises welfare, a separate question that Text 1 never addresses.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. funding) and paragraph E (i.e. welfare).
Integrate both texts into a balanced position on zoos.
questions.a: Zoos have kept 41 species alive, returned the Arabian oryx to the desert, and send about $230 million a year into the field, and visitors leave more willing to support conservation. But fewer than one in ten species held are part of any reintroduction program, and welfare varies sharply: elephants and wide-ranging carnivores do badly while small territorial species do well. The defensible zoo keeps the animals it can house properly.

questions.q:
accredited: An accredited zoo has been inspected and approved against a set of standards.
reintroduction: Reintroduction is returning animals raised in captivity to live in the wild again.
Describe the connection between an animal’s natural range and how it does in a zoo.
questions.a: Because a species that normally travels many miles cannot be given that distance in an enclosure, wide-ranging animals like elephants and large carnivores show pacing and shortened lives, while species that naturally hold a small territory find an enclosure closer to normal.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "the oryx was extinct in the wild in 1972" or "small territorial species often fare well." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: Two Texts: The Dust Bowl
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Integrate information from two texts on the same topic in order to write or speak about the subject knowledgeably.
 Spiral: RI.4.1 details and inferences · RI.4.2 main idea · RI.4.4 word meaning · RI.4.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: TEXT 1 · Oral history, recorded 1978. "April 14, 1935. We called it Black Sunday afterward. The morning was clear and warm and people hung wash out."

paras.label: B
paras.text: "The cloud came from the north and it was not a rain cloud. It was two thousand feet high and it was brown. My mother put wet sheets over the windows and it still came in. You could not see a lamp across the room."

paras.label: C
paras.text: "We had six good years on that land before that. People say the farmers should have known. Nobody told us. The government men came out and taught contour plowing in 1937, two years after."

paras.label: D
paras.text: TEXT 2 · From an agricultural history. The southern Plains were grassland whose deep roots held the soil through drought cycles that recurred every twenty years or so.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Between 1925 and 1930, tractor farming broke roughly 5 million acres of that sod for wheat. Wheat roots are shallow and annual. When the drought arrived on schedule in 1931, there was nothing holding the soil.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Federal soil-conservation programs began in 1935 and taught contour plowing, terracing, and shelterbelts. By 1938 soil loss in demonstration counties had fallen by 65 percent.

paras.label: A
paras.text: TEXT 1 · Oral history, recorded 1978. "April 14, 1935. We called it Black Sunday after. The morning was clear and warm and people hung wash out."

paras.label: B
paras.text: "The cloud came from the north and it was not a rain cloud. It was two thousand feet high and brown. My mother put wet sheets over the windows and it still came in."

paras.label: C
paras.text: "We had six good years on that land before that. People say the farmers should have known. Nobody told us. The government men came and taught contour plowing in 1937, two years after."

paras.label: D
paras.text: TEXT 2 · From an agricultural history. The southern Plains were grassland whose deep roots held the soil through droughts that came about every twenty years.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Between 1925 and 1930, tractors broke about 5 million acres of that sod for wheat. Wheat roots are shallow. When the drought came in 1931, nothing held the soil.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Federal soil programs began in 1935 and taught contour plowing and shelterbelts. By 1938 soil loss in those counties had dropped by 65 percent.

questions.q: Use the timeline to explain why the good years came before the disaster.
questions.a: The sod broken between 1925 and 1930 grew wheat well while the rain held, which is the six good years the speaker remembers. The drought returned on its usual cycle in 1931, and because wheat roots are shallow there was nothing left holding the soil.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. blame) and paragraph E (i.e. plowing).
Integrate both texts to explain what caused the Dust Bowl.
questions.a: Deep-rooted grassland had carried the southern Plains through droughts recurring every twenty years or so. Tractors broke about 5 million acres of that sod for shallow-rooted wheat between 1925 and 1930, which produced the six good years the speaker recalls. When drought returned in 1931 nothing held the soil, and by Black Sunday in 1935 a brown cloud two thousand feet high crossed the region. Conservation programs begun that year cut soil loss 65 percent by 1938.

questions.q:
sod: Sod is the top layer of soil held together by grass roots.
contour plowing: Contour plowing means plowing across a slope instead of up and down it, so water and soil stay put.
Describe the connection between shallow wheat roots and soil blowing away.
questions.a: Because wheat roots are shallow and die back each year, they could not grip the soil the way grass roots had, so when drought dried the surface there was nothing to hold it and the wind lifted it.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "wet sheets over the windows" or "drought cycles recurred every twenty years." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: Two Texts: Sleep and Memory
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Integrate information from two texts on the same topic in order to write or speak about the subject knowledgeably.
 Spiral: RI.4.1 details and inferences · RI.4.2 main idea · RI.4.4 word meaning · RI.4.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: TEXT 1 · From a science magazine. Sleep is when the brain files what it learned. During deep sleep, patterns of activity recorded in the hippocampus during the day are replayed, faster, and copied into longer-term storage in the cortex.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Experiments show the effect plainly. Students taught a list of word pairs and then allowed to sleep recall about 40 percent more than students taught at the same hour and kept awake the same length of time.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The same holds for physical skills. Typing a new finger sequence improves overnight without further practice, and the improvement shows up in sleep, not in the hours of wakefulness before it.

paras.label: D
paras.text: TEXT 2 · From a sleep laboratory’s guidance for schools. The replay finding is robust, and it is often used to argue that students should simply sleep more. The harder part is that not all sleep does this work equally.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Deep sleep is concentrated in the first half of the night; the REM sleep tied to skill and emotional memory clusters in the last two hours before waking. A student who sleeps seven hours instead of nine does not lose a slice of each. She loses most of her REM.

paras.label: F
paras.text: This is why a shortened night hurts skill learning more than fact learning, and why sleeping in on weekends does not repay the debt evenly.

paras.label: A
paras.text: TEXT 1 · From a science magazine. Sleep is when the brain files what it learned. In deep sleep, patterns recorded during the day are replayed faster and copied into longer-term storage.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Experiments show it clearly. Students taught word pairs and then allowed to sleep recall about 40 percent more than students kept awake for the same time.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The same holds for skills. Typing a new finger pattern improves overnight without more practice, and the gain shows up during sleep.

paras.label: D
paras.text: TEXT 2 · From a sleep lab’s guidance for schools. The replay finding is solid, and it is used to argue that students should sleep more. The harder part is that not all sleep does this work equally.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Deep sleep comes in the first half of the night. The REM sleep tied to skills comes in the last two hours before waking. A student who sleeps seven hours instead of nine loses most of her REM, not a slice of each.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That is why a short night hurts skill learning more than fact learning.

questions.q: Use the diagram to explain why a short night hurts skill learning most.
questions.a: Deep sleep, which handles facts, falls in the first four hours and survives a short night. REM, which handles skills, is concentrated in hours eight and nine, so cutting two hours off the end removes most of the REM and leaves the fact-storing sleep nearly untouched.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. evidence) and paragraph E (i.e. timing).
Integrate both texts into advice you could give a student.
questions.a: Sleep replays the day’s patterns and copies them into long-term storage, which is why sleeping students recall about 40 percent more word pairs and why a typing sequence improves overnight. But the two kinds of sleep are not spread evenly: deep sleep runs early and REM runs in the last two hours. Cutting a night short removes mostly REM, so a student practicing a skill loses more than one studying facts.

questions.q:
hippocampus: The hippocampus is the part of the brain that records new experiences before they are stored long term.
robust: A robust finding is one that holds up when the experiment is repeated.
Describe the connection between sleeping and getting better at a skill without practicing.
questions.a: Because the brain replays the finger sequence during sleep rather than during waking hours, the movement is rehearsed internally overnight, so performance improves by morning even though no additional practice took place.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "replay runs faster than the original" or "weekend sleep does not repay the debt evenly." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: The Seed Vault in the Ice
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of year, read and comprehend informational texts, including history/social studies, science, and technical texts, in the grades 4–5 text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.
 Spiral: RI.4.1 details and inferences · RI.4.2 main idea · RI.4.3 events and procedures · RI.4.4 word meaning · RI.4.7 visual information
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: On a Norwegian island 800 miles from the North Pole, a concrete entrance juts out of a mountainside. Behind it, a tunnel runs 400 feet into permafrost.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The Svalbard Global Seed Vault holds backup copies of crop seeds from almost every country. More than a million samples are stored there, each sealed in a foil packet inside a labeled box.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The vault does not own the seeds. Each depositing country keeps ownership and can withdraw its own boxes at any time, the way a bank holds a safe-deposit box it cannot open.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The site was chosen for its cold. Even if the refrigeration fails, the surrounding permafrost keeps the chambers below freezing without power.

paras.label: E
paras.text: There has been one withdrawal. In 2015 researchers in Syria, cut off from their own gene bank by war, requested their deposits back. They grew the seeds elsewhere, harvested new ones, and returned fresh samples to Svalbard.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That sequence is the vault working exactly as designed. It is not a museum. It is a spare copy.

paras.label: A
paras.text: On a Norwegian island 800 miles from the North Pole, a concrete entrance sticks out of a mountainside. Behind it a tunnel runs 400 feet into frozen ground.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The Svalbard Global Seed Vault holds backup copies of crop seeds from almost every country. More than a million samples are stored there in sealed foil packets.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The vault does not own the seeds. Each country keeps its own boxes and can take them back, like a bank holding a box it cannot open.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The site was chosen for its cold. If the freezers fail, the frozen ground keeps the rooms below freezing without power.

paras.label: E

paras.label: F

questions.q: Use the diagram to explain why the vault was built inside a frozen mountain.
questions.a: The rock puts 400 feet between the seeds and any storm, flood, or conflict outside, and the surrounding permafrost keeps the chambers below freezing even if the refrigeration loses power.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. ownership) and paragraph E (i.e. withdrawal).
Summarize what the vault is for and how the Syrian withdrawal showed it working.
questions.a: The vault stores backup copies of more than a million crop seed samples from nearly every country, each still owned by its depositor. When war cut Syrian researchers off from their own gene bank in 2015, they withdrew their deposits, grew the seeds elsewhere, and returned fresh samples, which is the cycle the vault was designed for.

questions.q:
permafrost: Permafrost is ground that stays frozen all year, even in summer.
deposits: Deposits are things placed somewhere for safekeeping, to be taken back later.
Describe the connection between the location and what happens if the power fails.
questions.a: Because the chambers are surrounded by ground that never thaws, a power failure does not warm them, so the seeds stay frozen while repairs are made.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "800 miles from the North Pole" or "seeds are sealed in foil packets." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: The Sound of a Stadium
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of year, read and comprehend informational texts, including history/social studies, science, and technical texts, in the grades 4–5 text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.
 Spiral: RI.4.1 details and inferences · RI.4.2 main idea · RI.4.3 events and procedures · RI.4.4 word meaning · RI.4.7 visual information
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: A crowd of 70,000 people can be measured. At Arrowhead Stadium in Kansas City, the noise has reached 142 decibels, louder than a jet engine at close range.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Decibels do not work the way most numbers do. The scale is logarithmic: every increase of 10 means the sound is ten times more intense. A 120-decibel crowd is not slightly louder than a 110-decibel crowd. It is ten times as intense.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The shape of the building matters more than the size of the crowd. A bowl with a low roof traps sound and reflects it back down onto the field. An open stadium of the same capacity measures far quieter.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Teams have learned to use it. A visiting quarterback cannot be heard calling plays, so the offense must use silent signals, and false-start penalties rise.

paras.label: E
paras.text: There is a cost. Sustained exposure above 100 decibels damages hearing, and stadium workers are exposed for whole seasons rather than single afternoons.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Some clubs now issue earplugs to staff. Almost none issue them to fans, who generally decline.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A crowd of 70,000 people can be measured. At one stadium in Kansas City, the noise has reached 142 decibels, louder than a jet engine up close.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Decibels do not work like most numbers. Every increase of 10 means the sound is ten times more intense. A 120-decibel crowd is ten times as intense as a 110-decibel crowd.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The shape of the building matters more than the size of the crowd. A bowl with a low roof traps sound and sends it back down. An open stadium the same size is much quieter.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Teams use it. A visiting quarterback cannot be heard calling plays, so the offense uses silent signals and makes more mistakes.

paras.label: E
paras.text: There is a cost. Long exposure above 100 decibels damages hearing, and workers are there all season.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Some clubs give earplugs to staff. Almost none give them to fans.

questions.q: Use the chart to explain why 142 decibels is far worse than it sounds.
questions.a: The scale multiplies rather than adds. Every 10 decibels is ten times the intensity, so the gap from 100 to 142 is not a small step past the damage threshold but thousands of times more intense sound.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. architecture) and paragraph E (i.e. cost).
Summarize why some stadiums are louder than others and what that costs.
questions.a: Crowd size matters less than shape: a low-roofed bowl reflects sound back onto the field while an open stadium of the same capacity is far quieter. The noise helps the home team, because visiting offenses cannot hear play calls and make more errors. It also damages the hearing of workers exposed to it all season.

questions.q:
logarithmic: A logarithmic scale multiplies at each step instead of adding the same amount.
sustained: Sustained means kept up over a long period rather than happening once.
Describe the connection between a stadium’s roof and how loud it is.
questions.a: Because a low roof stops sound from escaping upward, the noise reflects back down onto the field and adds to what the crowd is producing, so the same number of people sound far louder than in an open stadium.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "false-start penalties rise" or "some clubs issue earplugs to staff." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: The Man Who Refused to Fly
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of year, read and comprehend informational texts, including history/social studies, science, and technical texts, in the grades 4–5 text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.
 Spiral: RI.4.1 details and inferences · RI.4.2 main idea · RI.4.3 events and procedures · RI.4.4 word meaning · RI.4.7 visual information
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1930s Britain, a stockbroker named Nicholas Winton planned a skiing holiday. A friend asked him instead to come to Prague and see what was happening to refugee families there.

paras.label: B
paras.text: He went. Czechoslovakia had already lost its border regions to Germany, and thousands of families had fled inland with nowhere to go and no country willing to take them.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Britain would admit children under seventeen, but only with a sponsor, a foster family, and a £50 guarantee for each child. Winton set up an office in a hotel and began collecting names.

paras.label: D
paras.text: He sent lists to newspapers, forged entry documents when the paperwork ran behind, and arranged eight trains. Six hundred sixty-nine children reached London.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A ninth train, carrying 250 children, was scheduled for September 1, 1939. Germany invaded Poland that morning and the borders closed. That train never left.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Winton told almost no one. His wife found the scrapbook of names in the attic in 1988, nearly fifty years later.

paras.text: In 1930s Britain, a stockbroker named Nicholas Winton planned a skiing holiday. A friend asked him instead to come to Prague and see what was happening to refugee families.

paras.label: B

paras.label: C
paras.text: Britain would take children under seventeen, but each needed a sponsor, a foster family, and a £50 payment. Winton set up an office in a hotel and started collecting names.

paras.label: D
paras.text: He sent lists to newspapers, forged papers when the paperwork was slow, and arranged eight trains. Six hundred sixty-nine children reached London.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A ninth train, carrying 250 children, was set for September 1, 1939. Germany invaded Poland that morning and the borders closed. That train never left.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Winton told almost no one. His wife found the scrapbook of names in the attic in 1988.

questions.q: Use the timeline to explain why Winton could not simply move all the children at once.
questions.a: Britain required a sponsor, a foster family, and a £50 guarantee for every single child, so each name on his list needed months of separate arrangements before that child could board a train.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. organizing) and paragraph E (i.e. the closing).
Summarize what Winton did and what stopped him.
questions.a: Winton went to Prague in 1938, opened an office in a hotel, and matched refugee children one at a time to the sponsors, foster families, and £50 guarantees Britain demanded. Eight trains carried 669 children to London. A ninth carrying 250 was due to leave on September 1, 1939, the morning Germany invaded Poland and the borders closed.

questions.q:
refugee: A refugee is someone forced to leave home to escape war or danger.
guarantee: A guarantee is a promise, often backed by money, that something will be covered.
Describe the connection between the invasion of Poland and the ninth train.
questions.a: Because the invasion that morning closed the borders the train had to cross, the 250 children who were already scheduled and approved could not leave, and the rescue ended where it stood.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "he forged entry documents" or "his wife found the scrapbook in 1988." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: What a Tree Ring Remembers
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of year, read and comprehend informational texts, including history/social studies, science, and technical texts, in the grades 4–5 text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.
 Spiral: RI.4.1 details and inferences · RI.4.2 main idea · RI.4.3 events and procedures · RI.4.4 word meaning · RI.4.7 visual information
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: Cut a tree across and you get a record. Each pale band and dark band together make one year of growth.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The width of a ring is a weather report. A wet year with good light produces a wide ring. A drought year produces a narrow one. A tree that lived 400 years carries 400 measurements.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Because every tree in a region shares the same weather, their patterns match. Scientists overlap the ring patterns of living trees with those in old beams and buried logs, extending the record back thousands of years.

paras.label: D
paras.text: That overlapping makes tree rings a calendar. A beam in a cliff dwelling can be dated to the exact year it was cut, not a century or a range.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The rings recorded something else in the American Southwest: a drought lasting from 1276 to 1299. Within that window, the large cliff settlements were abandoned.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The rings do not say the drought caused people to leave. They establish that the two happened at the same time, which is the kind of fact an argument has to start from.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Cut a tree across and you get a record. Each pale band and dark band together make one year of growth.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The width of a ring is a weather report. A wet year makes a wide ring. A dry year makes a narrow one. A tree that lived 400 years carries 400 measurements.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Every tree in an area shares the same weather, so their patterns match. Scientists overlap patterns from living trees, old beams, and buried logs to reach back thousands of years.

paras.label: D
paras.text: That overlap makes tree rings a calendar. A beam in a cliff dwelling can be dated to the exact year it was cut.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The rings recorded something else in the Southwest: a drought from 1276 to 1299. In those years the large cliff settlements were abandoned.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The rings do not say the drought made people leave. They show the two happened at the same time.

questions.q: Use the diagram to explain how rings from a living tree help date a wooden beam.
questions.a: Trees in one region share weather, so their ring patterns match. A scientist finds where the pattern in the beam lines up with the pattern in a living tree, which fixes the beam’s rings to known years and gives the exact year it was cut.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. overlapping) and paragraph F (i.e. caution).
Summarize what tree rings can and cannot tell us.
questions.a: Each ring records one year, and its width records whether that year was wet or dry, so a single tree holds centuries of weather. Overlapping patterns from living trees, beams, and buried logs turn that into a calendar accurate to the year, which showed a drought from 1276 to 1299 in the Southwest. The rings date that drought alongside the abandonment of the cliff settlements but do not prove it caused them.

questions.q:
drought: A drought is a long stretch of time with far less rain than usual.
abandoned: Abandoned means left behind and no longer lived in or used.
Describe the connection between two events happening at the same time and one causing the other.
questions.a: Because the rings only show that the drought and the abandonment fall in the same years, they establish timing rather than cause, and an argument about why people left has to add other evidence.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "a 400-year tree carries 400 measurements" or "a beam can be dated to the exact year." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: The Machine That Reads the Sea Floor
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of year, read and comprehend informational texts, including history/social studies, science, and technical texts, in the grades 4–5 text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.
 Spiral: RI.4.1 details and inferences · RI.4.2 main idea · RI.4.3 events and procedures · RI.4.4 word meaning · RI.4.7 visual information
 Lower range: LL 610 – 690

paras.label: A
paras.text: A survey ship looking for a wreck does not look. It listens.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A sonar unit towed behind the ship sends out a pulse of sound and measures how long the echo takes to return. Sound travels through seawater at about 1,500 meters per second, so the delay converts directly into depth.

paras.label: C
paras.text: One pulse gives one depth. A modern multibeam unit fans out hundreds of beams at once, sweeping a strip of sea floor as wide as the water is deep.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The ship then drives back and forth in overlapping lanes, the way a mower crosses a lawn. A search area of a few hundred square miles can take weeks.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The result is not a photograph. It is a grid of depths, colored by height, in which a wreck appears as a shape a few meters proud of a flat plain.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Most of what the sweep finds is not the target. Analysts sort through boulders, rock ridges, and containers lost off cargo ships before anything worth a second pass turns up.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A survey ship looking for a wreck does not look. It listens.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A sonar unit towed behind the ship sends out a pulse of sound and times the echo. Sound travels through seawater at about 1,500 meters per second, so the delay gives the depth.

paras.label: C
paras.text: One pulse gives one depth. A modern multibeam unit sends hundreds of beams at once, sweeping a strip of sea floor as wide as the water is deep.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The ship drives back and forth in overlapping lanes, like mowing a lawn. A few hundred square miles can take weeks.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The result is not a photo. It is a grid of depths, colored by height, where a wreck shows up as a shape a few meters above a flat plain.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Most of what the sweep finds is not the target. Analysts sort through boulders, rock ridges, and lost shipping containers first.

questions.q: Use the diagram to explain why the travel time is divided in half.
questions.a: The sound has to travel down to the sea floor and back up to the ship, so the measured time covers the distance twice. Halving it gives the one-way depth.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. sweeping) and paragraph F (i.e. sorting).
Summarize how a survey ship finds a wreck.
questions.a: Sonar sends pulses of sound to the bottom and times the echoes, converting the delay into depth at about 1,500 meters per second. A multibeam unit does this with hundreds of beams at once, covering a strip as wide as the water is deep, and the ship runs overlapping lanes until the area is mapped. The result is a colored depth grid in which analysts look for a shape standing a few meters above the flat sea floor.

questions.q:
sonar: Sonar finds objects underwater by sending out sound and timing the echo.
analysts: Analysts are people whose job is to study data carefully and decide what it shows.
Describe the connection between the width of one sweep and how long a search takes.
questions.a: Because each pass only covers a strip as wide as the water is deep, a shallow area needs far more lanes to cover the same ground, so the number of passes rather than the size of the ship sets how many weeks the search will run.

articles.note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "the ship works in overlapping lanes" or "lost containers show up in the data." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

articles.title: The Bees That Dance
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Quote accurately from a text when explaining what the text says explicitly and when drawing inferences from the text.
 Spiral: RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.3 relationships · RI.5.4 word meaning · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: A honeybee that finds a patch of flowers comes home with more than nectar. She carries a map. Back inside the dark hive, she climbs onto the honeycomb and begins to move in a pattern her sisters can feel through the wax.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The pattern is called a waggle dance. The bee runs forward in a straight line while shaking her body from side to side, loops back, and runs the same line again. Other workers crowd around her and press their antennae against her body.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The straight run carries the message. Its direction, measured against straight up on the vertical comb, tells the other bees the angle to fly relative to the sun. A run pointed straight up means fly toward the sun.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The length of the run tells distance. A longer waggle means a longer flight. A run lasting one second sends the hive roughly a kilometer from home, and the bees adjust for wind without being told.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Karl von Frisch spent decades watching marked bees through glass walls before he worked out what the dance meant. In 1973 he shared a Nobel Prize for it. Many scientists had assumed insects were too simple to pass along anything so exact.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The dance is not perfect. Bees make small errors, and the hive sends out scouts in slightly different directions as a result. Researchers now think the error is useful, because it spreads the search instead of crowding every forager onto one patch.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A honeybee finds a patch of flowers. She comes home with nectar. She also brings a map. Inside the dark hive she climbs onto the honeycomb and starts to move.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The move is called a waggle dance. The bee runs forward in a straight line. She shakes her body side to side. Then she loops back and runs the line again.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The straight run holds the message. Its direction tells the other bees which way to fly. A run that points straight up means fly toward the sun.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The length of the run tells how far. A longer waggle means a longer flight. One second of waggle means about one kilometer.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Karl von Frisch watched bees through glass walls for years. He worked out what the dance meant. He won a Nobel Prize in 1973.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The dance is not perfect. Bees make small errors. That may help them. The errors spread the search over more flowers.

questions.q: What two things does the waggle dance tell the other bees?
questions.a: The direction of the straight run tells them the angle to fly relative to the sun, and the length of the run tells them how far away the flowers are.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. direction) and paragraph D (i.e. distance).
Summarize how a honeybee tells the hive where she found flowers.
questions.a: She dances on the honeycomb, running in a straight line while waggling. The direction of the run gives the angle to the sun and its length gives the distance, so other workers can fly to the same patch.

questions.q:
waggle dance: the pattern a bee runs on the comb to tell other bees where flowers are.
forager: a bee that leaves the hive to collect nectar.
Describe the connection between the small errors in the dance and the hive's search for food.
questions.a: Because bees make small errors, scouts leave in slightly different directions, which spreads the search over more flowers instead of crowding every forager onto one patch.

articles.note: Students may quote any accurate detail, i.e. "a run lasting one second sends the hive roughly a kilometer from home." Check that the quote is copied exactly, which is what RI.5.1 asks for.

articles.title: The Pony Express
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Quote accurately from a text when explaining what the text says explicitly and when drawing inferences from the text.
 Spiral: RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.3 relationships · RI.5.4 word meaning · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: In April of 1860, a mail company promised something that sounded impossible. A letter would cross from Missouri to California in ten days. At the time, the fastest mail went by ship around South America and took close to a month.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The plan was a relay of riders. Stations stood roughly ten miles apart along a 1,900-mile trail. A rider galloped in, threw a leather mochila of mail over a fresh horse, and was gone again in two minutes.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Riders were chosen for being light. One advertisement asked for young, skinny, wiry fellows and added that orphans were preferred. Each man carried about twenty pounds of mail and almost nothing else, because weight slowed the horse.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The route crossed the Sierra Nevada in winter and the Great Basin in summer. Riders went through snowdrifts, dust storms, and territory where war had broken out between settlers and the Paiute. Some stations were burned before a rider reached them.

paras.label: E
paras.text: It worked. Lincoln's inaugural address reached Sacramento in seven days and seventeen hours, the fastest the country had ever moved news that far.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The company still failed. The telegraph line reached California in October of 1861, and a message that took ten days by horse took seconds by wire. The Pony Express shut down two days later, after eighteen months.

paras.label: A
paras.text: In April of 1860, a mail company made a promise. A letter would cross from Missouri to California in ten days. Before that, mail went by ship and took a month.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The plan was a relay of riders. Stations stood about ten miles apart. A rider rode in, threw his mail bag onto a fresh horse, and left in two minutes.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Riders had to be light. One ad asked for young, skinny, wiry men. Each rider carried about twenty pounds of mail and little else.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The trail was hard. Riders crossed deep snow in the mountains and dust in the desert. Some stations were burned before a rider got there.

paras.label: E
paras.text: It worked. Lincoln's speech reached Sacramento in seven days and seventeen hours. No news had ever moved that fast.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The company still failed. The telegraph reached California in 1861. A message took seconds by wire. The Pony Express closed two days later.

questions.q: Why did the Pony Express shut down?
questions.a: The telegraph line reached California in October of 1861, and a message that took ten days by horse took seconds by wire, so the company closed two days later.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. the relay) and paragraph F (i.e. the telegraph).
Summarize what the Pony Express was and how long it lasted.
questions.a: It was a relay of riders carrying mail 1,900 miles from Missouri to California in about ten days. Stations stood ten miles apart and riders changed horses in two minutes. It ran for eighteen months and closed when the telegraph arrived.

questions.q:
relay: a system in which each rider carries something part of the way and hands it on.
mochila: the leather mail bag a rider threw over a fresh horse.
Describe the connection between the weight a rider carried and the choice of riders.
questions.a: Weight slowed the horse, so the company wanted light riders and asked for young, skinny, wiry fellows who carried about twenty pounds of mail and almost nothing else.

articles.note: The eighteen months are worth drawing out: the Pony Express is remembered far better than it worked, and the text says plainly that the company failed.

articles.title: What a Leaf Loses in Autumn
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Quote accurately from a text when explaining what the text says explicitly and when drawing inferences from the text.
 Spiral: RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.3 relationships · RI.5.4 word meaning · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: A maple leaf in July is not simply green. It already holds yellow and orange pigments, but the green of chlorophyll is so strong in summer that nothing else shows through.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Chlorophyll is the chemical a leaf uses to turn sunlight into sugar. A tree rebuilds it constantly through the growing season, because sunlight breaks it down almost as fast as the leaf can make it.

paras.label: C
paras.text: As nights lengthen in autumn, the tree stops the rebuilding. A thin layer of cells forms where the leaf stalk meets the branch and begins to seal the connection. Water and nutrients no longer move freely in or out.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The green fades first, because nothing is replacing it. The yellow and orange pigments that were there all along are left behind, and the leaf appears to change color when in fact it is only losing one.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Red is different. Many trees make red pigments in autumn, using sugar trapped in the dying leaf. Bright, cool days produce the deepest reds, which is why one autumn is spectacular and the next is dull.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Finally the sealing layer finishes its work. The leaf falls, and the tree keeps the nutrients it pulled back from it. The color a person drives out to see is the last stage of the tree reclaiming what it can.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A maple leaf in July is not only green. It already holds yellow and orange. The green of chlorophyll is so strong that nothing else shows.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Chlorophyll turns sunlight into sugar. A tree makes it all summer long. Sunlight breaks it down almost as fast as the leaf can build it.

paras.label: C
paras.text: In autumn the nights get longer. The tree stops rebuilding chlorophyll. A thin layer of cells seals the leaf stalk to the branch.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The green fades first. Nothing replaces it. The yellow and orange were there all along. The leaf is not gaining a color. It is losing one.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Red is different. Many trees make red pigments in autumn from sugar in the leaf. Bright, cool days make the deepest reds.

paras.label: F
paras.text: At last the leaf falls. The tree keeps the nutrients it pulled back. The colors are the last stage of that work.

questions.q: Why does a leaf look green in summer even though yellow pigments are present?
questions.a: The green of chlorophyll is so strong in summer that nothing else shows through, because the tree rebuilds chlorophyll constantly through the growing season.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. losing green) and paragraph E (i.e. making red).
Summarize why leaves change color in autumn.
questions.a: As nights lengthen, the tree stops rebuilding chlorophyll and seals the leaf stalk. The green fades and the yellow and orange that were there all along show. Some trees also make red pigments from sugar trapped in the leaf.

questions.q:
chlorophyll: the green chemical a leaf uses to turn sunlight into sugar.
pigment: a substance that gives something its color.
Describe the connection between the sealing layer and the color of the leaf.
questions.a: The sealing layer stops water and nutrients from moving, so chlorophyll is no longer replaced and the green fades, which lets the yellow and orange show and traps the sugar used to make red.

articles.note: The common answer is that leaves turn yellow. The text says the opposite for yellow and orange: those were already there, and the leaf loses green. Red is the one that is genuinely made in autumn.

articles.title: Ellis Island
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Quote accurately from a text when explaining what the text says explicitly and when drawing inferences from the text.
 Spiral: RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.3 relationships · RI.5.4 word meaning · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: Between 1892 and 1954, about twelve million people entered the United States through a building on a small island in New York Harbor. Most of them had spent one to two weeks at sea to get there.

paras.label: B
paras.text: First and second class passengers were inspected on the ship and usually walked straight off onto the pier. Everyone in steerage, the cheapest section below deck, was ferried to Ellis Island instead.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The first test came before anyone spoke. Doctors watched arrivals climb a flight of stairs carrying their luggage, looking for anyone short of breath or limping. That climb was called the six-second physical.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Inspectors in the Great Hall asked a list of twenty-nine questions: name, trade, destination, how much money a person carried. The questions were meant to find out whether an arrival could support themselves.

paras.label: E
paras.text: About two in every hundred were sent back. The most common reasons were contagious disease and a judgment that a person was likely to need public support. Families were sometimes separated by that decision.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The island is a museum now. Its records are searchable, and many Americans can find the exact line where an ancestor's name, age and trade were written down by an inspector.

paras.label: A
paras.text: From 1892 to 1954, about twelve million people came into the United States through Ellis Island. It sat on a small island in New York Harbor. Most had been at sea for one or two weeks.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Rich passengers were checked on the ship. They walked straight off onto the pier. People in the cheapest part of the ship were taken to Ellis Island.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The first test came before anyone spoke. Doctors watched people climb the stairs with their bags. They looked for anyone short of breath.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Inspectors asked twenty-nine questions. They asked for a name, a trade, and a destination. They asked how much money a person had.

paras.label: E
paras.text: About two in every hundred were sent back. The usual reasons were illness or no way to earn a living. Some families were split up.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The island is a museum now. The records can be searched. Many Americans can find an ancestor's name on a page.

questions.q: Why were first and second class passengers treated differently from people in steerage?
questions.a: First and second class passengers were inspected on the ship and walked straight off onto the pier, while everyone in steerage was ferried to Ellis Island to be inspected there.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the stairs) and paragraph D (i.e. the questions).
Summarize what happened to an arrival at Ellis Island.
questions.a: A person in steerage was ferried to the island, watched by doctors while climbing the stairs, and then asked twenty-nine questions in the Great Hall about name, trade and money. About two in every hundred were sent back.

questions.q:
steerage: the cheapest section of a ship, below deck.
contagious: able to spread from one person to another.
Describe the connection between the stairs and the doctors' work.
questions.a: Doctors watched arrivals climb the stairs carrying luggage so they could spot anyone short of breath or limping, which is why the climb was called the six-second physical.

articles.note: Two in every hundred is worth putting on the board as a fraction. Students often picture Ellis Island as a place that turned people away, and the text says ninety-eight of every hundred went through.

articles.title: How a Volcano Builds an Island
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Quote accurately from a text when explaining what the text says explicitly and when drawing inferences from the text.
 Spiral: RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.3 relationships · RI.5.4 word meaning · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: The Hawaiian Islands sit in the middle of a tectonic plate, far from the edges where most volcanoes form. The reason is a hot spot: a column of unusually hot rock rising from deep inside the Earth.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The hot spot stays roughly in place. The Pacific Plate above it does not, drifting northwest at about the speed a fingernail grows, four inches a year.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Where the plate passes over the hot spot, magma burns through and erupts onto the seafloor. Cold water chills the lava instantly, and it piles up in rounded lobes called pillow lava, layer on layer.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Building an island this way takes hundreds of thousands of years. The pile must rise through three miles of ocean before any part of it breaks the surface and becomes land.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Then the plate carries the new island away from its source. Cut off from the magma, the volcano goes quiet, and waves and rain begin to wear it down faster than it can grow.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The whole chain records the process. Kauai, in the northwest, is old and deeply carved by valleys. The Big Island, still over the hot spot, is erupting. Southeast of it, a seamount is building toward the surface.

paras.label: A
paras.text: The Hawaiian Islands sit in the middle of a plate. Most volcanoes form at the edges. These islands form over a hot spot. That is a column of hot rock from deep inside the Earth.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The hot spot stays in one place. The plate above it moves. It drifts northwest about four inches a year.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Magma burns through the plate and erupts on the seafloor. Cold water chills the lava fast. It piles up in rounded lobes called pillow lava.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Building an island takes a very long time. The pile has to rise through three miles of ocean. Only then does it become land.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Then the plate carries the island away. The volcano goes quiet. Waves and rain wear it down.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The chain shows each step. Kauai is old and carved by valleys. The Big Island still erupts. A new seamount is rising to the southeast.

questions.q: Why are the Hawaiian Islands in the middle of a plate instead of at its edge?
questions.a: They form over a hot spot, a column of unusually hot rock rising from deep inside the Earth, rather than at the plate edges where most volcanoes form.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. the moving plate) and paragraph F (i.e. the chain).
Summarize how the hot spot builds a chain of islands.
questions.a: Magma from the hot spot erupts onto the seafloor and piles up until it breaks the surface. The plate then carries that island away, the volcano goes quiet, and a new one begins over the hot spot.

questions.q:
hot spot: a column of unusually hot rock rising from deep inside the Earth.
seamount: an underwater mountain that has not yet reached the surface.
Describe the connection between the moving plate and the ages of the islands.
questions.a: Because the plate drifts northwest while the hot spot stays in place, islands made earlier are carried away and worn down, so Kauai in the northwest is old while the Big Island is still erupting.

articles.note: Four inches a year is a useful number to compare with the age of the chain. Ask what else the class knows that moves at the speed a fingernail grows.

articles.title: The Erie Canal
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine two or more main ideas of a text and explain how they are supported by key details; summarize the text.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.3 relationships · RI.5.8 reasons and evidence · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1817, New York began digging a ditch four feet deep and forty feet wide across the width of the state. Critics in Washington called it Clinton's Ditch, after the governor who pushed it, and refused to pay for any of it.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The problem it solved was cost. Moving a ton of flour from Buffalo to New York City by wagon took three weeks and cost about a hundred dollars. The same ton by canal boat would cost less than ten.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Nobody in the country had built anything like it. The engineers were surveyors and lawyers who learned on the job, inventing a stump puller and a cement that would harden underwater because they could not buy either one.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The land itself was the obstacle. Lake Erie sits almost six hundred feet above the Hudson River, so the canal needed eighty-three locks, each one a chamber that raised or lowered a boat like a step.

paras.label: E
paras.text: It opened in 1825, eight years after the first shovel. Freight costs fell by ninety per cent, and towns strung along the route grew faster than almost anywhere else in the country.

paras.label: F
paras.text: New York City was the biggest winner. The canal made it the cheapest door to the whole interior of the continent, and within fifteen years it handled more trade than Boston, Baltimore and Philadelphia together.

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1817, New York began digging a ditch across the whole state. It was four feet deep and forty feet wide. Critics called it Clinton's Ditch. Washington would not pay for it.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The canal solved a cost problem. A ton of flour from Buffalo to New York City cost about a hundred dollars by wagon. By canal boat it would cost less than ten.

paras.label: C
paras.text: No one had built anything like it. The engineers were surveyors and lawyers. They learned on the job. They invented a stump puller and a cement that hardened underwater.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The land was the hard part. Lake Erie sits almost six hundred feet above the Hudson River. The canal needed eighty-three locks. Each lock raised or lowered a boat like a step.

paras.label: E
paras.text: It opened in 1825. Freight costs fell by ninety per cent. Towns along the route grew fast.

paras.label: F
paras.text: New York City won the most. The canal made it the cheapest door to the interior. Soon it handled more trade than three other big ports together.

questions.q: Name two main ideas of this article and one detail that supports each.
questions.a: One main idea is that the canal cut the cost of moving freight, supported by the ton of flour falling from about a hundred dollars to less than ten. Another is that the canal made New York City the country's busiest port, supported by its handling more trade than Boston, Baltimore and Philadelphia together.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. the cost) and paragraph D (i.e. the locks).
Summarize the Erie Canal in three sentences.
questions.a: New York dug a canal across the state between 1817 and 1825. It needed eighty-three locks to climb almost six hundred feet from the Hudson River to Lake Erie. Freight costs fell by ninety per cent and New York City became the cheapest door to the interior.

questions.q:
lock: a chamber on a canal that raises or lowers a boat like a step.
freight: goods carried from one place to another.
Describe the connection between the eighty-three locks and the height of Lake Erie.
questions.a: Lake Erie sits almost six hundred feet above the Hudson River, so the canal needed eighty-three locks to raise and lower boats that whole distance in steps.

articles.note: RI.5.2 asks for two or more main ideas. Accept any two the text supports, i.e. cost, engineering learned on the job, or the rise of New York City, so long as the student names a detail for each.

articles.title: The Owl's Silent Wing
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine two or more main ideas of a text and explain how they are supported by key details; summarize the text.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.3 relationships · RI.5.8 reasons and evidence · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: A pigeon taking off from a branch can be heard across a yard. A barn owl crossing the same yard is nearly silent, and the difference is in the feathers rather than the bird's care.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Noise in flight comes from turbulence. Air rolling off the sharp back edge of a wing breaks into swirls, and those swirls make the rushing sound a person hears when a bird passes overhead.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The leading edge of an owl's wing is not smooth. It carries a comb of stiff bristles that splits the oncoming air into smaller streams before it can build into one large, noisy swirl.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The back edge is frayed rather than sharp. It ends in a soft fringe that lets the separated streams rejoin gradually, and the wing surface itself is covered in a velvety down that absorbs the high notes.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The quiet costs the owl something. The same soft feathers soak up water, so owls hunt poorly in heavy rain, and the structures only work at the slow speeds an owl flies.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Engineers have copied the design. Serrated edges based on owl feathers now appear on wind turbine blades and aircraft landing gear, where they cut noise without changing how the surface carries a load.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A pigeon taking off can be heard across a yard. A barn owl is nearly silent. The difference is in its feathers, not in how carefully it flies.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Noise in flight comes from turbulence. Air rolls off the back edge of a wing. It breaks into swirls. Those swirls make the rushing sound.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The front edge of an owl's wing is not smooth. It has a comb of stiff bristles. The comb splits the air into smaller streams.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The back edge is frayed, not sharp. A soft fringe lets the streams join again slowly. The wing is also covered in velvety down.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The quiet costs the owl something. The soft feathers soak up water. Owls hunt poorly in heavy rain.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Engineers have copied the design. Wind turbine blades now use serrated edges like owl feathers. They cut the noise.

questions.q: Name two main ideas of this article and one detail that supports each.
questions.a: One main idea is that feathers rather than care make an owl quiet, supported by the comb of stiff bristles on the leading edge. Another is that the quiet has a cost, supported by the soft feathers soaking up water so owls hunt poorly in heavy rain.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the leading edge) and paragraph D (i.e. the back edge).
Summarize how an owl flies silently.
questions.a: A comb of stiff bristles on the leading edge splits the oncoming air into smaller streams, a soft fringe at the back lets them rejoin gradually, and velvety down absorbs the high notes, so no large noisy swirl ever forms.

questions.q:
turbulence: air breaking into swirls as it rolls off a wing.
serrated: having a row of small teeth or notches along an edge.
Describe the connection between the owl's feathers and the design of wind turbine blades.
questions.a: Engineers copied the serrated edges of owl feathers onto turbine blades because the same structure cuts noise without changing how the surface carries a load.

articles.note: Paragraph E is the one students skip. A good second main idea has to account for the cost of the quiet, not only the cleverness of it.

articles.title: The Boys Who Planted a Forest
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine two or more main ideas of a text and explain how they are supported by key details; summarize the text.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.3 relationships · RI.5.8 reasons and evidence · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1933, a quarter of American workers had no job. One of the first programs of the new administration put young men to work outdoors, in a corps that would last nine years and enroll about three million of them.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The deal was plain. A man between eighteen and twenty-five signed up for six months, lived in a camp, and earned thirty dollars a month. Twenty-five of those dollars were sent home to his family.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The work was the kind no company would pay for. Crews built trails, fought fires, strung telephone line, and cut the roads and shelters that turned raw land into usable state parks.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Above all they planted trees. The corps put roughly three billion seedlings into the ground, more than half of all the trees planted in the United States up to that time.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The camps taught as well as worked. Many enrollees arrived unable to read, and evening classes in the camps taught more than forty thousand men to do so before they went home.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The corps was not open to everyone equally. Camps were segregated by race after 1935, and women were excluded entirely, which belongs in the record alongside the trails and the trees.

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1933, a quarter of American workers had no job. A new program put young men to work outdoors. It lasted nine years. About three million men joined.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The deal was plain. A man signed up for six months. He lived in a camp. He earned thirty dollars a month. Twenty-five dollars went home to his family.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The work was the kind no company would pay for. Crews built trails and fought fires. They cut roads and built shelters in state parks.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Most of all they planted trees. The corps planted about three billion seedlings. That was more than half of all the trees planted in the country up to then.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The camps also taught. Many men arrived unable to read. Evening classes taught more than forty thousand of them to read.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The corps was not open to everyone. Camps were segregated by race after 1935. Women could not join at all.

questions.q: Name two main ideas of this article and one detail that supports each.
questions.a: One main idea is that the corps gave jobless young men work and pay, supported by the thirty dollars a month with twenty-five sent home. Another is that the work changed the land, supported by the roughly three billion seedlings the corps planted.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. the trees) and paragraph F (i.e. who was left out).
Summarize what the corps was and what it did.
questions.a: From 1933 it enrolled about three million young men for six months at a time, paying thirty dollars a month with twenty-five sent home. They built trails, fought fires and planted roughly three billion seedlings, and evening classes taught more than forty thousand of them to read.

questions.q:
corps: an organized body of people working together under one command.
segregated: kept apart by race.
Describe the connection between the pay a man earned and his family at home.
questions.a: A man earned thirty dollars a month and twenty-five of those dollars were sent home, so his family was supported by work he did in a camp far away.

articles.note: Paragraph F is deliberately not a footnote. A summary that leaves out the segregated camps has left out a main idea, not a detail.

articles.title: The Tide and the Moon
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine two or more main ideas of a text and explain how they are supported by key details; summarize the text.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.3 relationships · RI.5.8 reasons and evidence · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: Twice a day most coasts rise and fall by several feet. The cause is gravity, but not quite in the way most explanations suggest, because there are two bulges of water and only one moon.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The moon pulls hardest on the water nearest it, raising a bulge on that side of the Earth. It also pulls the solid Earth away from the water on the far side, which leaves a second bulge behind.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The Earth turns underneath those bulges. A given beach passes through both of them in a day, which is why most places get two high tides and two low tides in about twenty-five hours.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The sun pulls too, with less than half the effect. When sun and moon line up, the bulges add together into the large spring tides; when they sit at right angles, the smaller neap tides result.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Shape matters as much as gravity. In the open ocean the bulge is barely three feet high, but a funnel-shaped bay can squeeze it upward, and the Bay of Fundy regularly sees a range above fifty feet.

paras.label: F
paras.text: All that water moving twice a day carries energy. Tidal power stations in France and South Korea run turbines on the flow, and unlike wind or sun, the schedule is known for centuries ahead.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Twice a day most coasts rise and fall. Gravity is the cause. But there are two bulges of water and only one moon.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The moon pulls hardest on the water nearest it. That raises a bulge. It also pulls the Earth away from the water on the far side. That leaves a second bulge.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The Earth turns under those bulges. A beach passes through both in a day. That is why most places get two high tides and two low tides.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The sun pulls too, but less. When the sun and moon line up, the tides are large. When they sit at right angles, the tides are small.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Shape matters as well. In the open ocean the bulge is about three feet. A narrow bay can squeeze it higher. The Bay of Fundy sees more than fifty feet.

paras.label: F
paras.text: All that water carries energy. Tidal power stations run turbines on the flow. The schedule is known for centuries ahead.

questions.q: Name two main ideas of this article and one detail that supports each.
questions.a: One main idea is that the moon raises two bulges rather than one, supported by its pulling the solid Earth away from the water on the far side. Another is that the shape of a coast decides the size of a tide, supported by the Bay of Fundy's range above fifty feet.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. two bulges) and paragraph E (i.e. the shape of a bay).
Summarize what causes the tides.
questions.a: The moon raises a bulge of water on the near side of the Earth and leaves a second on the far side. The Earth turns through both, giving most coasts two high tides a day, and the sun and the shape of a bay make them larger or smaller.

questions.q:
bulge: a swelling of water raised by gravity.
range: the distance between high tide and low tide.
Describe the connection between the position of the sun and the size of a tide.
questions.a: When the sun and moon line up their pulls add together and the tides are large, and when they sit at right angles the tides are small.

articles.note: The second bulge is the part worth slowing down for. Most students will say the moon pulls the water up, which explains one high tide a day, not two.

articles.title: The Silk Road
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine two or more main ideas of a text and explain how they are supported by key details; summarize the text.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.3 relationships · RI.5.8 reasons and evidence · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: The Silk Road was never a road, and silk was only part of what moved along it. The name describes a web of routes that linked China to the Mediterranean for roughly fifteen hundred years.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Almost nobody travelled the whole distance. Goods changed hands at market after market, so a bolt of silk that began near Xi'an might pass through a dozen owners before a Roman bought it.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Each exchange raised the price. Silk in Rome cost many times what it cost in China, and Roman writers complained about the silver leaving the empire to pay for cloth.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Ideas travelled in the same packs. Paper making moved west from China, Buddhism moved east into China, and both arrived with traders rather than with armies.

paras.label: E
paras.text: So did disease. The plague that struck Europe in the fourteenth century is thought to have followed trade routes west, carried by fleas on rats in the holds and packs of merchants.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The routes faded when ships got better. Once Portuguese and later Dutch vessels could carry a cargo from Asia to Europe by sea, the overland journey cost more than it was worth.

paras.label: A
paras.text: The Silk Road was not a road. Silk was only part of what moved on it. The name means a web of routes. They linked China to the Mediterranean for about fifteen hundred years.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Almost no one travelled the whole way. Goods changed hands at market after market. A bolt of silk might pass through a dozen owners.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Each trade raised the price. Silk in Rome cost many times what it cost in China. Roman writers complained about the cost.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Ideas travelled too. Paper making moved west from China. Buddhism moved east into China. Traders carried both.

paras.label: E
paras.text: So did disease. The plague that struck Europe is thought to have followed the trade routes west. Fleas on rats carried it.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The routes faded when ships got better. Ships could carry cargo from Asia to Europe by sea. The overland journey cost too much.

questions.q: Name two main ideas of this article and one detail that supports each.
questions.a: One main idea is that goods changed hands many times rather than travelling with one merchant, supported by a bolt of silk passing through a dozen owners. Another is that more than goods moved, supported by paper making travelling west and Buddhism travelling east.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. ideas) and paragraph E (i.e. disease).
Summarize what the Silk Road was and why it faded.
questions.a: It was a web of overland routes linking China to the Mediterranean for about fifteen hundred years, along which goods, ideas and disease passed from market to market. It faded once ships could carry cargo from Asia to Europe more cheaply by sea.

questions.q:
overland: across land rather than by sea.
bolt: a long roll of cloth as it is sold.
Describe the connection between the number of times goods changed hands and the price of silk in Rome.
questions.a: Each exchange raised the price, so silk in Rome cost many times what it cost in China and Roman writers complained about the silver leaving the empire.

articles.note: The title is the lesson. Ask what the class pictured before reading paragraph A, and what the text says instead.

articles.title: The Beaver and the Flood
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Explain the relationships or interactions between two or more individuals, events, ideas, or concepts in a historical, scientific, or technical text based on specific information in the text.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.5 structure · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: A beaver does not set out to build a wetland. It is responding to a sound. Running water triggers an urge to pile sticks and mud against it, and the beaver keeps piling until the sound stops.

paras.label: B
paras.text: What the animal makes, almost by accident, is a pond. Water backs up behind the dam, spreads sideways across flat ground, and soaks into soil that a fast stream would have carried past.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That stored water changes the stream below. In a heavy rain the pond holds part of the surge and lets it out slowly, so the flood peak downstream arrives lower and later than it otherwise would.

paras.label: D
