paras.text: The same pond helps in the opposite weather. Water that soaked into the banks seeps back out through the dry months, keeping a trickle in channels that would run dry without it.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Other species follow the water. Dead standing trees in the flooded ground become nest holes for woodpeckers and ducks, and the slow water suits frogs, dragonflies and young fish far better than the old stream did.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Trappers removed most North American beavers by the middle of the nineteenth century, and the streams changed with them. Several states now move beavers back on purpose, as cheaper flood control than anything a crew can build.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A beaver does not plan to build a wetland. It is answering a sound. Running water makes it pile sticks and mud. It piles until the sound stops.

paras.label: B
paras.text: What it makes is a pond. Water backs up behind the dam. It spreads across flat ground. It soaks into the soil.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That water changes the stream below. In heavy rain the pond holds part of the surge. It lets the water out slowly. The flood downstream is lower and later.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The pond helps in dry weather too. Water soaks into the banks. It seeps back out through the dry months. Channels keep a trickle.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Other animals follow the water. Dead trees become nest holes for woodpeckers and ducks. Frogs, dragonflies and young fish like the slow water.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Trappers removed most beavers by the 1850s. The streams changed with them. Some states now move beavers back on purpose.

questions.q: What makes a beaver begin building a dam?
questions.a: The sound of running water triggers an urge to pile sticks and mud against it, and the beaver keeps piling until the sound stops.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. floods) and paragraph D (i.e. dry months).
Summarize how one beaver dam changes a stream.
questions.a: The dam backs water up into a pond that soaks into the ground. In heavy rain the pond holds part of the surge so the flood downstream is lower and later, and in dry months the stored water seeps back out to keep a trickle running.

questions.q:
surge: a sudden rush of water.
channel: the bed a stream runs along.
Describe the connection between the beaver's dam and the birds that nest nearby.
questions.a: The dam floods the ground and kills standing trees, and those dead trees become nest holes for woodpeckers and ducks.

articles.note: RI.5.3 wants the interaction named, not just the two things. Push for because and so: the dam stores water, so the flood peak arrives lower and later.

articles.title: The Interpreter on the Expedition
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Explain the relationships or interactions between two or more individuals, events, ideas, or concepts in a historical, scientific, or technical text based on specific information in the text.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.5 structure · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: When Lewis and Clark set out up the Missouri River in 1804, they could speak none of the languages of the nations whose land they were crossing. Every conversation would have to pass through somebody.

paras.label: B
paras.text: At a Mandan village that winter they hired a French Canadian trader named Charbonneau. The reason was his wife. Sacagawea was Lemhi Shoshone, taken from her people as a child, and the expedition would need the Shoshone.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The need was horses. To cross the Rocky Mountains the party had to leave the river and buy pack animals, and the Shoshone had them. Without horses the expedition would have stopped at the mountains.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Communication ran through a chain. Sacagawea spoke Shoshone to a captured Shoshone speaker, who spoke Hidatsa to Charbonneau, who spoke French to a soldier, who spoke English to the captains. One question could take several minutes.

paras.label: E
paras.text: When the party finally met a Shoshone band in August of 1805, the chief turned out to be Sacagawea's brother. The expedition got its horses and a guide over the pass.

paras.label: F
paras.text: She did more than translate. A travelling party that included a woman and an infant read as a peaceful one, and Clark wrote in his journal that her presence reassured every group they met.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Lewis and Clark went up the Missouri River in 1804. They spoke none of the languages of the nations there. Every talk had to pass through someone.

paras.label: B
paras.text: At a Mandan village that winter they hired a trader named Charbonneau. The reason was his wife. Sacagawea was Shoshone. The expedition would need the Shoshone.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The need was horses. The party had to cross the Rocky Mountains. They had to leave the river and buy pack animals. The Shoshone had them.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Talk ran through a chain. Sacagawea spoke Shoshone. A man turned that into Hidatsa. Charbonneau turned that into French. A soldier turned that into English.

paras.label: E
paras.text: In August of 1805 the party met a Shoshone band. The chief was Sacagawea's brother. They got their horses and a guide.

paras.label: F
paras.text: She did more than translate. A party with a woman and a baby looked peaceful. Clark wrote that she reassured every group they met.

questions.q: Why did the expedition need to reach the Shoshone?
questions.a: To cross the Rocky Mountains the party had to leave the river and buy pack animals, and the Shoshone had the horses they needed.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the horses) and paragraph D (i.e. the chain of languages).
Summarize Sacagawea's part in the expedition.
questions.a: She was hired with her husband because she spoke Shoshone, and the party needed Shoshone horses to cross the Rocky Mountains. She translated through a chain of four languages, the Shoshone chief turned out to be her brother, and her presence made the party look peaceful.

questions.q:
interpreter: a person who turns speech from one language into another.
expedition: a journey made by a group with a set purpose.
Describe the connection between Sacagawea's childhood and the success of the expedition.
questions.a: She had been taken from the Lemhi Shoshone as a child, so she could speak Shoshone, and when the party met a Shoshone band the chief turned out to be her brother, which is how they got their horses.

articles.note: The chain in paragraph D is worth acting out with four students. It makes the point that the expedition's survival ran through one person's childhood language.

articles.title: The Fig and the Wasp
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Explain the relationships or interactions between two or more individuals, events, ideas, or concepts in a historical, scientific, or technical text based on specific information in the text.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.5 structure · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: A fig is not a fruit in the ordinary sense. It is a hollow ball lined on the inside with hundreds of tiny flowers, all of them facing inward where no bee can reach them.

paras.label: B
paras.text: One insect can get in. A female fig wasp, about the size of a grain of rice, pushes through a narrow opening at the end of the fig, usually tearing off her wings and antennae on the way.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Inside, she lays eggs in some flowers and leaves pollen on others. The pollinated flowers become seeds; the ones holding eggs become galls, small chambers where wasp larvae grow. Then she dies inside the fig.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The next generation mates in the dark. Wingless males chew exits through the fig wall and die; the winged females collect pollen, crawl out through those tunnels, and fly off to find another tree.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Neither species can manage alone. A fig tree without its wasp sets no seed, and a wasp without a fig has nowhere to lay eggs, so each depends on the other for its next generation.

paras.label: F
paras.text: There are more than seven hundred fig species, and most are pollinated by a wasp species found in no other fig. That pairing is one of the tightest partnerships known in nature.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A fig is not an ordinary fruit. It is a hollow ball. Hundreds of tiny flowers line the inside. They all face inward where no bee can reach.

paras.label: B
paras.text: One insect can get in. A female fig wasp is about the size of a grain of rice. She pushes through a narrow hole at the end of the fig. She often tears off her wings.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Inside, she lays eggs in some flowers. She leaves pollen on others. The flowers with pollen become seeds. The flowers with eggs become small chambers for larvae. Then she dies.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The next young mate in the dark. Wingless males chew exits through the wall and die. The winged females take pollen and crawl out. They fly to another tree.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Neither one can manage alone. A fig tree with no wasp makes no seed. A wasp with no fig has nowhere to lay eggs.

paras.label: F
paras.text: There are more than seven hundred kinds of fig. Most have one wasp found in no other fig.

questions.q: Why can a bee not pollinate a fig?
questions.a: The flowers are inside a hollow ball and all face inward, so no bee can reach them and only a wasp small enough to push through the narrow opening can get in.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. what she does inside) and paragraph E (i.e. why neither can manage alone).
Summarize how a fig and its wasp depend on each other.
questions.a: A female wasp pushes into the hollow fig, lays eggs in some flowers and leaves pollen on others, then dies inside. Her young mate in the dark and the females carry pollen to another tree, so the fig gets its seeds and the wasp gets somewhere to lay eggs.

questions.q:
pollen: the dust a flower needs from another flower in order to make seed.
gall: a small chamber in a plant where an insect larva grows.
Describe the connection between the number of fig species and the number of wasp species.
questions.a: There are more than seven hundred fig species and most are pollinated by a wasp found in no other fig, so the two groups have paired off almost one for one.

articles.note: Students usually ask whether they are eating wasps. The text says she dies inside, and the fig digests her; that is worth answering plainly rather than dodging.

articles.title: The Telegraph and the Railroad
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Explain the relationships or interactions between two or more individuals, events, ideas, or concepts in a historical, scientific, or technical text based on specific information in the text.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.5 structure · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: Two inventions arrived in America within a few years of each other, and neither one worked well until it was paired with the other. One moved goods; the other moved words.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Early railroads ran on single tracks. Two trains headed toward each other on the same rail had no way to know it, and the schedule printed on paper was the only thing keeping them apart.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Collisions were common enough to have a name. A head-on crash was called a cornfield meet, and in 1851 a superintendent on the Erie Railroad used a telegraph line to hold one train while another passed.

paras.label: D
paras.text: That order was the beginning of dispatching. From then on a man at a desk could know where every train on a line actually was, not where a printed timetable said it ought to be.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The railroad returned the favor. Telegraph companies strung their wire along the cleared, fenced, patrolled strip of land a railroad already owned, which was the cheapest right of way in the country.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The two spread together across the continent. Where the rails went, the wire went beside them, and a town that got one almost always got the other in the same year.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Two inventions arrived in America at about the same time. Neither worked well alone. One moved goods. The other moved words.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Early railroads ran on single tracks. Two trains could head toward each other on the same rail. Only the paper schedule kept them apart.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Crashes were common. A head-on crash even had a name. In 1851 a man on the Erie Railroad used a telegraph to hold one train while another passed.

paras.label: D
paras.text: That order began dispatching. A man at a desk could know where every train really was. He did not have to trust the timetable.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The railroad helped back. Telegraph companies strung wire along land the railroad already owned. It was cleared and fenced. It was the cheapest route in the country.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The two spread together. Where the rails went, the wire went beside them. A town that got one usually got the other.

questions.q: Why were collisions common on early railroads?
questions.a: Early railroads ran on single tracks, so two trains headed toward each other on the same rail had no way to know it and only the printed schedule kept them apart.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. dispatching) and paragraph E (i.e. the right of way).
Summarize how the telegraph and the railroad helped each other.
questions.a: The telegraph let a dispatcher know where every train actually was instead of where the timetable said, which stopped head-on crashes on single tracks. In return the railroad gave telegraph companies cheap cleared land to string wire along, so the two spread across the continent together.

questions.q:
dispatching: directing trains from a central desk using live information.
right of way: a strip of land a company has the right to run a line along.
Describe the connection between the railroad's land and the spread of the telegraph.
questions.a: Telegraph companies strung wire along the cleared, fenced, patrolled strip a railroad already owned, which was the cheapest right of way in the country, so the wire spread wherever the rails went.

articles.note: This is a two-way relationship, which is harder than cause and effect. Ask for one sentence in each direction before accepting an answer.

articles.title: Why the Sahara Feeds the Amazon
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Explain the relationships or interactions between two or more individuals, events, ideas, or concepts in a historical, scientific, or technical text based on specific information in the text.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.5 structure · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: The Amazon rainforest grows on soil that is surprisingly poor. Heavy rain washes nutrients down past the roots year after year, and phosphorus in particular drains away faster than the forest can replace it.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Some of the replacement comes from four thousand miles away. Every year winds lift dust from the Sahara and carry it west across the Atlantic in a haze that satellites can follow from space.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Most of that dust starts in one place. The Bodele Depression in Chad is the dried bed of an ancient lake, and the sediment there is packed with the remains of freshwater organisms rich in phosphorus.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Satellite measurements put the delivery at roughly twenty-eight million tons of dust a year, of which about twenty-two thousand tons is phosphorus, close to what the rain strips out of the soil.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The link runs on the seasons. The dust blows in winter, when the trade winds are strongest and the Sahara is driest, and much of it falls out over the basin in the rains that follow.

paras.label: F
paras.text: It is a reminder that the parts of the Earth are not separate. A dry lake bed in Chad helps keep the largest rainforest on the planet in leaf.

paras.label: A
paras.text: The Amazon rainforest grows on poor soil. Heavy rain washes nutrients past the roots. Phosphorus drains away fastest of all.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Some of it is replaced from four thousand miles away. Winds lift dust from the Sahara each year. They carry it west across the Atlantic.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Most of that dust starts in one place. The Bodele Depression in Chad is a dried lake bed. The sediment there is rich in phosphorus.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Satellites measure the dust. About twenty-eight million tons cross each year. About twenty-two thousand tons of that is phosphorus.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The link runs on the seasons. The dust blows in winter when the winds are strongest. Much of it falls in the rains that follow.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The parts of the Earth are not separate. A dry lake bed in Chad helps keep the Amazon in leaf.

questions.q: Why is the soil of the Amazon poor?
questions.a: Heavy rain washes nutrients down past the roots year after year, and phosphorus in particular drains away faster than the forest can replace it.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. where the dust comes from) and paragraph E (i.e. when it blows).
Summarize how the Sahara helps the Amazon.
questions.a: Rain strips phosphorus out of Amazon soil, and winter winds carry about twenty-eight million tons of Saharan dust across the Atlantic each year. About twenty-two thousand tons of that is phosphorus, close to what the rain removes.

questions.q:
phosphorus: a nutrient plants need in order to grow.
sediment: material that settles out of water and builds up over time.
Describe the connection between an ancient lake in Chad and the trees of the Amazon.
questions.a: The dried lake bed holds sediment packed with the remains of freshwater organisms rich in phosphorus, and the dust blown from it replaces the phosphorus that Amazon rain washes away.

articles.note: Pair this with a globe. The distance is the part that makes the relationship memorable, and students should trace the route before they explain it.

articles.title: The Words on a Dollar Bill
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of general academic and domain-specific words and phrases in a text relevant to a grade 5 topic or subject area.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.7 multiple sources · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: A dollar bill is covered in words, and most of them are doing legal work rather than decoration. Reading them carefully is a short lesson in what money actually is.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Across the top it says Federal Reserve Note. A note is a promise to pay, and the Federal Reserve is the central bank that issues it. The bill is a claim, not a piece of valuable material.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Below the portrait runs a line saying the note is legal tender for all debts, public and private. Legal tender means a creditor must accept it to settle a debt. It does not mean a shop must accept it for a sandwich.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Two signatures appear, the Treasurer of the United States and the Secretary of the Treasury. Their presence marks the note as officially issued, in the way a signature marks a check.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The Latin motto E pluribus unum means out of many, one. Annuit coeptis, printed above the pyramid on the back, is usually translated as he approves of our undertakings.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Older bills said something different. Before 1964 a silver certificate promised to pay the bearer one silver dollar on demand. The promise was dropped, and the words on the bill changed with it.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A dollar bill is covered in words. Most of them do legal work. Reading them shows what money really is.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Across the top it says Federal Reserve Note. A note is a promise to pay. The Federal Reserve is the central bank. The bill is a claim, not a valuable thing.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Below the portrait is a line about legal tender. Legal tender means a person who is owed money must take it to settle a debt. It does not mean a shop must take it.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Two signatures appear on the bill. One is the Treasurer. One is the Secretary of the Treasury. They mark the note as officially issued.

paras.label: E
paras.text: E pluribus unum is Latin. It means out of many, one. Another motto sits above the pyramid on the back.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Older bills said something else. Before 1964 a silver certificate promised one silver dollar. The promise was dropped. The words changed with it.

questions.q: What does legal tender mean on a dollar bill?
questions.a: Legal tender means a creditor must accept the note to settle a debt; it does not mean a shop must accept it for a sandwich.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. the word note) and paragraph C (i.e. legal tender).
Summarize what the words on a dollar bill tell you about money.
questions.a: The bill calls itself a note, which is a promise to pay issued by the central bank rather than a valuable material. It is legal tender for debts, it carries two Treasury signatures, and older bills promised silver until that promise was dropped.

questions.q:
tender: something offered in payment.
certificate: a document that states a promise or a fact.
Describe the connection between the silver certificate and the wording on bills today.
questions.a: A silver certificate promised to pay the bearer one silver dollar on demand, and when that promise was dropped after 1964 the words on the bill changed to the Federal Reserve Note wording used now.

articles.note: Hand out a real bill if you can. RI.5.4 is about meaning in context, and the context here is an object every student has handled without reading.

articles.title: Naming the Clouds
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of general academic and domain-specific words and phrases in a text relevant to a grade 5 topic or subject area.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.7 multiple sources · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: Before 1802 clouds had no shared names. A farmer and a sailor might describe the same sky in completely different words, and no two accounts of the weather could be compared with each other.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A London chemist named Luke Howard proposed a system built out of Latin pieces. Cumulus means heap, stratus means layer, cirrus means curl, and nimbus means rain.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The pieces combine. A cumulonimbus is a heap cloud that is raining, and the name carries both facts in one word without any need for a picture.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Height is added in front. Alto marks the middle level of the sky, so altostratus is a layer cloud at middle height, while plain stratus sits low.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The power of the system is that it describes rather than labels. A person who knows four roots can look at a cloud they have never seen before and say roughly what it is and what it is doing.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Howard's names were adopted internationally and are still in use more than two centuries later. The World Meteorological Organization now recognizes ten main types, all of them built from his original pieces.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Before 1802 clouds had no shared names. A farmer and a sailor might describe the same sky in different words. No two reports could be compared.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Luke Howard was a London chemist. He built a system out of Latin pieces. Cumulus means heap. Stratus means layer. Cirrus means curl. Nimbus means rain.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The pieces combine. A cumulonimbus is a heap cloud that is raining. The name holds both facts in one word.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Height is added in front. Alto marks the middle of the sky. Altostratus is a layer cloud at middle height. Plain stratus sits low.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The system describes instead of labels. Learn four roots and you can read a cloud you have never seen.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Howard's names spread around the world. They are still used today. Ten main types are built from his pieces.

questions.q: What does the name cumulonimbus tell you about a cloud?
questions.a: Cumulus means heap and nimbus means rain, so a cumulonimbus is a heap cloud that is raining.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. the Latin roots) and paragraph D (i.e. height).
Summarize the system Luke Howard invented.
questions.a: He named clouds from Latin roots: cumulus for heap, stratus for layer, cirrus for curl and nimbus for rain, with alto in front for middle height. The pieces combine, so a name describes what a cloud is and what it is doing.

questions.q:
root: a word part that carries meaning and combines with others.
cirrus: a curl of cloud high in the sky.
Describe the connection between knowing the Latin roots and reading a new cloud.
questions.a: Because each root describes a shape or a behavior, a person who knows four of them can look at a cloud they have never seen and say roughly what it is and what it is doing.

articles.note: Build the words on the board from the pieces rather than giving them whole. The point of RI.5.4 here is that a reader can take a long word apart.

articles.title: What a Map's Legend Tells You
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of general academic and domain-specific words and phrases in a text relevant to a grade 5 topic or subject area.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.7 multiple sources · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: A map is a set of agreements. Every line and color on it stands for something, and the box that spells out those agreements is called the legend, or sometimes the key.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The scale is the first agreement to find. A bar scale shows how far a given length on the paper reaches on the ground, so one inch might stand for ten miles or for ten feet.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Symbols carry the rest. A dashed line is usually a trail, a double line a divided highway, a small cross a church or a cemetery, and a dotted blue line a stream that runs only part of the year.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Color is a shorthand too. On a topographic map green means vegetation, blue means water and brown means the contour lines that show the shape of the land.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Contour lines are the hardest part of a legend to read. Each line joins points of equal elevation, so lines crowded together mean a steep slope and lines far apart mean nearly flat ground.

paras.label: F
paras.text: None of these are universal. A symbol that means one thing on a hiking map can mean another on a city plan, which is why every careful reader starts with the legend rather than the picture.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A map is a set of agreements. Every line and color stands for something. The box that explains them is the legend, or the key.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Find the scale first. A bar scale shows how far a length on the paper reaches on the ground. One inch might stand for ten miles.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Symbols carry the rest. A dashed line is usually a trail. A double line is a divided highway. A dotted blue line is a stream that dries up.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Color is a shorthand too. Green means plants. Blue means water. Brown means the lines that show the shape of the land.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Contour lines are the hardest part. Each line joins points at the same elevation. Lines close together mean a steep slope.

paras.label: F
paras.text: None of this is the same on every map. A symbol can change meaning. Careful readers start with the legend.

questions.q: What does it mean when contour lines are crowded together?
questions.a: Each contour line joins points of equal elevation, so lines crowded together mean a steep slope and lines far apart mean nearly flat ground.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. the scale) and paragraph E (i.e. contour lines).
Summarize what a legend does for a map reader.
questions.a: It states the agreements the map is built on: the scale that turns a length on paper into a distance on the ground, the symbols for trails, highways and streams, and the colors for vegetation, water and the contour lines showing the shape of the land.

questions.q:
legend: the box on a map that explains what its symbols mean.
elevation: how high a point is above sea level.
Describe the connection between the last paragraph and the advice to read the legend first.
questions.a: A symbol that means one thing on a hiking map can mean another on a city plan, so the legend is the only place a reader can learn what this particular map's lines and colors stand for.

articles.note: Two maps of the same place with different legends make this concrete in about four minutes.

articles.title: What a Chance of Rain Really Means
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of general academic and domain-specific words and phrases in a text relevant to a grade 5 topic or subject area.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.7 multiple sources · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: A forecast that says a forty per cent chance of rain is one of the most misread sentences in daily life. It does not mean forty per cent of the area, and it does not mean rain for forty per cent of the day.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The number is a probability of precipitation, and it has a definition. It is the chance that measurable rain, meaning at least one hundredth of an inch, falls at any given point in the forecast area.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Forecasters reach it by combining two judgments: how confident they are that rain will form at all, and how much of the area it would cover if it did. A forty per cent chance can come from either one.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The word measurable is doing real work. A drizzle that wets the pavement but never reaches a hundredth of an inch does not count, which is why a day can feel damp and still be recorded as dry.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Forecasts are checked afterward. Over many days carrying a forty per cent forecast, rain should fall on close to forty per cent of them, and forecasters track that record for themselves.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Knowing the definition changes what a person does with it. Forty per cent is not a promise about the sky; it is a statement about how often a day like today turns out wet.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A forty per cent chance of rain is often misread. It does not mean forty per cent of the area. It does not mean rain for forty per cent of the day.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The number is a probability of precipitation. It has a definition. It is the chance that measurable rain falls at any one point in the area.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Forecasters mix two judgments. One is how sure they are that rain will form. One is how much area it would cover. Either can give forty per cent.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The word measurable matters. A drizzle that never reaches a hundredth of an inch does not count. A damp day can still be recorded as dry.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Forecasts get checked later. Over many forty per cent days, rain should fall on about forty of every hundred.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The definition changes how to use it. Forty per cent is not a promise. It says how often a day like today turns out wet.

questions.q: What does a forty per cent chance of rain actually mean?
questions.a: It is the chance that measurable rain, meaning at least one hundredth of an inch, falls at any given point in the forecast area.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. the definition) and paragraph D (i.e. the word measurable).
Summarize how a forecaster arrives at a chance of rain.
questions.a: The forecaster combines how confident they are that rain will form with how much of the area it would cover, and the result is the chance that at least a hundredth of an inch falls at any given point.

questions.q:
probability: how likely something is, given as a number.
precipitation: rain, snow or any water falling from the sky.
Describe the connection between the definition of measurable rain and a day that feels damp but counts as dry.
questions.a: Measurable rain means at least one hundredth of an inch, so a drizzle that wets the pavement without reaching that amount does not count and the day is recorded as dry.

articles.note: Collect the class's guesses before reading paragraph A. Most rooms produce all three wrong readings, which makes the definition land.

articles.title: The Vocabulary of an Election
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of general academic and domain-specific words and phrases in a text relevant to a grade 5 topic or subject area.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.7 multiple sources · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: Election coverage runs on a vocabulary that is rarely explained. The words are ordinary enough to slide past a reader, and specific enough that missing one changes the meaning of a whole sentence.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A candidate stands for office; an incumbent is the one who already holds it. The distinction matters because incumbents win far more often than challengers, so the label carries a prediction with it.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A primary is an election to choose a party's candidate. A general election is the one held between parties. A voter can take part in both, and the two can produce very different turnout.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Turnout is the share of eligible voters who actually vote. A race decided by a landslide in the count can still be decided by a minority of the people entitled to take part.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A ballot is the list a voter marks, and a ballot measure is a question put directly to voters rather than to a legislature. Several states decide major laws that way.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The word poll does double duty. A polling place is where ballots are cast, while a poll is a survey of what people say they will do, which is a guess rather than a count.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Election news runs on special words. They are ordinary enough to slide past. Missing one can change a whole sentence.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A candidate runs for office. An incumbent already holds it. Incumbents win far more often than challengers.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A primary chooses a party's candidate. A general election is the one between parties. A voter can take part in both.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Turnout is the share of eligible voters who vote. A race won by a landslide can still be decided by a minority of them.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A ballot is the list a voter marks. A ballot measure is a question put straight to voters. Some states decide big laws that way.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The word poll does two jobs. A polling place is where ballots are cast. A poll is a survey of what people say they will do.

questions.q: What is the difference between a primary and a general election?
questions.a: A primary is an election to choose a party's candidate, and a general election is the one held between parties.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. incumbent) and paragraph F (i.e. the two meanings of poll).
Summarize what the words in this article let a reader understand.
questions.a: They separate a candidate from an incumbent, a primary from a general election, and a polling place from a poll. They also name turnout, the share of eligible voters who vote, and a ballot measure, a question put directly to voters.

questions.q:
incumbent: the person who already holds the office.
turnout: the share of eligible voters who actually vote.
Describe the connection between turnout and a landslide result.
questions.a: Turnout is the share of eligible voters who actually vote, so a race decided by a landslide in the count can still be decided by a minority of the people entitled to take part.

articles.note: The two meanings of poll in paragraph F are the ones that cause real confusion in news reports. Ask for a sentence using each.

articles.title: Two Texts: How a Hurricane Forms
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Compare and contrast the overall structure of events, ideas, concepts, or information in two or more texts.
 Spiral: RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.3 relationships · RI.5.6 point of view · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: A science museum and a state emergency agency both publish a page about hurricanes. The facts in them barely differ. The order of those facts differs completely, and the order is what each page is for.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The museum page is a chronology. It starts with warm ocean water, moves to rising air and falling pressure, then to the spiral of thunderstorms, and ends with a named storm crossing a coast.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Reading it, a person learns how one stage leads to the next. The question it answers is how does this happen, and it answers it in time order from first to last.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The agency page is problem and solution. It opens with what a storm surge does to a house, then gives the actions a family should take at seventy-two hours, forty-eight hours, and twenty-four hours before landfall.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Reading that one, a person learns what to do. It answers a different question, which is what should I do, and it is organized by how much time is left rather than by how a storm forms.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Neither structure is better. A student writing a report needs the chronology; a family watching a forecast needs the problem and solution. Noticing the structure tells a reader which text will answer their question.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A science museum and a state agency both write about hurricanes. The facts are nearly the same. The order is not. The order is what each page is for.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The museum page is a chronology. It starts with warm ocean water. Then air rises and pressure falls. Then thunderstorms spiral. Then a named storm crosses a coast.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Reading it, a person learns how one stage leads to the next. It answers the question how does this happen.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The agency page is problem and solution. It opens with what a storm surge does to a house. Then it lists what a family should do at seventy-two, forty-eight and twenty-four hours.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Reading that one, a person learns what to do. It is ordered by how much time is left.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Neither structure is better. A student needs the chronology. A family needs the solutions. The structure tells you which text answers your question.

questions.q: How are the two pages the same, and how are they different?
questions.a: The facts in them barely differ, but the order does: the museum page runs in time order from warm ocean water to landfall, and the agency page runs from the problem of storm surge to the actions a family should take.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. the chronology) and paragraph D (i.e. problem and solution).
Summarize why the same facts are arranged two different ways.
questions.a: The museum page is a chronology because it answers how a hurricane happens, and the agency page is problem and solution because it answers what a family should do. Each structure serves the question that page exists to answer.

questions.q:
chronology: an account arranged in time order.
landfall: the moment a storm crosses from the sea onto the coast.
Describe the connection between a reader's question and the structure they should choose.
questions.a: A student writing a report needs the chronology that explains how one stage leads to the next, while a family watching a forecast needs the problem and solution page organized by how much time is left.

articles.note: RI.5.5 is about structure, not topic. Ask students to name the structure before they say anything about hurricanes.

articles.title: Two Texts: The Gold Rush
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Compare and contrast the overall structure of events, ideas, concepts, or information in two or more texts.
 Spiral: RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.3 relationships · RI.5.6 point of view · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: Two accounts of the California gold rush sit side by side in a textbook. One is a timeline; the other is a cause and effect chain. They cover the same eight years.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The timeline begins in January of 1848, when gold was found at a sawmill on the American River, and runs forward: the news reaching the east, the ships, the overland crossings, statehood in 1850.

paras.label: C
paras.text: It is easy to follow and easy to quote. What it does not explain is why any of it followed from the rest.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The second account starts with an effect and works backward. San Francisco grew from about a thousand people to twenty-five thousand in two years, and the text asks what made that happen.

paras.label: E
paras.text: It then lays out the chain: a discovery, a newspaper story, cheap passage around Cape Horn, and a port that was the only place to land. Each link is given a reason.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Together the two show something neither shows alone. The timeline gives a reader the order of events; the cause and effect account gives the reader why that order was not an accident.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Two accounts of the California gold rush sit side by side. One is a timeline. One is a cause and effect chain. Both cover the same eight years.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The timeline begins in January of 1848. Gold was found at a sawmill. Then the news reached the east. Then came the ships. Then statehood in 1850.

paras.label: C
paras.text: It is easy to follow. It is easy to quote. It does not explain why one thing led to the next.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The second account starts with an effect. San Francisco grew from a thousand people to twenty-five thousand in two years. The text asks what made that happen.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Then it lays out the chain. A discovery. A newspaper story. Cheap passage around Cape Horn. A port that was the only place to land.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Together they show more than either one alone. The timeline gives the order. The other gives the reasons.

questions.q: What does the timeline leave out?
questions.a: It gives the order of events but does not explain why any of it followed from the rest.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. the timeline) and paragraph E (i.e. the chain of causes).
Summarize how the two accounts of the gold rush are organized.
questions.a: One is a timeline running from the discovery at the sawmill in 1848 forward to statehood in 1850. The other starts with San Francisco's growth and works backward through a chain of causes: the discovery, the newspaper story, cheap passage and a single port.

questions.q:
timeline: an account that lists events in the order they happened.
passage: a journey by ship, or the fare paid for it.
Describe the connection between the growth of San Francisco and the chain of causes the second text gives.
questions.a: The second account begins with San Francisco growing from about a thousand people to twenty-five thousand in two years, then explains it through the discovery, the newspaper story, cheap passage around Cape Horn and a port that was the only place to land.

articles.note: Have students draw both shapes before writing: an arrow for the timeline, a chain of boxes for the causes. The drawing usually makes the comparison easy.

articles.title: Two Texts: Plastic in the Ocean
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Compare and contrast the overall structure of events, ideas, concepts, or information in two or more texts.
 Spiral: RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.3 relationships · RI.5.6 point of view · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: A research summary and a campaign leaflet both describe plastic in the ocean. The numbers in them match. The shape of the two documents does not.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The research summary is organized by category. One section covers where the plastic comes from, one covers where it ends up, one covers what it does to animals, and one covers what is still unknown.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That structure makes the gaps visible. A reader can see that estimates of the total amount vary widely, because the text gives a whole section to what nobody has measured.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The leaflet is problem and solution, and it is much shorter. It states the problem in two sentences and then gives five things a reader can do this week.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Its structure hides the uncertainty on purpose. A leaflet that spent half its space on what is unknown would not move anybody to act, so the doubt is left out.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Both are honest about their facts, and they are built for different work. A reader who wants to know what is settled should not take the leaflet, and a reader who wants to act should not wait for the summary.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A research summary and a campaign leaflet both describe plastic in the ocean. The numbers match. The shape of the two documents does not.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The research summary is sorted by category. One part covers where the plastic comes from. One covers where it ends up. One covers what it does to animals. One covers what is still unknown.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That structure makes the gaps easy to see. Estimates of the total amount vary widely. A whole section says so.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The leaflet is problem and solution. It is much shorter. It states the problem in two sentences. Then it lists five things a reader can do.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Its structure hides the doubt on purpose. A leaflet full of what is unknown would not move anyone to act.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Both are honest about their facts. They are built for different work. One tells you what is settled. One asks you to act.

questions.q: Why does the leaflet leave out what is unknown?
questions.a: A leaflet that spent half its space on what is unknown would not move anybody to act, so the doubt is left out on purpose.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. categories) and paragraph D (i.e. problem and solution).
Summarize how the two documents are built differently.
questions.a: The research summary is organized by category, with sections on where plastic comes from, where it ends up, what it does to animals and what is unknown. The leaflet is problem and solution: two sentences of problem and five things a reader can do this week.

questions.q:
category: a group that things are sorted into.
estimate: a careful guess at an amount that has not been measured exactly.
Describe the connection between the structure of a text and the job it is meant to do.
questions.a: The summary gives a whole section to what nobody has measured because its job is to show what is settled, and the leaflet states the problem in two sentences because its job is to get a reader to act this week.

articles.note: Paragraph F keeps this from becoming a lesson about one text being dishonest. Both are accurate; they are built for different readers.

articles.title: Two Texts: The Great Migration
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Compare and contrast the overall structure of events, ideas, concepts, or information in two or more texts.
 Spiral: RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.3 relationships · RI.5.6 point of view · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: Between 1916 and 1970, about six million Black Americans left the South for cities in the North and West. Two texts about that movement take almost opposite shapes.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first is a statistical overview. It gives decade by decade figures: how many people left, which states they left, which cities they reached, and how the populations of Chicago and Detroit changed.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Its structure is comparison. Column against column, the text sets the South beside the North and one decade beside the next, so the size of the movement is impossible to miss.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The second text follows one family from Mississippi to Chicago in 1937. It is a narrative, in time order, and it covers four days of a journey rather than fifty years of one.

paras.label: E
paras.text: What the narrative gives is the reason a column of numbers cannot. It shows a wage, a train car, a landlord, and a decision made at a kitchen table.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A reader who has both can do something neither text alone allows: place one family inside six million people, and recognize the six million as that many separate kitchen tables.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Between 1916 and 1970, about six million Black Americans left the South. They moved to cities in the North and West. Two texts about it take opposite shapes.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first is an overview of numbers. It gives figures by decade. How many left. Which states. Which cities. How Chicago and Detroit changed.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Its structure is comparison. It sets the South beside the North. It sets one decade beside the next. The size is impossible to miss.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The second text follows one family from Mississippi to Chicago in 1937. It is a narrative in time order. It covers four days, not fifty years.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The narrative gives what numbers cannot. It shows a wage, a train car, a landlord, and a choice made at a kitchen table.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A reader with both can do more. One family can be placed inside six million people. And six million can be seen as that many kitchen tables.

questions.q: How many people left the South, and over what years?
questions.a: About six million Black Americans left the South between 1916 and 1970 for cities in the North and West.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. comparison) and paragraph D (i.e. narrative).
Summarize how the two texts about the Great Migration are structured.
questions.a: The first is a statistical overview built on comparison, setting the South beside the North and one decade beside the next. The second is a narrative in time order following one family from Mississippi to Chicago over four days in 1937.

questions.q:
narrative: an account that tells a story in the order it happened.
overview: a broad account that gives the whole picture rather than the detail.
Describe the connection between the numbers in the first text and the family in the second.
questions.a: The narrative shows a wage, a train car and a decision made at a kitchen table, which lets a reader place one family inside the six million people the overview counts.

articles.note: The last sentence of paragraph F is the one to read aloud twice. It names what comparing two structures is actually for.

articles.title: Two Texts: The Return of the Bald Eagle
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Compare and contrast the overall structure of events, ideas, concepts, or information in two or more texts.
 Spiral: RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.3 relationships · RI.5.6 point of view · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1963 there were about 417 nesting pairs of bald eagles in the lower forty-eight states. By 2019 there were more than seventy thousand. Two accounts explain that recovery in different shapes.

paras.label: B
paras.text: One is a cause and effect text. It begins with the pesticide DDT, explains how it thinned eggshells so that eggs broke under the weight of a sitting parent, and traces the collapse from there.

paras.label: C
paras.text: It then follows the effects of a single decision: DDT was banned in 1972, eggshells thickened again, and the number of nesting pairs began to climb within a decade.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The other account is a sequence of actions. It lists the protections in order, the 1940 eagle act, the 1972 ban, the 1973 endangered species listing and the 2007 delisting, with a date on each.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The sequence is better for a timeline on a wall. The cause and effect version is better for answering why the eagles recovered rather than simply when.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A careful reader uses the sequence to check the chain. If eggshells had thickened before the ban, the cause and effect account would be wrong, and the dates are what make that test possible.

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1963 there were about 417 nesting pairs of bald eagles in the lower forty-eight states. By 2019 there were more than seventy thousand. Two accounts explain it in different shapes.

paras.label: B
paras.text: One is a cause and effect text. It begins with the pesticide DDT. The chemical thinned eggshells. Eggs broke under a sitting parent.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Then it follows one decision. DDT was banned in 1972. Eggshells thickened again. The number of nesting pairs began to climb.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The other account is a list of actions in order. The 1940 eagle act. The 1972 ban. The 1973 listing. The 2007 delisting.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The list is better for a timeline on a wall. The cause and effect text is better for answering why.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A careful reader uses the dates to check the chain. If eggshells thickened before the ban, the first account would be wrong.

questions.q: What did DDT do to bald eagles?
questions.a: It thinned eggshells so that eggs broke under the weight of a sitting parent, and the number of nesting pairs collapsed.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. cause and effect) and paragraph D (i.e. the sequence of actions).
Summarize how the two accounts of the eagle's recovery differ.
questions.a: One is cause and effect: DDT thinned eggshells, the ban in 1972 let them thicken, and nesting pairs climbed. The other is a sequence of protections with a date on each, from the 1940 eagle act to the 2007 delisting.

questions.q:
pesticide: a chemical used to kill insects.
sequence: things set out in the order they happened.
Describe the connection between the dates in one text and the chain of causes in the other.
questions.a: The dates let a reader test the chain, because if eggshells had thickened before the ban in 1972 the cause and effect account would be wrong.

articles.note: Paragraph F is the real skill: using one structure to check another. It is worth more class time than naming the structures.

articles.title: Two Views of the Boston Massacre
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze multiple accounts of the same event or topic, noting important similarities and differences in the point of view they represent.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.5 structure · RI.5.8 reasons and evidence · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: On the night of March 5th, 1770, British soldiers fired into a crowd on King Street in Boston. Five men died. Almost everything else about the event was disputed within a week.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Paul Revere's engraving, sold around the colonies within three weeks, shows a line of soldiers firing on command into an unarmed, orderly crowd. An officer stands behind them with his sword raised.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The engraving is not a record. The street is drawn wider than it was, the crowd is drawn calm, and the clubs and snowballs that witnesses described are nowhere in the picture.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Captain Preston's own account, written days later, describes a mob throwing ice and swinging sticks, a soldier knocked down, and shots fired without any order from him at all.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A third account came out of the trial. John Adams defended the soldiers, and the jury heard dozens of witnesses contradict each other about whether the word fire was ever spoken.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The point of view in each one can be read from who made it. Revere was selling a cause, Preston was facing a hanging, and the court was deciding guilt. None of them was simply describing.

paras.label: A
paras.text: On the night of March 5th, 1770, British soldiers fired into a crowd in Boston. Five men died. Almost everything else was disputed within a week.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Paul Revere's engraving sold around the colonies in three weeks. It shows soldiers firing on command. The crowd is unarmed and orderly. An officer stands behind with his sword raised.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The engraving is not a record. The street is drawn wider than it was. The crowd is drawn calm. The clubs and snowballs are not in the picture.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Captain Preston wrote his own account days later. He describes a mob throwing ice and swinging sticks. A soldier was knocked down. He says he gave no order.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A third account came from the trial. John Adams defended the soldiers. Witnesses contradicted each other about the word fire.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Who made each account explains its view. Revere was selling a cause. Preston was facing a hanging. The court was deciding guilt.

questions.q: What do the three accounts agree on?
questions.a: They agree that British soldiers fired into a crowd on King Street in Boston on the night of March 5th, 1770, and that five men died.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. what the engraving leaves out) and paragraph F (i.e. who made each account).
Summarize the three accounts and how they differ.
questions.a: Revere's engraving shows an orderly crowd fired on by command. Preston's written account describes a mob throwing ice while he gave no order. The trial produced dozens of witnesses who contradicted each other about whether the word fire was spoken.

questions.q:
engraving: a picture printed from lines cut into metal.
disputed: argued about, with people claiming different things.
Describe the connection between who made an account and what it shows.
questions.a: Revere was selling a cause so his crowd is calm and the clubs are missing, Preston was facing a hanging so his account has a mob and no order given, and the court was deciding guilt so it heard witnesses contradict each other.

articles.note: Show the engraving. Students who have only read about it will not notice how calm the crowd is drawn until they see it.

articles.title: Who Saw the Shape of DNA
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze multiple accounts of the same event or topic, noting important similarities and differences in the point of view they represent.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.5 structure · RI.5.8 reasons and evidence · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: The 1953 paper announcing the double helix is one page long and carries two names, James Watson and Francis Crick. The story of how the shape was found takes more names than that.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Rosalind Franklin, working at King's College London, made X-ray photographs of DNA fibers. One of them, labelled Photo 51, showed a cross pattern that a trained reader could use to measure the shape.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Watson was shown that photograph by a colleague of Franklin's, without her knowledge. He later wrote that the moment he saw it, his mouth fell open and his pulse began to race.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Accounts of what happened next differ sharply. Watson's book describes Franklin as an obstacle; Franklin's notebooks show she had already worked out that the molecule was a helix with the backbones outside.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The Nobel Prize went to Watson, Crick and Maurice Wilkins in 1962. Franklin had died of cancer four years earlier at thirty-seven, and the prize is not awarded after death.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Reading several accounts changes the answer to a simple question. Who discovered the structure of DNA has one name in a textbook, two on the paper, and at least four in the record.

paras.label: A
paras.text: The 1953 paper announcing the double helix is one page long. It carries two names. The story of how the shape was found takes more names.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Rosalind Franklin worked at King's College London. She made X-ray photographs of DNA fibers. One was labelled Photo 51. It showed a cross pattern.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A colleague showed Watson that photograph. Franklin did not know. He later wrote that his mouth fell open.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Accounts of what happened next differ. Watson's book calls Franklin an obstacle. Her notebooks show she had already worked out the helix.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The Nobel Prize went to three men in 1962. Franklin had died four years earlier at thirty-seven. The prize is not given after death.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Reading several accounts changes the answer. Who discovered DNA has one name in a textbook and at least four in the record.

questions.q: What did Photo 51 show?
questions.a: It was an X-ray photograph of DNA fibers showing a cross pattern that a trained reader could use to measure the shape.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. the accounts that differ) and paragraph F (i.e. the answer changing).
Summarize why the question of who discovered DNA's structure has more than one answer.
questions.a: The paper carries two names, but Franklin's X-ray photograph was shown to Watson without her knowledge and her notebooks show she had already worked out the helix. Watson's book and Franklin's notebooks tell the story differently, and the prize went to three men after her death.

questions.q:
helix: a shape that winds around like a spiral staircase.
obstacle: something standing in the way.
Describe the connection between Franklin's death and the Nobel Prize.
questions.a: The prize went to Watson, Crick and Wilkins in 1962, four years after Franklin died at thirty-seven, and the prize is not awarded after death.

articles.note: This is a point of view standard, not a villain hunt. The useful question is what each account was written for, not who was good.

articles.title: Two Letters Home from the Trail
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze multiple accounts of the same event or topic, noting important similarities and differences in the point of view they represent.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.5 structure · RI.5.8 reasons and evidence · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: Two letters written on the same wagon train in 1852 survive. They describe the same two weeks on the Platte River and leave a reader with two different journeys.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first is from a man of twenty-six travelling to take up land. He writes about distance made each day, the condition of the oxen, and the price of flour at Fort Laramie.

paras.label: C
paras.text: His letter has almost nothing in it about people. The word company appears four times and always means the wagons, never the families inside them.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The second letter is from a woman of thirty-one with three children. Hers counts the graves they pass, names two families who turned back, and describes washing clothes in a river at the end of a day of walking.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Both are accurate. The man was responsible for stock and supplies; the woman was responsible for children and for everything that happened once the wagons stopped.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A reader who has only one of them will get the trail wrong. Together they show that what a person notices on a journey depends on what that person is answerable for.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Two letters from the same wagon train in 1852 survive. They cover the same two weeks on the Platte River. They leave a reader with two different journeys.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first is from a man of twenty-six going to take up land. He writes about distance made each day. He writes about the oxen and the price of flour.

paras.label: C
paras.text: His letter says almost nothing about people. The word company appears four times. It always means the wagons.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The second letter is from a woman of thirty-one with three children. She counts the graves they pass. She names two families who turned back. She describes washing clothes in a river.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Both are accurate. The man looked after stock and supplies. The woman looked after children and everything that happened once the wagons stopped.

paras.label: F
paras.text: One letter alone gives the trail wrong. Together they show that what a person notices depends on what that person is answerable for.

questions.q: What does the first letter write about?
questions.a: It writes about the distance made each day, the condition of the oxen, and the price of flour at Fort Laramie.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. what the first letter leaves out) and paragraph D (i.e. what the second letter counts).
Summarize how the two letters differ.
questions.a: The man writes about distance, oxen and the price of flour and says almost nothing about people. The woman counts graves, names families who turned back and describes washing clothes at the end of a day of walking.

questions.q:
company: a group of wagons travelling together.
answerable: responsible for something, and expected to account for it.
Describe the connection between what each writer was responsible for and what their letter notices.
questions.a: The man was responsible for stock and supplies so he wrote about oxen and flour, and the woman was responsible for children and for everything that happened once the wagons stopped, so she wrote about graves, families and washing.

articles.note: Paragraph C is the sharpest evidence in the piece. Counting one word four times is something students can do themselves with any text.

articles.title: The Argument About Pluto
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze multiple accounts of the same event or topic, noting important similarities and differences in the point of view they represent.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.5 structure · RI.5.8 reasons and evidence · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: Pluto was called a planet from its discovery in 1930 until a vote in 2006. Nothing about Pluto changed in those seventy-six years. What changed was what astronomers had found around it.

paras.label: B
paras.text: By 2005 telescopes had turned up hundreds of icy bodies beyond Neptune, and one of them, Eris, appeared to be larger than Pluto. Either the solar system had a tenth planet, or it had fewer than nine.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Astronomers chose a definition with three parts: a planet orbits the sun, is round under its own gravity, and has cleared other objects out of its orbital path.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Pluto fails the third test. It crosses Neptune's path and shares its region with thousands of other bodies, so it was reclassified as a dwarf planet.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Many planetary scientists objected, and still do. They argue the third rule describes where an object sits rather than what it is, and that by the same rule a planet moved into a crowded orbit would stop being one.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Both sides are reading the same facts. The disagreement is about what a word should mean, which is a different kind of argument from one about what is true.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Pluto was called a planet from 1930 until a vote in 2006. Nothing about Pluto changed. What changed was what astronomers found around it.

paras.label: B
paras.text: By 2005 telescopes had found hundreds of icy bodies beyond Neptune. One of them, Eris, looked larger than Pluto. The solar system had a tenth planet, or fewer than nine.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Astronomers chose a definition with three parts. A planet orbits the sun. It is round under its own gravity. It has cleared its orbital path.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Pluto fails the third test. It crosses Neptune's path. It shares its region with thousands of other bodies. It was called a dwarf planet.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Many scientists objected, and still do. They say the third rule describes where an object sits, not what it is.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Both sides read the same facts. The argument is about what a word should mean. That is not an argument about what is true.

questions.q: Why was Pluto reclassified?
questions.a: It fails the third part of the definition, because it crosses Neptune's path and shares its region with thousands of other bodies rather than having cleared its orbital path.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the definition) and paragraph E (i.e. the objection).
Summarize the argument about Pluto.
questions.a: Telescopes found hundreds of icy bodies beyond Neptune, so astronomers wrote a three-part definition of a planet. Pluto fails the third part and was reclassified as a dwarf planet, and many scientists object that the rule describes where an object sits rather than what it is.

questions.q:
orbit: the path one body follows around another.
reclassified: put into a different group than before.
Describe the connection between the discovery of Eris and the vote in 2006.
questions.a: Eris appeared to be larger than Pluto, so the solar system either had a tenth planet or fewer than nine, and astronomers wrote a definition to settle which.

articles.note: Paragraph F separates two kinds of disagreement. Students who grasp that distinction will read science news better for the rest of their lives.

articles.title: The Same Flood in Two Newspapers
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze multiple accounts of the same event or topic, noting important similarities and differences in the point of view they represent.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.5 structure · RI.5.8 reasons and evidence · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: A river rose over its banks on a Tuesday night and two papers covered it on Wednesday morning. Both front pages are accurate. They are not the same story.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The city paper leads with the count: homes flooded, roads closed, people in shelters, dollars of damage estimated by the county. Its first quotation is from the emergency manager.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The town weekly leads with one street. It names six families, says which of them had flooded before, and prints what a woman said while standing in her kitchen.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The city paper's readers mostly live elsewhere. They need to know how big this is and whether their own roads are open, so scale comes first and names come later.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The weekly's readers live on that street or two streets over. They already know how big it is. What they do not know is who needs help and where to take it.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Comparing the two teaches something about every account a reader meets. Whose questions a writer is answering shapes what goes in the first paragraph and what never appears at all.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A river rose over its banks on a Tuesday night. Two papers covered it on Wednesday. Both front pages are accurate. They are not the same story.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The city paper leads with the count. Homes flooded. Roads closed. People in shelters. Dollars of damage. Its first quotation is from the emergency manager.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The town weekly leads with one street. It names six families. It says which of them had flooded before. It prints what a woman said in her kitchen.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The city paper's readers mostly live elsewhere. They need to know how big this is. They need to know whether their roads are open.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The weekly's readers live on that street. They already know how big it is. They do not know who needs help.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Comparing the two teaches something useful. Whose questions a writer answers shapes what goes first and what never appears.

questions.q: What does the city paper put first?
questions.a: It leads with the count: homes flooded, roads closed, people in shelters, and dollars of damage estimated by the county.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. the city readers) and paragraph E (i.e. the weekly's readers).
Summarize why two accurate papers tell different stories.
questions.a: The city paper leads with scale because its readers live elsewhere and need to know how big the flood is and whether their roads are open. The weekly leads with six families on one street because its readers already know how big it is and need to know who needs help.

questions.q:
estimated: worked out approximately rather than counted exactly.
weekly: a newspaper printed once a week.
Describe the connection between who reads a paper and what its first paragraph says.
questions.a: Whose questions a writer is answering shapes the opening, so the city paper opens with the count for readers who live elsewhere and the weekly opens with named families for readers on that street.

articles.note: Bring in two real coverages of one local event if you can. The structure shows up faster in print the students recognize.

articles.title: Three Sources on a Snowstorm
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Draw on information from multiple print or digital sources, demonstrating the ability to locate an answer to a question quickly or to solve a problem efficiently.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.4 word meaning · RI.5.9 integrating sources · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: A storm is forecast for Thursday and a family needs three different answers: whether school will close, whether the roads will be drivable at six in the morning, and how much snow to expect in total.

paras.label: B
paras.text: No single source answers all three. The weather service forecast gives amounts and timing but says nothing about any particular school district or road.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The district website or its text alert answers the school question and nothing else. It will usually not post until early morning, because the district is waiting on the same forecast.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The state transportation department runs the third source: a map of plow locations and road conditions updated through the night. It answers the driving question and ignores the other two.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Knowing which source holds which answer is the whole skill. A person who checks only the forecast will guess at the roads; a person who checks only the alert will not know what is coming after.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The order matters too. Read the forecast on Wednesday to plan, check the road map at five, and look for the district alert last, because it is the only one that cannot come early.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A storm is forecast for Thursday. A family needs three answers. Will school close? Will the roads be drivable at six? How much snow will fall?

paras.label: B
paras.text: No single source answers all three. The weather service gives amounts and timing. It says nothing about one school district or road.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The district website answers the school question. It answers nothing else. It will not post until early morning.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The state transportation department runs the third source. It is a map of plows and road conditions. It is updated through the night.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Knowing which source holds which answer is the skill. Check only the forecast and you are guessing at the roads.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The order matters too. Read the forecast on Wednesday. Check the road map at five. Look for the district alert last.

questions.q: Which source answers whether the roads will be drivable?
questions.a: The state transportation department's map of plow locations and road conditions, updated through the night.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. the forecast) and paragraph D (i.e. the road map).
Summarize how a family gets all three answers.
questions.a: Read the weather service forecast for amounts and timing, check the state transportation map for road conditions, and watch the district alert for the school closing. Each source answers one question and ignores the others.

questions.q:
forecast: a statement of what the weather is expected to do.
alert: a short message sent out to warn people of something.
Describe the connection between when the district posts and what it is waiting for.
questions.a: The district will usually not post until early morning because it is waiting on the same forecast, so the alert is the only one of the three that cannot come early.

articles.note: RI.5.7 is about speed. Give the class the three questions and time them finding each answer, rather than reading the article first.

articles.title: Checking a Photograph
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Draw on information from multiple print or digital sources, demonstrating the ability to locate an answer to a question quickly or to solve a problem efficiently.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.4 word meaning · RI.5.9 integrating sources · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: A photograph of a flooded street is shared a hundred thousand times with a caption naming a city and a date. Checking whether the caption is true takes about four minutes and three sources.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first is a reverse image search. Upload the picture and a search engine will list every earlier page it appeared on, which often shows the same image carrying a different date.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second is a map. Street view and satellite images let a reader compare buildings, signs and the shape of a corner against what the photograph shows.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The third is a weather record. Archived observations say whether that city had rain on that day, and a flood without rain anywhere in the record is worth doubting.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Any one source can mislead on its own. An image may be new even if a search finds nothing, and a street can change between a satellite pass and a storm.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Together they are strong. A photograph that appeared online two years earlier, shows a corner that does not match the city, and falls on a dry day is not what the caption says.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A photograph of a flooded street is shared a hundred thousand times. The caption names a city and a date. Checking it takes four minutes and three sources.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first is a reverse image search. Upload the picture. A search engine lists earlier pages. The same image often carries a different date.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second is a map. Street view and satellite pictures show buildings and signs. A reader can compare them to the photograph.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The third is a weather record. It says whether that city had rain that day. A flood with no rain is worth doubting.

paras.label: E
