paras.text: Any one source can mislead. An image may be new even if a search finds nothing. A street can change over time.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Together they are strong. The photo appeared two years earlier. The corner does not match. The day was dry. The caption is wrong.

questions.q: What does a reverse image search tell a reader?
questions.a: It lists every earlier page the picture appeared on, which often shows the same image carrying a different date.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the map) and paragraph E (i.e. why one source is not enough).
Summarize the three checks and what each one does.
questions.a: A reverse image search finds earlier appearances and their dates, a map lets a reader compare buildings and corners against the photograph, and a weather record says whether that city had rain on that day.

questions.q:
caption: the words printed under a picture saying what it shows.
archived: stored as a record so it can be looked up later.
Describe the connection between using three sources and the weakness of any one of them.
questions.a: An image may be new even if a search finds nothing and a street can change between a satellite pass and a storm, so no single check is reliable, but a photograph that fails all three is not what the caption says.

articles.note: Do this live with one real image. Four minutes is an honest estimate and the class will remember beating it.

articles.title: Finding a Bird's Name
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Draw on information from multiple print or digital sources, demonstrating the ability to locate an answer to a question quickly or to solve a problem efficiently.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.4 word meaning · RI.5.9 integrating sources · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: A brown bird with a streaked chest lands on a feeder and a child wants its name. There are about eight hundred bird species in North America, and dozens of them are brown with streaked chests.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A field guide narrows it by region first. Range maps at the back show which species occur where, and a guide used properly cuts eight hundred down to perhaps forty before any feather is examined.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Then it narrows by shape. Bill thickness tells a reader whether a bird cracks seeds or probes for insects, which divides the forty again without needing any color at all.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A sound recording does work no picture can. Many look-alike species sound nothing alike, and an app that matches a recording to a library will often name a bird the eye cannot separate.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The third source is a local sightings list. Birders post what they have seen that week, and a species nobody has reported within a hundred miles is probably not the one at the feeder.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Used together the three take minutes. Used alone, any one of them can send a beginner to a species that has never occurred in the state.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A brown bird with a streaked chest lands on a feeder. A child wants its name. North America has about eight hundred bird species. Dozens are brown with streaked chests.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A field guide narrows it by region first. Range maps show which species live where. That can cut eight hundred down to forty.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Then it narrows by shape. Bill thickness tells you whether a bird cracks seeds or probes for insects. That divides the forty again.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A sound recording does what a picture cannot. Look-alike species often sound different. An app can match a recording to a library.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The third source is a local sightings list. Birders post what they have seen that week. A species nobody has reported is probably not the one.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Together the three take minutes. Alone, any one can send a beginner to the wrong species.

questions.q: What does a range map do for a reader?
questions.a: It shows which species occur where, so a guide used properly cuts about eight hundred species down to perhaps forty before any feather is examined.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. region) and paragraph D (i.e. sound).
Summarize how to name an unknown bird quickly.
questions.a: Use a field guide's range maps to cut the list by region, then use bill shape to cut it again, match a sound recording against a library, and check a local sightings list to rule out species nobody has reported nearby.

questions.q:
range: the area where a species is normally found.
species: one particular kind of living thing.
Describe the connection between the sightings list and a wrong answer from a field guide.
questions.a: A species nobody has reported within a hundred miles is probably not the one at the feeder, so the sightings list catches the mistake a guide alone can lead a beginner into.

articles.note: The method generalizes. Narrow by place, narrow by shape, confirm by a second sense, check against what others have found.

articles.title: Planning a Visit to a National Park
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Draw on information from multiple print or digital sources, demonstrating the ability to locate an answer to a question quickly or to solve a problem efficiently.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.4 word meaning · RI.5.9 integrating sources · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: A family has two days at a national park in July and wants to see three particular places. Doing that well is a research problem, and the park publishes most of the answer in pieces.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The official park site holds the hours, the entrance fee, and the alerts. Alerts matter most: a road closed by rockfall in June will make a planned route impossible in July.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The campground reservation system is a separate source with its own calendar. Sites in popular parks open on a fixed date months ahead and are gone within minutes of opening.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Trail conditions come from a third place. Rangers post recent reports on snow, water crossings and insects, and a trail that is open on the map can still be impassable that week.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A fourth source is the weather forecast for the elevation, not for the nearest town. A trailhead four thousand feet higher than the town can be twenty degrees colder and under cloud.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Reading them in the right order saves the trip. Check alerts, then reservations, then conditions, then weather, because each one can make the next question pointless.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A family has two days at a national park in July. They want to see three places. The park publishes the answer in pieces.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The official park site holds the hours, the fee and the alerts. Alerts matter most. A road closed by rockfall will ruin a planned route.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The campground booking system is a separate source. It has its own calendar. Sites open months ahead and are gone within minutes.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Trail conditions come from a third place. Rangers post reports on snow, water and insects. An open trail can still be impassable.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A fourth source is the weather forecast for the elevation. A trailhead can be much colder than the town below it.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Reading them in order saves the trip. Alerts, then reservations, then conditions, then weather. Each one can make the next question pointless.

questions.q: Why do alerts matter most on the park site?
questions.a: A road closed by rockfall in June will make a planned route impossible in July, so an alert can cancel a plan before anything else is decided.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. reservations) and paragraph E (i.e. weather at elevation).
Summarize the order a family should read the sources in.
questions.a: Check the park site's alerts first, then the campground reservation calendar, then the ranger reports on trail conditions, then the forecast for the elevation rather than the town, because each one can make the next question pointless.

questions.q:
alert: a notice warning of a change or a hazard.
elevation: how high a place is above sea level.
Describe the connection between the elevation of a trailhead and the forecast a family should read.
questions.a: A trailhead four thousand feet higher than the town can be twenty degrees colder and under cloud, so the forecast for the town is the wrong one to plan from.

articles.note: Paragraph F is the transferable idea: sequence the sources so a dead end shows up before any work is wasted on it.

articles.title: Reading a Nutrition Label
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Draw on information from multiple print or digital sources, demonstrating the ability to locate an answer to a question quickly or to solve a problem efficiently.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.4 word meaning · RI.5.9 integrating sources · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: Two cereal boxes sit on a shelf and one claims to be healthier. Deciding whether that is true means reading three parts of the package rather than the front of it.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The serving size at the top of the label governs every number below it. A cereal listing 110 calories per serving is not lower in calories if its serving is three quarters of a cup against the other's full cup.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The ingredient list is the second source. Ingredients appear in order of weight, so a product with sugar in the first three places contains more sugar than most of what else is in the box.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Sugar also travels under other names. Cane syrup, dextrose, fruit juice concentrate and honey are each listed separately, which can keep any one of them out of the first three places.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The third place to look is the percent daily value column. It converts an unfamiliar number of milligrams into a share of a day, which is far easier to compare between two boxes.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The front of the box is not a source. Words like natural and wholesome are not defined by any rule, and the claim a shopper can actually check is always on the back.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Two cereal boxes sit on a shelf. One claims to be healthier. Checking that means reading three parts of the package. The front is not one of them.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The serving size at the top governs every number below. One box lists 110 calories. But its serving is smaller than the other box's serving.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The ingredient list is the second source. Ingredients appear in order of weight. Sugar in the first three places means a lot of sugar.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Sugar also travels under other names. Cane syrup, dextrose and honey are listed separately. That can keep any one of them out of the top three.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The third place is the percent daily value column. It turns milligrams into a share of a day. That is easier to compare.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The front of the box is not a source. Words like natural follow no rule. The claim a shopper can check is on the back.

questions.q: Why does the serving size matter?
questions.a: The serving size at the top of the label governs every number below it, so a cereal listing 110 calories per serving is not lower in calories if its serving is smaller.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. ingredient order) and paragraph D (i.e. the names of sugar).
Summarize the three parts of a package worth reading.
questions.a: The serving size, because it governs every number below it; the ingredient list, which runs in order of weight and can hide sugar under several names; and the percent daily value column, which turns milligrams into a share of a day so two boxes can be compared.

questions.q:
serving: the amount of food a label's numbers are based on.
concentrate: a liquid with most of its water removed.
Describe the connection between the several names for sugar and the order of the ingredient list.
questions.a: Ingredients appear in order of weight, so listing cane syrup, dextrose, fruit juice concentrate and honey separately can keep any one of them out of the first three places even when the total sugar is high.

articles.note: Bring two real boxes. Students who compare the serving sizes first find the trick without being told it is there.

articles.title: The Case for Keeping the Old Bridge
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Explain how an author uses reasons and evidence to support particular points in a text, identifying which reasons and evidence support which point(s).
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.6 point of view · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: A town council has to choose between repairing a ninety-year-old bridge and replacing it. A letter from the historical society argues for repair, and it is worth reading for how it argues.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Its first point is cost. The letter gives an engineer's estimate of four million dollars for repair against seven million for replacement, and cites the report by date and page.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Its second point is time. It claims a repair closes the bridge for eight months and a replacement for two years, and supports that with the schedule from a nearby town that replaced a similar span.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Its third point is character, and here the support is different. The letter offers photographs, a quotation from a resident, and the fact that the bridge appears on the town seal.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A careful reader sorts those. The first two points rest on numbers that could be checked and disputed; the third rests on what people value, which no report can settle.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The letter is stronger for keeping them separate. It does not pretend that liking the bridge is a cost figure, and it does not hide the cost figures behind a photograph.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A town council must choose. Repair a ninety-year-old bridge, or replace it. A letter from the historical society argues for repair. How it argues is worth study.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Its first point is cost. An engineer estimates four million dollars for repair. Replacement would cost seven million. The letter cites the report.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Its second point is time. A repair closes the bridge for eight months. A replacement takes two years. A nearby town's schedule is the proof.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Its third point is character. Here the support is different. The letter offers photographs, a quotation, and the town seal.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A careful reader sorts those. The first two rest on numbers that can be checked. The third rests on what people value.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The letter is stronger for keeping them apart. Liking a bridge is not a cost figure. A photograph does not hide one.

questions.q: What evidence supports the letter's point about time?
questions.a: It supports the claim of eight months against two years with the schedule from a nearby town that replaced a similar span.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. cost) and paragraph D (i.e. character).
Summarize the three points and the support for each.
questions.a: Cost is supported by an engineer's estimate of four million against seven million. Time is supported by a nearby town's schedule showing eight months against two years. Character is supported by photographs, a resident's quotation and the town seal.

questions.q:
estimate: a careful calculation of what something will cost.
span: the part of a bridge that reaches from one support to the next.
Describe the connection between the kind of point being made and the kind of evidence used.
questions.a: The cost and time points rest on numbers that could be checked and disputed, and the character point rests on photographs and what people value, which no report can settle.

articles.note: RI.5.8 asks which evidence supports which point. A three-column chart with point, evidence and whether it could be checked does the work.

articles.title: Why Not to Feed Ducks Bread
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Explain how an author uses reasons and evidence to support particular points in a text, identifying which reasons and evidence support which point(s).
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.6 point of view · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: A park sign asks visitors not to feed bread to ducks. The sign gives three reasons, and the evidence behind them is not equally strong.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first reason is nutrition. Bread fills a duck without feeding it, and studies of waterfowl raised on a high-bread diet show deformed wing growth, a condition called angel wing.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That evidence is direct. Birds were raised under measured conditions and the result was recorded, so the claim and the study are about the same thing.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The second reason is water quality. Uneaten bread decays, feeding bacteria and algae that lower the oxygen in a pond, which is supported by measurements taken at heavily fed ponds.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The third reason is crowding. The sign says feeding draws more birds than a pond can support, which spreads disease. The support here is weaker: it rests on reasoning rather than on a count at that pond.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A reader who sorts the three is better placed than one who either believes all of them or dismisses the sign. Two reasons carry measurements; one carries an argument.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A park sign asks visitors not to feed bread to ducks. The sign gives three reasons. The evidence behind them is not equally strong.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first reason is nutrition. Bread fills a duck without feeding it. Birds raised on a high-bread diet grow deformed wings.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That evidence is direct. Birds were raised under measured conditions. The result was recorded.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The second reason is water quality. Uneaten bread decays. It feeds bacteria and algae. Those lower the oxygen in a pond.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The third reason is crowding. Feeding draws more birds than a pond can support. That spreads disease. This support is weaker. It rests on reasoning.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A reader who sorts the three does better than one who believes all of them. Two reasons carry measurements. One carries an argument.

questions.q: What is angel wing, and what causes it?
questions.a: It is a deformed wing growth seen in waterfowl raised on a high-bread diet, because bread fills a duck without feeding it.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. direct evidence) and paragraph E (i.e. the weaker support).
Summarize the sign's three reasons and how well each is supported.
questions.a: Nutrition is supported by studies of birds raised on bread that developed angel wing. Water quality is supported by measurements at heavily fed ponds. Crowding is supported only by reasoning, not by a count at that pond.

questions.q:
waterfowl: birds such as ducks and geese that live on water.
decay: to rot and break down.
Describe the connection between uneaten bread and the oxygen in a pond.
questions.a: Uneaten bread decays and feeds bacteria and algae, and those lower the oxygen in the pond, which is supported by measurements taken at heavily fed ponds.

articles.note: Weaker support is not the same as wrong. Paragraph E says the reasoning may well be right; it says nobody counted at that pond.

articles.title: The Argument for a Crosswalk
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Explain how an author uses reasons and evidence to support particular points in a text, identifying which reasons and evidence support which point(s).
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.6 point of view · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: Students at a middle school asked their city council for a crosswalk outside the front gate. Their presentation is a clean example of matching each kind of evidence to the claim it is meant to support.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Their first claim was that people already cross there. The support was a tally: two students counted crossings for five mornings and recorded 412 of them, with the sheets attached.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Their second claim was that the crossing is dangerous. Here they used the city's own crash records, which listed two collisions and one injury at that corner in four years.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Their third claim was that a crosswalk would help. That one needed outside evidence, so they cited a transportation study of marked crossings with a pedestrian island.

paras.label: E
paras.text: They also named what they could not show. Nobody could prove a future collision would be prevented, and the presentation said so rather than overstating the study.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The council approved the crosswalk. The tally mattered most, because it was the only piece of evidence nobody in the room could dispute: the students had gone out and counted it themselves.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Students at a middle school asked their city for a crosswalk. It would go outside the front gate. Their presentation matched evidence to each claim.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Their first claim was that people already cross there. Two students counted crossings for five mornings. They recorded 412 of them.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Their second claim was that the crossing is dangerous. They used the city's own crash records. Those listed two collisions and one injury in four years.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Their third claim was that a crosswalk would help. That needed outside evidence. They cited a transportation study of marked crossings.

paras.label: E
paras.text: They also named what they could not show. Nobody could prove a future crash would be stopped. The presentation said so.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The council approved the crosswalk. The tally mattered most. Nobody could dispute it. The students had counted it themselves.

questions.q: What evidence supported the claim that people already cross there?
questions.a: Two students counted crossings for five mornings and recorded 412 of them, with the tally sheets attached.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. the tally) and paragraph E (i.e. what they could not show).
Summarize the three claims and the evidence for each.
questions.a: People already cross there, supported by a tally of 412 crossings over five mornings. The crossing is dangerous, supported by city crash records listing two collisions and one injury in four years. A crosswalk would help, supported by a transportation study of marked crossings.

questions.q:
tally: a count kept by marking each item as it happens.
collision: a crash between two moving things.
Describe the connection between the students' own counting and the council's decision.
questions.a: The tally mattered most because it was the only piece of evidence nobody in the room could dispute, since the students had gone out and counted the 412 crossings themselves.

articles.note: Paragraph E is the part to praise. Naming the limit of your own evidence makes the rest of it more believable, not less.

articles.title: Should the School Put Solar Panels on the Roof?
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Explain how an author uses reasons and evidence to support particular points in a text, identifying which reasons and evidence support which point(s).
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.6 point of view · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: A school board received two reports on putting solar panels on the gym roof. Both were written by engineers, both used real numbers, and the two reached opposite recommendations.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first report supports the panels. Its central evidence is a twenty-five year total: the system costs $340,000 and would save about $620,000 in electricity over its life.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second report opposes them. Its central evidence is the roof itself, which has eleven years left before replacement, and removing and reinstalling panels would cost $45,000.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Neither report is hiding anything. They disagree because they chose different time spans, and a twenty-five year argument and an eleven year argument can both be true at once.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The board found the question underneath the disagreement. It was not whether solar panels save money, but whether to replace the roof first, and neither report had been asked to answer that.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That is what reading for reasons and evidence is for. The strongest move a reader can make is noticing which question the evidence was gathered to answer.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A school board got two reports on solar panels for the gym roof. Both were written by engineers. Both used real numbers. They reached opposite answers.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first report supports the panels. The system costs $340,000. It would save about $620,000 in electricity over twenty-five years.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second report opposes them. The roof has eleven years left. Taking the panels off and putting them back would cost $45,000.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Neither report hides anything. They chose different time spans. Both can be true at once.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The board found the real question. It was not whether panels save money. It was whether to replace the roof first.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That is what reading for evidence is for. Notice which question the evidence was gathered to answer.

questions.q: Why did the two reports disagree?
questions.a: They chose different time spans: one argued over twenty-five years and the other over the eleven years the roof has left, so both could be true at once.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. the savings) and paragraph C (i.e. the roof).
Summarize the two reports and what the board concluded.
questions.a: One report found the system costs $340,000 and would save about $620,000 over twenty-five years. The other found the roof has eleven years left and removing and reinstalling the panels would cost $45,000. The board decided the real question was whether to replace the roof first.

questions.q:
recommendation: the course of action a report advises.
span: a stretch of time from one point to another.
Describe the connection between the time span a report uses and the recommendation it reaches.
questions.a: A twenty-five year span makes the electricity savings of about $620,000 decisive, while an eleven year span makes the $45,000 cost of removing and reinstalling the panels decisive, so the same numbers support opposite recommendations.

articles.note: This is the hardest of the five and the most useful. Two honest reports, no villain, and the disagreement sitting in the question rather than the data.

articles.title: Naming the Park
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Explain how an author uses reasons and evidence to support particular points in a text, identifying which reasons and evidence support which point(s).
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.6 point of view · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: A city asked residents to propose a name for a new park, then published the three finalists with the case made for each. The three cases are not built the same way.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first proposes the name of a teacher who ran a free summer program on that land for thirty years. The case rests on testimony: eleven letters from former students, quoted at length.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second proposes a name from the language of the people who lived there first, and that case rests on documents, a treaty map and a historical society's record of the place name.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The third proposes naming it after the creek that runs through it. The case is practical: the name is already in use, appears on maps, and would need no explanation to anyone.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Each case is strong for a different reason. Testimony shows what a place has meant, documents show what it was called, and practicality shows what will actually be said out loud.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The council will have to decide which reason counts most, and no amount of further evidence will settle that. Choosing between good reasons is a different task from weighing evidence.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A city asked residents to propose a name for a new park. It published three finalists and the case for each. The three cases are not built the same way.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first proposes a teacher's name. She ran a free summer program on that land for thirty years. The case rests on eleven letters from former students.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second proposes a name from the language of the people who lived there first. That case rests on documents. A treaty map and a historical record.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The third proposes naming it after the creek. The case is practical. The name is already in use. It appears on maps.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Each case is strong for a different reason. Testimony shows what a place has meant. Documents show what it was called. Practicality shows what people will say.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The council must decide which reason counts most. More evidence will not settle that. Choosing between good reasons is a different task.

questions.q: What kind of evidence supports the first proposed name?
questions.a: Testimony: eleven letters from former students of the teacher who ran a free summer program on that land for thirty years, quoted at length.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. documents) and paragraph E (i.e. what each kind shows).
Summarize the three cases and what each rests on.
questions.a: A teacher's name rests on testimony from eleven former students. A name from the language of the people who lived there first rests on a treaty map and a historical record. The creek's name rests on being already in use and on maps.

questions.q:
testimony: a statement by someone about what they know or saw.
practical: useful and workable in everyday life.
Describe the connection between the kind of evidence a case uses and what that case can prove.
questions.a: Testimony shows what a place has meant to people, documents show what it was called, and practicality shows what will actually be said out loud, so each kind of evidence can only settle its own kind of question.

articles.note: A class vote after the reading makes paragraph F land: the room will split, and no further evidence will move anybody.

articles.title: Three Texts on the Monarch Butterfly
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Integrate information from several texts on the same topic in order to write or speak about the subject knowledgeably.
 Spiral: RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.5 structure · RI.5.7 multiple sources · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: A student writing about monarch butterflies has three texts on the desk: a life cycle diagram, a tagging study, and a news article about milkweed. None of them is the report, and together they are.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The diagram gives the sequence. Egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, adult, and the detail that an adult born in late summer lives eight months while one born in June lives about five weeks.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The tagging study gives the distance. Volunteers put numbered stickers on wings in Canada and the tags turned up in Mexico, which is how the three-thousand-mile migration was first proved.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The news article gives the problem. Milkweed is the only plant monarch caterpillars eat, and it has been cleared from most farm edges in the midwest over the last thirty years.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Put together they answer a question none of them asks. The long-lived late-summer generation is the one that makes the whole journey, and it needs milkweed at both ends of a route it has never flown.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That is what integrating sources means. The student is not summarizing three texts in turn but using them to say something none of their authors wrote down.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A student is writing about monarch butterflies. Three texts sit on the desk. A life cycle diagram. A tagging study. A news article about milkweed.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The diagram gives the sequence. Egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, adult. An adult born in late summer lives eight months. One born in June lives five weeks.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The tagging study gives the distance. Volunteers put numbered stickers on wings in Canada. The tags turned up in Mexico.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The news article gives the problem. Milkweed is the only plant the caterpillars eat. Most of it has been cleared from farm edges.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Together they answer a new question. The long-lived generation makes the whole journey. It needs milkweed at both ends of a route it has never flown.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That is what integrating sources means. The student says something none of the three authors wrote down.

questions.q: How long does a monarch born in late summer live?
questions.a: About eight months, while one born in June lives about five weeks.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the tagging study) and paragraph E (i.e. putting the three together).
Summarize what the three texts together show.
questions.a: The diagram gives the life cycle and the two lifespans, the tagging study proves a three-thousand-mile migration, and the news article shows milkweed disappearing. Together they show that the long-lived late-summer generation makes the whole journey and needs milkweed at both ends.

questions.q:
migration: a regular journey animals make from one region to another.
chrysalis: the hard case a caterpillar forms before becoming an adult butterfly.
Describe the connection between the lifespan in the diagram and the distance in the tagging study.
questions.a: An adult born in late summer lives eight months rather than five weeks, which is what makes the three-thousand-mile journey the tags proved possible for a single butterfly.

articles.note: Paragraph F names the standard. A student who writes three paragraphs, one per source, has summarized rather than integrated.

articles.title: Three Texts on the Cliff Houses
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Integrate information from several texts on the same topic in order to write or speak about the subject knowledgeably.
 Spiral: RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.5 structure · RI.5.7 multiple sources · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: Three sources describe the stone houses built into the cliffs of the Colorado Plateau, and a reader who uses only one will come away with a picture that is partly wrong.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first is an archaeological report. It dates the main building period to the twelve hundreds, counts the rooms at Cliff Palace at about 150, and notes that the sites were occupied for less than a century.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second is a tree-ring record. Beams cut from the roofs can be dated to the year, and the rings show a severe drought across the region in the eleven seventies and again in the twelve seventies.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The third comes from Pueblo people today. Hopi and Zuni accounts describe the cliff sites not as a place that was abandoned but as one stop on a long migration that continued south.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A reader who has only the report thinks of an unsolved mystery. One who has only the tree rings thinks drought drove everyone out. One who has only the Pueblo accounts misses the dates.

paras.label: F
paras.text: All three together give something steadier: a hard climate, a decision to move, and descendants who never stopped describing the move as something their ancestors chose to do.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Three sources describe the stone houses in the cliffs of the Colorado Plateau. A reader who uses only one gets a picture that is partly wrong.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first is an archaeological report. The main building period was the twelve hundreds. Cliff Palace has about 150 rooms. The sites were used for less than a century.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second is a tree-ring record. Roof beams can be dated to the year. The rings show a severe drought in the eleven seventies and again in the twelve seventies.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The third comes from Pueblo people today. Hopi and Zuni accounts do not call the sites abandoned. They describe one stop on a migration that went south.

paras.label: E
paras.text: One source alone misleads. The report alone sounds like a mystery. The tree rings alone sound like drought drove everyone out.

paras.label: F
paras.text: All three together are steadier. A hard climate. A decision to move. Descendants who still describe that move.

questions.q: What do the tree rings show?
questions.a: Roof beams can be dated to the year, and the rings show a severe drought across the region in the eleven seventies and again in the twelve seventies.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. the Pueblo accounts) and paragraph E (i.e. what one source alone misses).
Summarize what the three sources together show.
questions.a: The archaeological report dates the building and counts the rooms, the tree rings date two severe droughts, and Pueblo accounts describe the sites as one stop on a migration rather than a place abandoned. Together they give a hard climate, a decision to move, and descendants who still describe it.

questions.q:
archaeological: having to do with the study of people through what they left behind.
drought: a long period with far less rain than usual.
Describe the connection between the Pueblo accounts and the word abandoned.
questions.a: Hopi and Zuni accounts describe the cliff sites not as a place that was abandoned but as one stop on a long migration that continued south, which changes what the archaeological dates mean.

articles.note: The word abandoned is the whole lesson. It is in most textbooks and the people whose ancestors lived there do not use it.

articles.title: Three Texts on Hibernation
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Integrate information from several texts on the same topic in order to write or speak about the subject knowledgeably.
 Spiral: RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.5 structure · RI.5.7 multiple sources · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: Hibernation sounds like one thing and is not. Three sources about three animals show that the word covers several different strategies for getting through a winter.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A ground squirrel account describes true hibernation. Body temperature falls to near freezing, the heart slows to a few beats a minute, and the animal wakes only every week or two to shiver warm again.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A bear account describes something else. A denning bear's temperature drops only a few degrees, it does not eat or drink for months, and it can wake and move within a minute if disturbed.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A frog account is stranger than either. Some wood frogs freeze solid, with ice between their cells and sugar packed inside them to keep the cells from bursting, and thaw in spring.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Reading only one gives a wrong rule. A student who learns the bear case will say hibernating animals wake easily; one who learns the squirrel case will say they cannot be roused at all.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Taken together the three give a better definition. Hibernation is any way of surviving a season on stored resources, and what the body does depends on how big it is and how cold it gets.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Hibernation sounds like one thing. It is not. Three sources about three animals show several ways to get through a winter.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A ground squirrel shows true hibernation. Its temperature falls near freezing. Its heart slows to a few beats a minute. It wakes every week or two.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A bear is different. Its temperature drops only a few degrees. It does not eat or drink for months. It can wake within a minute.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A frog is stranger still. Some wood frogs freeze solid. Ice forms between their cells. Sugar inside keeps the cells from bursting. They thaw in spring.

paras.label: E
paras.text: One source alone gives a wrong rule. The bear case says they wake easily. The squirrel case says they cannot be roused.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Together the three give a better definition. Hibernation is surviving a season on stored resources. What the body does depends on its size and the cold.

questions.q: How does a bear in a den differ from a hibernating ground squirrel?
questions.a: A bear's temperature drops only a few degrees and it can wake and move within a minute, while a ground squirrel's temperature falls to near freezing and its heart slows to a few beats a minute.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. the frog) and paragraph F (i.e. the better definition).
Summarize what the three accounts together say about hibernation.
questions.a: A ground squirrel cools to near freezing, a bear drops only a few degrees but can wake within a minute, and a wood frog freezes solid and thaws in spring. Together they show hibernation is any way of surviving a season on stored resources.

questions.q:
rouse: to wake something that is deeply asleep.
strategy: a plan or method for dealing with a situation.
Describe the connection between an animal's size and what its body does in winter.
questions.a: What the body does depends on how big it is and how cold it gets, which is why a small ground squirrel can cool to near freezing while a bear only drops a few degrees.

articles.note: Paragraph E is the argument for reading more than one source, stated as a mistake students will recognize having made.

articles.title: Three Texts on the Chicago Fire
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Integrate information from several texts on the same topic in order to write or speak about the subject knowledgeably.
 Spiral: RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.5 structure · RI.5.7 multiple sources · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: The fire that burned Chicago in October of 1871 destroyed about three and a half square miles of the city. Three kinds of source describe it, and they are useful for different things.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first is the fire department's own inquiry. It records the alarm raised at about nine on a Sunday evening, a wrong box pulled, and an engine sent to the wrong street for over an hour.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second is the set of newspaper accounts printed in the weeks after. They are vivid, and they are also where the story about a cow kicking over a lantern first appeared, which a reporter later admitted he had invented.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The third is the insurance record. Claims filed after the fire describe building materials street by street, and they show how much of the burned district was wooden, including the sidewalks.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Each has a weakness. The inquiry was written by people whose work was being judged, the newspapers were competing for readers, and the insurance claims covered only what was insured.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Used together they answer the real question. The fire spread as it did because of a dry autumn, a wooden city, and an hour lost at the start, and no cow was required.

paras.text: The fire that burned Chicago in October of 1871 destroyed about three and a half square miles. Three kinds of source describe it. Each is good for something different.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first is the fire department's inquiry. The alarm was raised at about nine on a Sunday evening. A wrong box was pulled. An engine went to the wrong street.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second is the newspaper accounts. They are vivid. They are also where the story of a cow and a lantern began. A reporter later admitted he invented it.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The third is the insurance record. Claims describe building materials street by street. Much of the burned district was wooden, even the sidewalks.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Each has a weakness. The inquiry judged its own writers. The newspapers competed for readers. The claims covered only what was insured.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Together they answer the real question. A dry autumn. A wooden city. An hour lost at the start. No cow was required.

questions.q: Where did the story about the cow come from?
questions.a: It first appeared in the newspaper accounts printed in the weeks after the fire, and a reporter later admitted he had invented it.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. the insurance record) and paragraph E (i.e. each source's weakness).
Summarize what the three sources together explain.
questions.a: The inquiry records an hour lost to a wrong box and a wrong street, the newspapers are vivid but invented the cow, and the insurance claims show how much of the district was wooden. Together they explain a fire spread by a dry autumn, a wooden city and a slow start.

questions.q:
inquiry: an official investigation into what happened.
claim: a request for payment from an insurance company.
Describe the connection between each source's weakness and the need for all three.
questions.a: The inquiry was written by people whose work was being judged, the newspapers were competing for readers, and the claims covered only what was insured, so no one source can be trusted on its own.

articles.note: Almost every student arrives knowing the cow. Paragraph C is a good moment to ask where they learned it and how they could have checked.

articles.title: Three Texts on Antarctic Ice
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Integrate information from several texts on the same topic in order to write or speak about the subject knowledgeably.
 Spiral: RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.5 structure · RI.5.7 multiple sources · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: Three sources describe the ice of Antarctica, and a reader who mixes them up will reach a conclusion that none of them supports.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first measures sea ice: frozen ocean water that forms each winter and melts each summer, covering an area larger than the continent at its peak and nearly vanishing by February.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second measures the ice sheet: fresh water locked on land, in places more than two miles thick, built up over hundreds of thousands of years of snowfall.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The two behave differently and matter differently. Melting sea ice does not raise sea level, because the ice is already floating; melting land ice does, because it adds water that was not in the ocean.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The third source is a satellite record of mass. Since 2002 a pair of satellites has weighed the continent by measuring tiny changes in gravity, and the land ice has been losing mass.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A headline about record ice can be true of the sea ice in the same year the ice sheet is shrinking. Knowing which ice a sentence is about is the difference between reading the news and misreading it.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Three sources describe the ice of Antarctica. A reader who mixes them up will reach a wrong conclusion.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first measures sea ice. That is frozen ocean water. It forms each winter and melts each summer. At its peak it is larger than the continent.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second measures the ice sheet. That is fresh water locked on land. In places it is more than two miles thick.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The two behave differently. Melting sea ice does not raise sea level. It is already floating. Melting land ice does raise it.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The third source is a satellite record. Since 2002 satellites have weighed the continent by measuring gravity. The land ice has been losing mass.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A headline about record ice can be about sea ice. The ice sheet can shrink in the same year. Knowing which ice is meant matters.

questions.q: Why does melting sea ice not raise sea level?
questions.a: The sea ice is already floating, so melting it adds no water that was not in the ocean, while melting land ice does.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. the difference) and paragraph F (i.e. reading a headline).
Summarize what the three sources measure.
questions.a: One measures sea ice, frozen ocean water that forms and melts each year. One measures the ice sheet, fresh water locked on land more than two miles thick in places. The third weighs the continent from satellites, and the land ice has been losing mass.

questions.q:
sea ice: frozen ocean water floating on the sea.
mass: how much matter something contains.
Describe the connection between which ice a headline means and whether it is misleading.
questions.a: A headline about record ice can be true of the sea ice in the same year the ice sheet is shrinking, so a reader who does not know which ice is meant will draw the wrong conclusion.

articles.note: A glass of water with an ice cube in it settles paragraph D in thirty seconds. Mark the level, let it melt, look again.

articles.title: The Mail That Went by Mule
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of the year, read and comprehend informational texts, including history/social studies, science, and technical texts, at the high end of the grades 4-5 text complexity band independently and proficiently.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.4 word meaning · RI.5.8 reasons and evidence
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: Until 2023 the United States ran one mail route that no vehicle could reach. Letters and parcels for the village of Supai, at the bottom of a side canyon of the Grand Canyon, went down on mules.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The village sits eight miles from the nearest road, down a trail that drops two thousand feet through switchbacks too narrow and too steep for a truck of any size.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A train of mules left the canyon rim most mornings carrying sorted mail in canvas panniers. Each animal took about a hundred and thirty pounds, and the trip down ran three to five hours.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Everything the village used came the same way. Groceries, building supplies, mattresses and school books were all weighed, balanced in pairs so the two loads matched, and roped on.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The mail was stamped with a special postmark, and the route was the last official pack-mule mail service in the country. Helicopters now carry much of the load.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The route lasted because the alternative was worse. Building a road would have cut through the canyon the village lives in, and for more than a century mules were simply the sensible answer.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Until 2023 one United States mail route had no road. Letters and parcels for the village of Supai went down on mules. The village is in a side canyon of the Grand Canyon.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The village sits eight miles from the nearest road. The trail drops two thousand feet. It is too narrow and steep for a truck.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A train of mules left the rim most mornings. Sorted mail rode in canvas bags. Each animal took about a hundred and thirty pounds.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Everything the village used came the same way. Groceries. Building supplies. Mattresses. School books. All of it was weighed and roped on.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The mail got a special postmark. It was the last pack-mule mail service in the country. Helicopters now carry much of the load.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The route lasted because the alternative was worse. A road would have cut through the canyon. Mules were the sensible answer.

questions.q: Why could no truck reach Supai?
questions.a: The village sits eight miles from the nearest road, down a trail that drops two thousand feet through switchbacks too narrow and too steep for a truck of any size.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the mule train) and paragraph F (i.e. why no road was built).
Summarize how mail reached Supai.
questions.a: Mules left the canyon rim most mornings carrying sorted mail in canvas panniers, about a hundred and thirty pounds each, down a two-thousand-foot trail in three to five hours. Groceries, supplies and school books went the same way.

questions.q:
pannier: a basket or bag carried on the side of a pack animal.
switchback: a sharp bend in a trail that climbs or drops steeply.
Describe the connection between the canyon and the decision not to build a road.
questions.a: Building a road would have cut through the canyon the village lives in, so for more than a century mules were simply the sensible answer.

articles.note: Paragraph F is worth lingering on. The route was not a leftover; it was a choice the village kept making.

articles.title: The Clock in Your Body
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of the year, read and comprehend informational texts, including history/social studies, science, and technical texts, at the high end of the grades 4-5 text complexity band independently and proficiently.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.4 word meaning · RI.5.8 reasons and evidence
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: Almost every cell in the human body keeps time. A small group of neurons behind the eyes sets the pace, and the rhythm it runs on is close to twenty-four hours but not exactly.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Light is what corrects it. Special cells in the retina, separate from those used for seeing, report brightness to that clock and shift it forward or back by a few minutes each day.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The shifting explains jet lag. Flown across six time zones, a traveller's clock is six hours out and moves at roughly an hour a day, which is why the body takes most of a week to agree with the local one.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The clock controls more than sleep. Body temperature, blood pressure, hunger and the release of several hormones all follow it, and some medicines work measurably better at particular hours.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Adolescence shifts the whole rhythm later. Through the teenage years the clock runs behind a child's or an adult's by one to three hours, which is a change in biology rather than a habit.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That shift is why school start times are argued about. A teenager told to sleep at nine is being asked to do something their clock is not yet releasing them to do.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Almost every cell in the body keeps time. A small group of neurons behind the eyes sets the pace. Its rhythm is close to twenty-four hours.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Light corrects it. Special cells in the retina report brightness to that clock. They shift it forward or back by a few minutes each day.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That explains jet lag. Fly across six time zones and your clock is six hours out. It moves about an hour a day. A week passes before it agrees.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The clock controls more than sleep. Body temperature, blood pressure and hunger follow it. Some medicines work better at certain hours.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Adolescence shifts the rhythm later. A teenager's clock runs one to three hours behind. That is biology, not a habit.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That shift is why school start times are argued about. A teenager told to sleep at nine cannot yet do it.

questions.q: What corrects the body's clock?
questions.a: Light does: special cells in the retina report brightness to the clock and shift it forward or back by a few minutes each day.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. jet lag) and paragraph E (i.e. the shift in adolescence).
Summarize what the body's clock does and what sets it.
questions.a: A group of neurons behind the eyes keeps a rhythm close to twenty-four hours, corrected daily by light reported from the retina. It controls sleep, body temperature, blood pressure, hunger and hormones, and it runs one to three hours later through adolescence.

questions.q:
retina: the layer at the back of the eye that takes in light.
adolescence: the years between childhood and adulthood.
Describe the connection between the teenage clock and arguments about school start times.
questions.a: Through the teenage years the clock runs one to three hours behind an adult's, so a teenager told to sleep at nine is being asked to do something their biology is not yet releasing them to do.

articles.note: Fifth graders are a year or two from paragraph E. Reading it before it happens to them is most of the point.

articles.title: The Woman Who Finished the Bridge
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of the year, read and comprehend informational texts, including history/social studies, science, and technical texts, at the high end of the grades 4-5 text complexity band independently and proficiently.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.4 word meaning · RI.5.8 reasons and evidence
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: The Brooklyn Bridge was designed by John Roebling, who died of tetanus before construction began. His son Washington took over, and within three years he could not leave his room.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The cause was the work underwater. Men dug in sealed chambers called caissons, under pressure, and rising too quickly left them with crippling pain that nobody yet knew how to prevent.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Washington was left partly paralysed and unable to speak above a whisper. The bridge had eleven years left to build and a chief engineer who could not go to the site.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Emily Roebling, his wife, became the link. She learned cable construction, stress analysis and the mathematics of catenary curves, and carried instructions and answers between her husband and the site every day.

paras.label: E
paras.text: For more than a decade she met the contractors and the trustees. When politicians moved to replace Washington, she argued the case for keeping him and the board voted with her.

paras.label: F
paras.text: She was the first person to ride across the finished bridge in 1883, carrying a rooster for luck. A plaque on the bridge names all three Roeblings, which is the honest version of the story.

paras.label: A
paras.text: The Brooklyn Bridge was designed by John Roebling. He died before building began. His son Washington took over. Within three years he could not leave his room.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The cause was work underwater. Men dug in sealed chambers under pressure. Rising too quickly left them in crippling pain. Nobody knew how to prevent it.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Washington was partly paralysed. He could not speak above a whisper. The bridge had eleven years left to build.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Emily Roebling, his wife, became the link. She learned cable construction and stress analysis. She carried instructions to the site every day.

paras.label: E
paras.text: For more than a decade she met the contractors and trustees. Politicians tried to replace Washington. She argued for him and the board agreed.

paras.label: F
paras.text: She was the first to ride across the finished bridge in 1883. She carried a rooster for luck. A plaque names all three Roeblings.

questions.q: Why could Washington Roebling not go to the site?
questions.a: Working underwater in pressurized caissons left him partly paralysed and unable to speak above a whisper.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. what Emily learned) and paragraph E (i.e. the vote).
Summarize Emily Roebling's part in building the bridge.
questions.a: She learned cable construction, stress analysis and the mathematics of catenary curves, carried instructions between her husband and the site every day for more than a decade, met the contractors and trustees, and argued successfully against replacing him.

questions.q:
caisson: a sealed chamber used for working underwater.
paralysed: unable to move part of the body.
Describe the connection between the caissons and Emily Roebling's role.
questions.a: The pressurized caissons left Washington partly paralysed and unable to reach the site, so Emily learned the engineering and became the link between him and the work for eleven years.

articles.note: She had no title for most of those years. Ask what the plaque naming all three Roeblings is correcting.

articles.title: The Channel That Carries Whale Song
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of the year, read and comprehend informational texts, including history/social studies, science, and technical texts, at the high end of the grades 4-5 text complexity band independently and proficiently.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.4 word meaning · RI.5.8 reasons and evidence
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: A fin whale's call can be detected by a listening station a thousand miles away. The reason is not the loudness of the whale alone but a layer of the ocean that behaves like a pipe.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Sound in water bends toward whatever slows it down. Speed falls as water gets colder and rises as pressure increases, so between the cold surface layers and the deep high-pressure water there is a depth where sound travels slowest.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Sound that enters that depth cannot easily leave. A wave angling upward bends back down, a wave angling downward bends back up, and the energy is trapped in a horizontal channel instead of spreading in all directions.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The layer sits around half a mile down in most oceans and is called the SOFAR channel. It was discovered in the nineteen forties, when researchers set off small charges and heard them hours later across an ocean basin.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Several baleen whales call at frequencies that suit it, low and long, below the range of most human hearing. Blue and fin whale calls are among the loudest sounds any animal makes.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Shipping noise sits in the same frequencies and the same channel. Recordings show whales raising the pitch and loudness of their calls where traffic is heavy, and the range a call carries has shrunk.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A fin whale's call can be heard a thousand miles away. The reason is not only the whale. A layer of the ocean acts like a pipe.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Sound in water bends toward whatever slows it down. Cold water slows it. High pressure speeds it. So there is a depth where sound is slowest.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Sound that enters that depth cannot leave easily. A wave angling up bends back down. A wave angling down bends back up. The energy stays in a channel.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The layer sits about half a mile down. It is called the SOFAR channel. It was found in the nineteen forties.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Several whales call at low frequencies that suit it. Blue and fin whale calls are among the loudest sounds any animal makes.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Shipping noise sits in the same channel. Where traffic is heavy, whales raise the pitch and loudness of their calls. The range a call carries has shrunk.

questions.q: Why can a whale call travel a thousand miles?
questions.a: Sound that enters the depth where it travels slowest is trapped in a horizontal channel, because a wave angling upward bends back down and a wave angling downward bends back up.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the trapping) and paragraph F (i.e. shipping noise).
Summarize how the SOFAR channel works.
questions.a: Sound in water bends toward whatever slows it down, and about half a mile deep the cold and the pressure balance so sound travels slowest there. Sound entering that depth bends back into it instead of spreading, so it carries horizontally for a thousand miles.

questions.q:
frequency: how high or low a sound is.
channel: a path that keeps something travelling in one direction.
Describe the connection between shipping noise and whale calls.
questions.a: Shipping noise sits in the same frequencies and the same channel, so where traffic is heavy whales raise the pitch and loudness of their calls and the range a call carries has shrunk.

articles.note: This is the densest article in the grade 5 set, which is what RI.5.10 asks for. Read paragraph B twice before going on.

articles.title: The Code Talkers
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of the year, read and comprehend informational texts, including history/social studies, science, and technical texts, at the high end of the grades 4-5 text complexity band independently and proficiently.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.4 word meaning · RI.5.8 reasons and evidence
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: During the Second World War, American forces in the Pacific needed a way to send orders by radio that the other side could not read. Machine codes existed, but encoding and decoding a message took half an hour.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The answer was a language rather than a cipher. Navajo was spoken by fewer than thirty people outside the Navajo Nation, had no written form in wide use, and was unrelated to any European or Asian language.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Around four hundred Navajo marines served as code talkers. They did not simply speak Navajo: they built a code inside it, with Navajo words standing for letters and for military terms.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A submarine became an iron fish, a dive bomber a chicken hawk, and a general a war chief. A message that took half an hour on a machine took about twenty seconds.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The code was never broken. It stayed classified until 1968, which meant the men who built it could not explain what they had done for more than twenty years after the war.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Many of them had been punished as children for speaking Navajo in government boarding schools. The language those schools tried to end became one the United States military could not do without.

paras.label: A
paras.text: In the Second World War, American forces in the Pacific needed secret radio orders. Machine codes existed. Encoding and decoding took half an hour.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The answer was a language, not a cipher. Navajo was spoken by fewer than thirty people outside the Navajo Nation. It had no widely used written form.

paras.label: C
paras.text: About four hundred Navajo marines served as code talkers. They did not simply speak Navajo. They built a code inside it.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A submarine became an iron fish. A dive bomber became a chicken hawk. A general became a war chief. A message took about twenty seconds.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The code was never broken. It stayed secret until 1968. The men could not explain what they had done for over twenty years.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Many had been punished as children for speaking Navajo at boarding schools. That language became one the military could not do without.

questions.q: Why was Navajo chosen?
questions.a: It was spoken by fewer than thirty people outside the Navajo Nation, had no written form in wide use, and was unrelated to any European or Asian language.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. the code words) and paragraph F (i.e. the boarding schools).
Summarize what the code talkers did.
questions.a: About four hundred Navajo marines built a code inside their own language, with Navajo words standing for letters and military terms, so a message that took half an hour on a machine took about twenty seconds. The code was never broken and stayed classified until 1968.

questions.q:
cipher: a system for turning a message into secret writing.
classified: kept officially secret.
Describe the connection between the boarding schools and the code.
questions.a: Many of the code talkers had been punished as children for speaking Navajo in government boarding schools, and that same language became one the United States military could not do without.

articles.note: Paragraph F is not an aside. Read it last, slowly, and let the room sit with it before asking anything.

articles.title: The Radium Dial Painters
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Cite textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.
 Spiral: RI.6.2 central idea · RI.6.3 development · RI.6.4 word meaning · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1917 a factory in New Jersey hired young women to paint watch dials with a glowing green paint called Undark. The work paid well for the time, and the women were told the paint was harmless.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The glow came from radium, an element discovered twenty years earlier and still treated as a marvel. Radium appeared in toothpaste, in face cream, and in tonics sold as cures for almost anything.

paras.label: C
paras.text: To keep a fine point on the brush, the painters were taught to roll the bristles between their lips. A dial has small numbers, and a sharp tip was the only way to fill them. Each worker did this hundreds of times a day.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Radium behaves chemically like calcium, so the body files it away in bone. Within a few years the women began to lose teeth, and their jaws broke under ordinary pressure. Doctors who had never seen the pattern called it a mystery.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The company's own consultants had warned of the danger as early as 1925, and the company kept the reports quiet. When five of the women sued in 1927, the firm argued that they had contracted syphilis instead.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The women won a settlement in 1928, and the case helped build the legal idea that a worker can sue an employer for an occupational disease. The dials they painted still register on a Geiger counter today.

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1917 a factory in New Jersey hired young women. They painted watch dials with a glowing green paint. They were told the paint was safe.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The glow came from radium. The element had been found twenty years before. People put it in toothpaste and face cream and thought it was healthy.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The painters had to keep a fine point on the brush. They were taught to roll the bristles between their lips. Each worker did this hundreds of times a day.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Radium acts like calcium in the body. The body stores it in bone. Soon the women lost teeth. Their jaws broke under light pressure.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The company's own experts had warned about the danger in 1925. The company kept those reports quiet. Five women sued in 1927.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The women won in 1928. The case helped make a new rule. A worker could sue a boss over a disease caught at work.

questions.q: Why did the dial painters put their brushes in their mouths?
questions.a: A dial has small numbers, so a sharp tip was the only way to fill them, and the painters were taught to roll the bristles between their lips to keep a fine point.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the brushes) and paragraph E (i.e. the warnings the company kept quiet).
Summarize what happened to the women who painted watch dials.
questions.a: They were hired in 1917 to paint dials with radium paint and taught to point their brushes with their lips. The radium settled in their bones, their teeth and jaws broke, and the company hid its own warnings. Five of them sued and won a settlement in 1928.

questions.q:
occupational disease: an illness a person gets from the work they do.
consultant: an expert a company hires to study a question and report back.
Describe the connection between the way radium behaves in the body and the injuries the women suffered.
questions.a: Radium behaves chemically like calcium, so the body files it away in bone, and that is why the women lost teeth and their jaws broke under ordinary pressure.

articles.note: RI.6.1 asks for evidence, so push for the sentence, i.e. "the company's own consultants had warned of the danger as early as 1925." An answer that only says the company knew is not yet cited.

articles.title: How a Glacier Moves
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Cite textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.
 Spiral: RI.6.2 central idea · RI.6.3 development · RI.6.4 word meaning · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: A glacier looks like a landscape that has stopped. Measure the same point for a year, though, and it will have traveled, sometimes a few centimeters and sometimes half a kilometer.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The motion has two parts. Ice under enough pressure deforms, with crystals sliding past one another deep in the body of the glacier, so the middle of the ice creeps forward even where the base is frozen fast.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second part is sliding. Meltwater collects underneath and lifts the ice just enough to break its grip on bedrock. A glacier with water under it can move ten times faster than one without.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Because the centre moves faster than the edges, the surface tears. The cracks are called crevasses, and they only open in the upper fifty meters or so, where the ice is brittle rather than plastic.

paras.label: E
paras.text: What a glacier carries, it eventually drops. Boulders frozen into the base scrape the rock beneath into long parallel grooves, and the ridge of rubble left at the front marks how far the ice once reached.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Those ridges are how glaciologists read the past. A moraine sitting in a valley in New York is a record of where the ice stood eighteen thousand years ago, long before anyone was there to measure it.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A glacier looks like a landscape that has stopped. But measure one point for a year. It will have moved. Sometimes it moves a few centimeters. Sometimes it moves half a kilometer.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The motion has two parts. Ice under great pressure bends. Crystals slide past each other deep inside. So the middle of the ice creeps forward.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second part is sliding. Meltwater gathers underneath. It lifts the ice off the rock. Ice with water under it moves ten times faster.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The centre moves faster than the edges. So the surface tears open. These cracks are called crevasses. They form only near the top, where the ice is brittle.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A glacier drops what it carries. Boulders in the base scrape long grooves in the rock. A ridge of rubble marks how far the ice reached.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Those ridges tell scientists about the past. A moraine in a New York valley shows where the ice stood. That was eighteen thousand years ago.

questions.q: What two kinds of motion make up the movement of a glacier?
questions.a: Ice deep in the glacier deforms under pressure as crystals slide past one another, and the whole glacier slides on meltwater that lifts it off the bedrock.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. deforming) and paragraph C (i.e. sliding on meltwater).
Summarize how a glacier moves and what it leaves behind.
questions.a: A glacier creeps forward as the ice deforms under pressure and slides on meltwater beneath it. The centre moves faster than the edges, so crevasses open at the surface, and the ice scrapes grooves in the rock and leaves a ridge of rubble called a moraine.

questions.q:
crevasse: a crack that opens in the brittle upper ice of a glacier.
moraine: the ridge of rock and rubble left where the front of a glacier once stood.
Describe the connection between meltwater under a glacier and how fast it travels.
questions.a: Meltwater lifts the ice just enough to break its grip on bedrock, so a glacier with water under it can move ten times faster than one without.

articles.note: Ask where the text actually says how fast, i.e. "a few centimeters" against "half a kilometer." Citing the range is stronger than citing one number.

articles.title: The Library of Alexandria
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Cite textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.
 Spiral: RI.6.2 central idea · RI.6.3 development · RI.6.4 word meaning · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: Alexandria's library was not a building full of books in the modern sense. It was a collection of scrolls, perhaps several hundred thousand of them, attached to a research institution the Ptolemies paid for out of the royal treasury.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The collecting was aggressive. Ships that docked at Alexandria were searched for texts. Anything found was copied, and the official policy was to keep the original and return the copy to the owner.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Scholars worked there on salary. Eratosthenes measured the circumference of the Earth from the length of two shadows. Euclid's geometry and the first serious editions of Homer came out of the same institution.

paras.label: D
paras.text: There was no single fire. Caesar's troops burned part of the harbour district in 48 BCE, later rulers cut the scholars' funding, and the Roman emperor Aurelian destroyed the quarter the library stood in around 270 CE.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Most of the loss was quieter than any of that. Papyrus rots in humid air, and a scroll survives only as long as someone keeps copying it. When the salaries stopped, the copying stopped.

paras.label: F
paras.text: We know what is missing mostly from references. Ancient authors quote works no one has read since, which is how we know, for example, that Sophocles wrote more than a hundred plays and that seven survive.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Alexandria's library was not a building full of books. It was a collection of scrolls. There may have been several hundred thousand. The kings of Egypt paid for all of it.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The collecting was aggressive. Ships that docked were searched for texts. Each text was copied. The library kept the original and gave back the copy.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Scholars worked there for pay. Eratosthenes measured the size of the Earth using two shadows. Euclid wrote his geometry there.

paras.label: D
paras.text: There was no single fire. Caesar's soldiers burned part of the harbour in 48 BCE. Later rulers cut the funding. A Roman emperor destroyed the quarter around 270 CE.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Most of the loss was quieter. Papyrus rots in damp air. A scroll lasts only as long as someone copies it. When the pay stopped, the copying stopped.

paras.label: F
paras.text: We know what is missing from references. Old authors quote works no one has read since. Sophocles wrote over a hundred plays. Seven survive.
