paras.text: Results says what happened. That is all it says. The discussion comes next. There the authors may say what it means.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The limitations paragraph sits near the end. The authors name what their study cannot show. A paper without one is usually claiming too much.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So the order is about trust. Each section has one job. The claims come after the evidence.

questions.q: Why does the methods section matter even though nobody reads it for pleasure?
questions.a: It exists so that another lab can run the same study, and a method too vague to repeat is a finding that cannot be checked.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. results against discussion) and paragraph F (i.e. limitations).
Summarize how a research paper is organized and why.
questions.a: It has five parts in a fixed order: an abstract written last, an introduction that narrows to one question, methods that let another lab repeat the study, results that state only what happened, and a discussion where the authors say what it means. The order keeps the claims after the evidence so a reader can check them.

questions.q:
abstract: the compressed version of a whole paper, placed first and written last.
limitations: the paragraph where authors name what their study cannot show.
Describe the connection between splitting results from discussion and what a reader can trust.
questions.a: Results states what happened and nothing else, and the discussion is where the authors are allowed to say what they think it means, so keeping those apart lets a reader separate the evidence from the interpretation.

articles.note: This is RI.6.5 at the scale of a whole text. Ask which paragraph could move and which could not, i.e. why limitations cannot come before results.

articles.title: The Turn in the Middle
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze how a particular sentence, paragraph, chapter, or section fits into the overall structure of a text and contributes to the development of the ideas.
 Spiral: RI.6.2 central idea · RI.6.3 development · RI.6.6 point of view · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: Most arguments worth reading change direction once. The writer builds a case, then stops and takes the other side seriously, then answers it. That stop is the turn, and it usually arrives in the middle.

paras.label: B
paras.text: You can find it by its words. However, admittedly, it is true that, critics argue — each one announces that the next sentence will not continue the paragraph before it.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The turn is not a weakness. A reader who has already thought of the objection will stop trusting a writer who pretends it does not exist, so naming it first is what keeps them reading.

paras.label: D
paras.text: What the writer does after the turn is the test. A strong piece concedes the part that is actually true and then shows why the main claim survives anyway. A weak one restates the objection and calls it silly.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Remove the turn and the piece gets shorter and worse. It becomes a list of reasons for one side, which persuades nobody who did not already agree.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So when you read an argument, find the turn first. It tells you what the writer thinks the strongest case against them is, and whether they were willing to say it out loud.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Most good arguments change direction once. The writer builds a case. Then the writer takes the other side seriously. Then the writer answers it. That stop is the turn.

paras.label: B
paras.text: You can find it by its words. However. Admittedly. Critics argue. Each one warns you that the next sentence will not agree with the last.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The turn is not a weakness. A reader may have thought of the objection already. If the writer hides it, the reader stops trusting the writer.

paras.label: D
paras.text: What comes after the turn is the test. A strong piece admits the part that is true. Then it shows the main claim still holds. A weak piece just calls the objection silly.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Take out the turn and the piece gets worse. It becomes a list of reasons for one side. It persuades nobody.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So find the turn first. It shows what the writer fears most. It also shows whether they would say it out loud.

questions.q: What words signal that a turn is coming?
questions.a: However, admittedly, it is true that, and critics argue each announce that the next sentence will not continue the paragraph before it.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. why the turn builds trust) and paragraph D (i.e. what the writer does after it).
Summarize what the turn is and what it does for an argument.
questions.a: The turn is the point where a writer stops building their case, states the other side seriously, and answers it. It usually comes in the middle and is marked by words such as however or critics argue. Naming the objection keeps a reader who already thought of it, and what the writer does after the turn shows whether the argument is strong.

questions.q:
concede: to admit that part of the other side's case is true.
objection: the strongest reason somebody might disagree with the claim.
Describe the connection between hiding an objection and losing a reader.
questions.a: A reader who has already thought of the objection will stop trusting a writer who pretends it does not exist, so naming it first is what keeps them reading.

articles.note: Have students mark the turn in a real opinion column. The piece with no turn in it is the one worth discussing.

articles.title: Why the Timeline Comes First
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze how a particular sentence, paragraph, chapter, or section fits into the overall structure of a text and contributes to the development of the ideas.
 Spiral: RI.6.2 central idea · RI.6.3 development · RI.6.6 point of view · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: Open a history chapter and the first thing on the page is usually a timeline. It is easy to skip, and skipping it is why the chapter gets harder three pages later.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A timeline does one job the prose cannot. It fixes the order of events in a single glance, so the reader is not holding dates in mind while also following an argument.

paras.label: C
paras.text: History writing rarely runs in order. A chapter may open in 1945, jump back thirty years for causes, and return. That structure is deliberate, and it only works if the reader has the straight sequence somewhere to check against.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The spacing carries information too. Four events in one year and then a gap of twenty tells you where the pressure was, which a list of dates in a paragraph would hide.

paras.label: E
paras.text: What a timeline leaves out is the argument. It will tell you that two things happened in order and never that one caused the other, and a reader who treats sequence as cause has misread it.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So read it twice. Once before the chapter, to get the order, and once after, when the dates have names and reasons attached and the gaps have become the interesting part.

paras.label: B

paras.label: C

paras.label: D
paras.text: The spacing tells you something too. Four events in one year, then a gap of twenty. That shows where the pressure was.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A timeline leaves out the argument. It shows that two things happened in order. It never shows that one caused the other.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So read it twice. Read it before the chapter for the order. Read it after, when the dates have reasons attached.

questions.q: What job does a timeline do that the prose cannot?
questions.a: It fixes the order of events in a single glance, so the reader is not holding dates in mind while also following an argument.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. the spacing) and paragraph E (i.e. what a timeline leaves out).
Summarize why a history chapter puts a timeline before the prose.
questions.a: History writing rarely runs in order, so a reader needs the straight sequence somewhere to check against while the chapter jumps between years. The timeline fixes that order at a glance and its spacing shows where events clustered, but it cannot show cause, so it is worth reading both before and after the chapter.

questions.q:
sequence: the order in which events actually happened.
chronological: arranged in time order, which a timeline is and a chapter often is not.
Describe the connection between the gaps on a timeline and where the pressure was.
questions.a: Four events in one year and then a gap of twenty tells you where the pressure was, which a list of dates in a paragraph would hide.

articles.note: Paragraph E is the one to hold on to, i.e. "a reader who treats sequence as cause has misread it." That error is the whole reason the section exists.

articles.title: Where a Lab Report Ends
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze how a particular sentence, paragraph, chapter, or section fits into the overall structure of a text and contributes to the development of the ideas.
 Spiral: RI.6.2 central idea · RI.6.3 development · RI.6.6 point of view · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: Students are often taught that a lab report ends with a conclusion, and then taught to write the conclusion as a summary. Those two instructions pull in opposite directions.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A summary repeats. A conclusion decides. The last section of a report is where the writer answers the question the first section asked, and a reader should be able to read those two paragraphs alone and understand the point.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Which means the conclusion is written against the hypothesis, not against the data. If the opening predicted that the salt water would freeze later, the ending says whether it did, in those words.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The sentence that makes a conclusion work is usually the one admitting what went wrong. A thermometer read in a warm room, a timer started late — naming it is not a confession, it is the reason the number came out as it did.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A conclusion that ends with what to do next is stronger than one that ends with a result. The next experiment is the evidence that the writer understood their own.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So the shape is a circle. The question at the front and the answer at the back hold the report together, and everything between them is there to get from one to the other.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Students are told a lab report ends with a conclusion. They are also told to write a summary. Those two instructions pull apart.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A summary repeats. A conclusion decides. The last section answers the question the first section asked. A reader should understand the point from those two parts alone.

paras.label: C
paras.text: So the conclusion is written against the hypothesis. The opening may predict that salt water freezes later. The ending says whether it did.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The best sentence often admits what went wrong. A thermometer read in a warm room. A timer started late. That is not a confession. It explains the number.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A conclusion that says what to do next is stronger. The next experiment shows the writer understood this one.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So the shape is a circle. The question at the front and the answer at the back hold the report together.

questions.q: What is the difference between a summary and a conclusion?
questions.a: A summary repeats and a conclusion decides, because the conclusion answers the question the first section asked.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. writing against the hypothesis) and paragraph D (i.e. naming what went wrong).
Summarize what the last section of a lab report is for.
questions.a: It answers the question the opening asked, written against the hypothesis in the same words, so the first and last sections can be read alone and still make sense. It should name what went wrong and say what to do next, which makes the report a circle from question to answer.

questions.q:
hypothesis: the prediction the report sets out to test.
conclusion: the section that decides the question rather than repeating the report.
Describe the connection between the first section of a report and the last one.
questions.a: The last section answers the question the first section asked, so the question at the front and the answer at the back hold the report together and everything between them is there to get from one to the other.

articles.note: Ask students to read only the first and last paragraphs of a real report. If the point does not survive that, the conclusion was a summary.

articles.title: The Sidebar and the Story
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze how a particular sentence, paragraph, chapter, or section fits into the overall structure of a text and contributes to the development of the ideas.
 Spiral: RI.6.2 central idea · RI.6.3 development · RI.6.6 point of view · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: A news feature often carries a box beside the main text, set in a different typeface and a tinted panel. The box is not an interruption. It is doing work the article cannot do without stopping.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The main story has to move. A sidebar holds the material that would break that movement: a definition, a short history, the numbers behind a claim, a second voice that does not fit the narrative.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Where it sits is a decision. A sidebar placed beside the paragraph it serves gets read; the same box at the end of the article usually does not, and editors argue about this.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A sidebar can also carry the part the writer is least sure of. A disputed figure, a claim from one source only — putting it in a box marks it as separate from the reporting without hiding it.

paras.label: E
paras.text: That means reading the box changes the article. A story about a factory closing reads one way beside a sidebar on the town's unemployment rate and another beside one on the owner's other plants.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So the question to ask is not what the sidebar says but why it is a sidebar. Something was kept out of the main column on purpose, and what it was tells you how the writer wanted the story to run.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A news feature often has a box beside the main text. It is set in a different typeface. The box is not an interruption. It does work the article cannot.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The main story has to move. A sidebar holds what would break that movement. A definition. A short history. The numbers behind a claim.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Where it sits is a decision. A sidebar beside the paragraph it serves gets read. The same box at the end usually does not.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A sidebar can hold the part the writer is least sure of. A disputed figure. A claim from one source. The box marks it as separate without hiding it.

paras.label: E
paras.text: So reading the box changes the article. A story about a factory closing reads one way beside the town's jobless rate. It reads another beside the owner's other plants.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So ask why it is a sidebar. Something was kept out of the main column on purpose. What it was tells you how the writer wanted the story to run.

questions.q: What kind of material goes in a sidebar?
questions.a: A definition, a short history, the numbers behind a claim, or a second voice that does not fit the narrative — material that would break the movement of the main story.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. where the box sits) and paragraph D (i.e. what the writer is least sure of).
Summarize what a sidebar does and why its placement matters.
questions.a: A sidebar holds material that would stop the main story moving, such as a definition, a short history or the numbers behind a claim, and it can mark a disputed figure as separate without hiding it. A box beside the paragraph it serves gets read and one at the end usually does not, so placement decides whether it changes the article at all.

questions.q:
sidebar: a boxed section beside an article carrying material that would interrupt it.
narrative: the line the main story follows from beginning to end.
Describe the connection between what is in the sidebar and how the main story reads.
questions.a: A story about a factory closing reads one way beside a sidebar on the town's unemployment rate and another beside one on the owner's other plants, so the box changes the article.

articles.note: Paragraph F turns the standard into a habit, i.e. ask "not what the sidebar says but why it is a sidebar." That question works on any text with a box in it.

articles.title: Who Wrote the Brochure
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text and explain how it is conveyed in the text.
 Spiral: RI.6.1 citing evidence · RI.6.4 word meaning · RI.6.8 claims and evidence · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: A national park brochure and a resort brochure for the same valley can both be accurate and leave opposite impressions. Neither has to lie to do it, and neither usually does.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Start with who paid. The park service brochure is funded by an agency whose job is protecting the place and whose budget depends on visitors behaving. The resort's is funded by somebody selling rooms.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The park brochure warns. It names the elevation, the afternoon storms, the distance to the nearest water, and the two trails that have killed people. Warning you is part of its purpose.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The resort brochure photographs the same trail in good light and does not mention the storms. Everything in it is true, and the storms are missing, and that absence is the point.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Word choice carries the rest. One says rugged and remote; the other says secluded and unspoiled. They are describing the same emptiness and asking you to feel differently about it.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So the question is not which brochure is honest. Both can be. It is what each one needs you to do after reading it — stay safe, or book a room — and every choice in it follows from that.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A park brochure and a resort brochure can describe the same valley. Both can be accurate. They leave opposite impressions. Neither has to lie to do it.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Start with who paid. The park service protects the place. Its budget depends on visitors behaving. The resort is selling rooms.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The park brochure warns. It gives the elevation. It gives the afternoon storms. It names two trails that have killed people.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The resort brochure shows the same trail in good light. It does not mention the storms. Everything in it is true. The storms are missing.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Word choice does the rest. One says rugged and remote. The other says secluded and unspoiled. The emptiness is the same.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So ask what each one needs you to do after you read it. Stay safe, or book a room. Every choice in it follows from that.

questions.q: Why can both brochures be accurate and still leave opposite impressions?
questions.a: Everything in the resort brochure is true and the storms are missing, so the absence does the work rather than a lie.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. who paid) and paragraph E (i.e. word choice).
Summarize how two accurate brochures about the same place can differ.
questions.a: The park service brochure warns because its purpose is keeping visitors safe, naming the elevation, the storms and the trails that have killed people. The resort brochure photographs the same trail in good light and leaves the storms out. Word choice carries the rest, and both follow from what each one needs the reader to do.

questions.q:
purpose: what a text is trying to get the reader to think or do.
omission: something true that has been left out, which can shape a reader as much as a claim.
Describe the connection between who paid for a brochure and what it leaves out.
questions.a: The resort's brochure is funded by somebody selling rooms, so it does not mention the storms, while the park service brochure is funded by an agency whose job is protecting the place and warning you is part of its purpose.

articles.note: Paragraph E is the cleanest pair of synonyms students will meet all year, i.e. "rugged and remote" against "secluded and unspoiled." Same fact, opposite feeling.

articles.title: The Scientist and the Press Release
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text and explain how it is conveyed in the text.
 Spiral: RI.6.1 citing evidence · RI.6.4 word meaning · RI.6.8 claims and evidence · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: A study is published, a university writes a press release about it, and a news site writes a story from the release. By the end of that chain the claim is often larger than the study.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The study is written to be careful. It says that an association was observed in a sample of a particular size, under particular conditions, and that further work is needed.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The press release is written to be noticed. It is produced by a communications office whose purpose is attention for the university, and its first sentence usually drops the conditions.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Researchers do not always see it before it goes out, and some have publicly objected to the version of their own work that ended up in the headline.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The news story then works from the release rather than the paper. Studies of this chain have found that most of the exaggeration in health reporting is already present in the release, not added by the journalist.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The tells are findable. A study says may be associated with; a release says could help prevent; a headline says prevents. Each step drops a hedge and nobody writes anything untrue.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So read in the other direction. Find the study, read what it says it measured and in how many people, and compare that to the sentence that reached you.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A study is published. A university writes a press release. A news site writes a story from the release. By the end the claim is often larger.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The study is careful. It says an association was seen in a sample of one size. It says the conditions were particular. It says more work is needed.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The press release is written to be noticed. A communications office produces it. Its job is attention for the university. The first sentence usually drops the conditions.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Researchers do not always see it first. Some have objected in public to the version of their own work in the headline.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The news story works from the release, not the paper. Studies of this chain found most of the exaggeration is already in the release.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The tells are findable. A study says may be associated with. A release says could help prevent. A headline says prevents.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So read backwards. Find the study. Read what it measured and in how many people. Compare that to the sentence you saw.

questions.q: Where does most of the exaggeration in health reporting come from?
questions.a: Studies of this chain have found that most of the exaggeration is already present in the release, not added by the journalist.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. who writes the release) and paragraph F (i.e. the dropped hedges).
Summarize how a careful study becomes an overstated headline.
questions.a: The study reports an association in a particular sample under particular conditions. A university communications office writes a release to attract attention and drops the conditions, often without the researchers seeing it. The news story works from the release rather than the paper, so each step removes a hedge without anybody writing something untrue.

questions.q:
hedge: a word that limits a claim, such as may or associated with.
press release: an announcement written by an organization's own communications office.
Describe the connection between the purpose of a communications office and the first sentence of a release.
questions.a: Its purpose is attention for the university, so the first sentence usually drops the conditions the study was careful to state.

articles.note: Paragraph F is a three-step ladder worth putting on the board, i.e. "may be associated with" to "could help prevent" to "prevents."

articles.title: A Letter to the Editor About the Dam
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text and explain how it is conveyed in the text.
 Spiral: RI.6.1 citing evidence · RI.6.4 word meaning · RI.6.8 claims and evidence · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: A letter in a small-town paper argues that the old dam should stay. It runs four hundred words and never says what the writer does for a living. It is signed with a name and a street.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The argument is about memory. The writer swam in that reservoir as a child, names three families who did the same, and asks what the town will be without it.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Not one sentence addresses the engineering report. The report says the spillway has failed inspection twice, and the letter does not mention a spillway at all.

paras.label: D
paras.text: That silence is the strongest clue to purpose. A writer who wanted to win on the merits would take on the report; a writer who wants the reader to feel something will stay where the feeling is.

paras.label: E
paras.text: It can still be worth reading. What the town loses is real, and it is a thing the engineering report does not measure and was never meant to.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So hold both. The letter is evidence about what people value and no evidence at all about whether the dam is safe. Treating it as either one alone gets the decision wrong, and only one of the two questions is one an engineer can answer.

paras.label: A

paras.label: B
paras.text: The argument is about memory. The writer swam in that reservoir as a child. The letter names three families who did the same. It asks what the town will be without it.

paras.label: C
paras.text: No sentence addresses the engineering report. The report says the spillway failed inspection twice. The letter never mentions a spillway.

paras.label: D
paras.text: That silence is the best clue to purpose. A writer who wanted to win on the merits would take on the report. A writer who wants you to feel something stays where the feeling is.

paras.label: E
paras.text: It can still be worth reading. What the town loses is real. The engineering report does not measure that.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So hold both. The letter shows what people value. It shows nothing about whether the dam is safe. Only one of those is a question an engineer can answer.

questions.q: What does the letter never mention?
questions.a: It never mentions the spillway, although the engineering report says the spillway has failed inspection twice.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. what the silence tells you) and paragraph E (i.e. what the letter is still good for).
Summarize what the letter argues and what it leaves out.
questions.a: It argues that the old dam should stay on the grounds of memory, naming families who swam in the reservoir and asking what the town will be without it. It never addresses the engineering report or mentions the spillway that has failed inspection twice, so it is evidence about what people value and none about whether the dam is safe.

questions.q:
spillway: the channel that lets water past a dam safely.
merits: the facts of a case, as opposed to how people feel about it.
Describe the connection between what the letter avoids and what the writer wants the reader to feel.
questions.a: A writer who wanted to win on the merits would take on the report, and a writer who wants the reader to feel something will stay where the feeling is, which is why the letter never mentions a spillway.

articles.note: Paragraph E keeps this honest. The letter is weak evidence about safety and real evidence about value, and students should be able to say both.

articles.title: Why the Museum Label Says Probably
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text and explain how it is conveyed in the text.
 Spiral: RI.6.1 citing evidence · RI.6.4 word meaning · RI.6.8 claims and evidence · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: A museum label is about forty words long and every one of them has been argued over. The hedges in it are not caution for its own sake. They are a record of how much is actually known.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Probably a burial site means the objects were found arranged the way burials usually are, and no body survived. Ritual object means nobody knows what it was for.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Attributed to means the museum is not certain who made it. Circle of means somebody in that workshop. After means a later copy. Each is a different distance from the artist's own hand.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Date ranges work the same way. 1480 to 1520 is not vagueness; it is the span the evidence allows, and narrowing it would be claiming more than the museum can support.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The labels also record how an object arrived. Acquired in 1897 and collected during the expedition are doing different work, and some museums now say removed from, which is a sentence about a dispute.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So read the hedges as the honest part. A label with no qualifiers anywhere is either very well evidenced or written by somebody who has stopped distinguishing what is known from what is assumed.

paras.label: A

paras.label: B
paras.text: Probably a burial site means the objects lay the way burials usually do. It also means no body survived. Ritual object means nobody knows what it was for.

paras.label: C

paras.label: D
paras.text: Date ranges work the same way. 1480 to 1520 is not vagueness. It is the span the evidence allows. Narrowing it would claim too much.

paras.label: E

paras.label: F
paras.text: So read the hedges as the honest part. A label with no qualifiers is either very well evidenced or written by somebody who has stopped checking.

questions.q: What does a date range like 1480 to 1520 on a label mean?
questions.a: It is not vagueness; it is the span the evidence allows, and narrowing it would be claiming more than the museum can support.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. attributed to, circle of and after) and paragraph E (i.e. how an object arrived).
Summarize what the hedges on a museum label are doing.
questions.a: They record how much is actually known. Probably a burial site means the arrangement looked like a burial and no body survived, ritual object means nobody knows what it was for, and attributed to, circle of and after each mark a different distance from the artist's hand. Date ranges give the span the evidence allows.

questions.q:
attributed to: assigned to a maker the museum is not certain about.
qualifier: a word that limits a claim, such as probably or circle of.
Describe the connection between a label's wording and what the museum can support.
questions.a: Narrowing a date range would be claiming more than the museum can support, so the span the evidence allows is what gets printed.

articles.note: Paragraph E is the live one, i.e. "collected during the expedition" against "removed from." Those are two accounts of the same event.

articles.title: The Company's Report on the River
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text and explain how it is conveyed in the text.
 Spiral: RI.6.1 citing evidence · RI.6.4 word meaning · RI.6.8 claims and evidence · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: When a plant is accused of polluting a river, three reports usually appear. The company writes one, the state agency writes one, and a university lab writes one, and all three may use the same samples.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The company's report is not required to lie and generally does not. It selects. It reports the readings downstream of the outfall after the spring melt, when the river is highest and anything in it is most dilute.

paras.label: C
paras.text: It also chooses the comparison. Measured against the legal limit, the number passes. Measured against the river above the plant, the same number is eleven times higher.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The agency report is bound by a procedure, which is its strength and its limit. It tests what the rules say to test, on the schedule the rules set, which a plant can plan around.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The university lab has the most freedom and the least power. It can sample where it likes and publish what it finds, and it cannot require anybody to do anything about it.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Who funded each one is printed somewhere in all three, usually near the back. It does not tell you which is wrong. It tells you which questions each was built to answer.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So compare the methods sections before the conclusions. Where they sampled, when, and what they compared it to will explain most of the disagreement before you reach anybody's opinion.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A plant is accused of polluting a river. Three reports usually appear. The company writes one. The state agency writes one. A university lab writes one. All three may use the same samples.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The company's report does not have to lie. It selects. It reports readings downstream after the spring melt. The river is highest then. Anything in it is most dilute.

paras.label: C
paras.text: It also picks the comparison. Against the legal limit, the number passes. Against the river above the plant, the same number is eleven times higher.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The agency report follows a procedure. That is its strength and its limit. It tests what the rules say to test. A plant can plan around the schedule.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The university lab has the most freedom and the least power. It can sample where it likes. It cannot make anybody act on what it finds.

paras.label: F
paras.text: All three print who funded them, usually near the back. That does not tell you which is wrong. It tells you what each was built to answer.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So compare the methods before the conclusions. Where they sampled, when, and what they compared it to explains most of the disagreement.

questions.q: How can the same reading both pass and fail?
questions.a: Measured against the legal limit the number passes, and measured against the river above the plant the same number is eleven times higher.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. when the company sampled) and paragraph C (i.e. what it compared the number to).
Summarize why three reports using the same samples can disagree.
questions.a: The company selects when and where to sample and which comparison to make, so its readings come from the most dilute moment and are measured against the legal limit. The agency follows a fixed procedure a plant can plan around. The university lab can sample freely but cannot require anything, so the disagreement sits in the methods.

questions.q:
outfall: the point where a pipe discharges into a river.
dilute: thinned out, so the same amount of a substance reads lower.
Describe the connection between the spring melt and the company's numbers.
questions.a: It reports the readings after the spring melt, when the river is highest and anything in it is most dilute, which makes the numbers read lower.

articles.note: Paragraph F is the move to teach, i.e. funding "does not tell you which is wrong, it tells you which questions each was built to answer." That is RI.6.6 without the cynicism.

articles.title: The Graph and the Glacier
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Integrate information presented in different media or formats, including visually and quantitatively, as well as in words to develop a coherent understanding of a topic or issue.
 Spiral: RI.6.1 citing evidence · RI.6.2 central idea · RI.6.9 comparing accounts · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: A photograph of a glacier taken in 1920 beside one from today is the most persuasive thing in any article about ice. It is also the least precise, and the two facts are related.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The photographs show that the front of the glacier has moved. They cannot say how fast, when most of it happened, or whether it is still happening. A century is a long gap between two frames.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The graph beside them does the rest. A line of annual mass balance, measured every year since 1950, shows the ice losing more each summer than it gains each winter, and the slope steepening after 1990.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The table underneath is where the numbers live. Mean loss per decade, in meters of water equivalent, with the uncertainty beside each figure — unglamorous, and the only part that lets you check the line.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Each format fails alone. The photographs have no scale, the graph has no sense of a place, and the table is unreadable at a glance. Together they say what none of them says by itself.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Watch what the article chose to lead with. A photograph pair at the top and the table in a footnote is a different piece from the same evidence arranged the other way round.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So read the caption last and the axis first. The axis tells you what was measured and over what span, and a graph with no units is a picture, not evidence.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A glacier photograph from 1920 beside one from today is persuasive. It is also the least precise thing in the article.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The photographs show the front of the glacier has moved. They cannot say how fast. They cannot say when it happened. A century is a long gap.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The graph does the rest. It shows mass balance each year since 1950. The ice loses more each summer than it gains each winter. The slope steepens after 1990.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The table holds the numbers. It gives mean loss per decade. It gives the uncertainty beside each figure. It is the only part you can check the line against.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Each format fails alone. The photographs have no scale. The graph has no sense of place. The table cannot be read at a glance.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Watch what the article leads with. Photographs at the top and the table in a footnote is a different piece. The evidence is the same.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So read the axis first. It tells you what was measured and over what span. A graph with no units is a picture.

questions.q: What can the two photographs not tell you?
questions.a: They cannot say how fast the front of the glacier moved, when most of it happened, or whether it is still happening.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the graph) and paragraph D (i.e. the table).
Summarize what each format contributes to an article about a glacier.
questions.a: The photographs show that the front has moved but have no scale and a century-long gap. The graph shows annual mass balance since 1950 and the slope steepening after 1990. The table holds the per-decade numbers and the uncertainty, which is the only way to check the line. Each one fails alone.

questions.q:
mass balance: the difference between the ice a glacier gains in winter and loses in summer.
uncertainty: the measured range a figure could fall within, printed beside it.
Describe the connection between where a format sits in the article and the impression it leaves.
questions.a: A photograph pair at the top and the table in a footnote is a different piece from the same evidence arranged the other way round.

articles.note: Paragraph G is the habit, i.e. "read the caption last and the axis first." Students will do the opposite unless they are told.

articles.title: A Map, a Table, and a Flood
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Integrate information presented in different media or formats, including visually and quantitatively, as well as in words to develop a coherent understanding of a topic or issue.
 Spiral: RI.6.1 citing evidence · RI.6.2 central idea · RI.6.9 comparing accounts · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: After a river floods, a town meeting usually has three documents on the table, and they do not agree about who was hurt.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The map shades the flooded area. It is the only one that shows where, and it treats every shaded house the same, whether the water came to the doorstep or the ceiling.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The table counts. Houses damaged, dollars claimed, days out of the home — it distinguishes severity, and it has no geography at all, so you cannot see that one street took most of it.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The photographs do what neither can. A single picture of a kitchen under four feet of water puts a number into a body, and it also shows one kitchen out of six hundred.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The disagreement is usually about scale. The map says twelve percent of the town flooded. The table says the average claim was eleven thousand dollars. Both are true and neither mentions that twenty families lost everything.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So the question for the meeting is which document the decision is being made from. A budget drawn from the average will not reach the twenty, and a budget drawn from the photograph will not reach the rest.

paras.label: A
paras.text: After a river floods, a town meeting has three documents. They do not agree about who was hurt.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The map shades the flooded area. It is the only one that shows where. It treats every shaded house the same. Water at the doorstep looks like water at the ceiling.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The table counts. It lists houses damaged and dollars claimed. It shows how bad each case was. It has no geography, so one hard-hit street does not show.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The photographs do what neither can. One picture of a flooded kitchen makes a number real. It also shows one kitchen out of six hundred.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The disagreement is about scale. The map says twelve percent of the town flooded. The table says the average claim was eleven thousand dollars. Neither mentions the twenty families who lost everything.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So ask which document the decision comes from. A budget built on the average will not reach those twenty.

questions.q: What does the map treat the same that the table does not?
questions.a: The map treats every shaded house the same, whether the water came to the doorstep or the ceiling, while the table distinguishes severity.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. what the table counts) and paragraph E (i.e. the disagreement about scale).
Summarize what each of the three documents shows and misses.
questions.a: The map is the only one that shows where the water went but treats a doorstep and a ceiling alike. The table records severity in houses, dollars and days but has no geography. The photographs make one case vivid and are one case out of six hundred. The averages leave out the families who lost everything.

questions.q:
severity: how badly each case was affected, as opposed to how many were affected.
average: a single figure standing for a whole group, which can hide the extremes inside it.
Describe the connection between which document is used and who a budget reaches.
questions.a: A budget drawn from the average will not reach the twenty families who lost everything, and a budget drawn from the photograph will not reach the rest.

articles.note: Paragraph E is the arithmetic that matters, i.e. twelve percent and eleven thousand dollars are both true and both leave the twenty families out.

articles.title: Reading a Population Pyramid
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Integrate information presented in different media or formats, including visually and quantitatively, as well as in words to develop a coherent understanding of a topic or issue.
 Spiral: RI.6.1 citing evidence · RI.6.2 central idea · RI.6.9 comparing accounts · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: A population pyramid is two bar charts laid back to back, men on one side and women on the other, with age rising from the bottom. The shape alone tells you most of what a country is about to face.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A wide base and a narrow top means many children and few old people. Those countries need schools now and will need jobs in fifteen years, and they can usually say exactly when.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A narrow base under a thick middle is the opposite problem. Japan's pyramid is shaped like a lightbulb, and every worker there supports a growing number of retired people.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Notches are history. A pinch in one age band marks a war, a famine, or a policy, and because that band also had fewer children, the pinch reappears twenty-five years higher up.

paras.label: E
paras.text: What a pyramid cannot show is movement. Migration in and out is invisible on it, which is why a country's pyramid and its actual population can diverge within a decade.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So read the shape, then the notches, then the year it was drawn. A pyramid is a photograph of a population, and the thing it is best at is telling you what happens next.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A population pyramid is two bar charts back to back. Men are on one side and women on the other. Age rises from the bottom. The shape tells you a lot.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A wide base and a narrow top means many children and few old people. Those countries need schools now. They will need jobs in fifteen years.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A narrow base under a thick middle is the opposite problem. Japan's pyramid looks like a lightbulb. Each worker supports more retired people.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Notches are history. A pinch in one age band marks a war or a famine. That band also had fewer children. So the pinch shows up again higher up.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A pyramid cannot show movement. Migration in and out is invisible on it. So a pyramid and the real population can drift apart.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So read the shape, then the notches, then the year. A pyramid is a photograph of a population. It is best at telling you what comes next.

questions.q: What does a wide base on a pyramid tell you?
questions.a: It means many children and few old people, so those countries need schools now and will need jobs in fifteen years.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. the notches) and paragraph E (i.e. what a pyramid cannot show).
Summarize what a population pyramid shows and what it hides.
questions.a: It is two bar charts back to back with age rising from the bottom, and its shape shows whether a country has many children or many retired people. Notches mark a war, famine or policy and reappear higher up a generation later. It cannot show migration, so it can drift from the real population.

questions.q:
population pyramid: two back-to-back bar charts of a population by age and sex.
migration: people moving into or out of a country, which a pyramid does not record.
Describe the connection between a notch and the one above it.
questions.a: A pinch in one age band also had fewer children, so the pinch reappears twenty-five years higher up.

articles.note: Paragraph D is the one students find striking, i.e. a famine showing up twice on the same chart twenty-five years apart.

articles.title: The Chart in the Doctor's Office
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Integrate information presented in different media or formats, including visually and quantitatively, as well as in words to develop a coherent understanding of a topic or issue.
 Spiral: RI.6.1 citing evidence · RI.6.2 central idea · RI.6.9 comparing accounts · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: A growth chart is a sheet of curved lines, and a child's height is a dot somewhere among them. Parents read the dot. Doctors read which line it is following.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The lines are percentiles. A child on the fiftieth is taller than half of children that age; one on the fifth is taller than one in twenty. None of those is a grade, and the chart does not have a passing line.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A dot low on the chart is not the concern. A child who has tracked the tenth percentile since birth is growing exactly as expected, and the expected thing is to stay on your line.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Crossing lines is what gets attention. A child who moves from the fiftieth to the tenth over two years has not become short; something has changed, and the chart found it because two dots were compared and not just read.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The chart also only works for what it was built from. Different charts exist for different populations and for premature infants, and using the wrong one produces a worrying dot and no actual problem.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So the useful object is not the dot. It is the line of dots across years, which is why the nurse measures a child who has obviously grown and writes it down anyway.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A growth chart is a sheet of curved lines. A child's height is a dot among them. Parents read the dot. Doctors read which line it follows.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The lines are percentiles. A child on the fiftieth is taller than half of children that age. A child on the fifth is taller than one in twenty. None of those is a grade.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A low dot is not the concern. A child on the tenth percentile since birth is growing as expected. Staying on your line is the expected thing.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Crossing lines gets attention. A child who moves from the fiftieth to the tenth has not become short. Something has changed. Two dots were compared, not just read.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The chart only works for what it was built from. There are different charts for different groups and for premature babies. The wrong chart makes a worrying dot and no real problem.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So the useful thing is not the dot. It is the line of dots across years. That is why the nurse measures and writes it down every time.

questions.q: What do doctors look at that parents often do not?
questions.a: Doctors read which line the dot is following rather than the dot itself.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. a low dot) and paragraph D (i.e. crossing lines).
Summarize how a growth chart is meant to be read.
questions.a: The curved lines are percentiles, not grades, and there is no passing line. A low dot is not a concern if the child has tracked that line since birth, because staying on your line is what is expected. Crossing lines is what gets attention, so the useful object is the line of dots across years rather than any one dot.

questions.q:
percentile: the position in a hundred, so the tenth percentile is taller than one child in ten.
tracking: staying on the same percentile line over time.
Describe the connection between measuring every visit and what the chart can show.
questions.a: The chart found the change because two dots were compared and not just read, which is why the nurse measures a child who has obviously grown and writes it down anyway.

articles.note: Paragraph B is worth saying out loud, i.e. "the chart does not have a passing line." Families read percentiles as scores constantly.

articles.title: The Seismograph and the Map
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Integrate information presented in different media or formats, including visually and quantitatively, as well as in words to develop a coherent understanding of a topic or issue.
 Spiral: RI.6.1 citing evidence · RI.6.2 central idea · RI.6.9 comparing accounts · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: An earthquake arrives at a seismograph as a wiggle on a line, and the wiggle is not a picture of the shaking. It is a record of two different waves arriving at two different times.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The fast wave comes first. P waves travel through rock at about six kilometers a second; S waves follow at roughly half that, and the gap between them on the trace is the only thing needed to find the distance.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That gives a distance, not a direction. A single station can say the quake was two hundred kilometers away and nothing more, which draws a circle of possible locations around it.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Three stations give a point. Three circles cross in one place, and that intersection is the epicenter, which is why a seismic network is useless with one instrument and precise with several.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The height of the wiggle is a separate measurement. Amplitude gives magnitude, and magnitude is a number about the quake itself rather than about how it felt anywhere in particular.

paras.label: F
paras.text: How it felt is a different map. Shaking intensity is collected from instruments and from people reporting what moved, and it depends on soil, depth and building type as much as on magnitude.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So a magnitude 6 is one number and the intensity map is a thousand. Reading only the number tells you what happened at the fault; reading only the map tells you nothing about what the fault did.

paras.label: A
paras.text: An earthquake reaches a seismograph as a wiggle on a line. The wiggle is not a picture of the shaking. It records two waves arriving at two times.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The fast wave comes first. P waves move through rock at about six kilometers a second. S waves follow at about half that. The gap between them gives the distance.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That gives a distance, not a direction. One station can say the quake was two hundred kilometers away. That draws a circle of possible places.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Three stations give a point. Three circles cross in one place. That crossing is the epicenter. One instrument is useless and several are precise.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The height of the wiggle is a separate measure. It gives magnitude. Magnitude is about the quake itself, not about how it felt.

paras.label: F
paras.text: How it felt is a different map. Intensity comes from instruments and from people reporting what moved. It depends on soil and depth and buildings.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So a magnitude 6 is one number. The intensity map is a thousand. The number tells you what the fault did. The map tells you what it was like.

questions.q: How does a single station work out how far away a quake was?
questions.a: The gap between the P wave and the S wave arriving on the trace is the only thing needed to find the distance.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. three stations) and paragraph F (i.e. the intensity map).
Summarize how a quake's location and size are worked out.
questions.a: The gap between the fast P wave and the slower S wave gives a distance, which draws a circle around one station, and three circles cross at the epicenter. The height of the wiggle gives magnitude, a number about the quake itself, while shaking intensity is a separate map that depends on soil, depth and buildings.

questions.q:
epicenter: the point on the surface above where a quake began.
magnitude: a single number for the size of the quake itself, not for how it felt anywhere.
Describe the connection between the number of stations and knowing where a quake was.
questions.a: A single station can say only that the quake was two hundred kilometers away, which draws a circle of possible locations, so three stations are needed because three circles cross in one place.

articles.note: Paragraph G is the pairing to teach, i.e. magnitude "is one number and the intensity map is a thousand." One is about the fault and one is about people.

articles.title: Should the City Build a Bike Lane?
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Trace and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, distinguishing claims that are supported by reasons and evidence from claims that are not.
 Spiral: RI.6.1 citing evidence · RI.6.5 structure · RI.6.6 point of view · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: The proposal would take one of four traffic lanes on Market Street and make it a protected bike lane. The council packet runs eleven pages. Four of its claims carry evidence and three do not.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The supported ones are easy to check. The city counted 1,340 cyclists a day on Market Street in September, and the fire department's own letter says a protected lane does not narrow the path for an engine.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The crash figure is supported and smaller than it sounds. Collisions involving cyclists fell 38 percent on Oak Street after its lane was built, which is six fewer crashes a year on one street over three years.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Three claims have nothing behind them. The packet says the lane will bring shoppers downtown, that property values will rise, and that traffic will not get worse. No study, no comparison city, no figure.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The last of those is the one to press. Taking a lane away and expecting no change in traffic is a claim that could be tested, cheaply, by measuring Oak Street before and after. Nobody did.

paras.label: F
paras.text: An argument can be worth supporting and badly made at the same time. The cyclist count and the fire department letter are reasons. The property values are a hope with a sentence around it.

paras.label: A
paras.text: The plan would turn one of four traffic lanes into a protected bike lane. The council packet runs eleven pages. Four claims carry evidence. Three do not.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The supported ones are easy to check. The city counted 1,340 cyclists a day in September. The fire department wrote that a protected lane still fits an engine.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The crash figure is supported and smaller than it sounds. Crashes with cyclists fell 38 percent on Oak Street. That is six fewer crashes a year.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Three claims have nothing behind them. The packet says the lane will bring shoppers. It says property values will rise. It says traffic will not get worse.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The last one is the one to press. Taking a lane away and expecting no change could be tested. Nobody measured Oak Street before and after.

paras.label: F
paras.text: An argument can be worth supporting and badly made. The cyclist count is a reason. The property values are a hope.

questions.q: Which claims in the packet carry evidence?
questions.a: The city counted 1,340 cyclists a day on Market Street in September, the fire department's letter says a protected lane does not narrow the path for an engine, and collisions fell 38 percent on Oak Street.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. the three unsupported claims) and paragraph E (i.e. the one that could have been tested).
Summarize which parts of the bike lane argument are supported and which are not.
questions.a: The cyclist count, the fire department letter and the Oak Street crash figure all carry evidence, although the crash drop is six fewer a year. The claims that the lane will bring shoppers, raise property values and not worsen traffic have no study or figure behind them, and the traffic claim could have been tested cheaply.

questions.q:
protected lane: a bike lane separated from traffic by a physical barrier.
unsupported: stated without a study, figure or comparison behind it.
Describe the connection between the 38 percent figure and what it means in crashes.
questions.a: Collisions involving cyclists fell 38 percent on Oak Street, which is six fewer crashes a year on one street over three years.

articles.note: Paragraph F is the point of the whole standard, i.e. an argument can be "worth supporting and badly made at the same time." Students want those to be one question.

articles.title: The Claim That Sharks Do Not Get Cancer
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Trace and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, distinguishing claims that are supported by reasons and evidence from claims that are not.
 Spiral: RI.6.1 citing evidence · RI.6.5 structure · RI.6.6 point of view · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: A 1992 book called Sharks Don't Get Cancer sold well and built an industry. Shark cartilage pills were being sold for hundreds of dollars a bottle within a few years.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The argument ran in three steps. Sharks do not get cancer; their skeletons are cartilage; therefore cartilage prevents cancer. Each step was offered as support for the next.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The first step is false. The Registry of Tumors in Lower Animals has documented dozens of tumors in sharks, including cancers of the cartilage itself, which were on record before the book was written.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The second step is true and does no work. Sharks do have cartilage skeletons, and that fact supports nothing about cancer unless the first step holds.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The third step does not follow even if the first two did. A substance in an animal's body is not a drug you can swallow; cartilage is mostly protein, and protein is digested rather than delivered.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Trials settled it. Controlled studies of shark cartilage in patients with advanced cancer found no benefit, and regulators have acted against companies for claiming otherwise.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The cost was not only money. Shark populations were fished down for the pills, and some patients took them instead of treatment that worked.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A 1992 book called Sharks Don't Get Cancer sold well. It built an industry. Shark cartilage pills soon cost hundreds of dollars a bottle.

paras.label: B

paras.label: C
paras.text: The first step is false. A registry has recorded dozens of tumors in sharks. Some were cancers of the cartilage itself. They were on record before the book.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The second step is true and does no work. Sharks do have cartilage skeletons. That supports nothing unless the first step holds.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The third step does not follow either. A substance in an animal is not a drug you can swallow. Cartilage is mostly protein. Protein is digested.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Trials settled it. Studies in patients with advanced cancer found no benefit. Regulators have acted against companies for claiming otherwise.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The cost was not only money. Sharks were fished down for the pills. Some patients took them instead of treatment that worked.

questions.q: Why is the first step of the argument false?
questions.a: The Registry of Tumors in Lower Animals has documented dozens of tumors in sharks, including cancers of the cartilage itself.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. the step that does no work) and paragraph F (i.e. the trials).
Summarize the argument and what is wrong with each step.
questions.a: It claims sharks do not get cancer, that their skeletons are cartilage, and therefore that cartilage prevents cancer. The first step is false because tumors in sharks were already on record, the second is true but does nothing on its own, and the third does not follow because cartilage is protein and is digested. Trials found no benefit.

questions.q:
cartilage: the flexible tissue a shark's skeleton is made of.
controlled study: a trial that compares a treatment against no treatment to see whether it works.
Describe the connection between the three steps and whether the conclusion holds.
questions.a: Each step was offered as support for the next, so because the first step is false the second supports nothing about cancer and the conclusion does not follow.

articles.note: This is a chain argument, and chains are the clearest case for RI.6.8: one false link and nothing downstream survives, however true the other links are.

articles.title: Is Bottled Water Worth It?
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Trace and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, distinguishing claims that are supported by reasons and evidence from claims that are not.
 Spiral: RI.6.1 citing evidence · RI.6.5 structure · RI.6.6 point of view · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: A flyer handed out at a school fair argues that families should stop buying bottled water. It makes five claims, and the strong ones are not the loud ones.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The cost claim is solid. A gallon from the tap costs a fraction of a cent in most American cities, and the same gallon in bottles runs a few dollars, which is a comparison anyone can check on a bill.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The safety claim is weaker than the flyer suggests. Municipal water in the United States is tested more often than bottled water is, which is true, and that does not make every tap safe — Flint had tested water and a lead problem.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The plastic claim is supported and overstated. Bottles really do take centuries to break down, and the flyer's figure of ninety-one percent unrecycled is a global number quoted as if it were local.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The taste claim is not an argument. Whether tap water tastes worse varies by city and by person, and the flyer offers it as though it settled something.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The one missing piece is the exception. Some people cannot drink their tap water, and a flyer that never says so is making a weaker case than it could, because it leaves itself one obvious counterexample.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A flyer at a school fair says families should stop buying bottled water. It makes five claims. The strong ones are not the loud ones.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The cost claim is solid. A gallon from the tap costs a fraction of a cent. The same gallon in bottles costs a few dollars. Anyone can check that on a bill.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The safety claim is weaker than it sounds. City water is tested more often than bottled water. That is true. It does not make every tap safe. Flint had tested water and a lead problem.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The plastic claim is supported and overstated. Bottles do take centuries to break down. The flyer's ninety-one percent figure is a global number used as a local one.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The taste claim is not an argument. Taste varies by city and by person. The flyer offers it as if it settled something.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The missing piece is the exception. Some people cannot drink their tap water. A flyer that never says so makes a weaker case than it could.

questions.q: Which claim in the flyer is the strongest?
questions.a: The cost claim, because a gallon from the tap costs a fraction of a cent and the same gallon in bottles runs a few dollars, which anyone can check on a bill.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the safety claim) and paragraph F (i.e. the missing exception).
Summarize which of the flyer's claims hold up.
questions.a: The cost claim is solid and checkable. The safety claim is true about testing but does not make every tap safe. The plastic claim is supported and quotes a global recycling figure as a local one. The taste claim is not an argument at all, and the flyer never mentions people who cannot drink their tap water.

questions.q:
municipal: belonging to a city, as in the water a city supplies and tests.
counterexample: a single case that a claim fails to cover.
Describe the connection between naming the exception and the strength of the flyer's case.
questions.a: Some people cannot drink their tap water, and a flyer that never says so is making a weaker case than it could, because it leaves itself one obvious counterexample.

articles.note: Paragraph F is the counter-intuitive one worth arguing about: naming the exception makes the argument stronger, not weaker.

articles.title: The Advertisement for the Memory Pill
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Trace and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, distinguishing claims that are supported by reasons and evidence from claims that are not.
 Spiral: RI.6.1 citing evidence · RI.6.5 structure · RI.6.6 point of view · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: A full-page advertisement promises better memory in thirty days. It reads like an argument and is built out of things that are not evidence.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It opens with a doctor. The photograph is of a person in a white coat, the name has letters after it, and nothing says what the letters are or whether the person studied memory.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Then come the testimonials. Four people say the pill worked, and a testimonial cannot show that a pill works because nobody collected the people it did nothing for.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The study it cites is real and the sentence about it is not. The advertisement says clinically proven; the study had eleven participants, no comparison group, and ran for two weeks.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The graph has no numbers on the vertical axis. The bars rise, and without units a rising bar can represent any difference at all, including none worth noticing.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The small print carries the actual claim. These statements have not been evaluated by the Food and Drug Administration, it says, and that sentence contradicts the headline above it.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So the test is not whether an argument sounds like science. It is whether any part of it could come out the other way, and nothing in this advertisement could.

paras.label: B

paras.label: C

paras.label: D

paras.label: E

paras.label: F

paras.label: G
